News.title: Four in 10 Gen Z Brits wouldn’t be confident hanging a mirror & many feel unsure about assembling flat-pack furniture
News.content:
Next

A POLL of 2,000 adults found only 23 per cent 18 to 24-year-olds feel comfortable doing basic DIY tasks such as unblocking a sink (62 per cent), putting up a set of shelves (63 per cent) or changing a fuse (76 per cent).

More than a quarter (27 per cent) claimed they’ve never been taught practical DIY skills, while 30 per cent avoid tackling jobs themselves for fear of doing a bad job and facing an expensive bill to put it right.



However, 41 per cent of youngsters would be confident setting up a home WiFi network without any help, as well as building a website (36 per cent) and troubleshooting internet connection issues (35 per cent).

It also emerged 80 per cent of 18 to 25-year-olds have used AI tools to create, write or build something within the past year – including websites and side hustles.



The research was commissioned by Tiiny Host, a simple drag-and-drop platform designed to quickly launch and share static websites, PDFs and files online.

Elston Baretto, founder of the platform, said: “DIY hasn’t disappeared – it’s evolving – and for previous generations, making something yourself might have meant picking up a drill or opening a toolbox.



“Today, that same instinct to create, learn and figure things out for yourself is increasingly happening online.

“What’s exciting is that technology and AI are giving more people the confidence to turn an idea into something real – whether that’s a website, a creative project, a side hustle or even the beginnings of a business.

“You no longer need years of technical experience or a team of experts to get started.

“People are teaching themselves, experimenting and building independently in a way that simply wasn’t possible before.”



The study also revealed Gen Z are more likely to have created something using AI in the past year than put up a shelf (34 per cent vs 26 per cent).

With 25 per cent of this age range having learned their technology skills directly from tools, such as ChatGPT and Copilot, themselves.

But it’s not just the younger generation leading the digital way, as 45 per cent of all adults have used artificial intelligence for a specific purpose within the same timeframe.

While almost a quarter (23 per cent) have used their digital skills to make money, according to the OnePoll.com data.

It also emerged 72 per cent of those polled feel confident in their technology and digital skills, compared with 60 per cent who say the same about DIY and home maintenance.



What’s more, Millennials are the generation most likely to feel at home using technology than tackling household DIY tasks (41 per cent vs 18 per cent).

Tiiny Host’s Elston Baretto added: “This isn’t about replacing traditional DIY or saying one set of skills matters more than another, it’s about recognising that what it means to ‘do it yourself’ has expanded.

“A new generation is using a different toolbox – AI, digital platforms and technology – but the instinct behind it is exactly the same: I have an idea, I can learn how to do this, and I can make it happen

News.title: Pornography showing incest and strangulation to be BANNED after warning over ‘devastating consequences’
News.content:
EXPLICIT CRACKDOWN Pornography showing incest and strangulation to be BANNED after warning over ‘devastating consequences’







Next

ONLINE pornography showing incest or strangulation will be banned after a warning that normalising sexual violence will have “devastating consequences”.

The new rules mean it will be illegal to possess or publish porn depicting strangulation or suffocation, sexual activity between people who are related adults, or adults role-playing as children under 16.

The regulations will come into force from November 6 for England and Wales and are designed to better protect children and young people.

This comes after a 2025 review into pornography regulation found that “around half of all sexual abuse cases against children were perpetrated by step-parents”.





Conservative peer Baroness Gabby Bertin, who published the review, also warned the “rife” depictions of choking in online pornography had led to it becoming normalised among young people.

Her independent review referenced one account of a 14-year-old boy asking a teacher how to choke girls during sex.

Today she welcomed the Government’s announcement and said it had come “not a moment too soon”.

Baroness Bertin added that it would send a message to porn companies and to society that “extreme and violent content that encourages real-life harm is not acceptable”.

Speaking to the Today programme she said showing strangulation had “absolutely sort of normalised this kind of sexual violence”.

She added that this “has to come to an end”.

The law changes are the start of an effort to “marry up” the legal disparity between what is acceptable online and offline, she said.

While non-consensual, non-fatal strangulation is already an offence, its depiction online is still legal.



Justice minister Alex Davies-Jones said this was not about “criminalising harmless sexual preferences”.

But stopping content which “normalises or even glorifies” violence against women shaping how young people view healthy relationships.

The maximum penalty for publishing any of the soon to be criminal content is five years’ imprisonment.

This includes uploading, posting or sharing the content to someone online.

Possession of images depicting sexual activity between adults role-playing as children under 16 could lead to three years behind bars.



Images of strangulation and suffocation or penetrative sexual activity between certain relatives – including step or foster relations – both carry maximum sentences of two years.

The House of Lords agreed by a majority of one to ban videos and images depicting relationships that would not be allowed in real life in March.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

They also agreed by 142 votes to 140, majority two, to bring intimate pictures and videos of adults pretending to be children in line with similar images of real children.
