News.title: Ex-rugby player, 48, dies during charity cycle ride raising money for tragic teammate as tributes pour in
News.content:
CYCLING TRAGEDY Ex-rugby player, 48, dies during charity cycle ride raising money for tragic teammate as tributes pour in







Next

A POPULAR rugby player who was “one of the world’s good guys” died on a charity cycle ride while raising cash for a former teammate.

Dan Singer, 48, was taking part 500-mile ride to support his friend, Crawford Henderson, who has been battling a brain tumour.



Tragically, Dan died during the six day charity ride from Scotland to London on October 1.

Fellow riders completed a short ride to Rosslyn Park in his honour, and cancelled the remainder of the challenge following the devastating news of his death.



The former Welsh rugby player was loved by many, and donors have given over £95,000 to the charity cycle fundraise in his memory.

The Good, The Bad & The Rugby podcast, hosted by James Haskell, Mike Tindall and Alex Payne, paid tribute.



A podcast spokesman said: “Our thoughts are with Dan’s wife Michelle, his family, friends and everyone at Rosslyn Park and the wider rugby community. Sending our deepest condolences to all who knew and loved Dan.”

Dan spent his education in Wycliff school in Gloucestershire, where he was captain of the Rugby team, hockey team, and cricket team.

He also was a youth player for Porthcawl RFC in Porthcawl, near Bridgend, south Wales, before he went on to join the Rosslyn Park team.

After some time as a Welsh rugby player, he moved to London to become a bond trader for J P Morgan in 2013 and played for Rosslyn Park.



A spokesman for Rosslyn Park said: “It is with profound sadness that we share the news that our former player and much-loved friend Dan Singer tragically passed away on Thursday while taking part in the RFC500 charity cycle ride in support of his former teammate Crawford Henderson.

“Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with Dan’s wife Michelle, his family and friends, and all those who were riding alongside him.

“RFC500 was conceived as a celebration of friendship and the enduring bonds created through rugby, bringing together former teammates for a 500-mile journey from Scotland to Rosslyn Park to raise funds for The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity and The Brain Tumour Charity, through the Lewis Moody Foundation.”

Porthcawl RFC said Dan “remained a friend of the club” and always visited when he was back in the area.

A statement from Porthcawl RFC said: “It is with great sadness that we share the news that our former player and friend, Dan Singer, tragically passed away recently while taking part in the RFC500 charity cycle ride.



“Dan joined the club as a youth player in the mid 1990s before going on to play senior rugby for several years while studying at university. He remained a friend of the club and always made time to visit when back in the area.

“We last saw Dan at the club last year, when he was home from Paris with his family for an international match in Cardiff.

“Our sincere condolences go to Dan’s family and friends at this sad time. Rest in peace, Dan.”

The charity ride was to raise money for The Royal Marsden and the Lewis Moody foundation.

Paying tribute, on friend said: “Dan – one of the world’s good guys! You’ll be missed dearly.”



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Another said: “Dan – it’s hard to find the words. You believed in me and gave me a chance, I am forever grateful and was lucky to call you a great friend.”

One said: “Dan Singer, you were doing something yet again for others. Your kindness, leadership and high standards are examples to all of us. Love you.”

News.title: New vape ban is being introduced in less than a fortnight – plus extended age restrictions
News.content:
Next

A NEW vape ban will come into force across the UK in just under a fortnight.

It comes as the government is continuing its crackdown on the devices.

Come October 29, vape vending machines will no longer be allowed to operate across the UK.



The updated rules mean it will be an offence for all businesses, such as a pub, to have one of these machines on their premises.



However, in England and Wales, vending machines for vaping products will continue to be allowed within an area of a mental health hospital that is intended for inpatient use.

The stricter regulations come as the government is looking to tackle a rise in youth vaping as part of its mission to create a “smoke-free generation”.

On the same day, the age of sale for all vaping and nicotine products will be age 18 and over.

It means it will be an offence to sell these products to a person under the age of 18.

Meanwhile, it will also be an offence for an adult to buy vaping or nicotine products for someone aged under 18.

Giving away vaping products as part of a promotion or coupons to reduce the costs of the products is also set to become an offence.

At the start of the month, the cost to buy vape products also increased.



The change has seen a flat rate of 22p per millilitre or £2.20 per 10ml on vaping liquid, regardless of how much nicotine it contains.

It means a single 10ml bottle of juice that previously scanned in at £3.99 has now risen to £6.63.

News.title: Influencer Jennifer Burnham reveals four-year-old son Baxter’s cause of death in emotional update on his final months
News.content:
Next

INFLUENCER Jennifer Burnham has revealed the heartbreaking cause of her four-year-old son’s death after opening up about his final months.

The devastated mom shared an emotional video with her thousands of followers, revealing the devastating diagnosis that turned her family’s life upside down.



Baxter, who died on October 5, had been battling an incurable brain tumor for six months, Jennifer revealed in an Instagram video on Thursday.

The lifestyle blogger, who lives in California, explained that her little boy had been diagnose with diffuse midline glioma, an aggressive type of brain tumor, after doctors initially suspected he had a common eye condition.



Jennifer, who shares Baxter and one-year-old son Barron with husband Bryce Burnham, said her eldest child had been perfectly healthy before the shocking discovery.

“Basically, my son was a totally healthy, happy four-year-old. He went to school, was on a T-ball team, did karate, had tons of friends,” she said.

“I mean, just like the happiest little guy, loved his Hot Wheels cars—just couldn’t have been happier or healthier. And I think that’s why this was so shocking.”

The grieving mom explained that Baxter had started crossing his left eye, prompting the family to take him to an ophthalmologist.

Doctors initially believed he had strabismus, a condition that causes the eyes to point in different directions.

Baxter was given an eye patch, and surgery was scheduled for mid-April to correct the problem.



However, a routine MRI carried out ahead of the procedure revealed something far more sinister.

“When we did the MRI, they told us that they found he had a brain tumor and we needed to go to the hospital immediately,” Jennifer recalled.

Further scans confirmed Baxter had diffuse midline glioma, a devastating diagnosis that left his parents desperately searching for treatment options.

“In the brain tumor world, that is essentially the worst type of brain tumor that you can have, unfortunately, because it’s in the brain stem and that’s inoperable – meaning it’s incurable,” she explained.

Jennifer said doctors discovered that part of the tumor extended into Baxter’s cerebellum, an area where surgery was possible.



Just three days after receiving the diagnosis, the little boy underwent an operation to remove that portion of the tumor.

The family then traveled to San Diego, where Baxter received targeted proton radiation therapy.

But Jennifer and Bryce refused to give up hope, spending the following months researching possible treatments and contacting specialists across the country.



Their desperate search for answers even took them to Europe twice over the summer.

The couple also pursued alternative therapies, including red light therapy, hyperbaric oxygen and oxygen baths, in an effort to help their son.

Jennifer did not suggest that those treatments had been proven effective against Baxter’s condition.

“We talked to every doctor in the country, any specialist, anyone that could put eyes on our son’s case to try to figure out what our options were to get rid of this,” she said.

Despite their efforts, the location of Baxter’s tumor meant doctors could not surgically remove it completely.



Jennifer explained that the brain stem controls vital neurological functions, making the diagnosis particularly devastating.

“That’s the hardest part because it’s just so difficult to watch your child going through something like this, and you’re literally helpless,” she said.

“It’s every parent’s worst nightmare, and we’ve been living in this nightmare for six months. It’s the most difficult thing we’ve ever gone through.”

The heartbroken mom praised Baxter’s strength through his battle, describing him as a fighter who remained cheerful despite everything he endured.

“He was so strong and such a fighter, and literally fought until the very last day,” she said.



“He had a smile on his face and just was the happiest guy. I’m so proud of him because no child should ever go through this, no parent should ever go through this, and I hate that our family is going through this.”

Jennifer also explained why she had chosen to share the painful details of her son’s illness, saying she hoped Baxter’s story could help other families facing similar diagnoses.

“No person should go through this alone,” she said.



The mom admitted that she was still struggling to comprehend life without her eldest son but found some comfort in believing he was no longer suffering.

“I know he’s in heaven, just playing with his cars and trucks and eating cookies and ice cream and having the best time,” she said.

“That gives me comfort as a mom, just knowing that he’s no longer in pain.”

She added: “It doesn’t change the fact that my heart is broken, and I’m not sure how to continue living every day because it’s so hard to just fathom my life without him since he is such a big, full part of it.”

The emotional update comes just days after Jennifer announced Baxter’s death in a heartbreaking Instagram tribute on Monday.



The content creator, who has around 96,000 followers, shared a touching video celebrating her little boy’s life.

“Heaven welcomed our angel Baxter last Monday, October 5th,” she wrote.

“From the moment you were born, you have always been our dream come true.”

Jennifer regularly shares lifestyle, motherhood and cooking content with her Instagram audience, which includes Ivanka Trump.

Baxter had become a familiar face on her social media accounts, appearing in family videos documenting his childhood.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Jennifer and Bryce welcomed Baxter Scott Burnham on January 25, 2022, announcing his arrival in a joyful Instagram post.

Over the years, Jennifer shared glimpses of Baxter playing with his toys, spending time with the family dog and enjoying special moments with his parents.

News.title: Car ‘tried to smash into cop van’ after woman, 26, stabbed to death in street – as man, 25, arrested over ‘murder’
News.content:
STREET STABBING Car ‘tried to smash into cop van’ after woman, 26, stabbed to death in street – as man, 25, arrested over ‘murder’







Next

A CAR reportedly tried to smash into a police van after a woman was stabbed to death in the street.

Alisha Samuels, 26, was found with stab wounds in a Manchester suburb and police have arrested a 25-year-old man on suspicion of murder.



Residents said they heard “screams” outside their homes in Newton Heath and saw a car smash into a police van.

Moments later a man was reportedly dragged out the vehicle and arrested.



One local told Manchester Evening News: “They arrested a man, I couldn’t see what he looked like because it was dark.

“They dragged him out of a car after he tried to drive into a police van.”



A small white car which looked like it had been crashed into was allegedly later seen close to the crime scene.

Officers have also arrested a 61-year-old man and a 38-year-old woman on suspicion of assisting an offender.



All three remain in custody while enquiries continue.

Greater Manchester Police were called to reports of a disturbance on Dorking Avenue in the early hours of yesterday morning.

Residents have said they heard “screaming and shouting” between 1am and 2am.

Witnesses reported seeing a forensic tent on Staplehurst Road which was shut alongside Edmonton Road and part of Briscoe Lane as officers investigated yesterday morning.

One resident added: “All the road is taped off. Police are not allowing any residents to drive out of the street.”



Another said one officer told her “you wouldn’t want to see what was further up the street”.

The force said Alisha’s family has asked for privacy while they deal with “the devastating loss of their loved one”.

Detective Inspector Paul Costello from Greater Manchester Police Major Incident Team previously said: “Firstly, my thoughts go out to the victim’s family, friends, and loved ones at this incredibly difficult time.



“Formal identification has not yet been conducted, but the believed family have been made aware and are being supported by specialist officers.

“This was an awful and tragic attack, but I would like to reassure the community that we have three people in our custody, and my team are working tirelessly to identify anyone else who may have been involved.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“There will be a significant police presence in the area, and multiple scenes are in place whilst our investigations continue.

“I urge anyone who may be able to help with our enquiries to please come forward.”

News.title: Half of Brits regularly clock into a ‘second shift’ to pursue side hustles and passion projects, study finds
News.content:
DOUBLE DUTY Half of Brits regularly clock into a ‘second shift’ to pursue side hustles and passion projects, study finds







Next

HALF of Brits regularly clock into a “second shift” – putting in 214 extra hours in the evening per year to pursue side hustles and passion projects.

A poll of 2,000 adults found 49 per cent now regularly work towards a personal ambition after their day job ends, doing so at least once a week.



While 14 per cent are even more dedicated, hustling every day from Monday to Friday.

The average person with a second shift dedicates four hours a week to projects that could shape their future.



The emerging ‘5-9 economy’ sees the average second shift begin between 7pm and 7.59pm, with 17 per cent saying some of their most productive hours happen after they have officially finished work.

The research was commissioned by Samsung to highlight its Galaxy Tab S12 Series, combining long-lasting battery life with an expansive display that gives users the space to learn, research, create and pursue personal projects after hours.



Side hustles are the biggest driver of the UK’s after-hours output boom, with 24 per cent currently running one alongside their main job.

But making extra money isn’t the only motivation, as some spend their evenings learning a new skill, either out of personal interest (32 per cent) or to develop their career (23 per cent).

Millennials are the most focused on career development, with 31 per cent using their evenings to build their skills in this area, compared to just 11 per cent of Gen X and nine per cent of Boomers.

Creative ambitions also factor in, as 16 per cent use their evenings to create content.



London has also emerged as the UK’s “hustle capital”, with 61 per cent of residents clocking in to their ‘5–9’ at least once a week, ahead of Manchester (54 per cent) and Bristol (49 per cent).

The desire for greater independence is helping drive Britain’s second shift, with 22 per cent wanting to gain more control over their future.

While 15 per cent hope their evening efforts will open up new career opportunities as 12 per cent use this time to study towards a qualification.

The second shift also has the potential to transform the first, with 15 per cent of side-hustlers hoping their evening project will become their full-time career.

Whereas 12 per cent of those studying or developing new skills hope to use these to move into a different role.



But turning these ambitions into progress takes commitment, with finding the time (37 per cent) and keeping their energy up after a full working day (45 per cent) the two biggest challenges.

Technology also helps power this second shift, in the form of online tutorials (25 per cent), task management apps (16 per cent), and digital creative tools (15 per cent).

Charlie Nordfeldt, from Samsung UK and Ireland, said: “Finishing the workday is often when personal ambitions truly take flight.

“Whether you are studying for a qualification, launching a new business idea, or bringing a creative project to life, those evening hours make a real difference.”

News.title: Zara Tindall's witty remark about Prince William after learning of awkward encounter
News.content:
Zara Tindall's witty remark about Prince William after learning of awkward encounter

Princess Anne's daughter Zara Tindall shared her thoughts about the awkward moment involving Prince William during a podcast appearance

View 3 Images The royal cousins are thought to be close (Image: Getty)

Zara Tindall couldn't resist making a sarcastic quip after hearing an anecdote about her cousin, Prince William. The royal was appearing on the Talk Horse podcast alongside hosts Pippa Funnell MBE and Made in Chelsea star Tristan Phipps when Pippa recounted an awkward encounter with the future King.

‌



‌



Pippa revealed that she met William while she was "covered in blood and mud" after suffering a nasty fall from her horse.

‌



She shared: "I don't know if I've said this story on Talk Horse, but the one and only time I've met your cousin was at Badminton.

‌



"[The] horse left a leg at the gate going to Huntsman's Close, fell off, [it was] a really wet day, mud studded, I had to take a helicopter so I'd be back in time for my second horse because I had a wound, a stud wound.

"And [with] the second horse, exactly the same thing happened. [I] fell off at the same gate, left the same leg, fell on the same piece of mud on the second horse," she explained.

View 3 Images Zara and Mike Tindall were guests on the Talk Horse podcast (Image: TALKHORSEPODCAST)

‌



Pippa went on to describe how she encountered William while making her way back to the stables.

"And then I was walking back to the stables, the walk of shame back through Badminton, who should come along? Prince William and he said, 'You had a good day?' And I'm thinking, I'm covered in blood and mud," she laughed.

Zara responded with a sarcastic quip of her own, asking: "Does it look like it?", which prompted laughter.

‌



The daughter of Princess Anne had joined the pair to discuss her eventing career and family commitments before her husband, Mike Tindall, joined the conversation.

After hearing Pippa's gory account, Mike suggested the incident could serve as an "icebreaker" if she were to cross paths with William again.

Tristan, however, joked that the Prince might struggle to recognise Pippa without the blood and mud covering her.

‌



Zara is believed to share a particularly close bond with her cousin and has reportedly never shied away from telling him when he is being "pompous".

View 3 Images Zara Tindall with her cousin Prince William (Image: Getty)

Royal author Robert Jobson told the Daily Mail that Zara "can tell the heir to the throne he is being pompous" and claimed that "he takes it".

Article continues below

"She knew him before he was a headline," the expert added, before stating that she "has no angle" when she tells the future King how it is.

Zara is also one of the godmothers to Prince George, the eldest of William and Princess Catherine's three children.

The equestrian also shares three children with her husband Mike; Mia, 12, Lena, eight, and Lucas, five.

News.title: Fake weight-loss jabs worth £2m seized from 'filthy Birmingham warehouse'
News.content:
Fake weight-loss jabs worth £2m seized from 'filthy Birmingham warehouse'

More than 12,000 counterfeit weight-loss pens were discovered at a Birmingham industrial unit, along with packaging for around 30,000 more products. The MRA warned the jabs could contain harmful substances

View 3 Images The MHRA warned the seized pens had not been checked for safety and could contain harmful substances

Fake weight-loss injection pens worth £2million have been seized in a raid on a “filthy warehouse” in Birmingham.

‌



‌



Officers found more than 12,000 counterfeit retatrutide and tirzepatide pens at the industrial unit, along with packaging for around 30,000 more products. The raid was a joint operation by West Midlands Police and the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA).

‌



Among the pens were products labelled retatrutide, an experimental weight-loss drug known online as “reta”. Counterfeit versions have been promoted on social media despite the drug being unavailable for public use.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 3 Images The Birmingham discovery was the latest in a series of raids on illegal weight-loss medicines (Image: Getty Images)

Retatrutide is being studied as the first drug to tackle weight loss in three distinct ways. But it has not been approved anywhere in the world, and its developer, Eli Lilly, says it is only available through its clinical trials.

‌



Products bearing its name has been found online and can put people's health at serious risk. Tim Duffield, Head Intelligence at the MHRA’s Criminal Enforcement Unit said: “We are tackling the organised criminal gangs whose illegal trade in unauthorised medicines puts people at risk of serious harm.

“Our officers seized around £2 million worth of fake weight loss medicines from a filthy warehouse on an industrial estate. These products have not been assessed for safety, quality or effectiveness, and there is no guarantee of what they contain or whether they have been contaminated with harmful substances.”

View 3 Images The MHRA warned there was no guarantee what the counterfeit pens contained (Image: Getty Images)

‌



The seizure was the latest in a series of MHRA raids targeting unauthorised weight-loss medicines. In May, two people were arrested after officers raided a country estate believed to have been used to make, assemble and distribute unlicensed weight-loss drugs.

They recovered around 12,000 doses, as well as packaging and suspected pharmaceutical substances. Another 2,000 doses awaiting dispatch were seized in February, alongside manufacturing equipment, suspected ingredients, packaging and commercial vehicles.

In October 2025, the MHRA dismantled the first illicit weight-loss medicine production facility discovered in the UK. Officers seized 5,000 unauthorised retatrutide and tirzepatide pens, thousands of empty pens and raw chemical ingredients.

Article continues below

Tim added: “Retatrutide has not been authorised for use in the UK. Products being sold as retatrutide outside legitimate clinical trials are being supplied illegally and could pose serious risks to public health. We urge people to avoid buying weight-loss medicines from unregulated sources.

"Anyone considering GLP-1 treatment should speak to a healthcare professional and only obtain medicines from a registered pharmacy against a valid prescription.”

News.title: Helicopter declares mid-air emergency moments after taking off from Aberdeen
News.content:
Helicopter declares mid-air emergency moments after taking off from Aberdeen

The Airbus H175 helicopter, operated by Offshore Helicopter Services, took off from Aberdeen heliport before it declared a mid-air emergency over the North Sea this morning

View 2 Images The aircraft was travelling out to a platform in the North Sea (Image: Flightradar24)

A helicopter travelling to a North Sea platform was forced to make an urgent landing after it declared a mid-air emergency this morning.

‌



‌



The Airbus H175 took off from Aberdeen heliport shortly before 8am and headed north-east over the North Sea.

‌



However the chopper, operated by Offshore Helicopter Services, was forced to turn back part-way through its journey out to one of the platforms in the area.

‌



Just minutes into the flight, the helicopter crew issued a 7700 squawk code, the air traffic control code of a general emergency.

The aircraft, which typically holds up to 18 passengers, made a U-turn over the ocean before heading back to Aberdeen heliport for a safe landing.

View 2 Images The Airbus H175 helicopter declared a mid-air emergency (Image: Bloomberg via Getty Images)

‌



No information has been released about the exact nature of the emergency so far. The helicopter reportedly returned to Aberdeen as a precautionary measure.

The Mirror has contacted Offshore Helicopter Services for comment.

The news comes after a United Airlines flight from London to New Jersey declared an emergency on Thursday afternoon and returned to Heathrow shortly after take-off.

‌



Flight UA941 departed London Heathrow shortly after 4pm on Thursday, bound for Newark Liberty International Airport, where it was due to arrive at 7.20pm local time.

Shortly after take-off, the crew transmitted squawk code 7700 - the international code for a general emergency - and requested an immediate return to Heathrow due to a "technical issue", according to aviation outlet Air Live.

The Boeing 767-300 was initially expected to dump around 20 tonnes of fuel to reduce its landing weight before returning to Heathrow, the outlet reported. However, the crew reportedly abandoned the plan and opted to return directly to the airport.

Article continues below

Aircraft often have to burn fuel before making an unscheduled landing. This is because many aircraft were designed to land after a long flight during which they would have burned most of their fuel.

Planes take off much heavier than they can land, and airliners must burn or dump fuel before an emergency landing to reduce the aircraft's total weight to the safe maximum landing weight.

Landing while carrying too much weight runs the risk of extreme physical stress on the landing gear, wings and fuselage.

News.title: Robert Jenrick tied in knots after being accused of 'deflecting' Reform row questions
News.content:
Robert Jenrick tied in knots after being accused of 'deflecting' Reform row questions

WARNING: DISTRESSING CONTENT. Robert Jenrick was tied in knots in a radio interview after being accused of 'deflecting' questions about Reform politicians being filmed making concerning remarks

View 3 Images Reform's Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick was forced to deny deflection tactics (Image: TalkTv)

Tetchy Robert Jenrick was tied in knots in a radio interview after being accused of "deflecting" questions about Reform politicians being filmed making a series of racist, sexist and other concerning remarks.

‌



‌



Reform's Treasury spokesman was forced to deny deflection tactics after he tried to talk about other parties when he was interrogated on the revelations about Reform in an undercover probe by ITV. He suggested Reform doesn't have a particular problem and all parties have "bad apples".

‌



Mr Jenrick - who defected to Reform from the Tory party earlier this year - said his party will "never have any place for racism" and pointed to Reform having suspended individuals in question. And he insisted Reform has "very strong vetting", saying the Conservatives have " absolutely no vetting whatsoever by the central party for local councillors."

‌



He also brushed off footage showing Reform MP Sarah Pochin saying the party's press team are "f***ing chauvinistic", saying it is "not my experience of Reform" and accused the presenter of "trying to make something where there is nothing".

Footage released on Wednesday by ITV, who went undercover in Reform's ranks during a year-long investigation, showed Reform councillor Alan Feeney, the deputy mayor of Solihull, claim that his area was "infested" with Asian homeowners. He was seen suggesting the government should "drag them out of their homes".

Reform launches racism probes into politicians after undercover TV investigation READ MORE :

View 3 Images ITV went undercover in Reform's ranks during a year-long investigation (Image: Will Colebourne/the Press Association)

‌



Another clip showed South London councillor, Dean Miller, saying the King should be beheaded after claiming the monarch is secretly a Muslim. He also described Black children as "f***** animals".

And Raymond Dunning, who claimed to have been asked by Reform to run as an MP, said on camera: "I'm so far-right it's unbelievable." Further clips showed councillor Chris Whelen making vile sexual remarks about a female Reform colleague.

Further footage released on Thursday showed a Reform aide saying Dr Chris Parry, Reform’s candidate to be the Mayor of Hampshire and the Solent, was "clearly a racist". Dr Parry at the time faced questions after posting on social media that the then Deputy Prime Minister David Lammy “must go home to the Caribbean where [his] loyalty lies”. He had also questioned in social media posts the loyalty of eight other prominent Black and Muslim politicians.

‌



Mr Farage was filmed saying; “It's showing a bit of... bit of sorrow. Look, ‘I'm sorry’ is probably a good thing to hear. Just take the f***ing deal. Trouble is he's a Rear Admiral. That's the problem." He adds that Dr Parry should apologise and move on. Footage also showed Reform’s Director of Communications, Ed Sumner, suggesting Mr Farage was “protecting" Dr Parry.

Footage also showed Sarah Pochin, Reform MP for Runcorn and Helsby, saying the party needs welcoming a female undercover reporter posing as a press officer. "We so need women press officers," she said.

"They are so chauvinistic. I go out on all the shows and go: ‘Oh no, it's lovely, they're all so welcoming'. S***. They just exclude you if you are a woman. There's a bit of a male issue going on."

‌



In an interview on BBC R4's Today programme, Mr Jenrick said: " Well, I didn't like what I heard in the documentary or what I've seen of it. The party has acted immediately.

"We have, and will never have, any place for racism or comments of that kind in Reform, and so we acted to suspend or remove all of the individuals in question, including the councillor Feeney from Solihull that you just referenced, and we couldn't do more than that. I don't accept that this happens any more in Reform than any other party."

He added: " In my experience, all political parties have bad apples."

‌



View 3 Images Andy Burnham said Reform UK must take 'immediate and firm action' against party members caught in ITV's footage (Image: Gary Oakley/the Press Association)

Asked whether he had spoken to Ms Pochin since her comments emerged, he added: " I have, and I speak to Sarah all the time. I wasn't in Reform when she made those comments, and you obviously have to talk to her about them. But that is not my experience of Reform, and she's a very valued colleague of mine who, you know, I work with every day."

Told that he wasn't a woman and asked if he was supporting her, he said: "Y ou're trying to make something where there is nothing. As I said, I've spoken to Sarah many times. We are colleagues and friends, and she knows that she can always rely me.

‌



"But it's not my experience that the party has problems of that kind. Although, as I said before, in all political parties, there are bad individuals."

After repeatedly trying to talk about Labour or the Conservatives during the rest of the interview, BBC host Emma Barnett said nobody was suggesting other parties don't have issues but that he was being asked about his own party.

She added: "It risks, if you every time you're asked about this, if you deflect to what other parties have done... you need to address what is happening within your party." Mr Jenrick insisted he was not deflecting.

‌



On Thursday, Andy Burnham said Reform UK must take “immediate and firm action” against party members caught in ITV's footage. Asked by reporters about the investigation during a visit to the North West, the Prime Minister said: “We’ve allowed a poison into our politics in recent years, and it’s time to draw a line under it."

After the latest footage was released on Thursday, Labour chair Bridget Phillipson said: “These latest shocking and deeply disturbing revelations go right to the top of Reform UK. Nigel Farage needs to wake up and realise the buck stops with him.

“Time and again Farage has had every opportunity to demonstrate leadership and get Reform’s house in order and every single time he has failed."

‌



A Reform spokesperson said: "Not all individuals covertly recorded by ITV are members of Reform UK. Where members, activists and councillors have clearly behaved inappropriately, investigations have commenced. In some cases, there have been suspensions and due process must be followed.

“Reform UK has improved and prioritised its vetting procedures, but from time to time, a handful of individuals who do not share our values will initially make it through vetting. This is the same for all organisations."

In a statement sent to The Mirror, Mr Miller said he had resigned the party whip, adding: "This decision was taken due to a catastrophic, multi-layered failure of the duty of care and safeguarding by party leadership at both local and national levels."

‌



He continued: "Any footage obtained by undercover operatives occurred when I was suffering from acute physical and neurological distress, sleep deprivation, and heavily under the influence of strong, legally prescribed neurological pain medications. Any remarks captured during this period of severe cognitive impairment does not reflect my character, my beliefs, or my years of dedicated humanitarian and public health service."

Responding to the latest revelations, Mr Sumner said: “Nothing in the excerpts [of filming] discloses any wrongdoing, criminal activity or breaches of Reform UK policy by me. I do not endorse extremism or bigotry, or any concealment of extremism and bigotry”.

Dr Parry told ITV: “I would urge people to go back to the original contexts and tweets to see what was said and why.

Article continues below

“They related to reparations and failures by the police and government. They will see I always exercise my right to criticise anyone in power or the public eye, whom I judge to be acting against the interests of the British people.”

News.title: Pharmacist shares ‘little known’ amlodipine side effect - when to seek medical help
News.content:
Pharmacist shares ‘little known’ amlodipine side effect - when to seek medical help

A TikTok pharmacist has highlighted a common side effect of a widely prescribed blood pressure medication

View 2 Images Amlodipine may cause some serious side effects (Image: Getty Images)

Amlodipine is prescribed to treat high blood pressure and prevent angina, helping relax and widen blood vessels so blood can flow more easily. But there are some lesser-known side effects that could make life quite difficult.

‌



‌



Pharmacist Dose of Jit used one of his recent TikTok videos to highlight one of them, acting out a conversation with a patient where he realised he'd forgotten to give them important advice about their prescription. He explained: "It can actually cause swollen ankles because it dilates the blood vessels, increases pressure into the capillaries, pushing fluid into surrounding tissues."

‌



Amlodipine belongs to a group of medicines called calcium channel blockers, which work by relaxing blood vessels. The NHS says this type of medication can cause peripheral oedema, where fluid builds up in the tissues, commonly affecting both ankles and feet.

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

The swelling can be uncomfortable and may make shoes feel tighter than usual, particularly towards the end of the day. Although it can be linked to amlodipine, the severity of the swelling and whether it affects one or both legs can help a healthcare professional assess what might be causing it.

‌



Swelling can have other causes, including injuries, problems with the veins, or conditions affecting the heart, kidneys or liver. Anyone who develops swelling that is new, persistent or getting worse should seek advice from a pharmacist or GP rather than assume the medication is responsible.

The NHS advises people to seek urgent medical help if swelling in one leg or foot has no clear cause, starts suddenly, is severe or painful, or the area becomes red or hot. If swelling occurs alongside breathing difficulties or chest pain, call 999.

View 2 Images Side effects can vary with amlodipine (Image: Getty Images)

Article continues below

People who suspect amlodipine is causing side effects should speak to their doctor or pharmacist, who can discuss the best way to manage them. They should not stop taking the medicine without medical advice, as untreated high blood pressure can increase the risk of serious health problems.

A healthcare professional may review the symptoms, check for other possible causes and discuss whether any changes to treatment are appropriate. Anyone concerned about a suspected side effect can also report it through the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency's Yellow Card scheme.

News.title: Brit dad fined £2,500 after son, 2, plunged nearly 40ft to death from Cyprus hotel
News.content:
Brit dad fined £2,500 after son, 2, plunged nearly 40ft to death from Cyprus hotel

Joshua Foster pleaded guilty to causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act after his two-year-old son plunged to his death from a hotel window in Cyprus

Joshua Foster arrives to be sentenced for causing death of son in Cyprus

A British man has been fined for causing the death of his two-year-old son, who fell nearly 40ft from a fourth floor window of a hotel in Cyprus during a family holiday.

‌



‌



Joshua Foster placed the toddler on a windowsill at the five-star King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort in Chlorakas to show him the view of a waterpark, not realising the window was open, Paphos District Court previously heard.

‌



The 37-year-old pleaded guilty to causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act and was today fined 3,000 euro (£2,500) at Paphos District Court. Foster, who worked as an auditor, wore a light blue shirt and held back tears as his sentence was read out by District Judge Froso Christodoulidou.

‌



Speaking to reporters after this sentencing, Foster said: “Thank you for the support. I’m looking forward to going home and being with my wife and daughter.”

View 2 Images Joshua Foster has been fined £2,500 (Image: Annabel Lee-Ellis/the Press Association)

Rapist who killed police officer at World Cup fan zone gets one year in prison READ MORE :

It was previously heard that Foster thought there was protective glass and the window was shut when he “lost control” of his young son. Foster, his wife, two children, and in-laws had arrived in Cyprus in the early hours of July 12.

‌



After spending the day carrying out activities, the family returned to their rooms to get ready to go out for dinner. Foster, his father-in-law and son left their rooms and walked towards the elevator at around 6pm.

As they approached the lift, the boy noticed a waterpark outside, Foster’s lawyer Alexandros Alexandrou told an earlier hearing.

Foster pushed the elevator button, placed the child on the windowsill, the boy looked out, and the “inconceivable” happened before Foster had a chance to react, the court was told.

‌



View 2 Images The King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort in Chlorakas, Cyprus (Image: Annabel Lee-Ellis/the Press Association)

Prosecutor Chryso Pergandi said that at around 6.40pm on July 12, police received reports that a child had fallen from the fourth floor of the beachfront hotel in unknown circumstances. The boy was taken to Paphos General Hospital where, despite efforts to resuscitate him, he was pronounced dead.

Foster’s father-in-law said the defendant had picked up his son and placed him on the window to “see the view” before he fell, it was heard. Foster gave a voluntary statement to police and said his son “fell before he had a chance to grab him”.

‌



Mr Alexandrou said the moment will “haunt him for the rest of his life”, adding: “We’re allowed, even when we’re happy, to lose our concentration. And in that moment he was happy, he held his child.”

The court heard the window was 2.85 metres (9.3ft) wide and 1.2 metres (3.9ft) high.

In a statement outside Paphos District Court today, Foster’s lawyer Mr Alexandrou paid tribute to his client as an “exemplary family man”.

Article continues below

Speaking through a translator, he said: “I met an incredible father, a very good husband and an exemplary family man with a beautiful family behind him, that support him, that embraces him, that has always been by his side with all the means that they have at their disposal.”

He added that Foster is “very emotional” after the sentencing and the family needed time to grieve properly. Mr Alexandrou said: “They (the family) need to go back (to the UK) to grieve properly and allow themselves to grieve (after) they have been in a defence mode during this procedure.”

News.title: Celebrity Traitors live updates - Rob Beckett and Hannah Fry out as star told off by bosses
News.content:
The production team behind the Celebrity Traitors has reportedly been accused of being "like human traffickers" for preventing the cast from contacting their loved ones whenever they wanted to.

A source has claimed that one of the show's stars lashed out over not being allowed to speak to family and friends in the breaks between filming. Producers and the other contestants were said to have been left confused by the outburst, as the strict rules of the show were made clear to participants before they signed up to the BBC show. Speaking to the Sun, the source said: "The celeb couldn't understand why they couldn't just call home – despite this being clearly explained to them at the start of the process.

"They kicked off and in a rant, compared the team on the show to being like human traffickers. Show insiders told the publication that phone rules are in place to 'protect the integrity of the game'."

The Sun has claimed that participants are allowed to make calls, but that this is at the producers' discretion and can only be made at select times, on a producer's phone while a member of the production team is present.

The Mirror understands that it is usual practice for a show that is such an immersive experience to limit players' contact to the outside world to protect the integrity of the game.

News.title: Indian restaurant in Liverpool loved by A-list stars gets ZERO hygiene rating
News.content:
Indian restaurant in Liverpool loved by A-list stars gets ZERO hygiene rating

Holdi, an Indian restaurant in Liverpool loved by A-list celebrities, has been handed a zero food hygiene rating following a visit from health inspectors

View 2 Images Elijah Wood at Holdi in 2024 (Image: HOLDI)

A well-loved restaurant frequented by sports stars and celebs has been hit with a zero food hygiene rating.

‌



‌



Holdi, an Indian restaurant in Liverpool popular with TV and movie stars and footballers, is widely regarded as one of the best curry houses in the city. It was named by last year’s Curry Awards in the top 10 Liverpool curry houses.

‌



It quickly became a favourite of soap stars from Hollyoaks and Coronation Street in the years after it opened, the Liverpool Echo reports. And in 2024, Holdi welcomed a Hollywood A-lister when Elijah Wood and his Lord of the Rings co-star Billy Boyd dined there when they were in the city for the annual Comic Con convention. Wood reportedly told staff the meal was the "best Indian he had ever had."

‌



Football stars including Anthony Gordon, Harvey Elliott and Sean Dyche have all been known to eat at the restaurant. UFC Star Paddy Pimblett is another fan of their food, and was pictured with staff at the restaurant after enjoying a meal with a group of friends in September of this year.

View 2 Images Holdi, based in Woolton, is one of the best-known curry houses in Liverpool (Image: Facebook)

Over 110 Brewers Fayre and Beefeater restaurants reopening across UK – all the locations confirmed so far READ MORE :

But just a few days after it welcomed the UFC Baddy - on September 14 - Holdi in Woolton got a visit from Liverpool City Council environmental health inspectors.

‌



According to a report from the Food Standards Agency, Holdi was handed a zero rating out of five for food hygiene - with "urgent improvement is necessary".

The report also detailed that major improvement was necessary in terms of structural compliance, meanwhile urgent improvement was required in terms of the agency's confidence in the restaurant's management of these areas.

Inspectors cited a "poor track record of compliance, with little or not technical knowledge, no appreciation of hazards or quality control and no food safety management system".

‌



Najer Hossain, owner of Holdi, blamed their poor scores on electrical problems as business had been forced to resort to using a generator for power while waiting for council approval to carry out groundworks to fix issues with their supply.

On the night of September 13 the generator switched off “due to our own carelessness of not leaving it with enough diesel, something we have been extra cautious about since,” Mr Hossain said.

He went on: "This had again affected the temperature of our fridge and freezers, we then had inspectors visit on the 14th, this was before we were due to open, and before any staff had arrived. As we had done previously, we realised we’d need to voluntarily close that day due to temperatures not being to the required level.

‌



"The health inspector also saw this as a major issue, the wiring was not to a satisfactory standard going through the kitchen and windows upstairs and this affected our ability to to reach certain parts of the kitchen when cleaning and had gathered food debris.

"During this time our operational manager and main chef had been off on paternity leave at the same time, it led to some of the cleanliness of the restaurant caused by electrical works overlooked. It is important to point out we had voluntarily closed, and the inspectors had asked us to contact them again when we feel it’s safe to reopen.

"We closed this time for just over a week, in this time we contacted our generator supplier to come in and tidy up the wiring so that it didn't impact our ability to keep the restaurant clean, this was done within a day. We also were able to clean up the areas in the restaurant that were difficult to reach previously, provide staff with adequate health and safety training, and equip the restaurant with plenty of disinfectant and hand washes, as a couple of the smaller sinks had been missing hand wash during the inspection.”

Article continues below

Following a revisit on September 24 and a satisfactory health inspection, the establishment has now re-opened. Mr Hossain said: "This restaurant has always been a five-star star rated restaurant from previous inspections, [however] due to recent issues this has caused us a lapse in concentration in focusing on the things that matter.

“We are happy all staff and management have had the opportunity to retrain and we hope we are able to acquire and get back to the very high standards we hold ourselves to.”

Mr Hossain added that permission has been granted for the electrical works to go ahead and the power supply should return to normal by the end of October. He has requested another visit from health inspectors to be given a new score.

News.title: Community 'heartbroken and horrified' after Oregon school shooting
News.content:
Three children and a teacher were shot dead by a 16-year-old at a primary school in the US state of Oregon before he was killed by a bystander, police have said.

The suspect, who has not been named, forced his way into Silver Rail Elementary School in the city of Bend on Thursday afternoon by shooting at locked doors.

"We are stunned and heartbroken by this senseless tragedy," Steven Cook, the top administrative official of the local school district, said in a statement.

News.title: Banks expect to be hit with higher taxes in Budget
News.content:
Chancellor John Healey is planning to increase taxes on the bank sector, senior banking executives have told the BBC.

Healey has described banks as part of "the crown jewels" of the UK economy, but leaders in the sector have said it will be "on the menu" at the Budget in two weeks' time.

The biggest four banks collectively made about Â£15bn profit in the first six months of this year, and trade unions have called for them to face additional taxes.

The trade body for the banking sector, UK Finance, warned "further increases in bank taxes would weaken competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government's ambition to deliver growth in every postcode".

Shares in banks including Lloyds and NatWest fell on Friday on expectations that the sector would be hit by tax hikes. The firms were among the biggest fallers on the UK stock market, with both dropping more than 2%.

Barclays fell only slightly and HSBC actually rose as both have large international businesses and would be less affected by a hike in UK taxes.

There are a number of ways the chancellor could extract more money from the sector.

One option is for Healey is to reverse a reduction in the surcharge that banks pay on corporation tax, from 8% to 3%, introduced in 2023, by Conservative chancellor Jeremy Hunt.

Critics argue this would be unfair noting the cut coincided with a rise in corporation tax from 19% to 25%.

Healey could also raise the bank levy - a small percentage charged on loans.

The BBC understands that the Treasury is leaning towards changing the surcharge if they were to go ahead as it is easier to change an existing tax rather than impose a new windfall tax.

Reversing the 2023 surcharge rate would raise around Â£2bn. However, the last government was persuaded that adding 8% on top of corporation tax of 25% would leave UK banks struggling to compete with European and US rivals - so it may be that it is raised, but not all the way back to the 8% level.

Speaking to the press in Bangkok, Healey praised the role banks play in the British economy.

Adding that he has "decisions to take in the Budget", he said: "My observation on the banks is that people too often see âthem as big, distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future â prospects."

In the past banks have successfully argued that higher taxes would risk making the UK uncompetitive with other jurisdictions and would reduce their ability to lend, and therefore be anti-growth.

Sir Philip Augar, an author and former banker in the City of London, told the BBC's Today programme there was "room for a moderate increase" in taxes on the sector that could raise up to Â£3bn a year.

He said lenders were enjoying "booming conditions", benefiting from higher interest rates which boost their profits.

Rising interest rates have expanded the margin between the rate at which banks lend to customers and the rate they pay savers.

Sir Philip added that when the banking sector "hits really rocky times it expects the taxpayer to bail them out - when it hits boom times, it expects some kind of special treatment".

He said banks cannot simultaneously be "too big to fail and too big to tax".

Paul Nowak, general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, which represents trade unions, said Britain's four biggest banks are making a billion pounds a week, with bonuses at post-financial crash records. "These are bumper profits - driven by high interest rates and households' mortgage misery," he said.

"Now it's time to make sure banks pay their fair share," he added.

"But if the chancellor does ask the Banks to pay a fairer share of tax in the Budget, that's 100% the right call," he added.

News.title: Police officer who raped two women jailed for 12 years
News.content:
A former police sergeant who was found guilty of a catalogue of sex crimes, including raping two women, has been jailed for 12 years.

Campbell Petrie had been convicted of eight charges involving physical and sexual abuse towards the women in Glasgow over a 17-year period between 2006 and 2023.

Petrie, who had denied the allegations, will be supervised and monitored in the community for a further three years after his release.

He is one of four serving or former Police Scotland officers who have been exposed as rapists in the space of five months.

In May, Alan Greer took his own life just days after a police raid on his home as part of an investigation into offences dating back to 2012.

An investigation has since established that the officer was a violent serial sex offender with at least 15 victims.

In July, former constable Cameron Ross was jailed for 10 years for raping two women and abusing a third.

And on Thursday, serving officer John Williamson was found guilty of raping a teenage girl and a woman in Shetland. He will be sentenced in December.

News.title: Sparks fly at the Celebrity Traitors round table and a 'terrifying' death parade
News.content:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the fifth episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

Things are hotting up a bit in the castle, not least for Ross Kemp, who doesn't seem to be enjoying it very much.

"I'm quite angry," he said, his brow furrowing even more than usual.

"I've suffered at the hands of the traitors and now they've put heat on me, so I'm quite angry about that," he said.

"They're using me like a donkey."

Clearly they aren't hitching rides on him at the seaside - that would be another show entirely - he's referring to them pointing the finger of suspicion at him by making him stand out when he doesn't want to.

Firstly they kept the former EastEnders star and documentary maker above ground at the grave-digging task, sparing him from being buried.

In this episode, he was one of four celebrities who had to sit alone in a tomb, before one of them was murdered.

This was intended to get tongues wagging about him, deflecting suspicion away from the actual traitors.

Joanne McNally was convinced enough by this to say: "The vibe with Ross is off. His eyes do not close.

"He has not blinked since we've been here. He is giving cyborgs."

News.title: Doctor regrets not going to police earlier about Lucy Letby
News.content:
A senior doctor who raised suspicions about Lucy Letby has said he should have gone to police sooner.

Dr Stephen Brearey was the lead neonatal consultant at the Countess of Chester Hospital when the nurse murdered seven babies and attempted to murder seven others.

In his first interview since the publication of the Thirlwall Inquiry report into what happened, Brearey reflected on the effect on staff and said he had "naively" assumed senior managers would respond to suspicions about the nurse's involvement in a series of baby deaths.

The inquiry found a "toxic negativity" within the NHS that continued to discourage staff from speaking out, despite stronger whistleblowing guidance, and said regulation was lacking.

Brearey claimed his warnings about Letby were repeatedly ignored by bosses at the hospital, which is now under new management - and also fears cultural change at the NHS will take time to implement.

"I was naively thinking that raising concerns with senior managers, they had the same values that I did and, once they got it, they would be thinking the same way," he said.

The doctor led a group of seven consultants who shared the same concerns about Letby.

Hospital bosses carried out a series of internal reviews into increased infant mortality in 2015 and 2016, but Cheshire Police was not asked to investigate until May 2017.

Letby remained employed at the hospital until her arrest more than a year later.

"I think one of the reasons we got through this and ended up picking up a police investigation is that the seven of us stuck together," he said.

"But obviously in retrospect, clearly, if we'd known what was ahead of us, we would have gone to the police earlier."

News.title: Ten-year-old Willow among children to benefit from pioneering same-day test to spot infections
News.content:
"The fact that they had a test there available to her was paramount. It saved her life," said Stacey.

"It's a miracle she's here and we're extremely grateful for that," added Willow's dad, Russ.

With the right treatment, Willow was eventually able to recover from her infection, but needed several months in hospital.

She is one of many patients at the children's hospital to benefit from the new type of testing.

During a study in 2024-5 metagenomic testing was used on 122 critically ill children in the paediatric intensive care unit (ICU) at GOSH.

The results have now been published in the Lancet Microbe.

Metagenomic testing analyses all genetic material in a sample and can detect thousands of different pathogens.

By contrast, the most common method of identifying bacteria is by trying to culture them in Petri dishes, a technology that has been used since Victorian times.

Another test, PCR, can identify viruses and some bacteria, but doctors need to specify what they are trying to detect.

Metagenomics testing at GOSH was able to identify around nine in 10 bacteria and viruses and all fungi in samples.

News.title: Wildlife park reopens after man killed by tiger
News.content:
Yorkshire Wildlife Park has reopened for the first time since a man was killed by a tiger in an enclosure.

William Chapman, 24, was mauled to death at the park near Doncaster on Saturday. The public were evacuated after the incident with the attraction closed since then.

An inquest that opened into Chapman's death on Thursday heard of his history of mental illness and a diagnosis of schizophrenia. His family expressed concerns about his contact with mental health services leading up to his death.

City of Doncaster Council, which is responsible for licensing the park, is carrying out a health and safety investigation and said it would share the outcome with the coroner, the inquest was told.

On Thursday, Yorkshire Wildlife Park confirmed it would reopen on Friday following "engagement with the relevant authorities".

In a previous statement on social media, the park said "many, many people" had contacted it about Altai, the Amur tiger involved in the incident, and it confirmed he was "safe and well" and would not be euthanised.

A spokesperson said its "Land of the Tiger" area, where Saturday's incident took place in front of staff and members of the public, would also reopen.

Several hundred cars could be seen at the popular attraction on Friday morning, with many young families and wildlife enthusiasts carrying cameras heading in.

Among them was Taylor, who was visiting with her partner and their two children, aged one and three, for the youngest child's birthday.

She said: "We just want to support the centre, it's just very sad and we feel for staff who must have been through a lot.

"We will go to the tiger enclosure and feel safe."

Glyn, an animal enthusiast, was "glad to be coming" and also remarked on the "sad incident".

He said he never "felt unsafe" at the park, adding that the animals were "secure".

News.title: Mother of Henry Nowak's killer could be released early
News.content:
The mother of the man who murdered Henry Nowak could be released from prison early as part of the government's plan to tackle overcrowding in jails.

Kiran Kaur, 53, was jailed for three years in July for removing the knife her son, Vickrum Digwa, used to kill the 18-year-old student in Southampton in December.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight Police and Crime Commissioner (PCC) Donna Jones said Kaur's early release would be "a significant blow for Henry's family".

Under the Sentencing Act 2026, which came into force on 1 October, most prisoners serving fixed-term sentences of up to two and a half years are automatically released on licence after serving a third of the time, rather than half.

Kaur, who is appealing against her sentence, would serve the rest of it in the community on licence, and could be recalled to prison if she breached her licence conditions.

She spent 221 days on remand, which the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said was taken into account when she was sentenced.

Her crime of assisting an offender is not one of the offences excluded from changes to the early release scheme.

Jones told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "She wasn't even sentenced until July this year, which was just three months ago, and here we are now talking about her potential release."

She said she would write to Justice Secretary Alex Norris asking for "clarity" so she could continue supporting the family.

The MoJ said offenders released on licence faced tougher controls, including:

a presumption that all prison leavers will be tagged, from October

restriction zones confining dangerous offenders to a pre-agreed area

giving victims a say in licence conditions

near real-time location data for probation officers, to be rolled out nationally by the end of 2026

It is not known whether Kaur could face deportation, as her immigration status is unclear.

The government, which does not comment on individual cases, said it would "always seek to deport foreign criminals at the first opportunity".

Foreign nationals jailed for 12 months or more are generally considered for deportation, although there are exceptions and decisions can be appealed.

If Kaur holds dual British nationality, the home secretary would first have to try to remove her British citizenship before she could be deported.

Kaur's appeal against her sentence is due to be heard at the Court of Appeal on 5 November.

Her son, Digwa, was jailed for life with a minimum term of 21 years on 1 June for the murder of Nowak, after falsely claiming the student had racially abused him.

Digwa has been given permission to challenge the length of that sentence at the Court of Appeal on 5 November.

News.title: Reform faces questions over candidate vetting after undercover filming
News.content:
Reform UK is facing further questions about its vetting procedures for candidates, after undercover filming broadcast by ITV News, external.

In the film, gathered over the course of a year, an undercover reporter is advised by a local party chairman to delete social media posts supportive of far-right activist Tommy Robinson, before being encouraged to apply to stand to be a councillor for the party.

It also shows a former Reform candidate claiming he failed the party's vetting process twice but was still allowed to stand to be a councillor. Reform denies the individual failed vetting in the first place.

Reform said the party had "improved and prioritised its vetting procedures".

In a statement, the party said that "from time to time, a handful of individuals who do not share our values will initially make it through vetting" but added: "This is the same for all organisations."

It follows undercover filming broadcast on Wednesday night, which showed some of Reform's councillors and candidates using racist, violent and sexist language.

Reform MP Robert Jenrick said all political parties had "bad apples".

Speaking to the BBC's Today programme, he said he "didn't like what I heard in the documentary" but argued that the party had acted quickly, removing or suspending those in the undercover film.

"I don't accept this happens any more in Reform than in any other party," he added.

The party said: "There is no room for racism in Reform UK. We always respect due process of investigations and whilst these are ongoing it would not be appropriate to comment on individual cases."

Reform also accused the ITV investigation of "extreme methods of deception" and using false information to obtain an undercover role in Reform's headquarters.

Jenrick said he believed the undercover reporters had wanted to find evidence of party leader Nigel Farage "acting in an inappropriate way" but had not succeeded.

Two years ago, Farage vowed to vet candidates more "rigorously", after the party dropped a series of candidates following reports they had made offensive or racist comments.

However, the party has continued to face questions over the strength of its vetting processes.

Speaking on Thursday, before the latest filming was broadcast, Farage told BBC Look East his party vetted "to a much higher standard than other parties" but "you can't vet for future comments".

News.title: 'Massive challenge' to protect paedophile Donaldson from harm in jail
News.content:
Donaldson represents a "very complex challenge to the Northern Ireland Prison Service", Acheson added.

"There are always hierarchies within prisons - and there are even hierarchies within sex offenders - and the lowest of the low and the most vulnerable in terms of hostility from others are those who've been convicted of sexual violence against a minor," he said.

But he said it would also be necessary to "examine potential political or sectarian targeting" relating to Donaldson's leadership of the DUP and his service in the Ulster Defence Regiment, a former Army unit.

"The prison has a duty of care to protect him and he is uniquely vulnerable," Acheson told BBC Radio Ulster's Talkback programme.

"Maghaberry, in previous inspections, has indicated that it operates an integrated regime, where sex offenders can be safely managed in the wider prison community.

"I don't think that is remotely viable for Jeffrey Donaldson, given those offence characteristics and his background.

"So either he is kept, in effect, in conditions of solitary confinement for years and years or another solution has to be found.

"I don't think it's acceptable to keep him in conditions of solitary confinement - it may not even be legal."

News.title: Trans people should use hospital spaces according to biological sex, NHS England says
News.content:
Trans patients should be cared for on single-sex hospital wards or bays that align with their biological sex rather than their gender identity, according to new NHS England (NHSE) guidance.

It says when this is not "clinically appropriate" then alternative arrangements should be made and the dignity and safety of all patients should be maintained.

The guidance also says staff facilities should be used by people based on their biological sex, while trusts should ensure enough alternatives to single-sex facilities, such as single-occupancy toilets, are offered.

Previous NHSE guidance suggested patients and staff could be accommodated on wards or use facilities based on their gender identity.

That meant that a trans woman â a biological male who identifies as a woman â could have chosen to be on a women's ward, or a trans man â a biological female who identifies as a man â could have opted for a men's ward.

That guidance was withdrawn following the Supreme Court ruling in April 2025 that under equality law the term "sex" means biological sex and "woman" refers to a biological woman.

The judgment said for a space or service to be single sex it should only allow those of the same biological sex to use it.

Also under the new guidance issued on Thursday, NHSE emphasised that in order to avoid discriminating against trans people they should be offered gender neutral spaces.

But the guidance also says decisions may have to be made on a case-by-case basis and must ensure clinical needs are met.

It also makes clear that there are circumstances where clinical need is the overriding priority, including on emergency units and urgent care settings.

In addition to the patient document of the guidance, NHSE has published advice for trusts on how to organise changing rooms, toilets and other single-sex facilities for staff.

Again, it says they should be used by people based on their biological sex, not their gender identity.

The document encourages NHS trusts in England to carry out an audit to ensure they are offering enough alternatives to single-sex facilities, for instance, gender neutral or single occupancy toilets.

Pressures on hospitals mean many have already struggled to keep wards single sex.

NHSE data shows that the number of breaches of the previous mixed-sex accommodation guidance has been growing every year since 2021- where members of the opposite sex were placed on a single-sex ward.

The most recent figure for August 2026 shows there were 5,520 breaches, compared to 3,853 in June 2025.

Sex-based rights charity Sex Matters has welcomed the guidance as a "momentous shift back to reality", but is concerned about how it will be applied.

"NHS patient data is a mess, with potentially thousands of trans-identifying people recorded as the opposite sex," CEO Maya Forstater said.

Trans rights organisations TransActual and Trans+ Solidarity Alliance have said they are concerned NHS staff will be unclear on how to safely look after trans patients.

"This guidance will not survive contact with reality in resource-strapped hospitals and will create unworkable operational challenges," they said.

The NHS has been at the centre of a number of high-profile arguments over the interpretation of equality law and workplace regulations.

In January 2026, Darlington Memorial Hospital was found to have violated the dignity of a group of nurses who complained about a transgender colleague - a biological male who identified as a woman - being allowed to use the female changing rooms. The nurses were told they should change somewhere else if they objected.

The tribunal concluded that the trust had indirectly discriminated against them.

The nurses are currently seeking Â£400,000 from the NHS to cover their legal costs.

One of the nurses who brought the action, Bethany Hutchison, who is now president of the Darlington Nurses Union, says they welcome the "clear and necessary guidance" from NHSE, but the test will be whether trusts follow it.

"The Darlington nurses should never have had to take their own employer to court to secure privacy, dignity and lawful single-sex facilities," she said.

"Enforcement cannot continue to depend on the courage and personal sacrifice of individual nurses."

In Scotland, another employment tribunal found, in December 2025, that a nurse, Sandie Peggie, had been harassed by NHS Fife over its interpretation of rules on single sex spaces.

Peggie had complained about a doctor, who was a trans woman, using the female changing rooms.

She was suspended after raising concerns. The tribunal dismissed her other claims of discrimination and victimisation.

An appeal is under way and expected to reach the courts next year.

News.title: Russell Brand accuser says he turned 'monster-like' before alleged rape
News.content:
Under cross-examination Brand's barrister, Ian Winter KC put it to the complainant that when she first met Brand she welcomed his attention.

"I welcomed his company, not what followed," the woman replied.

He then suggested that she fell under his spell and that she wanted to spend more time with him.

The woman replied: "That's incorrect. I did not fall under his spell and I did not find him attractive. "

Asked by the defence why she agreed to go back to the hotel room with Brand, she responded: "I'm telling you... I thought he was a gay man, very softly spoken, very effeminate.

"I felt safe â I felt sexually safe with him. He was very intelligent and that appealed to me, not in a sexual sense. "

The woman became tearful a number of times while giving her evidence from the witness box.

At one point the judge told the witness to "take a moment, catch your breath", after she became emotional.

Brand's barrister later challenged the complainant about why she did not run back into the bathroom or leave the room when she realised Brand had removed some of his clothes.

She replied: "What was I supposed to do? Hide in bathroom? Walk out the room? Walk past him? I had no phone, no reception, no idea where I was. Run into the night with him following me?"

Referring to photographs she had taken of Brand, she said: "I took those photographs, he told me to take them, he was showing off, he was prancing around... I was scared... I couldn't fight him.

"I blame myself for allowing him back into my room," the woman said.

She was also challenged by the defence barrister about why she didn't report her allegation about Brand to the police in Bournemouth.

She said: "I didn't report it as I didn't want anyone to know. I didn't think anyone would believe me."

The woman told the jury that after she says she was raped by Brand she blamed herself "in that moment".

"I hate that I blamed myself, I shouldn't have to blame myself."

She also told jurors: "I regret to this day the error in judgment thinking this man would not rape me.

News.title: Severe drought declared in parts of southern England
News.content:
South East Water's operations director Douglas Whitfield said standpipes remained part of the company's drought plan but were unlikely to be needed.

Whitfield said a wet winter had been forecast but timings were not clear and the firm was making any adjustments it could to protect supplies.

Whitfield said South East Water, which supplies more than two million customers, said 92 repair crews were out across Sussex and Kent tackling leaks to minimise loss from the network.

In an email sent to customers South East Water said it was optimising water pressure across the county and had more than doubled the number of teams tackling leaks in the region, increasing from seven to 16.

It said the number of leaks in the affected area had fallen from 181 to 97 and that more than 1,300 leaks had been repaired since 1 April.

Wessex Water, which supplies customers from Wimbleball, introduced its first hosepipe ban in 50 years in August and said the restrictions would remain in place for the foreseeable future.

The water company said it had increased leak repairs, moved water into the area from more resilient sources and adjusted water pressure in some communities to conserve supplies and urged customers to continue using water carefully.

Will Willoughby, director of water supply at Wessex Water, said: "We saw record levels of demand through the network - and it sustained above the 400 million litres a day for 48 days, which is far and away the toughest year that we've seen in terms of that height in demand."

He said customer impact "should be none" but encouraged customers to continue to be mindful about water usage.

Paul Tompkins, deputy president of The National Farmers' Union (NFU) said it had been a "torrid year for farmers", where the conditions proved "very difficult" to harvest crops, provide water for livestock, and a "potential dry winter could have implications for next year's crops".
