News.title: Temperatures to drop for weekend as stormy weather could return next week
News.content:
A brighter but chillier weekend is forecast as high pressure takes hold across the UK, following a week of fluctuating temperatures.

Northerly winds on Friday will bring in colder air, with daytime temperatures falling back to around the October average of 10 to 16C (50-61F).

Some areas will see their coldest spell of the autumn so far. Clear skies and light winds overnight could lead to patchy fog and some frost away from coastal areas.

The cooler conditions follow unseasonably warm weather earlier this week when it felt more like late summer in some areas, with exceptionally mild nights.

News.title: Watch: Harry and Meghan at first joint engagement since UK return
News.content:
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have arrived in Nottingham to cheers from crowds in their first joint engagement since returning to the UK.

Harry and Meghan were pictured arriving at the Community Recording Studio charity on Thursday. They are expected to visit two more locations in the East Midlands city during the visit.

The decision to visit Nottingham bears some significance as it is the city where the couple - who are no longer working royals - made their first joint appearance after announcing their engagement in 2017.

The BBC's Royal correspondent Noor Nanji reports from Nottingham.

More on this story.

News.title: Emotional TV plea for cancer research leads to meeting with PM
News.content:
Swimmer Archie Goodburn has been successful in his efforts to improve brain cancer care for patients as the UK government announce new measures.

The Scottish athlete, who was diagnosed with three inoperable brain tumours two years ago, met Prime Minister Andy Burnham after making an emotional plea on BBC Breakfast for more investment to be put into brain cancer research.

After the meeting, Burnham announced a new national brain cancer clinical lead and promised a review of brain cancer progress and action to get patients treatment sooner.

Goodburn, 25, thanked the prime minister and said all three of his requests have been "promised to some extent" but "fleshing out" needs to be done on the details.

The prime minister described the swimmer an "inspiration to us all" and said he was "delighted" to welcome him to Downing Street.

News.title: Hilary Swank: 'There’s a lot of backlash to older women having children but not men'
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Hilary Swank has addressed the "backlash" that older pregnant women receive after announcing she is expecting another baby at the age of 52.

The Oscar-winning actress is expecting the child with her husband, businessman Philip Schneider, in December.

The couple are also parents to three-year-old twins Aya and Ohm. Swank has said women face “a lot of backlash” for having children at an older age.

Speaking on the Drew Barrymore Show, Swank said: “There’s a lot of backlash women get for having children older but not men, which is interesting.”

Barrymore replied: “I mean, it is weird. Men have babies in their, like, 80s. That is not a euphemism or a joke.

“You had babies in your 40s and people weren’t always gracious about it.”

Hilary Swank during her first pregnancy in 2023 ( AFP/Getty )

Swank replied: “There’s one story that I found really interesting and I think that I was attracted to this particular story because this one woman said, ‘How dare you, you’re too old and you won’t be old enough when your kids are older. My dad was my favourite person and he died when I was in my early 20s and it’s just devastation’.”

Swank said she related to this because her father, Stephen Swank, died in 2021.

She added: “He was one of my favourite people on Earth so I was drawn to that. “And I thought, myself, I would rather be born and have that person that was my favourite person and experience that than not at all. “So that’s how I took what she said.”

The actress announced her pregnancy on Instagram. She shared a neon stick animation of her family which showed her with a pregnant belly alongside her announcement.

She wrote on Instagram: “A lot of people have been asking what project I’m doing next, this one releases in December.”

Swank married her husband in 2018 after two years of dating.

She was married to actor Chad Lowe for nine years until 2006. She was also engaged to professional tennis player turned financial adviser Ruben Torres, but they split in 2016.

The actress has won two Academy Awards for Best Actress. The first was for Boys Don’t Cry in 2000, and the second for Million Dollar Baby in 2005.

News.title: FBI investigates mystery white powder sent to Democratic senators and election officials weeks before midterms
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The FBI has launched an investigation after suspicious letters, some containing unidentified white powder, were sent to election officials and Democratic lawmakers across the United States just weeks before the crucial midterm elections.

Federal authorities confirmed Thursday that they intercepted multiple suspicious mailings, including letters addressed to the offices of Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer and Democratic Sens. Alex Padilla of California and Chris Murphy of Connecticut.

The alarming discoveries come less than three weeks before the November 3 elections, when control of Congress will be at stake and millions of Americans are expected to cast their ballots by mail.

open image in gallery The FBI and US Postal Service's law enforcement arm said on Thursday they were investigating suspicious mailings, including some sent to state election officials ( AP )

The FBI said some of the letters contained an unknown substance, while the US Postal Inspection Service confirmed it was working to identify those responsible.

"This incident is a stark reminder of the very real dangers facing those who serve the public and who help administer our elections," Padilla said in a statement.

The House of Representatives' sergeant at arms also warned congressional staff that public officials had received letters containing suspicious white powder, according to an email Reuters obtained.

Authorities have not established whether the mailings are connected or identified the sender.

Suspicious letters intercepted across multiple states

The National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors said Wednesday that suspicious letters had been mailed to election offices across the country.

open image in gallery Postal carrier Marc Jacques delivers the mail in a neighborhood in Miami ( Getty )

Some were intercepted before reaching their intended recipients, including letters destined for election offices in Pennsylvania, Ohio and Idaho.

In Wisconsin, election officials confirmed Thursday that the state's Elections Commission had received a letter containing an unidentified powdery substance.

Officials later determined the substance was not hazardous.

"Let this be very clear: this incident will not shake us," Wisconsin's chief election official, Meagan Wolfe, declared.

Brendan Donahue, deputy chief inspector of the Postal Inspection Service, confirmed that investigators were examining the mailings and that some letters had been stopped before delivery.

open image in gallery The threats come as President Donald Trump ramps up his war on mail-in-voting prior to the midterms ( AFP/Getty )

"We are committed to protecting our nation's election officials from threatening and dangerous mail," Donahue told reporters.

"Any threat or attack on an election official is unacceptable."

A warning circulated to Senate staff indicated that some suspicious envelopes might carry postmarks inconsistent with their return addresses.

The email included an image of an envelope bearing a New York City return address marked "DSA," although authorities have not publicly established whether that label has any connection to the sender's identity or an organization.

Postal Service braces for millions of ballots

The investigation comes as the Postal Service prepares for another election in which mail-in voting could play a significant role.

Postmaster General David Steiner insisted Thursday that the agency was "absolutely ready" to process millions of ballots ahead of Election Day.

open image in gallery Postmaster General David Steiner insisted Thursday that the agency was "absolutely ready" to process millions of ballots ahead of Election Day ( AP )

The Postal Service has announced what it describes as "extraordinary measures" for the 2026 midterms, including extended opening hours at selected locations, expedited ballot handling, additional deliveries and special collection arrangements.

The preparations follow a legal setback for President Donald Trump's efforts to tighten restrictions on voting by mail.

On September 14, the Supreme Court declined to allow the Postal Service to enforce a new rule affecting mail ballots.

The measure followed a March executive order from Trump seeking tighter controls over postal voting.

Under the blocked rule, states would have been required to provide the Postal Service with lists of voters receiving mail ballots and use approved envelopes carrying unique barcodes.

The agency could then have refused to process ballots that failed to comply with those requirements or were linked to voters absent from the supplied lists.

The Postal Service said it would not enforce the rule following the court's order.

Election security concerns mount ahead of November vote

Mail voting remains a major feature of American elections.

During the 2024 presidential contest, the Postal Service handled approximately 99.2 million ballots traveling to and from voters.

open image in gallery During the 2024 presidential contest, the Postal Service handled approximately 99.2 million ballots traveling to and from voters ( AFP/Getty )

Around 30 percent of votes were cast by mail that year, compared with 46 percent during the pandemic-era election in 2020.

Surveys have consistently found that Democratic voters are more likely than Republicans to vote by mail, making restrictions on the practice a particularly contentious political issue.

Trump and his Republican allies are fighting to retain control of Congress in November, with the results expected to shape the remainder of his second term.

The suspicious mailings have introduced another security concern for election administrators already preparing to oversee voting in a politically charged environment.

Federal investigators have not disclosed the origin of the letters, whether they were intended to intimidate recipients or whether any of the unidentified substances posed a genuine health threat.

For now, officials insist that neither the investigation nor the threatening nature of the mailings will disrupt election preparations.

News.title: Nick Clegg’s wife says Gibraltar is Spanish, not British
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Gibraltar is Spanish, not British, the wife of former deputy prime minister Sir Nick Clegg has said.

Miriam González Durántez made the remarks while she was promoting Democracia 21, the party she has started ahead of Spain’s upcoming general election.

Speaking to Spanish current affairs programme En boca de todos, Ms González Durántez was asked whether Gibraltar was Spanish. She replied: “Yes, of course”.

Asked whether her husband agrees with her, she said: "We try not to talk about Gibraltar. He will defend his position and I defend mine.”

She added: "Women don’t think the same as their husbands; we have minds of our own”.

open image in gallery ‘Women don’t think the same as their husbands’, Ms González Durántez said ( Getty )

Ms González Durántez started her new party as an attempt to offer an alternative to Spain’s current system which is dominated by two political parties – the governing Socialists and the conservative People’s Party.

Gibraltar was ceded to Britain in 1713, but Spain has maintained its sovereignty claim ever since.

The contested British Overseas Territory of 38,000 people is perched at the southern tip of the Iberian Peninsula, located just miles from Morocco at a point where the Atlantic Ocean meets the Mediterranean Sea.

Over the summer, a physical border between Gibraltar and Spain was removed following Britain’s exit from the EU, making life easier for the thousands who travel between the two every day.

The move allows a new freedom of movement under a historic European Union-UK treaty that came after years of post-Brexit wrangling. The UK’s Foreign Office minister Stephen Doughty said that the agreement secured Gibraltar’s long-term economic future and interests.

open image in gallery The physical border between Spain and Gibraltar was removed earlier this year ( AFP/Getty )

In Britain’s 2016 Brexit referendum, 96 per cent of voters in Gibraltar supported remaining in the EU. But when Britain finally left the bloc in 2020, the relationship between Gibraltar and the EU had been left unresolved.

Previous talks on a deal to ensure people and goods could keep flowing across the border had made halting progress. In 2025, the EU and UK announced an agreement on those issues, with the two sides and Gibraltar’s government signing a treaty on Tuesday that eases border crossings.

Without a deal, Gibraltar could have a faced a hard land border with full passport checks, posing economic risks for the territory deeply dependent on some 15,000 Spaniards – almost half of Gibraltar’s workforce – who cross the frontier every day for work.

Travelers to Gibraltar from countries outside the Schengen area will have to contend with the EU Entry-Exit System, or EES, that was rolled out in Europe in April and replaced passport stamps with biometric data collected through photographs and digital fingerprints.

News.title: What is ‘dark tourism’? Why tourists visit destinations with tragic histories
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Almost two million people visited the Auschwitz museum on the former concentration camp site in Poland last year. The United States island where the notorious Alcatraz prison once operated welcomes around 1.2 million visitors annually. Just under 15 million people took a trip to Hiroshima throughout 2025, the 80th anniversary of the atomic bombing that devastated the city.

It is clear that travelling to places associated with death and tragedy, referred to as “dark tourism”, has widespread popularity. But the reasons behind parting with money to confront uncomfortable topics on holiday still mystify many.

From monuments to museums, areas where atrocities took place and the remains of natural disasters, tourists are drawn to sites that now serve as places of remembrance of lives lost and also as a reminder of what the world is capable of.

Everyone has their motives for visiting these heart-rending sites: for some, it’s confronting a part of their past or family history, and for others, it’s the immense intrigue and motivation to learn the history of an event, no matter how heinous.

Whether it’s looking upon a pile of personal belongings left behind by those killed at Auschwitz or reading the names of people who lost their lives at the 9/11 memorial, these sites remain important to those who have a personal connection to the tragedies and offer the chance for others to partake in keeping memories of those affected alive.

What is dark tourism?

The basic definition of dark tourism is visiting a place that is associated with a tragic event in history, usually surrounded by death and suffering.

Dr Philip Stone, who founded the Institute of Dark Tourism Research at the University of Central Lancashire in 2012, told The Independent that dark tourism chiefly portrays and commemorates “our noteworthy dead within visitor economies, through museums and exhibitions, monuments and sites, as well as visitor attractions”.

“It represents tragedies or calamities for the contemporary tourist experience and the ‘difficult heritage’ that often entails,” he said. “Dark tourism is bound up in contested memory, memorialisation, and the visitor experience.”

“The dead in dark tourism can warn us of our own fights, follies, or misfortunes,” he added.

Some people are not totally on board with dark tourism. This might be due to concerns about tragic sites becoming commercialised or because it’s not how certain countries want to represent themselves in the tourism sector.

Dr Stone explained that dark tourism is “full of managerial dilemmas” and “political quandaries” as visiting places with a dark past can be “ethically laden”.



What isn’t dark tourism?

Why humans are drawn to dark tourism has been studied by academics extensively. At the Institute of Dark Tourism Research, they examine the multi-dimensional aspects of dark tourism in society and culture, and the business of managing such provocative visitor sites, museums, and attractions.

“The line between commemorating and commercialising the dead is becoming increasingly blurred,” said Dr Stone. “Whilst we never encounter the corpse in dark tourism, we encounter touristified narratives of the demise and the significant dead can mediate our own sense of mortality.

“Dark tourism can entail a kind of secular pilgrimage where journeys in the footsteps of the dead are made, for instance at battlefields or at conflict sites.

“Ironically, in a world that seems to spin ever faster, dark tourism is focused on death and the dead, but it perhaps tells us more about life and living.”

The creator of the online guide dark-tourism.com says that the practice is a “respectful and enlightened” engagement in history and its dark sides, in a way that educates people without sensationalising events of the past.

The website adds that there are several misconceptions about dark tourism, such as that it includes visiting impoverished areas, known as “slum tourism”, visiting current war zones (”war tourism”) or taking part in extreme activities that could put people in danger, such as exploring caves (“danger tourism”).

Dark tourism also does not promote tourists being disrespectful at historical sites, the website says, such as what has been seen over the years at Auschwitz with people taking selfies or posing for photos.

Many monuments, museums and places of interest aim to be places of remembrance where people can come to terms with history, while also serving as stark reminders.

Dr Duncan Light, a principal academic in tourism management at Bournemouth University who has written review papers on dark tourism research, told The Independent that there are many other misconceptions about dark tourism.

“One of the big ones is that the people who visit places of death and suffering have a sick and morbid fascination with death,” he said. “However, there’s been a lot of research into why tourists go to places of death, and it’s found virtually no evidence of such motivations.

“Instead, the main reasons why people say they visit places of death and suffering are to do with learning about the past; remembrance of tragic events, connecting with tragic events by seeing for themselves where it happened, paying respect to victims of suffering, visiting places associated with their family’s history and visiting places that are significant for national identity.

“None of these motives are particularly dark,” Dr Light added.



Dark tourism places of interest

1. Auschwitz-Birkenau

Poland

open image in gallery Auschwitz-Birkenau museum was opened in 1947, less than two years after the Second World War ended ( Getty )

One of the largest Nazi concentration camps, Auschwitz was established in 1940 and built more than 40 sub-camps that exploited prisoners as slave labourers. In less than five years, at least 1.1 million people were murdered at the camp; no other camp or extermination centre under the Nazis saw the level of mass murder of Jews as Auschwitz did during the Second World War. Today, the site is a museum, where the original camp blocks and barracks stand, and tens of thousands of objects have been preserved. Personal possessions such as shoes, suitcases, camp garments and works of art made by prisoners are on display, as well as objects that bear testimony to the living conditions within the camps. The memorial and museum are found in Oświęcim, Poland and are open almost every day of the year. Almost two million people visited the museum in 2025, a seven per cent increase on the previous year.

2. Chernobyl

Ukraine

open image in gallery Chernobyl tours have not been operating since the start of the Ukraine-Russia war ( Getty/iStock )

The Chernobyl nuclear power disaster in 1986 forced around 350,000 people to eventually evacuate and left 28 dead from acute radiation syndrome, along with two who died on the night of the explosion – though some say it is likely more people died. The explosion and fires released at least five per cent of the radioactive reactor core into the environment. As a result of the Ukraine-Russia war, tours of the exclusion zone are currently not running, but the site has been frequently visited by many dark tourist enthusiasts in the past. The UK Foreign Office currently advises against all travel to parts of Ukraine.

3. National 9/11 Memorial & Museum

New York, USA

open image in gallery The memorial at 9/11 is dedicated to the thousands killed in 2001 ( Getty )

Located at the World Trade Center in New York City, often referred to as ground zero, the 9/11 Memorial & Museum was created to tell the story of the 9/11 terror attacks in 2001 and the 1993 World Trade Center bombing. On the site where the twin towers once stood, the museum has a collection of artefacts, media and narratives that tell personal stories and give visitors the opportunity to learn about the history of the attacks and the aftermath. Also at the site is a memorial to the 2,977 people killed on 9/11, as well as the six people killed in the 1993 bombing, with the names of those who died inscribed on bronze parapets. The memorial is open daily, while the museum is open Wednesday to Monday. Its newest exhibition, which opened this year in commemoration of the 25th anniversary of 9/11, examines the countless acts of service that followed the tragedy.



4. War Remnants Museum

Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam

open image in gallery From photographs to artefacts, the War Remnants Museum tells the story of the Vietnam war ( Getty )

The War Remnants Museum has nine permanent exhibitions, each displaying photos, documents and artefacts relating to the Vietnam war and the first Indochina war. The exhibitions tell the story of the atrocities, politics and history through the eyes of photojournalists, as well as with artefacts such as torture devices from prisons and information from people around the world who stood in solidarity with the Vietnamese during the war. Two exhibitions are dedicated to Agent Orange, a chemical herbicide used by the US military during the war that contaminated 2.6 million hectares of land and caused serious health impacts on millions of Vietnamese and future generations. The museum is regarded as one of Ho Chi Minh City’s most prominent cultural sites and is open every day.

5. Pompeii

Italy

open image in gallery Despite being buried thousands of years ago, Pompeii is considered by some to be a dark tourist site ( Getty/iStock )

While this Unesco World Heritage site does not deliver the same contemporary history as other dark tourism destinations, the archaeological site of Pompeii still attracts many visitors to bear witness to the area that was engulfed by Vesuvius’s eruption in 79AD. The eruption of the volcano buried two Roman towns, Pompeii and Herculaneum, being buried by volcanic ash along with thousands of residents. The excavations can be visited from Naples, Italy and the site is open year-round. Due to record numbers of visitors causing issues in 2024, Pompeii now has a daily limit of 20,000 admissions year-round.

6. Crumlin Road Gaol

Belfast, Northern Ireland

open image in gallery Tours around the former prison shine a light on its role during the Troubles ( Getty/iStock )

While Crumlin Road Gaol offers experiences more suited to visitors interested in ghost-hunting and the supernatural, the former Northern Irish prison also draws dark tourists who want to learn about the over 150 years of justice history, such as the detention of both republicans and loyalists during the Troubles and the imprisonment of suffragettes. The prison was open between 1845 and 1996, and during this time 17 people were executed, numerous escapes were undertaken, and many infamous inmates were detained. A self-guided tour will take visitors through an underground tunnel that once connected the gaol to the Crumlin Road Courthouse, view all the wings from the circle, and pay a visit to the condemned man’s cell, before seeing the execution cell where the majority of death sentences were carried out. Crumlin Road Gaol is open seven days a week.

7. Choeung Ek Killing Fields

Cambodia

open image in gallery Choeung Ek Genocidal Center is one of several places dedicated to the memory of those who lost their lives during the Khmer Rouge regime ( Getty )

The Choeung Ek Genocidal Center sits on the former mass execution site used by the Khmer Rouge regime to kill the vast majority of 18,000 prisoners at S-21, a notorious interrogation centre, and is one of the well-known Killing Fields. The brutal regime, whose supposed goal was to make Cambodia into an agrarian utopia, claimed the lives of around two million people through murder, starvation and disease. At Choeung Ek, a large Buddhist stupa with glass fronting shows stacks of skulls of more than 5,000 victims whose remains were found in the surrounding graves. The Tuol Sleng Genocide Museum, also in Phnom Penh, at the site of the former S-21 interrogation site and detention centre, has exhibitions giving visitors a chance to learn about the history, living conditions and lasting impact of the Khmer Rouge regime. The museum is open every day.

8. Kigali Genocide Memorial

Rwanda

open image in gallery The Kigali Genocide Memorial is dedicated to the memory of the Rwandan genocide ( Getty )

The Kigali Genocide Memorial was opened as a place of remembrance, dedicated to the victims of the genocide in Rwanda in 1994 that saw some 800,000 killed. The Rwandan genocide happened in just 100 days, led by Hutu militias who targeted the Tutsi minority community and some moderate Hutus. The memorial sits next to mass graves, the final resting place of 250,000 people killed, and includes three permanent exhibitions, the largest of which documents the genocide. The museum can be visited through a guided tour that is often led by survivors or an audio guide. The memorial is open seven days a week and no visitors under the age of 12 are permitted to visit.

9. Hiroshima

Japan

open image in gallery Hiroshima has a whole area of its city dedicated to the remembrance of those killed in the explosion ( AFP via Getty )

At 8.15am on 6 August 1945, the Japanese city of Hiroshima was devastated by an atomic bomb, the first to be used as a weapon of war. Around five square miles of the city were destroyed, and about 140,000 people were killed by the explosion or the effects of burns and radiation. There are several sites around the city where visitors go to remember the victims or learn more about the history. The Hiroshima Peace Memorial, commonly known as the Atomic Bomb Dome, is the only structure left standing in the area where the bomb exploded and has been preserved by the city. Just across the river is the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park, home to an arched cenotaph that contains registries of the names of all known victims and the Atomic Bomb Memorial Mound, which is placed in the ashes of thousands of unclaimed or unidentified victims. At the other end of the park is the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum, which houses exhibitions of personal belongings left behind by victims, testimonies from survivors and photographs from the time. The museum is open every day for most of the year.

10. Alcatraz Island

United States

open image in gallery Visitors can reach Alcatraz, which is now a state park, by ferry ( Getty Images/iStockphoto )

Alcatraz, a small island just off the coast of San Francisco, was once home to one of the most well-known maximum-security federal prisons. It also served as a military fortification, military prison and was also occupied for 19 months by a Native American community. Today, the island is a state park accessible by an Alcatraz City Cruise ferry, which provides visitors with an audio tour of the main three-story Cellhouse. Several high-profile criminals were locked up on the island, including Al Capone, George "Machine-Gun" Kelly, Alvin Karpis (the first "Public Enemy #1"), and Arthur "Doc" Barker. It also once housed Robert Stroud, known as the "Birdman of Alcatraz", who spent 54 years of his life behind bars. Most of the prisoners incarcerated at Alcatraz were sent there after refusing to conform to the rules at other penitentiaries, were considered violent and dangerous, or were believed to be escape risks.

News.title: England driven by memory of semi-final loss ahead of Tonga World Cup rematch
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

England captain George Williams is convinced his squad have learned the lessons of their heartbreaking 2022 semi-final defeat as they prepare for a potentially crucial opening game of the Rugby League World Cup against Tonga in Perth on Saturday.

Williams was part of the side that were stunned by a sudden-death 27-26 loss to Samoa at the Emirates Stadium and acknowledged that in a career sprinkled with Grand Final glory but also his fair share of disappointments, that was the toughest to take.

“The one in the last World Cup was probably the most difficult loss of my career to date,” admitted Williams. “It does sit there and you can’t hide away from what happened, but it can give you the drive and motivation and there’s still players in the group who felt that.”

Williams arrived in Perth fresh from another knock-back after failing to sign off from his Warrington career by leading the club to an elusive Grand Final win. The 31-year-old will stay in Australia with NRL side Dolphins following the conclusion of the World Cup.

open image in gallery George Williams is keen to erase the pain of Warrington’s recent Grand Final defeat (Cody Froggatt/PA) ( PA Archive )

He added: “There was a lot riding on that game and it was not the way I wanted go out out. But sometimes that happens in life and sport and you have to crack on. I didn’t have much time to dwell on it, but now there is a determination to get back to winning ways.”

Williams will partner Wigan’s Harry Smith in the halves in a starting 13 that features eight players currently contracted to clubs in Australia’s NRL. Three more Wigan players – Junior Nsemba, newly-crowned Man of Steel Brad O’Neill and debutant Zach Eckersley – complete the line-up.

England beat Tonga in all three of their 2023 Test matches but the South Seas side is crammed with NRL talent and they arguably start as favourites for a match which, due to the competition’s complicated cross-group format, could have a real impact on both sides’ hopes of booking a semi-final place.

The strength of the southern hemisphere sides has already been emphasised by Australia’s classic opening win against New Zealand and Samoa’s 14-try rout of a France team filled with Super League players in Parramatta on Friday.

“We’ll probably go into the match as underdogs,” admitted Williams, whose side will be led by new head coach Brian McDermott for the first time. “Tonga are a stacked team and have been for a number of years now. We will have to bring our best game tomorrow night against a great team.”

open image in gallery England beat Tonga in three back-to-back Tests in 2023 (Martin Rickett/PA) ( PA Archive )

England follow their opener against Tonga with subsequent games against France and Papua New Guinea. They must secure a top-two place in a pool that includes both the Tongans and Samoans in order to secure their passage straight into the semi-finals.

Williams added: “It’s a mad set-up, I don’t know how they’ve worked it out with no quarter-finals, but we’ve just got to win our games and do our job and it starts tomorrow.

“I know everyone will say the same thing, but I do think this group is hungry. I’m not going to tell you all the tricks, but it’s been different and enjoyable. The group has bought into what Brian wants to do, and hopefully you’ll see that on Saturday.”

England’s women also begin their campaign on Saturday against World Cup debutants Wales in a match which will immediately precede the men’s match in Perth.

News.title: The way our time works has just changed forever
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The way our clocks work is set to change after an international timekeeping body voted to ditch “leap seconds”.

The vote by the International Bureau of Weights and Measures on Thursday means that keep atomic time will no longer be kept strictly in line with astronomical time.

Leap seconds have been implemented 27 times since 1972 to keep our clocks in sync with Earth’s position to the Sun.

The practice first became problematic with the emergence of the World Wide Web and satellite communications, with Amazon, Google, Meta and other tech giants campaigning to have the “devastating” time quirk scrapped.

Scientists claim that replacing leap seconds with a leap hour is less disruptive and would rarely need to be used.

open image in gallery The leap second has been used 27 times since its introduction 50 years ago ( Meta )

The world’s international time system, known as Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), is maintained by ultra-precise atomic clocks, such as those at the National Physical Laboratory in the UK.

Much of today’s infrastructure and technologies, such as smartphones and financial markets, rely on this dependable and consistent way of measuring time.

Applying leap seconds to this system is tricky to implement and can cause significant disruption to telecommunications, global navigation systems and grid synchronisation.

Rather than implementing a leap second every couple of years or so, scientists say that shifting to a leap hour would require an update once every thousand years.

“The decision taken today reduces the risk to systems that depend on precise and continuous time synchronisation, including national infrastructure that we rely on daily,” said Setnam Shemar, principal scientist at the National Physical Laboratory.

“Leap seconds can be difficult to implement reliably, and if not applied correctly they can cause differences in time across networks, potentially leading to the failure of systems such as mobile phone networks or electricity grids.”

open image in gallery Clocks of the art installation 'Zeitfeld' (time field) by German artist Klaus Rinke are seen in Duesseldorf, western Germany, on 28 March, 2024 ( AFP/Getty )

In recent years, the unusual possibility of a negative leap second has arisen due to an acceleration in the Earth’s rotation.

It would be the first time a negative leap second has ever been implemented, which could further increase the risk of disruption.

The vote means that from 20 May 2027, a difference of up to 1 hour will be allowed between UTC and astronomical time (UT1) before intervention is needed.

“The relationship between UTC and UT1 is important for some applications, such as astronomy and celestial navigation,” Dr Shemar said.

“The decision would not sever that link: UT1 will continue to be monitored and its difference from UTC will continue to be disseminated through established international services.”

News.title: ‘Outrageous’ backroom deals put progress fighting AIDS at risk, campaigners warn
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Hard-won progress against HIV and Aids globally could be undone if the UK withdraws its full support for a flagship UN programme, activists have warned.

UNAIDS, which coordinates worldwide efforts to end Aids as a public health threat by 2030, risks being “sunset” before achieving its goal because of “outrageous” backroom dealings by wealthy donors, campaigners claim.

UNAIDS is in the middle of a major transformation and has shed more than half of its staff since 2025 in response to global aid cuts, mainly from the US. Its board will meet later this month to decide how the organisation should work in the future, including its level of presence in countries worldwide, how big a budget it needs, and how many staff should remain in a central coordinating hub.

A split has emerged between donors like the UK who want a low budget organisation with limited presence on the ground in countries, and civil society groups and governments from countries most affected by HIV. The latter group say UNAIDS is still needed on the ground in the immediate future, to support them as they navigate smaller budgets after US aid withdrawals amid a complicated geopolitical climate.

The UK provided $5.5 million (£4.2m) to UNAIDS in 2026. For 2027 it plans only £1m, The Independent understands. The government has said it will reduce aid spending from 0.5 per cent of Gross National Income (GNI) to 0.3 per cent over the next few years, in order to fund increased defence spending. The Independent has called on the UK to protect spending on efforts to stop the AIDS epidemic.

Asia Russell, executive director of Health GAP, said: “The time to end UNAIDS is once we have defeated this pandemic. Anything else is absurd. And parallel work by powerful donors in backrooms to try to sweep aside legitimate concerns regarding transitioning UNAIDS is outrageous.”

In 2025, around 41 million people globally were living with HIV, and 1.2 million people newly acquired the virus. Around 570,000 people died from Aids-related illnesses.It comes as funding for HIV responses in low- and middle-income countries fell by $2.1 billion (£1.6bn) last year after Donald Trump’s administration made substantial cuts to global health funding.

Donor funds decreased by a quarter compared to the previous year, recent reports from KFF and the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS show. It marks the lowest funding level since 2007, with total disbursements dropping to from $8.3 billion in 2024 to $6.2bn in 2025.

Mike Podmore, CEO of UK advocacy network STOPAIDS, said: “The UK’s support is fundamental to the future of UNAIDS and the direction of the global HIV response.

“If donor decisions are driven by aid cuts rather than by listening to and standing side by side with the countries and communities most affected, we risk UNAIDS closing prematurely and hard-won progress being undone.

“We urge the UK to honour its legacy as an HIV leader: provide ongoing funding to UNAIDS; support it to keep a country presence defending human rights and gender equality; and protect community leadership in its governance.”

Initial proposals by UN secretary general António Guterres to sunset UNAIDS by the end of 2026 as part of wider UN reforms were scrapped, but a working group has been meeting for months to establish a transition plan for the organisation.

Its final document proposes a smaller UNAIDS central hub that would focus on advocacy, data and governance, with some work currently carried out by UNAIDS instead done by other organisations such as the World Health Organisation.

The group sets out three proposals for annual ongoing budgets of between $35m and $90m. The current core budget is $63m. However, during talks, some donors suggested a lower annual budget of $25m to $35m.

The open letter to the UNAIDS Programme Coordinating Board (PCB), signed by more than 300 civil society groups, says the global HIV response is “at a critical moment”, and that the board’s decisions “will have a profound impact on our lives and on our shared goal of ending Aids as a public health threat by 2030”.

It adds: “We are concerned that discussions taking place outside or in parallel to the formal process could lead to PCB decisions that amount to a gradual sunsetting of UNAIDS without that outcome ever being agreed.”

Some options under consideration, including a $30m budget, 34-person staff and 12-month transition timeline are “obviously inadequate”, the letter says. It also urges the PCB to protect UNAIDS’ presence in countries around the world, and “resist unrealistic thinking” about other parts of the UN taking on work, saying they are unlikely to prioritise HIV when “faced with their own shrinking budgets and political threats”.

A UNAIDS spokeswoman said: “For more than 40 years, progress against Aids has come when countries stood together and acted in solidarity with the people and communities most affected by HIV. That principle matters just as much today.”

She said the working group’s conclusion was clear that “it is much too soon to contemplate sunsetting UNAIDS [...] the next steps should be shaped by what countries and communities say they need, guided by local realities and readiness, and focused on protecting hard-won gains for people living with and affected by HIV.”

A spokesperson for the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) said: "The UK priority remains securing an effective, efficient, and sustainable future for UNAIDS, and that is why we have committed a further £1m on top of our existing £4m provision to support their reform and transition efforts."

News.title: Israel stops commercial goods from entering Gaza
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Israel said that commercial goods will no longer enter the Gaza Strip, cutting off a key source of food and shelter supply for the war-torn territory as hungry Palestinians face the approach of winter.

COGAT, the Israeli military body that oversees humanitarian affairs in Gaza, announced the suspension of commercial goods in a Wednesday statement. It was not clear whether they made the decision. COGAT said it was relaying a statement from Gaza merchants, a claim Palestinians refuted.

The move stands to immediately reduce Gaza's supplies, because the closed-off territory is completely reliant on whatever goods Israel allows in through border crossings. The suspension also raised fears about affordability, with humanitarian workers saying a combination of aid and a robust commercial market is needed to keep prices under control.

“The humanitarian sector on its own cannot meet the needs of all the people,” said Shaina Low, a spokesperson for the Norwegian Refugee Council, an aid group. “The markets need to be functioning.”

The world’s leading authority on food insecurity reported earlier this year that conditions in Gaza had improved since famine was declared in the territory in August 2025, but were still at crisis levels. Most families in the war-battered enclave weren’t getting nearly enough to eat, said the report, adding that “even small disruptions to humanitarian access could rapidly reverse recent gains.”

In announcing the measure, COGAT claimed to be communicating a decision made by local merchants in Gaza who had grown tired of Hamas taxing their trucks and threatening them. Israel has long accused the militant group of levying fees on imports to fund its operations.

But the head of Gaza’s private truckers union, Nahed Sheheiber, disputed that, saying Israel had made the decision.

open image in gallery Palestinians walk among tents at a tent camp for displaced people in Gaza City, Friday, Oct. 16, 2026. (AP Photo/Abdel Kareem Hana) ( Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved. )

“The merchants are not the ones who stopped the shipments," he said. “The Israeli coordinator is claiming that Gaza’s merchants are responsible, but the truth is that the Israelis are the ones who imposed the restrictions.”

Following COGAT's announcement, Shehaiber's union met with Gaza's Ministry of Economy to express concern and say Israel was citing fees levied by the ministry as a pretext to cut off commercial goods.

The ministry had been asking merchants to pay 10,000 shekels (about $3,226) per truck entering Gaza, Shehaiber said. At the meeting, ministry Undersecretary Khaled Al-Raqab told the union that the amount was not a tax, but rather a donation sought by the ministry to help pay civil servants in the strip.

It was not clear from the COGAT announcement if aid agencies would be allowed to increase shipments into Gaza to compensate for the loss in commercial goods.

The agency claimed that Gaza's population — of roughly 2 million people — required approximately 250 truckloads of goods each day. That's far below the minimum of 600 trucks a day stipulated by a ceasefire brokered by the U.S. a year ago.

The war started when Hamas-led militants killed some 1,200 people on Oct. 7, 2023, and took 251 hostages. Israel responded with a massive bombardment and a ground invasion that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.

That includes over 1,400 Palestinians killed since the ceasefire took effect, the ministry says. Sporadic attacks have killed five Israeli soldiers in Gaza in the same period.

The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, maintains detailed records and is seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It does not distinguish between civilians and militants in its toll but says women and children make up around half the dead.

News.title: Pierre Sage’s Lyon return ends in disappointment for Crystal Palace
News.content:
Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of Thursday night’s European football with Crystal Palace, Sunderland and Bournemouth in Europa League action, and Brighton hosting Kauno Zalgiris in the Uefa Conference League.

Palace manager Pierre Sage managed Lyon between November 2023 and January 2025, and another sub-plot is American businessman John Textor’s involvement with the French club. The former Palace shareholder was the reason the club missed out on Europa League participation last season because Lyon were in the same competition and thus Palace were considered in breach of multi-club ownership rules. Textor sold his stake in Palace, but despite the club’s best efforts they had to settle for the Conference League, a competition they subsequently won.

Palace could have been three or four down against Nottingham Forest at the weekend but fought back for a much-needed Premier League victory. They made a winning start in Europe, beating Lech Poznan 4-0 at Selhurst Park in their opening Europa League game.

Bournemouth and Sunderland also made winning starts, despite both teams’ poor form domestically. Sunderland travel to Portuguese side Torreense, while Sturm Graz are the opposition for Bournemouth’s first ever European game at the Vitality Stadium (or Dean Court if you prefer). Bournemouth continue to be without Justin Kluivert, Eli Junior Kroupi and Alex Scott because of injury.

Brighton are favourites to win the Conference League and play their first game in the competition against Lithuanian club Kauno Zalgiris. Lifting the trophy in Istanbul at the end of the season would assure Brighton of a place in next season’s Europa League, though given their Premier League form and Manchester City’s predicament, Champions League qualification could be a realistic aspiration. Brighton won with 10 men at Sunderland on Saturday, and were successful in their appeal against Pascal Struijk’s red card.

Full team news on the way shortly.

News.title: Economy slows before Healey’s maiden Budget
News.content:
The Chancellor said banks are too often seen as “distant financial institutions”, in a sign he will not raise taxes on the industry in the Budget.

John Healey has faced pressure to impose a windfall tax on bank profits to help rebuild an expected decline in his wiggle room in the public finances.

John Healey said: “My observations on the banks are just that people too often see them as a big distant financial institutions when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future prospects.

“That said, you know I’ve got decisions to take in the Budget, and I will. I’ll set those out in two weeks’ time.

“And my special responsibility as Chancellor is to protect the resilience of the British economy for the future. That the resilience that the IMF has reported on this week by upgrading our growth figures in the UK this week, that the welcome monthly growth figures published this morning reinforce, and importantly, alongside that, the IMF reports said that Britain stands out for our deficit reduction plans, and will have his forecast actually a reflection not just on forecast plans but performance over the last couple of years. You know, a consolidation plan in place and underway.

“I’ve said from day one and week one, and I’ve had Andy Burnham in lockstep alongside me, I will meet those fiscal rules in full.

“That will be part of the Budget that I set out in two weeks’ time, and I think the IMF report reinforces that that is not just a not just a reinforcing the strength of Britain’s position, but something that they say they want to see other countries doing as well.”

News.title: Ukrainian Vampire drones drop food on town besieged by Russian army
News.content:
On Ukraine’s front lines, drones are the deadliest weapons in Kyiv’s arsenal, hunting Russian soldiers one by one with chilling precision.

But across the Dnipro River, the same machines have been given a very different mission: keeping trapped civilians from dying of starvation.

Since March, Ukrainian drones have been flying food and medicine into occupied Oleshky, on the river’s left bank, where residents are surviving on grass and weeds.

The town is less than three miles from Kherson, a city battered by Russian drones and shelling.

Since December, Oleshky has been under an effective blockade. Its roads are mined and shops have closed, with no food arriving by road since late May. Humanitarian agencies are blocked from entering, and the health system has all but collapsed.

Only around 2,000 of its 24,000 pre-war residents remain. For them, the drones are now their only lifeline.

“With the onset of winter, the situation is only getting worse,” said Elvina Osmanova of the Kherson regional military administration. “Food supplies are running out. People are facing a life-threatening choice: risk their lives trying to find food outside the city or remain without food.”

News.title: Man City dismantled by PSG in breathless Champions League battle
News.content:
When Manchester City play like this what a loss their football will be to the Premier League – and the Champions League – if they are heavily sanctioned later this season.

In what turned out to be a match for the ages, a night of brilliant, unbridled attack, we were treated to the ultimate game of two halves as the back-to-back European champions Paris St-Germain took City apart for 45 minutes. And then were left holding on.

City will hope this is a sign of what is to come in their Premier League fight. But with a different result. After suffering a resounding defeat at the hands of the Premier League’s independent commission, with 114 of the 115 charges against them proven, they maintain their innocence and are mounting an appeal.

Could they make a comeback? It would be incredible and highly improbable if they did so but, out on the pitch, and 3-0 down after a first half in which they were in danger of being humiliated by PSG, they created enough opportunities to save themselves.

The data backed that. City’s expected goals (xG) was 2.57 while PSG’s was 1.83. City had 27 shots to 15 and had more possession and more passes. Enzo Maresca made a triple substitution to devastating effect, especially with the introduction of new signings Ayyoub Bouaddi and Iliman Ndiaye.

In the end they clawed back two goals, both scored by Erling Haaland, who now has 61 in 60 games in this competition – seventh outright in the all-time list, before Ruud van Nistelrooy. And 37 of those for City, overtaking Sergio Agüero’s club record.

News.title: Barcola starts to justify £123m price tag with hat-trick as Liverpool hit LASK for six
News.content:
Of the five Premier League teams in the Champions League this season, Liverpool have the friendliest league-phase fixtures and they can secure back-to-back wins against Austrian side LASK in this evening’s early kick off.

Having already vanquished one of their pot one opponents by beating Atletico Madrid at Anfield, Andoni Iraola’s team really should be targeting one of the top spots.

They travel to Linz without some key players, though. Alexander Isak, Cody Gakpo and Dominik Szoboszlai missed the defeat by Manchester City and remain sidelined, while Hugo Ekitike is a long-term absentee.

There were positive aspects to Liverpool’s performance against City, but they collapsed like a deck of cards after Ryan Gravenberch’s harsh second yellow card.

Tonight’s game is one they should dominate, and it is a presentable opportunity for Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola to kick-start their seasons and respond to the recent criticism of their performances. Iraola hopes to have a stronger squad to choose from at the weekend, when Liverpool face a stringent test at Brentford. This is the second of nine matches in 28 days for Liverpool.

“You don’t have a lot of time to train,” said Iraola. “You try to prepare the games now a lot of times just with the videos and the tactics boards, just a little bit outside. You have to prioritise the freshness of the players.

“Especially now we are playing four games in 10 days, it’s keeping all the legs, all the energy in the games.

LASK are currently third in the Austrian league, but booked their place in this season’s Champions League proper with a remarkable comeback from 4-0 down on aggregate against Celtic.

They have injury problems of their own to contend with George Bello and Moses Usor limping off in the weekend’s defeat by league leaders Rapid Wien and Ramiz Harakate tearing his anterior cruciate ligament in July.

They do play on a grass pitch at the Raiffeisen Arena though Kasper Schmeichel, the former Celtic goalkeeper who was working as a TV pundit for the game, was critical of the playing surface.

Full team news on the way shortly.

News.title: Second Ebola case confirmed in Kenya
News.content:
Kenya has recorded its second-ever case of Ebola after a relative of a patient who died last week tested positive for the virus, officials have said.

A 39-year-old man fell ill on Tuesday and has since been confirmed to be infected with Ebola, according to Kenyan health authorities.

The patient, who is now isolated, is a family member of Kenya’s first-ever Ebola case, who died in a hospital in Nairobi last Monday.

The index case, a 40-year old businessman, had travelled to Kenya from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), the epicentre of the deadly outbreak of the rare Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, which has so far killed more than 4,300 people.

Kenyan authorities have identified 128 of his contacts and have successfully tracked down 113 of them, who are having their temperatures checked daily for a period of three weeks, the country’s Director-General for Health, Dr Patrick Amoth, said in a statement.

“There is no evidence of spread in the wider community,” the statement, issued on Wednesday, added.

However, questions remain over whether more cases will crop up in the coming weeks.

News.title: I tried Apple’s new smart home hub – the brand faithful will love it
News.content:
HomeView can control smart lights, heating, security cameras and video doorbells via touch or voice, but devices must support Matter – the cross-brand smart home standard. That means you aren’t confined to Apple-approved gadgets, but you are still limited – Ring video doorbells, for example, aren’t Matter-compatible, so they won’t work with HomeView, which could be a deal-breaker for even the biggest Apple fan.

But for anyone put off by the complexity of setting up a smart home, Apple is trying to simplify things. It has partnered with LG on Home Collection – a range of devices, including security cameras and a video doorbell – that connect with a single tap, just as AirPods do with an iPhone. They won’t be available until later in the year, but they could mark a major step towards making smart home set-up less complicated.

My early verdict

HomeView is built for the Apple faithful: set-up requires an iPhone or iPad, personalised AI features need a recent Apple Intelligence-capable iPhone, and some apps work only when your phone is nearby. In a household split between iPhone and Android, Android users will get a much thinner experience, and Apple’s own services come first at every turn.

Still, HomeView is the most polished smart display I have seen. Face recognition makes it both a great shared and personalised device; the sound quality is excellent; and Siri AI is finally worth talking to, especially when it can draw on your personal context. I’ll need to live with it for a few weeks before giving a final verdict, but so far it’s a beautifully designed device I’d be happy to invite into my home.

News.title: Ed Miliband calls for ‘new deal on debt’ as developing countries face spiralling borrowing costs
News.content:
Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, has called for a “new deal on debt” as spiralling borrowing costs force developing countries to spend more on interest payments than on education or health.

In a speech in Bangkok on Wednesday, Mr Miliband warned that the global financial system is failing emerging markets, and promised to use the UK’s diplomatic heft to push for urgent reform.

He said: “The short-term repayments are crippling, and while many are not defaulting on their payments they are being forced, if you like, to default on the lives and prospects of future generations.

“So we need a new deal on debt, a deal that supports countries to repay over longer time horizons and, crucially, refinancing with better rates to give developing countries precious fiscal space.”

Although public debt is not inherently problematic, servicing costs are at a 25-year-high – squeezing government coffers just as conflict, climate change and a ‘Godzilla’ El Niño push food and fuel prices ever higher.

Emerging economies in particular have little headroom: according to the Rockefeller Foundation, average interest payments now exceed 10 per cent of revenue in developing nations, while UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) analysis found 3.7 billion people live in countries where debt servicing costs exceed spending on health or education.

At the same time, overseas development aid (ODA) spending from wealthy countries has plummeted – hitting social, infrastructure and humanitarian projects, and disaster response.

The mounting global debt pile has dominated discussions in Bangkok this week, where some 15,000 people have descended for the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank annual meetings.

This included the first meeting of the newly formed Borrowers’ Platform on Monday. A group of finance ministers and central bank governors from some 30 countries, it was formed to exchange ideas about how to deal with debt burdens – and how to avoid pitfalls.

Sports.title: Sir Alex Ferguson wouldn’t have let Lisandro Martinez rant happen and would have scolded him, admits ex-Man Utd star
Sports.content:
Next

SIR ALEX FERGUSON would never have allowed Lisandro Martinez’s explosive rant to happen, according to Gary Pallister.

Pallister, 61, starred at Manchester United under Ferguson between 1989 and 1998, winning 15 titles as the Red Devils became England’s biggest footballing force.



However, since Ferguson’s retirement in 2013 United have lost sight of those lofty standards and ambitions.

The club are currently on a five-game winless run under Michael Carrick and the latest defeat to Atletico Madrid saw senior star Martinez break rank by slamming the board for their lack of investment in the team over the summer.

“Michael probably won’t discuss it much in public, rightly so, it’ll be behind closed doors.

Sports.title: Man Utd star’s ex-wife opens up on ‘hell’ of shock divorce and says ‘it was like open-heart surgery’
Sports.content:
Next

MATTHIJS DE LIGT’S ex-wife has spoken out about their divorce “hell” that she compared to “open-heart surgery”.

AnneKee Molenaar, 27, split from the Manchester United defender last year.



The pair started dating when De Ligt was a teenager breaking through at Ajax and they got married in May 2024.

But their relationship broke down after eight years together before splitting last summer.



And Molenaar – who is a model and social media star – has now opened up on their turbulent break-up “hell” which left her “fragile and vulerable”.

She told RTL Boulevard: “It has been a tough year. A year with a lot of change, but also a year I am very grateful for.

“It is an abrupt change and you miss something and you are sad about that. You are in pain. I really experienced it as something physical. Just physical pain… that is really just a process of grieving.

“It was like I was having open-heart surgery and someone was blowing on my heart. That is how fragile and vulnerable I felt. Bruised.

“We had a wonderful time all those years, and yet last year we came to the conclusion that it is no longer there in a romantic way.”

She insisted there was still mutual respect between the pair despite going their separate ways.



She added: “There is a lot of love between Matthijs and me. There really is a lot of love.



“I think the most loving thing we did was saying: ‘you go this way and I go that way’.”

It has also been claimed De Ligt has since moved on by starting a new relationship with model Amber Yuusef.

According to reports in the Daily Star, De Ligt grew tired of Molenaar’s spiritual lifestyle, which included using crystals, tarot cards and alchemy.

De Ligt, 27, has not played for United in almost a year after undergoing surgery on a long-term back injury.

His last appearance for the Red Devils came during a 2-1 win over Crystal Palace on November 30, 2025.



De Ligt joined United from Bayern Munich in a £42million deal in 2024.

The Netherlands international has since played 56 times for the club, scoring three goals.

Sports.title: Man Utd flop Antony’s home raided while he played in Champions League as he shares emotional statement on family’s pain
Sports.content:
Next

EX-MANCHESTER UNITED player Antony revealed his home was burgled while on Champions League duty with Real Betis.

The winger helped Betis come from behind and beat Porto 3-2 on Wednesday with an assist that led to Cucho Hernandez’s equaliser at La Cartuja.



However, the 26-year-old couldn’t celebrate the big Champions League victory as he swiftly found out his home in Seville was broken into.

The Brazil international didn’t specify whether anyone was inside the residence when the robbers invaded.



However, the ex-Man Utd player was still left heartbroken as items were stolen and his personal space was violated.

The Betis star took to Instagram where he shared the news and revealed the impact that horrific incident had on his family.

Antony posted: “Today, I want to talk about something that made me very sad and angry.

“What should have been a beautiful night ended in anger and frustration. My house was robbed.

“It’s hard to describe the feeling of having your home broken into. Everything we worked so hard for and poured our hearts into obtaining was taken by someone who has no idea how much hardship we went through to get it.

“The most infuriating thing is not just the loss of belongings, but the loss of security in a place where we should feel most protected, and seeing the unease in my family’s eyes.



“But after all this, one thing makes me even more certain: in this world, no possession is more precious than the lives and safety of my family.

“What was lost, we can earn back. The effort will not stop, the dream remains, and the determination to win has not diminished in the slightest.

“What truly matters is that when I look at my family, I know we are still together, united, and have the strength to overcome this difficulty.

“The unease and anger still linger, but I am also more certain: our greatest wealth has never been the items in the house, but the loved ones who make it a home, because ultimately, my greatest achievement in life will always be my family.

Sports.title: Broncos overpower Seahawks to win in OT
Sports.content:
The Denver Broncos overpowered Sam Darnold and the Seattle Seahawks in a 17-14 overtime victory on Thursday night.

Will Lutz kicked a 53-yard field goal to win it at Mile High Stadium to move Denver to 4-2 and drop the defending champion Seahawks to 3-3.

Seattle had taken a first-quarter lead with a Jason Myers field goal, before the Broncos put together two scoring drives in the second - one ending with a JK Dobbins four-yard score and the other with RJ Harvey running in from the one.

They didn't find the end zone again and managed just 168 total yards compared to Seattle's 353, but kept the game close with a tremendous defensive performance that included five sacks and two interceptions of Seattle quarterback Darnold.

Image: Sam Darnold was sacked five times

Darnold completed just 27 of 51 attempts with a quarterback rating of 52.6, but was able to put together two scoring drives in the fourth quarter to send the game to overtime as Denver struggled to move the ball themselves. Broncos QB Bo Nix threw for just 107 yards in an underwhelming outing.

George Holani ran in from one yard out after an 11-play, 67-yard drive with five minutes remaining, with Darnold converting the two-point conversion to Rashid Shaheed with a tipped catch at the back of the end zone to bring Seattle within three.

The Seahawks defense held their own and after a Shaheed return had given Darnold excellent field position with less than a minute remaining, Myers was good from 34 yards to send the game to overtime.

However, on their first possession in OT, Broncos corner Ja'Quan McMillian stepped in front of Shaheed for an interception and the excellent field position allowed Lutz to kick the winner.

Sports.title: Crane 'buzzing' at England recall, wants more than Insta celebrity
Sports.content:
Mason Crane said he was "buzzing" to be back in the England fold, adding that his ambitions go beyond being a "highlights reel" leg-spinner as he looks to make the most of his second bite at international cricket.

Crane was capped three times as a 20-year-old, nine years ago, the last of which was his Test debut in the final match of England's 2017/18 Ashes tour in Sydney. He'd take a single wicket as the tourists signed off a 4-0 series drubbing with another defeat.

Speaking to the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast, Crane admitted that he was "resigned to the fact it may not come again" as a near decade passed without further recognition, until getting the call for England's upcoming ODI tri-series in Pakistan.

"I didn't really expect it, to be honest," Crane said. "It was a bit out of the blue. But it's really cool and I'm buzzing.

Image: Mason Crane made his Test debut for England in Sydney during the 2017/18 Ashes, taking one wicket

"I think there was a period a few years ago where I was sort of resigned to the fact it may not come again, where I maybe put a bit too much pressure on myself and wasn't particularly enjoying it.

"But the last couple of years I feel like I've I sort of got that spark back and the ambition that comes with it."

Following his initial England breakthrough in 2017, injuries ruined Crane's 2018 season and he struggled to nail down a regular spot for his county Hampshire, until a 2024 move to Glamorgan prompted a change in fortunes.

There, he thrived under the coaching of Richard Dawson, who has just left to join England's red-ball staff as assistant to the newly-appointed Stephen Fleming.

Image: Richard Dawson has been named assistant coach to Stephen Fleming in the England men's Test team

"Daws is a brilliant coach. He's been absolutely amazing for us," Crane said. "He has very high standards; he pushes you to become the best version of yourself, and we all sort of thrived off that.

"From a Glamorgan point of view, we'd obviously rather have kept him. But when you have someone like Daws as your coach, if we're if we're being brutally honest, I think you know at some point that he's going to go on to international cricket.

"He's such a brilliant manager of people. He'll be amazing in any role he does.

"It's amazing for England. And like I said, I'm sure one day he will be in a position to take over an international side. He's that kind of calibre of coach."

Crane on batting form - 'My confidence just grew and grew'

Crane's return to the England fold has as much to do with his hugely-improved form with the bat, as much as his performances with the ball.

Image: Mason Crane celebrates one of his two centuries for Glamorgan in the County Championship

Crane struck a maiden first-class century, swiftly following with a second, as Glamorgan finished safely in sixth place upon their first County Championship season in Division One since 2005.

"I've always believed I underperformed a bit with the bat," Crane said. "When I moved to Glamorgan and started playing a lot more regularly, I kind of realised I had a few more shots.

"My confidence just grew and grew. And then this year, to get a few big scores has been amazing.

"Ironically, that's helped my bowling because I'm now bowling in matches where I probably wouldn't be playing in to start with."

Crane claimed 34 wickets across 14 County Championship appearances in 2026, and 15 in 10 Vitality Blast outings. He also played three times for London Spirit in The Hundred, taking two wickets.

A couple of his dismissals went viral on social media, particularly those of Yorkshire batters George Hill and James Wharton as part of an eight-wicket match haul back in April, but Crane doesn't want to just be Insta-famous.

"I don't want to just be a highlights reel bowler, every now and then bowl a really good ball and just live off that," he added.

"I pride myself on trying to play to the situations really, trying to work out how I'm going to get the most out of a wicket and get a particular guy out.

"I've also given myself a bit more freedom, I guess, with the ball now. I try and bowl more variations, but I'm also better at bowling them now.

"It's about sort of adding as many strings to your bow. It's really important."

Sports.title: Rutter scores twice as Brighton win big and go top in Conference League
Sports.content:
Georginio Rutter scored twice and set up one as Brighton thrashed Kauno Zalgris 4-0 to get their Conference League campaign off to a winning start.

Brighton were dominant from the first whistle to the last against the Lithuanian Cup winners and took the lead through Rutter, but only after a VAR check. The ball had initially been deemed to have gone out of play before Ibrahim Osman's cut-back to the Frenchman, but the goal was awarded after review.

Image: Brighton and Hove Albion's Jack Hinshelwood (second right) is embraced by his team-mates

Rutter then turned provider as Brighton doubled their lead on the stroke of half-time when Hinshelwood - returning to the side for the first time since the Premier League opening weekend - slotted into the corner.

The third came after a lung-bursting run from Malick Yalcouye, who played Osman through to cross for Rutter to turn into the net with ease.

Matt O'Riley made it four with a header as he scored his first Brighton goal since August 2025. The Denmark international should have got his second with another header late on, but was denied by an excellent save from Tomas Svedkauskas.

It is now five straight wins in all competitions for Fabian Hurzeler's side who host rivals Crystal Palace in the Premier League on Sunday, live on Sky Sports.

Hurzeler: Disciplined performance sets us up

Brighton boss Fabian Hurzeler:

"We showed a good performance, a disciplined performance, a performance where we kept a clean sheet and a performance where a lot of players used the opportunities.

"This will be key for the season, that we can really rely on each other."

'Convincing win for Hurzeler's side'

Analysis from Sky Sports News' Sophie Evans:

"A convincing win for Fabian Hurzeler's side as they kick off the club's second chapter in Europe in style. The fans around the stadium are already confident of a strong run in this competition, chanting 'we're going to go to Istanbul'.

"The Brighton boss joined his team in applauding this evening's home support. He said that their energy would be crucial in making the Amex a fortress for the opposition this season.

"It's five wins in a row in all competitions for the Seagulls. They were already the favourites to win the Conference League and their dominant performance this evening will only drive that narrative."

Key moments from the Amex Stadium...

3: CLOSE! Costinha heads over from six yards out! Excellent early opportunity for Brighton.

14: SAVE! Gross shoots from the free-kick, but his effort is tipped over by the goalkeeper!

32: CLOSE! Dunk whips a shot at goal from distance that goes just over and lands on the roof of the net!

35: SAVE! Gross with an excellent delivery from the right for Hinshelwood who heads into the ground forcing the goalkeeper to make an acrobatic one-handed save.

43: GOAL! Rutter opens the scoring after turning in Osman's cross. The goal is awarded after a VAR check.

45+1: GOAL! Rutter turns provider and crosses for Hinshelwood who produces a tidy finish across the goalkeeper to double Brighton's lead.

49: SAVE! Gross picks out De Cuyper with a lovely ball, the substitute crosses on the volley for Hinshelwood whose header is tipped over.

53: GOAL! Rutter scores his second of the night after a quality ball from Yalcouye to Osman who cuts back for the Dutchman to apply the finish.

67: GOAL! O'Riley heads across the goalkeeper and into the net to make it 4-0 to the home side.

79: SAVE! Costinha with a header at the back post. Well saved by the goalkeeper!

82: SAVE! O'Riley's bullet-header is saved brilliantly by the Kauno Zilgris goalkeeper.
