Sports.title: Revealed: The death of possession football as Premier League teams are winning games with less of the ball than ever before... and goalkeepers are going longer instead of playing out from the back
Sports.content:
Revealed: The death of possession football as Premier League teams are winning games with less of the ball than ever before... and goalkeepers are going longer instead of playing out from the back

It was after a Champions League victory over Arsenal in 2015 that Pep Guardiola, then Bayern Munich manager, made clear his idea of a football utopia: 'What I want, my desire, is to have 100 per cent possession.'

Bayern had only enjoyed 66 per cent that night in a 5-1 victory over Arsene Wenger's side but even that wasn't enough to satisfy Guardiola's unquenchable pursuit of perfection.

After all, as his idol Johan Cruyff once said, 'if you play on possession, you don't have to defend, because there's only one ball.'

If the opponent doesn't have it, bar calamity or self-sabotage, they can't score.

It was this philosophy that Guardiola brought with him to Manchester City and the one that has since permeated every corner of the English game over the past decade. Who can forget that viral video of Rochdale, then in League One, scoring a sweeping team goal, playing out from the back, with the accompanying caption: 'Right, so f****** ROCHDALE scored this goal and you're telling me Pep Guardiola isn't having an influence on English football?'

Only, now, the pendulum has swung the other way. Football embraced the possession obsession, then began to rebel against it and, at last, is thriving in the face of it.

Pep Guardiola made clear his idea of a football utopia: 'What I want, my desire, is to have 100 per cent possession' back in 2015

Last season was the first since before Guardiola came to the Premier League that the average possession figure for winning matches dropped below 50 per cent and the first time it's happened since Opta records began in 2003-04. That has fallen again across the first 60 games of this campaign.

Over the weekend, only two of the 10 sides that had more than 50 per cent possession came out on top (and one of those was Manchester City so does that really count anyway). Five teams won with less than half of it.

Coventry thumped Newcastle on Monday night with only 33 per cent of the ball. Earlier in the season, Chelsea beat Brighton with just 26 per cent.

Last season, too, was the first since 2005-06 that clubs won more matches (139) with less than 50 per cent of the ball than with more of it (137). The current count is 22 to 19 in their favour again.

Beyond that, the days of teams wanting to completely dominate possession are gone, too, for now. Probably because when they do, they don't win as much as they once did.

Just three seasons ago, in 2023-24, there were 66 matches across the entire campaign in which a team had more than 70 per cent of the ball. Only 14 of them were by Guardiola's City. In all, 12 different sides managed it and one of them was Luton. Fifty-five per cent of them went on to win.

Then, it stopped. In 2024-25, there were just 29 matches where a team had 70 per cent possession and only 11 of those teams won. Last season, it happened just 19 times and only six of them won.

By this point, even Guardiola knew the game had changed. In January last year, he famously remarked that 'Today, modern football is the way Bournemouth, Newcastle, Brighton and Liverpool play. Modern football is not positional. You have to rise to the rhythm.'

But Premier League teams are winning games with less possession than ever before, including promoted side Hull, who are thriving in eighth place

This season, teams boasting 60 per cent possession have won just 35 per cent of their matches. In 2023-24, it was 54 per cent. Teams with less than 30 per cent of the ball now win a third of their games. Five seasons ago, they won less than 10 per cent of them.

We've seen it creep in over recent seasons, as more sides like Bournemouth under Andoni Iraola, now Liverpool manager, embraced fast, direct football as an antidote to death by 1,000 passes. Teams are quicker, stronger, better at man-to-man pressing and able to harangue and harass outfits who previously felt they had the divine right to play out from the back.

When they did, they could punish them. As those possession numbers dropped, so too have those for counter attacks soared. According to Opta, this season is the highest on record (since 2006-07) for fast breaks, shots from fast breaks and goals from fast breaks. Teams soak up pressure and then strike.

Teams also now look to beat the press by going over the press. The average length of goalkeeper passes from open play is on the rise again as it dropped considerably during the Guardiola years.

Gone, too, are the days of promoted sides battling to win their place in the Premier League only to try to play like Guardiola when they get here. Vincent Kompany did it with Burnley and went straight back down, Russell Martin tippy-tapped an instant return to the Championship with Southampton.

Not anymore. Coventry, Ipswich and Hull are averaging the lowest possession of any three promoted teams since Opta records began, with the Sky Blues having 38 per cent of it and eighth-placed Hull the lowest of any side in the division on 32 per cent. Hull sit in the top 10 of the Premier League, having beaten Manchester United and taken a point off Chelsea, while Coventry are level on points with Michael Carrick's side.

'Sergej knows what it takes to win, and having the ball is not that important to him,' one Hull dressing room source told Daily Mail Sport. 'Anybody that knows the game knows there are different ways to win and he plays completely to the strengths of the players that he's got.'

It's not the only barometer for success, of course, with the current top three sides in the division also the top three for possession. The difference, though, is that it's not the only way to win and teams will use whichever method is best. Pragmatism is thriving once again over principles. Teams no longer need to pretend to be something they are not.

Possession does not remain the same throughout a game, of course, and forever fluctuates depending on who's holding on to the lead, who's chasing it and who is pushing for a winner. It is never as simple as saying that the less possession you have, by itself, makes you more likely to win.

Yet what does appear to be becoming clear is that some sides, even when chasing a goal, are content to give up more of the ball because they know they can create more chances when they do.

When Everton came from behind to draw against United, their possession dropped from 47 per cent in the first half to 44.5 per cent as they went searching for an equaliser. It did the same when they snatched a point against Bournemouth, dropping from 42 per cent until the opening goal to 40 per cent until they went level and 37 per cent in the 10 minutes before their stoppage-time equaliser.

Football is often cyclical and the trend has, for now, shifted the other way. In Guardiola's old dream world, he longed for 100 per cent of the ball. In football's latest cycle, it would be the wish of many to let him try.

Sports.title: WILL JOSEPH and SEB ATKINSON interview: Gloucester's 'N'Golo Kante and Lamine Yamal' on turning electric club form into England centre pairing and the overhaul behind PREM leaders' flying start
Sports.content:
WILL JOSEPH and SEB ATKINSON interview: Gloucester's 'N'Golo Kante and Lamine Yamal' on turning electric club form into England centre pairing and the overhaul behind PREM leaders' flying start

Looking out across the Kingsholm car park, Gloucester's Seb Atkinson and Will Joseph have the sort of easy chemistry any good centre combination requires.

‘Maybe it’s something to do with Martin St Quinton, our owner,’ says Atkinson, eyeing up the unfamiliar Caterham 7 sports car in one of the bays.

‘Val Rapava-Ruskin (Gloucester's Georgian prop) used to drive a Maserati,’ adds Joseph. ‘You’ll be due a nice one soon, won’t you Seb? Kerching!’

‘I drive a VW Golf!’ replies Atkinson, who this summer was handed his first enhanced central contract by the RFU. ‘I’m like N’Golo Kante, the French midfielder with his Mini.’

‘That’s right… the Kante of the team,’ says Joseph. ‘Seb’s our workhorse, just like N’Golo. He’s relentless. He’s always got the highest metres. Whenever we train or play a game, Seb always checks the statistics. Always running. Always chasing kicks. Always at the top.’

One eye-catching statistic is that Atkinson, the inside centre, made more post-contact metres than any other back in the PREM last season. He brings muscle to Gloucester’s backline that is complemented by outside centre and fellow 24-year-old Joseph’s stardust.

Gloucester's Seb Atkinson (left) and Will Joseph (right) have the sort of easy chemistry any good centre combination requires

Positivity is running through Gloucester as the club prepare to host back-to-back European champions and French giants Bordeaux in their Champions Cup opener

Atkinson brings muscle to Gloucester’s backline that is complemented by outside centre Joseph’s stardust

‘If we’re going for footballers, then Will is like Lamine Yamal,’ says Atkinson, picking out the 19-year-old Barcelona winger who has already led Spain to World Cup and European Championship glory. ‘Fast and skilful. He does everything I can’t do. He’s very exciting on the ball and he’s really confident when he plays.

'You can prepare all week tactically but if you can beat your man with a bit of speed or footwork, then it doesn’t really matter what the defence looks like. I probably go too tactical at times and someone like Will brings that spark or flair that gets the crowd on their feet.’

Positivity is running through Gloucester as the club prepare to host back-to-back European champions and French giants Bordeaux in their Champions Cup opener on Friday night.

Having finished a disappointing eighth in the PREM last season, scraping into Europe's elite competition by a point over ninth-placed Harlequins, they are top of the table after three rounds, with their young backs flourishing.

Technical director Chris Boyd, the experienced Kiwi, oversaw a backroom restructure last season, bringing in forwards coach Brett Deacon, defence coach Joel Tomkins and recruitment chief Rob Burgess. The club then went out this summer and bolstered their pack by signing Springbok lock Jean Kleyn and Wales co-captains Dewi Lake and Jac Morgan, giving Atkinson and Joseph a platform to shine.

Gloucester are one of two PREM teams (along with Bristol) never to have lifted the league title, despite having played in all 40 seasons since the realignment to a national league system and topping the table on three occasions, only to have their hopes dashed each time in the play-offs. Is this the year the drought ends?

‘The vibe’s good,’ says Atkinson. ‘There was a little bit of an unknown in pre-season. We knew we had an opportunity to play some good rugby but we thought that in previous years and it hadn’t come through. There’s a belief that we can still get a lot better.

'Joel just wants to see physical people putting their body on the line, doing what it takes for the team, then getting up and doing it again. His northern accent makes a difference! We’re trying to make dominant tackles rather than just tackles.

‘The vibe’s good,’ says Atkinson. ‘We knew we had an opportunity to play some good rugby but we thought that in previous years. There’s a belief that we can still get a lot better'

Gloucester, who along with Bristol are one of only two current PREM teams never to have lifted the title, are top of the table after three rounds

Gloucester made major additions to their pack this summer, bringing in (L-R) Dewi Lake, Jean Kleyn and Jac Morgan

‘Then someone like Jean makes good points around training. If you see people getting frustrated, a few scuffles, he just says, “That’s not the team we want to be”.

'No one is reinventing rugby. They know what’s right and what’s wrong and people buy into that. It gives us trust and belief in our game plan so everything pushes in the right direction.

‘I’ve had some tough times at this club. We don’t want to get satisfied now and fall back into those periods. We’re not here for just a couple of good games.’

Friday night’s match against Bordeaux will be Gloucester’s toughest test in recent years. The visitors are loaded with stars such as Tom Willis, Maxime Lucu and Yoram Moefana, and have won each of their seven matches against English sides in the two Champions Cup-winning campaigns.

The French heavyweights sprung a surprise with their team selection, naming giant 23st Tonga prop Ben Tameifuna in the second row alongside 6ft 5in Cameron Woki.

For the hosts, Joseph will shift to the wing, lining up against French superstar Louis Bielle-Biarrey, a challenge he is not shying away from.

‘The double European champions are coming to our place on a Friday night,’ says Joseph. ‘Given how we’ve started the PREM, we definitely feel like we’ve got a chance to win that game and show the rest of Europe what we’re about.

'What a statement that could be. If you can’t get excited for this one then you’re in the wrong sport. It’s going to be like a Test match for us.’

As the man in possession of England’s No12 jersey, Atkinson knows the demands of Test rugby. Attack coach James Lightfoot-Brown celebrated his central contract in a team meeting, while the club hope the buzz around Kingsholm will convince Atkinson to sign a new deal. His current contract expires at the end of this season.

‘Things are looking positive so we’ll see,’ says Atkinson. ‘I’m enjoying being here and I’m enjoying playing with Will and everyone else. The contract with England is a funny one because it doesn’t guarantee selection in any way. It won’t change my mindset on things.

'It shows what I’ve been doing so far has been respected by the coaching set-up. With the World Cup lingering in the background, I want to continue on that trajectory. Everyone at the club gives you a pat on the back but it doesn’t change much in my mind. I’m gaining confidence every game I play. I want to push myself to be one of the best 12s in the world.’

Atkinson is the man in possession of England's No12 shirt, and this summer was awarded his first enhanced EPS contract by the RFU

Joseph's older brother Jonathan won 54 caps for England between 2012 and 2020, winning the Six Nations three times including a Grand Slam in 2016 (pictured left, with Anthony Watson)

‘I was 19 when I was called up by England,’ says Joseph of his senior debut in 2022 in Brisbane. ‘I went in with the attitude of having nothing to lose'

While Atkinson is looking to cement his place in Steve Borthwick’s midfield, Joseph is trying to force his way back into the conversation.

He has just one cap, earned four years ago, when Eddie Jones called him up as an apprentice for the victorious tour of Australia. Gloucester coach George Skivington believes the pair's complementary skillsets can see them thrive for country as well as club.

‘I was 19 when I was called up by England,’ says Joseph. ‘It’s all a bit of a blur. I went in as an apprentice player, probably not expecting to play. I went in with the attitude of having nothing to lose. That was pretty freeing. I trained pretty well and was given an opportunity.

‘I hadn’t played much rugby at all at that point. I was living in the academy house, pretty immature, developing as a young man. I’ve learned a lot about the game since then. Now I know what it takes to be a consistent Premiership player. It’s an environment I’d love to be part of in the future but for now I’m focused on Gloucester.’

Joseph’s older brother Jonathan was capped 54 times by England, winning three Six Nations titles including the 2016 Grand Slam, and the famous name carries weight.

‘When I was younger, I used to struggle with the expectancy,’ he admits. ‘I felt like I was always being compared to him. People had a perception of me and they would say, “You’re never going to be as good as your brother”. That used to get to me a bit. Now I’ve proven to myself that I belong here and deserve to be here. We’ve spoken a lot about confidence and belief and you can feel that around the building.’

Sports.title: Jon Rahm leaves £75.5MILLION on the table to walk away from LIV as bankrupt tour lets go of one of its biggest stars in major blow
Sports.content:
Jon Rahm has left a staggering multi-million-pound sum on the table after walking away from rebel tour LIV Golf following Saudi Arabia's exodus from the sport.

The Spanish star deemed the terms of the LIV 2.0 to be 'unacceptable', after Saudi's Public Investment Fund (PIF) announced that it would stop funding the tour at the end of the 2026 season.

The tour plans to rebuild with new backers BC Partners, a private equity group, but Rahm will not be part of the cohort playing in 2027 after coming to a 'consensual separation agreement' with LIV.

Rahm and LIV have reached a deal to release all of his monetary and economic claims against the league, with Rahm previously the organisation's largest unsecured creditor owed £5.7m of his contract after LIV filed for bankruptcy last month.

But in walking away, Rahm has also foregone the remainder of his contract, which adds up to a staggering £75.5m ($100m).

In exchange for doing so, the 31-year-old is believed to receive rights to his name, image and likeness in return.

Jon Rahm has walked away from the £75.5m outstanding from his lucrative contract with LIV

This will mean the return of his nickname 'Rahmbo' used on the tour, and his 'Legion XIII' team name, which he played under on the LIV tour.

Confirmation of Rahm's deal with LIV will come on November 5, when it will be judged by US Bankruptcy Court of New Jersey Judge Michael B Kaplan.

Rahm has won the past three seasons of the tour after being tempted to join the Saudi-backed rebels by a mammoth contract agreed at a reported £258m ($350m) - to be paid out over multiple years.

While LIV 2.0 will hope that many of their big-name stars stay and continue to play for the second coming of the tour, their filing for bankruptcy in New Jersey opened the door for stars like Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton to wrap up their time on the tour.

Daily Mail Sport reported last month that while Bryson DeChambeau's deal expired at the end of the 2026 season, he is expected to recommit in return for equity in the league.

The rebel golf circuit, which launched in 2022 with the financial backing of the PIF, paid nine-figure bonuses to lure top players like Brooks Koepka, Dustin Johnson, DeChambeau and Rahm away from the PGA Tour.

Further temptations including lucrative prize money, with some tournaments offering up to $20million in funds.

But it all began to fall apart earlier this year with PIF's withdrawal, prompting a number of events to be cancelled in 2026.

Sports.title: Alex Scott QUITS Disney's 'Gen Z' Women's Champions League football show, just two rounds of matches in, after saying she 'didn't agree with all decisions' on 'Match of the Day with a dog'
Sports.content:
Alex Scott has left her role as part of Disney+'s Women's Champions League coverage just weeks after taking part in the launch of new show 'The Hangout', which was widely criticised by fans.

The former Football Focus presenter had worked with the streaming service since they were awarded the rights to Europe's flagship competition in 2025, but Scott has now stepped away with a view to focusing on other projects.

In a statement released by Disney+ and shared with the Guardian, the broadcaster thanked Scott and wished her 'every success', adding: 'Her passion for the women's game and the competition shone through throughout her time with us, and we are grateful for all she contributed.'

A representative for Scott told Daily Mail: 'Alex is grateful for the opportunities she has had to work with the team at Disney+ and hopes that they continue to work together in the future.'

Scott leaves the streaming service shortly after the debut of a new Match of the Day-style programme launched for the competition which was mocked for its chaotic launch episode.

She fronted the programme alongside fellow former professional Lianne Sanderson, and influencers Tyra Mills and Alex Bailess.

Alex Scott has left Disney+'s coverage of the Women's Champions League just one season on from the broadcaster winning the rights

Scott celebrated her birthday on Wednesday evening, the day before the announced, with her partner musician Jess Glynne (Source: Instagram/Alex Scott)

A move to appeal to Gen Z viewers seems to have been made, with football at times seeming peripheral to discussions, and an influencer dog named Barley was also introduced, with the animal asked to pick the winner of the Champions League through food.

The show featured a 'watch party' with Dutch twins Sanne and Merel van Dongen, with Sanne a former basketball player and Merel a footballer.

Fans were left in disbelief at what was unfolding on social media, with one writing: 'Disney said they were a brand and ran with it. They thought a revolving sofa and dog would keep the attention of the girls whilst watching the football and stuck an ad mid game because no one's really watching. You get comments about how empty the stadiums are but how are we growing the game if it's still being dressed up with a pink bow on the top?

'Then bored men with no club football will s**g it off because some football account is making fun of it.

'If we like women's football, we like it for the game, for the players, for their skill, our clubs. JUST like you would for a men's game. Disney, the fans of women's football do not need cute, we'd love impartial analysis, post-match interviews with the team that's played and less dog.'

Another added: 'Sorry the dog in the Disney studio for the UWCL coverage is finishing me like am I watching the coverage for the football or Crufts?'

There was no explanation for why Barley was on the show, though his 137,000 Instagram followers were mentioned.

Disney's production levels were criticised elsewhere on match day, with the broadcaster coming in for further criticism when it cut to an unscheduled advert break in the middle of Arsenal's clash with HB Koge.

Scott is believed to be set to be focusing on her other commitments including her recently launched WSL show, One More Word WSL.

The presented waved goodbye to her role on Football Focus, with the end of the programme after 52 years on air on the final day of the season.

The long-running Saturday programme was the victim of BBC cuts amid a decline of viewing figures in recent years.

Scott was left in tears after being overcome with emotion during the final episode, with returning presenter Garth Crooks gifting her a photo of her and the programme's first host Bob Wilson.

'That's got me,' she said as she looked at her present which had: 'Alex, congratulations for all you have achieved', written on it.

She later added: 'Thank you Garth for being here today. For 52 years, wow, this show has done one thing. Week in week out, it has brought football into your Saturday afternoons whether it was Bob Wilson in 1974 or any of the brilliant presenters that sat in this chair after him, the thing that never changed was you, the fans.'

Sports.title: Cherries on top! Bournemouth make European history as Sunderland score last-gasp winner and Brighton enjoy easy win... but Crystal Palace fall to defeat in five-goal thriller against Lyon
Sports.content:
This was a night for Bournemouth to look back as much as it was to look forward. A night to reflect on how far they’ve come, from navigating a 17-point deduction that put their Football League status at risk in 2008 to playing – and winning – their first ever European home game, thanks to a sublime treble from Evanilson, Rayan and Alvaro Rodriguez, who added the cherry on top with a late penalty. There was a special tifo behind one goal to mark the historic night, with a record crowd of 12,010 packed in to witness it. It was Adam Smith, who has been with Bournemouth since 2010 when they played in League One, leading them out as club captain. Here was owner Bill Foley, seeing his vision to get Bournemouth into Europe, a target he ambitiously but explicitly set back in December 2022, occurring a year ahead of his five-year target. But when Smith’s cross in from the right was expertly flicked up into the air by Evanilson, looping over Sturm Graz goalkeeper Daniil Khudyakov, it was a moment for Bournemouth to look forward, too. Tournament favourites before they beat Real Sociedad in San Sebastian last time out and back-to-back European wins has done little to rubbish that label. Bournemouth have had to take the long way to the top but now they are here, they are showing just how much of a punch they pack. Evanilson scored Bournemouth's first European goal at home in their 3-0 win over Sturm Graz Bournemouth fans celebrated the club's journey pre-match, with the club now among the leading contenders to win the Europa League Boss Marco Rose, who made five changes for this one, described the weekend’s 5-1 drubbing at the hands of Chelsea as a ‘good slap’. Bournemouth were ruthlessly dismantled in south-west London. But to paraphrase the iconic ‘Tubthumping’, a song by British band Chumbawamba, when you get knocked down, you get up again, and that’s exactly what Rose’s side did. It was a suffocating first half for a Sturm Graz side that started with a back five before pivoting to a back four at the interval. Bournemouth had 10 efforts on goal to the visitors’ zero, with Ben Gannon-Doak and Evanilson a constant threat down the Bournemouth right. Good sides ride their luck at times, too, and Bournemouth are no different. Sturm Graz wanted a penalty just before half-time when Belmin Beganovic was clumsily felled by Smith, only for the referee to adjudge Beganovic to have dived. In a much improved second half, Graz struck the post when Jurgen Heil was picked out in the area. But when you’ve battled back from the brink of minus-seventeen in League Two, and all the perils that come with trying to gatecrash the Premier League elite from a starting base in the fourth tier, adversity in Europe is light work. Second halves have been an issue that have pockmarked Rose’s tenure on the south coast so far, coming into this one having led in six out of eight, only going on to win two of them. It was an irritation away to Sociedad, and here was proof that Rose and his players are learning lessons on the fly. Marco Rose wants his side to take their performance against Sturm Graz into the Premier League Justin Kluivert, Rayan and Ryan Christie all formed part of the cavalry sent on by Rose in a bid to settle the game and allow the party atmosphere to kick into another gear and that roll of the dice paid off with 15 minutes to go. Khudyakov dealt poorly with a Bournemouth corner and after dropping it in his six-yard box, Rayan smashed in as Rose threw both arms into the air in celebration. Rose is already looking ahead to how they can now secure their first league win of the season - starting on Sunday, when Sunderland visit the Vitality. 'Performance-wise, clean sheet, attitude, effort - a deserved win and now we have to continue, have to get consistent in these things and Sunderland is the next challenge,' said Rose. 'I believe in this team and know they are always confident despite a difficult situation. The squad is working, everyone is keen to play, everyone deserves to play and its good for us for the busy weeks to have a competitive squad. 'If we stick together and play like this and we have our fans then we are hard to play and it's hard to beat us. That's what we should take into the next game.' For all the fireworks, tifos, light shows, and noise that lit up the night sky, here was proof of just how far Bournemouth have come… and how much further this ascending group can go with Champions League football in their sights. Torreense 1-2 Sunderland: Sadiki scores last-gasp winner By Michael Pavitt Regis Le Bris was forced to call on the cavalry to rescue his side as Sunderland came from behind to win their first European away match in 53 years in stoppage time against Portuguese second division side Torreense. Noah Sadiki struck in the dying minutes prompting wild celebrations from the near 4,000 travelling supporters, who had earlier seen summer signing Jules Ahoka cancel out a spectacular opener from Torreense defender Volnei Feltes. The winner owed much to the creativity of Enzo Le Fee and Granit Xhaka as the pair, who began the night on the bench, underlined their importance to the Black Cats. Having watched their team-mates struggle to break down Torreense, Le Fee produced a delightful dinked pass into the penalty area to find Xhaka, with the Swiss flicking the ball first time into the path of Sadiki to score his first goal for the club. ‘When Granit touched it I heard him scream shoot and I didn’t think twice,' Sadiki said. 'I just hoped it was going in and the keeper wouldn’t save it. I’m really happy. It was a beautiful moment.’ Le Bris had taken the understandable risk by deciding to make seven changes for the fixture against arguably their weakest Europa League opponents, with Torreense currently lying 15th in the Portuguese second tier. Noah Sadiki scored a stoppage time winner as Sunderland beat Portuguese side Torreense Sunderland were forced to fight back following a stunning opener from Volnei Feltes With just four points in the Premier League and five matches left to play this month, this was the match to give an opportunity to fringe members of the squad. Torreense, though, have proved they are more than capable of springing a surprise. Their journey to the Europa League is one to rival Sunderland’s own having stunned Sporting Lisbon in last year’s Portuguese Cup final to qualify. Their opening goal proved just as unexpected as that triumph. Feltes was well inside his own half when he received possession and opted to embark on a forward run. After driving towards the Sunderland box, the Brazilian defender chopped between the challenges of Malick Fofana and Nilson Angulo and curled magnificently into the top corner. Whatever happens to the minnows, they will come away with one of the best goals of this year’s competition. Sunderland were forced to be patient when trying to break down their opponents, who dropped deep in the second half. Le Bris turned to his bench moments after Nilson Angulo saw a header superbly kept out by goalkeeper Lucas Paes, with Omar Alderete failing to convert the follow-up. His quadruple change of Xhaka, Le Fee, Reinildo and Nordi Mukiele proved crucial. The latter's cross for Ahoka to equalise with a header while Xhaka and Le Fee were central to Sadiki's winner. 'Winning this game just at the end is really special,' Le Bris said. 'It’s important for the club and the fans – they were fantastic once again. 'We are growing and we need experiences and I think the team showed the belief until the end which is really important for us. We showed again we have this mindset.' Lyon 3-2 Crystal Palace – Eagles defence struggles again By James Sharpe Now Pierre Sage knows how Oliver Glasner feels. He knows how it feels to return to your old stomping ground, one where you achieved great things, and come away with nothing. Just as Glasner took his new Nottingham Forest side back to Selhurst Park at the weekend and lost, so too did Sage as Crystal Palace endured a frustrating night in Lyon where he once helped save the French side from relegation. In truth, a night like this has been coming. Palace cannot keep defending like this, be so open and unorganised, and expect to win matches. Sooner or later, you leave yourself with too much of a hill to climb. It took Forest just three minutes to open the scoring at the weekend and Lyon needed only seven minutes and 31 seconds here. As always, it was all too easy. A bog-standard corner into a crowded six-yard box and, despite the hordes of black Palace shirts, the ball still dropped to Lyon captain Corentin Tolisso. Only this time, Lyon didn’t miss the rest of the chances that came their way like Forest did. On the stroke of half-time the hosts cut through Palace with simple passes and Keito Nakamura squared for Ernest Nuamah, who darted ahead of the defenders to finish. Tyrick Mitchell, for all his goalscoring exploits this season, made little effort to track his run. It was this leakiness that caused a few shudders in the Palace boardroom, letting in 11 goals in their opening four matches, and sparked rumblings that Sage could be the first Premier League managerial casualty of the season. Pierre Sage saw his Crystal Palace side fall to a 3-2 defeat against his former club Lyon Ernest Nuamah was among the scores as Lyon capitalised on poor Crystal Palace defending If there is a saving grace to which Palace can cling, it’s that when they do get it right under Sage, they do look menacing. There was little of that in a dreadful first half but, after the break, they clicked into gear. They are just, as yet, unable to find the balance. Having wantaway forward Ismaila Sarr back in the line-up always helps with his directness in the final third. And when you have the precision of Adam Wharton in your midfield, you will always stand a chance. It was his delightful first-time through ball to Yeremy Pino after a fine short corner routine that helped fire Palace back into the game. The introduction of Daichi Kamada swung momentum further Palace’s way. He was bundled over inside the box but Palace’s furious protests fell on deaf ears. He had a shot from close range saved and, eventually, found the net after some chaos inside the box. The only problem was that, by then, Lyon had already added a third courtesy of Pavel Sulc’s cheeky backheel flick. Palace kept pushing as Chris Richards saw a late header from a corner saved but, ultimately, in vain. This time, it wasn’t enough. This time, they didn’t get away with it. This time, they gave themselves too much to do. 'I’m really frustrated about the result but really frustrated with the way of playing in the first half,' Sage said. 'Our game started at half-time and it was too late. 'We play too quickly sometimes with the idea to play out the back quickly in transition but we are not a team like this, we have only one or two players able to run and make the difference with the speed. 'That’s why we have to move with the ball, travel with the ball, and we did that in the second half.' Brighton 4-0 Kauno Zalgiris – Seagulls cruise in Conference League By Kieran Gill It must be up there with the finest feelings in football – the relief that washes over when your team finally finds a way through that dastardly low block in front of them. For Brighton, that arrived just before half-time. There was no blaming Kauno Zalgiris for their tactical approach. Hardly anyone other than Fabian Hurzeler, who was perhaps being polite when listing the Lithuanian side’s attributes before kick-off, gave them a hope in hell of escaping their first-ever fixture in the main stage of a European competition without losing. Once Georginio Rutter found that first goal after 41 minutes, this turned into a much more enjoyable evening at the Amex Stadium. Even more so when Jack Hinshelwood, back from his ankle injury and appearing for the first time since August, added a second before the break. With that, the floodgates opened, Brighton started their Conference League campaign in style, and truthfully, this competition should sit high on Hurzeler’s priorities this term. Georginio Rutter scored the opening goal as Brighton overcame Lithuanian side Kauno Zalgiris While we often praise Brighton for the way in which they work – including in the talents they find that the richer clubs then seek to steal – all that is missing is the silverware to complement it all. Despite being brilliantly run, they have never won a major trophy in their history, and the Conference League is an opportunity to correct that. Other English clubs such as West Ham and Brighton’s rivals Crystal Palace have used it well. To sides such as Kauno Zalgiris, these are giants they are competing with, opponents competing on an entirely alien level to their own. While Hurzeler had explained why Kauno Zalgiris would be confident – he warned us they were the champions of Lithuania and that they had won the Lithuanian Cup at the weekend – Brighton are in a happy place, too. This made it five successive victories for them in all competitions. They are third in the Premier League behind only Manchester City and Arsenal, and into the fourth round of the Carabao Cup after winning away at Manchester United – a club now linked with liking Hurzeler in case they move on from Michael Carrick. With that, we had an inkling as to how this game would go. Brighton would attack, and Kauno Zalgiris would defend, and the opening 30 minutes was all about blocks. From Anton Tolordava, from Nosa Iyobosa Edokpolor, from any Kauno Zalgiris player with a body for throwing at the ball. But then arrived the breakthrough. It was a nice finish from Rutter despite the on-field officials thinking the ball had gone behind for a goal-kick in the build-up. It had not, and VAR overruled to award Brighton their opener. Hinshelwood added a second before the break before Rutter grabbed the third goal and Matt O’Riley the fourth. ‘We want to keep improving every game,' said Hinshelwood. 'What’s happened in the past has gone now. We want to look forward to the future.’ It was a good way to warm up for Palace in the Premier League on Sunday, though Brighton may be reminded by the Amex’s away end which side have won a trophy of late. Hurzeler should be embracing this European competition as a way to give his supporters a season to cherish.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson urges UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in a behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; there were allegations of spitting by an Israeli player at half-time, while the Israeli government criticised the Irish players for bowing their heads during the national anthem

Republic of Ireland: Heimir Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future after tense draw

Ireland's head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson has called for UEFA to keep his team and Israel separate in future

Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

The Ireland boss was speaking following his side's 1-1 UEFA Nations League draw with Israel behind closed doors in Serbia.

The games between the two nations this international break were overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

This continued in Serbia, as Ireland fitness coach Damien Doyle was allegedly spat on by an Israeli player at half-time, according to reports in the stadium.

Irish media reported that the incident took place as the teams went down the tunnel. Ireland boss Hallgrimsson confirmed there was an allegation, but he admitted he didn't see it and declined to comment further on it.

However, when asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Israeli Government accuses ROI of 'moral blindness'

The Israeli Government have accused the Ireland football team of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during their national anthem.

For the second time in a week, the Irish players, coaching team and FAI all bowed their heads while the Israeli national anthem was played pre-match.

Image: Republic of Ireland players bowed their heads during the national anthem

The official Israeli Government X account posted: "While some use the football field as their political theatre, for us this is personal.

"1939: Irish players raised their arms in salute to Nazi Germany.

"2026: Irish players bowed their heads during Israel's anthem.

"Different generations. The same moral blindness.

"Today, Israel's players wear black armbands to remember those brutally massacred by Hamas on October 7 - including former professional footballer Lior Asulin.

"Some of us have skin in the game. Others just make a show of it."

Sky Sports News has contacted the FAI for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged that a derogatory term had been used, which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. The term is not associated with antisemitic or anti-Israeli abuse.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying: "That's completely untrue," before bringing the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called following an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist, who said a microphone had been taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands that no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland draw with Israel in second Nations League meeting
Sports.content:
Match report and reaction as Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out after the break; sides clashed at half-time

Republic of Ireland 1-1 Israel: Troy Parrott scores again as sides draw second controversial Nations League meeting

The Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in the second controversial Nations League fixture between the sides.

Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out by Dor Peretz after the break in the behind-closed-doors game in Serbia.

The Republic's 'home' fixture was held on neutral territory at the 4,500-seat TSC arena in Backa Topola, due to "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil" according to a June Football Association of Ireland (FAI) statement.

Both sides wore black armbands. The Republic's, the same as in Hungary to acknowledge - as the Football Association of Ireland chief David Courrell explained before that contest - "all lives lost" in the ongoing Israel-Hamas conflict.

Israel's armbands - which read "7.10" - were to commemorate the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on southern Israel, their official X account confirmed.

The pitch featured no sponsored content or branding, just UEFA graphics with slogans like "football for all", a decision taken by the FAI.

Image: The referee pleads with the benches in Serbia

Tensions rose at half-time after a fracas broke out in front of the tunnel and players from both sides engaged in a heated argument, with the Israeli Government later accusing Irish players of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during Israel's national anthem, as they did in Monday's first match.

Officials broke up a second altercation in three minutes of added time, and there were more heated words exchanged after the final whistle.

On the pitch Parrott, who has now scored 10 times in his last seven competitive internationals, fired the Republic in front from the spot in the 39th minute before Dor Peretz drew the sides level two minutes after the restart.

The result puts Ireland third in Nations League Group B3, level on points with second-placed Kosovo.

Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future

Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

Speaking after the 1-1 draw, Hallgrimsson also declined to comment on the half-time fracas between the two sides.

When asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

On the half-time incident, he said in his post-match press conference: "I was there. I'm not going to comment on it. It's something that a disciplinary committee is probably going to look at."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called due to an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist who had the microphone taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there was no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Ireland news conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland vs Israel is being played in Serbia as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott; protests briefly halted Ireland's draw with Austria on Thursday over opposition to Sunday's Israel fixture

Republic of Ireland vs Israel: Heimir Hallgrimsson's press conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media

Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson's pre-match press conference ahead of Sunday's match against Israel in Serbia ended abruptly after a tense exchange with Israeli media.

The media access was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed they were racially abused by Irish players during their match in Hungary last Sunday.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close as one of his colleagues remonstrated with the reporter.

Image: Ireland's players bowed their heads before facing Israel in the reverse fixture last week

Hallgrimsson later labelled the accusation a "verbal attack" during a separate briefing for members of the Irish press.

The exchange in the main press conference took place after Hallgrimsson was also asked a question about a co-pilot who attacked a pilot and tried to hijack a flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv earlier this week.

The reporter's question was shut down by the FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there are no open UEFA investigations at this stage from the previous meeting between Israel and Ireland last weekend.

The FAI are conducting their own investigation into whether striker Adam Idah was racially abused by Israeli supporters during their 3-0 UEFA Nations League win but have yet to make an official complaint to UEFA.

Image: Protesters interrupted Ireland's draw with Austria by throwing tennis balls onto the pitch with Palestine flags on them

Despite the high-profile nature of the fixture, members of the Irish media later reported that there was no UEFA delegate present at the news conference.

Sky Sports News was told a UEFA match delegate does not have to attend press conferences. The duty is left to the venue media manager, whose job it is to report anything if there is an incident.

Sunday's match is being played in Backa Topola, Serbia, as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott.

Sky Sports News has approached the FAI for comment.

Sports.title: Ireland held by Austria despite Parrott double as protests interrupt game
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott scored twice but the Republic of Ireland were forced to settle for a 2-2 draw after Austria came back in the second half of their Nations League encounter at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin.

The contest was twice interrupted in the opening 45 minutes, first due to what campaign group Stop the Game later referred to in a statement as a "limited tennis ball protest", when - around the 20th minute - tennis balls wrapped in stickers featuring the Palestinian flag and the text '#StopTheGame' were launched onto the pitch.

The match paused a second time when an invader carrying what appeared to be a Palestine flag entered the pitch and was promptly tackled and carried off by security.

The protests came after Ireland's decision not to boycott their game against Israel last week - although goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu did make himself unavailable.

Ireland are due to face Israel again on Sunday.

Image: Tennis balls with Palestine flags were throw onto the pitch

Before the protests, Parrott scored a sensational 12th-minute opener, and then added a penalty on the stroke of half-time.

A pair of substitutes proved Ireland's undoing after Alexander Prass halved the deficit in the 71st minute and Michael Gregoritsch drew the sides level six minutes later.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had a chance to top Group B3 with a victory, but they sit third behind Austria and Kosovo at the halfway point of the group stage.

Hallgrimsson made three changes, including the reintroduction of Finn Azaz, who was greeted warmly when his name was announced over the PA system before the match.

Bazunu was back in the squad, while Liam Scales and John Egan were awarded starts.

There was a significant security and police presence outside the stadium, where a small group of protesters also gathered before kick-off.

There was an audacious early effort from Sasa Kalajdzic, who tried to catch Caoimhin Kelleher off his line with a lob from midfield, before Ireland enjoyed a couple of attacking spells deep in the visitors' half.

Image: Parrott is congratulated after scoring his second goal against Austria

It was a brilliant opener from Parrott, who realised he was on his own after bringing down Adam Idah's glanced-on header from a goal kick.

The Real Betis striker was sandwiched in a triangle of white shirts, before nutmegging Philipp Lienhardt and evading every other challenger with a mazy run before planting the ball past Florian Wiegele and into the bottom corner.

Image: A protestor was carried off the pitch during the game

Kelleher denied Patrick Wimmer and there were a few more promising spells for Austria before Parrott doubled their lead.

Ryan Manning won the penalty after he was clipped in the box by Nicolas Seiwald. Parrott stepped up after a VAR check and blasted it past the Austria 'keeper.

Austria cut the deficit after Liam Kitching was caught out and Austria worked the ball to the unmarked Prass, who blasted the ball beyond Kelleher. The offside flag was initially raised, but the decision was reversed after a VAR check.

The Brentford goalkeeper then failed to stop Gregoritsch's free-kick as Ralf Rangnick's side fought back for a point.

Ireland captain Dara O'Shea was denied by an excellent leaping Wiegele save, Gregoritsch directed a shot over the crossbar and both sides fended off attempts at a late winner.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson admits 'toughest days' of career after Ireland beat Israel
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in their controversial Nations League fixture at a neutral venue in Hungary.

Players did not shake hands with each other before their meeting at the Nagyerdei Stadion in Debrecen and there was no exchange between Ireland captain Dara O'Shea and Israel's Manor Solomon.

Ireland players also appeared to bow their heads while Israel's national anthem was played out before kick-off.

Black armbands were worn by Ireland players, which Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said was a gesture to recognise "all lives lost" in the Israel-Gaza conflict.

Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu was the only player who chose not to play after the squad voted to proceed with the match on Saturday amid calls for the game not to go ahead.

Goals from Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan sealed the victory for Heimir Hallgrimsson's side.

Moylan celebrated his goal by kissing and raising his black armband before kissing his badge.

Hallgrimsson: I couldn't be more proud of the players

Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"It has been some of the toughest days of my coaching career, but its not about me.

"The game, the desire the players showed to make a statement on the pitch - they are football players, they wanted to show on the pitch, make that talking with their feet.

"What they did was impressive. In tough times that's when you find your leaders, there were so many players that stepped up in these tough times. The energy levels they showed was impressive.

"The performance was good given all the preparation, the lack of training, all of our meetings were about something other than football.

"I couldn't be more proud of the players.

"By playing I know we are making some people unhappy. By playing we are making others happy. Winning probably pleases everyone, but there will still be people angry that we played the game.

"I hope we can settle that slowly down and stay together as a team. I wish people in Ireland continue supporting these boys, because they certainly deserve it."

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland slip to deserved defeat in Kosovo
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat away to Kosovo in their Nations League opener in Pristina.

The build-up to the League B3 encounter had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which Republic boss Heimir Hallgrimsson had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.

Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly at the Fadil Vokrri Stadium.

The home side saw two shots cleared off the line and Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher then clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrimsson's side got to the break on level terms.

Ireland - who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday and then again in a 'home' tie at another neutral venue in Serbia seven days later - dug in for the second half but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when Kosovo captain Muriqi bundled the ball in from close range.

Udinese defender James Abankwah was handed a first competitive start as part of a back five, with in-form Real Betis striker Troy Parrott the lone forward and Dara O'Shea taking the captain's armband.

Image: The Republic of Ireland have won two of their six games in 2026 so far

Ireland created what ended up being their only real clear chance in the 22nd minute. Abankwah got away down the right and ran into the Kosovo penalty area before cutting the ball back to Ogbene, who sent a curling effort over the crossbar.

Kosovo, who are in League B for the first time, went close on the half-hour mark when a cross from the left found its way through to Muriqi, whose angled shot was cleared off the line by Jayson Molumby.

Veldin Hodza then saw his 10-yard strike blocked in front of goal by O'Shea before Kelleher got up to claw away a looping header from Muriqi, which was set for the top corner.

Ireland made a positive start to the second half, with a deep cross from the right by Abankwah finding Parrott at the far post and his header was gathered by Kosovo goalkeeper Arijanet Muric.

Image: Vedat Muriqi scored the winner for Kosovo

Kosovo, though, continued to carry a threat themselves. Baton Zabergja sent a 20-yard effort just wide of the top corner, which again got the home supporters into full voice.

Muriqi forced Kelleher into another smart reaction save from an angled shot at the near post before Kosovo eventually made the breakthrough in the 83rd minute.

Ermal Krasniqi's shot was deflected onto the crossbar and Muriqi reacted quickest in a crowded six-yard box to nod the ball over the line.

Kosovo should have got a second late on when substitute Krasniqi dragged his shot wide after being set up by Muriqi following a break onto a long ball.

Ireland pay price for 'off day'

Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson told RTE:

"[Kosovo are] a good team, momentum with them, crowd with them, and to be honest they deserve the win.

"There was nothing that we didn't know about how they would play, where their threats would be, but [it was] an off day for a lot of our players and [it is] a tough place to come to if you have an off day, so a deserved win for Kosovo."

Hallgrimsson added: "We were the team that needed to defend today and didn't connect in possession or passes, not as sharp as we have done.

"We have to quickly find out the reason that we had an off day. We can all do better than we did today.

"It is a two-day turnaround for the next one, so we better be quick…and do better than this versus Israel. They are probably in the same position as us [having lost to Austria]."

Asked if the controversy from playing the fixtures against Israel had impacted on his team's performance against Kosovo, Hallgrimsson said: "I couldn't say now. It is difficult to measure that one."

He added: "This is the situation, we have to cope with it. And like I said before the game, this camp is a test of character.

"We need to do better in that area than we did here today. We knew that we needed to win the duels, win the one-vs-ones, but sadly they had the upper hand on all the basics."

What it means and next fixtures

Sports.title: Why have the Republic of Ireland's two games against Israel become so controversial?
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland will face Israel in a men’s football fixture for the first time since 2005 in this international break, but there have been calls for the two UEFA Nations League games not to be played at all.

Both meetings - the first played in Debrecen, Hungary on Sunday and the second scheduled for the Serbian town of Backa Topola on October 4 - have been overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

Uncertainty over the games going ahead might have subsided, but the tensions between the two nations have not.

Heimir Hallgrimsson, the Republic of Ireland head coach, has been accused of "stupidity and hypocrisy" by the Israel Football Association after last week suggesting his team would be "playing against genocide" when facing Israel, while his players are not ruling out their own protests ahead of the games.

The Athletic examines the key issues ahead of the first meeting this weekend.

Why have these games caused controversy?

This has been a contentious issue rolling down the tracks ever since the 2026-27 Nations League draw was made in February. Group B3 saw the Republic of Ireland pitted against Kosovo, their opening opponents this evening, and Austria, but it was the prospect of facing Israel which created immediate unease.

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) had overwhelmingly approved a motion that called on UEFA to ban Israel from its competitions just four months earlier due to violations of the governing body's statutes, including "the organisation of clubs in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank without the consent of the Palestinian Football Association".

The Nations League draw duly reignited the row. Irish politicians, including the FAI member Joanna Byrne, were quick to call for a boycott of the Israel games in the following days and protests ensued when Qatar visited Dublin's Aviva Stadium for a friendly in May. Tennis balls featuring the Palestine flag were thrown on the pitch by supporters, twice causing brief interruptions.

Image: Tennis balls with a Palestinian flag on were thrown onto the pitch in Dublin during protests in May 2026

The FAI had already confirmed its plans to go ahead with the Israel games by then, and that decision was formally approved at an EGM in July.

That saw only 32 votes in favour of a boycott, with 75 members voting for the games to be played. The FAI had argued that boycotting games would cause "significant and lasting harm to Irish football" due to the likely disciplinary sanctions from UEFA.

A measure of the opposition to the Republic of Ireland facing Israel also came with the acceptance that the "home" fixture would not be played in Dublin. The FAI cited "operational challenges (that) could impact the delivery of the game on home soil" and the decision was eventually made in late June, with the support of UEFA, to move the game to Backa Topola, a small town in northern Serbia, on Sunday week.

No tickets for the game will be made available to Ireland fans.

The FAI has subsequently revealed that a request to see the two nations kept apart in future competition draws has been rejected by UEFA.

"The answer I got was very clear," FAI chief executive David Courell told reporters on September 18. "That would not be possible because Ireland and Israel have never been in direct conflict."

What is the political backdrop?

The Republic of Ireland has consistently outlined its backing for the Palestinian people since the conflict with Israel began almost three years ago, joining Norway and Spain when officially recognising a Palestinian state in 2024. Taoiseach Micheal Martin has also made his stance clear, accusing Israel of committing "genocide" last year in comments reported by the Irish Mirror.

The conflict in Gaza began after Israel responded to attacks by Hamas militants on October 7, 2023, which saw around 1,200 people, mostly civilians, killed in Israel and 250 taken hostage. The war has subsequently seen 73,000 people killed, according to figures from the Gaza Health Ministry and used by the UN.

Strained relations between the Republic of Ireland and Israel have continued this year. Two Israeli government ministers were the subject of travel bans in June, while foreign minister Helen McEntee also confirmed Ireland's intent to limit goods trading with settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank this summer.

Image: Taoiseach Micheal Martin

A meeting between the Republic of Ireland and Israel on a football field this weekend has subsequently taken on enormous significance against such a backdrop.

There are similarities in Ireland's political stance with those of Norway, who faced similar calls for a boycott when Israel travelled to Oslo last October. The Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) had aligned itself with its government and said in a statement leading up to Israel's visit that the "tragic humanitarian suffering in Gaza" had made the fixture challenging.

That World Cup qualifier, won 5-0 by Norway, saw thousands take part in a protest march to the stadium.

Who has opposed the games taking place?

Moving a home game 1,500 miles away has not stopped the objections building ahead of the two teams meeting on Sunday. More than 160 Irish sportspeople signed an open letter asking their national team to boycott the Israel games under the banner of the Irish Sport for Palestine Group, who have also run the "Stop the Game" campaign that protested outside of the Irish team hotel in Dublin on Monday.

"This is a significant moment and with this moment you have an opportunity to do the right thing," the letter said.

Kevin Kilbane, the former Republic of Ireland international who holds 110 caps, has also been unequivocal in his views. "The Republic of Ireland should not be playing Israel… not while Israeli forces are committing genocide," he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.">he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.

Amnesty International also issued a fresh statement on Tuesday that said UEFA risked letting football "rubber-stamp apartheid" by allowing Israel's continued participation in its club and international competitions. A spokesperson for the Israeli FA responded to that by saying: "Their obsession with the idea of Israel as a state is incurable, as is their need of attention."

The Irish media, meanwhile, has faced its own dilemmas in the coverage of the Israel games. RTE, the public broadcaster behind Ireland's boycott of the Eurovision Song Contest in the last two years due to Israel's continued involvement, has stripped back its coverage. Contractual obligations will be met, RTE confirmed in a statement, but there would be no studio coverage or commentators sent to either fixture.

Image: Kevin Kilbane, former Ireland international, has spoken out

What have the key stakeholders said ahead of this weekend?

Relations between the two nations have grown increasingly hostile in the last week. Hallgrimsson appeared in front of the media to announce his squad for the upcoming friendlies and made pointed remarks when asked how his players would focus on football.

"We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," the former Iceland head coach told reporters. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."

The reaction to those words, in a social media post from the Israel FA account, raised temperatures further still. "We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way," it read. "Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by @IrelandFootball team coach. We're not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, we're playing against the coach who embodies them."

Martin, who was among the world leaders attending the UN General Assembly in New York, was then drawn back into debate on Tuesday. "I think those are unacceptable remarks. They should be withdrawn. Israel can't keep denying what the world knows and what the world understands."

The FAI has not addressed Hallgrimsson's comments publicly, but the Republic of Ireland's head coach said on Wednesday that he had been "grateful for the support" he had received.

"Maybe from a leadership point of view, it was not clever from me to take the attention (away) like this. It's a tricky time for us," Hallgrimsson said in his pre-match press conference ahead of facing Kosovo.

The same extends to his players, too. Dara O'Shea, the Ipswich Town defender, said, according to the BBC, that he and the rest of the players would come together on Friday to "openly discuss" the prospect of a protest ahead of the first Israel game in Debrecen on Sunday.

Image: Dara O’Shea, left, and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson during Wednesday’s press conference

Why are the games being played in Hungary and Serbia?

Hungary has acted as an adopted home for Israel since the start of the conflict. They first played there in November 2023, when resuming their attempts to qualify for Euro 2024 when hosting Switzerland at the Pancho Arena in Felcsut, a small village 26 miles west of Budapest.

Victor Orban, who lost his position as Hungary's prime minister this year, had been a long-standing ally of Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and claimed Hungary to be the "safest country in Europe" for Jews.

The World Cup 2026 qualifiers against Estonia, Norway and Italy were all held in Debrecen, which has also previously hosted European games for Israeli sides Maccabi Haifa and Maccabi Tel Aviv.

The Republic of Ireland's choice of Backa Topola, Serbia, is less clear. Dublin ceased to become an option, even behind closed doors, as the opposition to Israel visiting became clear, which left limited options for relocation.

It needed to be a nation sympathetic to Israel to avoid further protests and Serbia, neighbouring Hungary to the south, has forged strong diplomatic relations. According to the Associated Press, Serbia's president Aleksandar Vucic inaugurated an assembly factory for Israel-made drones last week, with plans for three more production sites.

A switch to Serbia was reliant on UEFA approval and it will be Backa Topola's home of the TSC Arena where this story ends on October 4.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

YouTube YouTube , which may be using cookies and other technologies. To show you this content, we need your permission to use cookies. You can use the buttons below to amend your preferences to enable YouTube cookies or to allow those cookies just once.
