World.title: India’s mass voter purge is hollowing out democracy
World.content:
Over the weekend, thousands of protesters demanding the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, faced mass detentions and a heavy police crackdown in New Delhi. The demonstrations, which have brought together youth activists and opposition parties, centre on the removal of more than 130 million names from India’s electoral rolls, raising profound questions about the state of Indian democracy.

The deletions are the result of the controversial Special Intensive Revision (SIR) undertaken by the Election Commission of India (ECI). The ECI periodically revises electoral rolls to add new voters and remove the names of those who have died or permanently moved away. The last intensive revision was completed in 2003-2004. What makes the current SIR unprecedented, however, is its scale, the arbitrariness and overreach of its procedures, and the mass disenfranchisement that has followed. The exercise has disproportionately affected Muslims, women, migrants and other marginalised communities while also raising questions about the legitimacy of the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party’s (BJP’s) electoral victories in Bihar and West Bengal.

Both the ECI and the ruling party have defended the exercise by using the language of “purification”. In a caste society, that rhetoric is deeply troubling but also revealing. The bureaucratic procedures and technological infrastructure underpinning the exercise barely mask its intention to create two classes of citizenship in India, one endowed with political voice through the right to vote and the other reduced to what the philosopher Giorgio Agamben calls “bare life”.



The SIR’s intent, procedures and outcomes reveal a sinister design: to maximise voter exclusions rather than enhance voter participation. This subverts the promise of universal adult suffrage, a cornerstone of India’s constitutional democracy. The ECI initially excluded the government-issued Aadhaar card from the list of documents accepted for voter verification during the SIR, supposedly because it was considered “overinclusive”. If that did not expose the exercise’s exclusionary intent, the ECI’s invention of the category “logical discrepancy” during the West Bengal SIR certainly did. This pseudo-legal innovation accounted for 2.7 million of the nearly 9 million names removed from electoral rolls in Bengal. The demand for educational certificates, land records, legacy documents and family trees as evidence also places a heavy burden on poor and marginalised voters, especially in regions still reeling under mass poverty, landlessness and rampant illiteracy. With the “burden of proof” shifted to ordinary voters, the SIR aims to achieve precisely what it set out to do: mass deletions and consequent disenfranchisement.

Customised apps and online forms, digitised electoral rolls and the requirement to upload scanned documents in prescribed formats are all presented as evidence of the SIR’s efficiency and objectivity. But this approach ignores the digital divide in a deeply unequal society. Technology does not operate outside relations of power. In fact, it often serves as a mechanism of control. The category of “logical discrepancy” relies on an AI-enabled application, ERONET (Electoral Roll Officers’ Network), which compares voters’ details with older electoral rolls and flags discrepancies in names and family relationships. The use of such centralised systems has also raised questions about who controls electoral data and how these discrepancies are assessed. Women are particularly vulnerable to these procedures. Many change their names or addresses after marriage and may lack the documents needed to establish links with older electoral records. The excessive exclusion of women demonstrates how ostensibly neutral technological procedures can reinforce existing inequalities and weaken people’s political voice.

The SIR’s purported neutrality is at odds with its effects, which fall heavily on the weak and the marginalised. Among religious minorities, Muslims across the country bear a particularly heavy burden of deletions. In Bengal, Muslims reportedly accounted for about 65 percent of the 2.7 million people removed from electoral rolls on grounds of “logical discrepancy”. With only 19 specially constituted tribunals to handle more than 3.8 million appeals, the corrective process in effect has remained inaccessible to many excluded voters. In Hyderabad, 1.94 million names were marked for deletion under the “absent, shifted, dead and duplicate” (ASDD) category. An estimated 40.7 percent of those entries appeared to belong to Muslim voters, compared with Muslims’ 30 percent share of the city’s population. In some constituencies in Hyderabad’s Old City, Muslims accounted for as much as 80 percent of the names marked for deletion. The pattern is repeated in the National Capital Region, Delhi, where nearly one-third of the existing electorate was missing from the draft SIR roll. Studies flag especially high rates of exclusion in areas with large minority and migrant populations and among residents of informal and unauthorised settlements. The disproportionate exclusion of Muslims suggests an ideological alignment between the SIR’s ostensibly impersonal bureaucracy and the social and political programme of the Hindu right.



As a political and ideological instrument, the exercise has proved to be doubly potent. Through mass deletion of voters from targeted social categories, such as Muslims, it has contributed to shrinking the electoral base of the BJP’s principal rivals. The elections in Bihar and Bengal after the SIR suggest a discernible pattern. In the 2020 Bihar Assembly elections, the Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD)-led alliance lost to the BJP-led alliance by just 0.03 percentage points in vote share. In contrast, in the 2025 elections after the removal of 6.8 million names from the existing rolls and the addition of 2.1 million new voters, the BJP alliance’s lead increased to nearly 9 percentage points. Analysis of the 2026 Bengal Assembly elections also points to the decisive role SIR deletions played in the electoral outcome. The exercise disproportionately affected Muslim, migrant and poorer voters in districts where the BJP had historically struggled to gain support. In many constituencies won by the BJP, the number of deleted or disputed voters exceeded the party’s margin of victory.

Furthermore, the bureaucratic exercise reinforces the larger ideological project of a “pure Hindu” nation. It has also legitimised calls for the expulsion of “Rohingyas”, “infiltrators” and “Bangladeshis”, terms used as dog whistles for Muslims, helping to polarise elections along communal lines. Although Bengali Hindus and others also found their names removed from electoral rolls, the political messaging around the SIR in a communally charged election campaign cast Muslims as a suspect community, imperilling their civil and social rights. Predictably, the newly elected BJP governments in Bihar and Bengal moved to deny Public Distribution System benefits to those who found their names expunged from the electoral rolls.

The SIR is thus fuelled by the imagined spectre of a vile and illicit intruder who must be expelled to preserve the existing order. It follows the Supreme Court-supervised National Register of Citizens (NRC) in Assam, which left 1.9 million of the state’s residents, mostly Bengali speakers, essentially stateless. It also resembles the Citizenship Amendment Act of 2019, which introduced religiously differentiated access to citizenship, an affront to the republic’s secular structure. The recently established High-Level Committee on Demographic Change, mandated to assess demographic changes occurring across India due to “illegal infiltration” and “abnormal” population changes among “religious and social communities”, is cut from the same cloth. Ultimately, the SIR is one of several instruments at play to criminalise, disenfranchise and denationalise social groups and communities considered inimical to the Hindutva vision of an ethnic state.

World.title: China-North Korea border bridge may do little to spur trade, experts say
World.content:
Sanctions and a North Korean leadership that prioritises security dim prospects for economic cooperation, analysts say.

Share China-North Korea border bridge may do little to spur trade, experts say on social media

As China and North Korea cut the ribbon on New Yalu River Bridge this week, officials described the new border crossing in momentous terms.

Chinese Premier Li Qiang said the 3km (1.9-mile) bridge, which links China’s Dandong and North Korea’s Sinuiju, would “vigorously promote” trade and “strengthen emotional bonds”.

North Korean Premier Pak Thae-song expressed his belief that the crossing would “accelerate the advance for the prosperity of the two countries” and “add fresh vigour” to their economic cooperation.

Analysts on China-North Korea ties are much more circumspect.

While the bridge is a concrete symbol of China and North Korea’s efforts to revitalise relations that have waned from their Cold War-era peak, the prospects for trade are hindered by obstacles ranging from international sanctions to a North Korean leadership that prioritises security above all else, experts say.

“It reflects China’s renewed effort to strengthen its relationship with North Korea at a time of changing regional alignments,” Phillip Park, a professor at the University of North Korean Studies in Seoul, South Korea, told Al Jazeera.

“But whether this leads to substantially deeper economic integration, greater North Korean dependence, or a significant shift in Pyongyang’s strategic orientation remains an open question.

“The bridge could facilitate trade and logistics, but it does not remove international sanctions,” Park added.

China, whose troops fought alongside Pyongyang in the 1950-53 Korean War, has long been North Korea’s most crucial economic benefactor.



China accounts for as much as 95 percent of official trade with the secretive country, which is among the world’s most diplomatically and economically isolated states.

Before the four-lane New Yalu River Bridge officially opened on Thursday, road and rail freight between Dandong and Sinuiju, the main route for China-North Korea trade, travelled exclusively via the ageing Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge.

Opened in 1943, the bridge, which has a single-lane road and a rail track, can only carry vehicles weighing a maximum of 20 tonnes.

Jae-woo Joo, a professor of Chinese foreign policy at Kyung Hee University in Seoul, said the new bridge could “tremendously” boost trade between the sides, including the transfer of components banned under sanctions against Pyongyang’s nuclear and missile programmes.

“It is therefore really significant to open this bridge with China,” Joo told Al Jazeera.

After coming under strain from North Korea’s nuclear weapons tests in the mid-2000s, Beijing-Pyongyang ties have warmed under Chinese President Xi Jinping and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

At Xi and Kim’s most recent meeting in June, their seventh summit since 2018, the leaders pledged to enhance cooperation in areas spanning trade, defence, agriculture, law, science and technology.

Analysts have, in part, cast Beijing’s deepening engagement with Pyongyang as a response to the latter’s growing ties with Moscow, which have included the deployment of thousands of North Korean troops to the front lines of Russia’s war in Ukraine.

Last month, North Korean and Russian officials opened the first road bridge linking their countries across the Tumen River.

North Korea and China’s two-way trade grew 25 percent in 2025 to reach $2.74bn, according to figures from China’s General Administration of Customs.

Bilateral trade has continued to grow in 2026, jumping nearly 20 percent to reach $1.5bn in the first half of the year, putting it on track to reach its highest volumes since the COVID-19 pandemic.

But while growing, trade remains relatively minuscule in the context of global commerce.

With China’s overall trade hitting $6.36 trillion in 2025, North Korea’s contribution to the total was a little more than 0.04 percent.

Official trade between the neighbours also remains substantially below its 2010s heyday.



Trade hovered around $5-6bn throughout much of the decade, peaking at $6.45bn in 2013.

Economists have offered explanations for the slowdown that range from tightened sanctions to China’s waning reliance on imports amid its efforts to boost economic self-reliance.

Christopher Green, a senior consultant for the Korean Peninsula at International Crisis Group, said the new border crossing’s significance should not be overstated, considering that China-North Korea trade “is fundamentally driven by politics”.

“Lack of cross-border transit routes is not the main obstacle,” Green told Al Jazeera.

“If the bridge opening signifies a political desire on both sides to give political cover to rising trade volumes, then a boost to trade should follow,” Green said, describing ties up until now as “steady-as-she-goes” economic engagement.

“Time will tell. But the key is the politics of national security, not economics.”

As much as officials have hailed the New Yalu River Bridge as a reflection of Chinese-North Korean cooperation, the project had a long and torturous road to completion.

Construction began in 2011 and was finished on the Chinese side in 2014.

But North Korean authorities only completed roads and customs facilities on their side of the river this year following repeated pauses in construction amid tensions with Beijing.

“The 12-year delay certainly suggests that economic cooperation is more conditional than the language of friendship might imply,” Marco Mari, a PhD researcher at Bocconi University in Italy who studies China-North Korea economic ties, told Al Jazeera.

“The bridge can facilitate supplies and economic activity, while Russian support gives North Korea alternatives that diminish Beijing’s leverage,” Mari added.

“This does not necessarily imply broader economic reform or a comparable improvement in ordinary people’s lives.”

Weiqi Zhang, an associate professor at Suffolk University who studies relations between North Korea and China, said the history of China-North Korea economic ties is littered with abortive projects, such as the Hwanggumpyong Special Economic Zone, a North Korean-Chinese development near Dandong.

“There were cases, like the Hwanggumpyong Special Economic Zone – established by China and North Korea – where China built infrastructure on its side, but North Korea didn’t even pave the road on their side,” Zhang told Al Jazeera.

“One reason is that, unlike its neighbours, North Korean government doesn’t really pay much attention to trade for economic development,” Zhang said.

“International trade is used by North Korea more like a foreign policy tool.”

With China wishing to demonstrate its “indispensability” as a trade partner and North Korea eager to strengthen their economic ties, trade is likely to grow, said Edward Howell, a lecturer in international Relations at the University of Oxford.



Even so, economic engagement will be subject to political considerations, Howell said.

“North Korea will obviously want to avoid facing any Chinese influence to change its economic model, but Pyongyang will want to reap the economic benefits of trade with its principal economic benefactor,” Howell told Al Jazeera.

World.title: Man Utd veering towards crisis as Man City cloud hangs over Premier League
World.content:
Lisandro Martinez apologises for his criticism after on-field spotlight shifts to Manchester United from City.

Share Man Utd veering towards crisis as Man City cloud hangs over Premier League on social media

Manchester United will travel to historic rivals Leeds for their next match as pressure mounts on manager Michael Carrick while Manchester City aim to extend their perfect Premier League start despite the uncertainty over their future.

Brighton could be one of the big winners should City suffer severe sanctions for breaking the Premier League’s financial rules.

The Seagulls are riding high, just two points behind second-placed Arsenal, before their grudge match on Sunday against Crystal Palace.

Martinez blast comes after Man Utd’s worst start for 40 years

United are off to their worst league start in 40 years and were plunged further into chaos by defender Lisandro Martinez’s attack on the club’s hierarchy over a lack of investment after Tuesday’s 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid.

The Argentinian took aim at Technical Director Jason Wilcox after the Red Devils added only three midfielders during the transfer window.

But Martinez himself has been one of those most culpable for a miserable start to the campaign for his part in goals conceded to Fulham and Tottenham in recent weeks.

United have won just one of their opening six league games and were also dumped out of the League Cup last month by Brighton.

Leeds last beat the Red Devils at Elland Road in 2002 but did inflict the only home defeat of Carrick’s interim spell in charge last season when the sides met in April.

Carrick is increasingly at risk of becoming the latest manager unable to turn around a sharp decline at Old Trafford since Alex Ferguson’s retirement in 2013.



But he said the hostile atmosphere that will await his side presents the perfect chance to bounce back.

“What a great game [on] Sunday to prepare for. It’s a fantastic game for us, for the club, for the history, for the supporters,” Carrick said.

“Everything to do with the game is a great game, so we’ll be ready for that.”

Martinez has since apologised for his comments.

Man City charges leave Premier League in limbo

Manchester City sit pretty at the top of the table with six wins from six league games, but that may all count for nothing if they do not successfully overturn a guilty verdict on more than 100 charges of breaking Premier League rules.

Enzo Maresca’s men shut out that distraction to win 3-0 at Liverpool last weekend and rallied impressively in the second half despite losing 4-2 to Paris Saint-Germain in a thrilling Champions League tie on Tuesday.

But the uncertainty over their future has left the entire league in limbo.

City deny any wrongdoing, and a case that began eight years ago has at least a few months left to run before the appeal is heard and a potential sanction announced.

“My underlying thought is none of this is good for football and there are no winners,” former England manager Gareth Southgate said.

City can stretch their lead at the top to six points when Ipswich visit the Etihad on Saturday. Arsenal are not in action until 24 hours later at Nottingham Forest.

The football regulator in England said after City’s appeal that he expects an outcome by January.

‘Ruthless’ Brighton eye Champions League

Arsenal’s only defeat this season came in a 3-0 trouncing by Brighton, whose remarkable rise could reach new heights this season with many of the other established giants struggling.

Brighton have soared through the divisions and into Europe on the back of owner Tony Bloom’s expertise in data analytics.

But they are yet to play Champions League football.

Despite routinely selling their prized assets to wealthier clubs, Brighton’s smart recruitment of both players and coaches has allowed them to continue to thrive.

That has also made them a neutral’s favourite, but manager Fabian Hurzeler wants his side to show their nasty side against rivals Palace on Sunday.

“We want to be ruthless. We want to create this energetic atmosphere where it makes it so hard to come to this place,” Hurzeler said. “We have to keep building this together with our fans and not be the nice football club any more.”

World.title: Indian police launch New Delhi clampdown for Cockroach Party rally
World.content:
Cockroach Janta Party standoff with government extended as youth-led movement calls protest over jailing of activists.

Authorities have tightened security in New Delhi after the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) called for a new protest over the jailing of two of its activists.

Thousands of additional police officers were deployed in the Indian capital on Friday as the Indian government appeared to prepare for further confrontations. The youth-led CJP movement has held a series of protests in recent weeks to demand India’s election chief resign. Its demonstrations have been met with a tough crackdown.

CJP supporters have been called to gather in New Delhi’s Central Park at 5pm (11:30am GMT). The rally was called after two of the movement’s leaders were jailed for five days this week for allegedly trespassing at a protest site.

Authorities have closed the park, citing “administrative reasons”, and set up metal barricades at key intersections.

CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke suggested police may try to arrest him before the protest but declared he and his supporters are “not afraid” and are “ready” to go to jail.

In a social media post, Dipke accused the government of hypocrisy and denounced police crackdowns against the movement.

Members of the government may never have come to power had they experienced similar protest restrictions, he asserted.

“The very party that is in power today spent decades organising protests, taking to the streets and questioning the governments of the day when it was in opposition,” Dipke said.

“Had the same restrictions, intimidation and police crackdowns been used against them, many of those who occupy positions of power today might never have reached where they are.”

The rally is just the latest facing a crackdown by the authorities.



The CJP has held almost daily demonstrations this month demanding electoral reforms and the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

The commissioner oversaw the removal of more than 130 million names from the electoral roll and is accused by the CJP of voter fraud. Election authorities said the changes were made to remove duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries.

The CJP was founded in May amid anger over the leaking of exam papers and the poor prospects facing India’s youth.

The movement swiftly became a conduit for India’s Gen Z, many of whom feel disenfranchised during an unemployment crisis under Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s right-wing government. The movement has since forced the resignation of the education minister.

With the political opposition quick to support the protests, Modi has come under intense pressure with some analysts saying he is now facing the worst crisis since he came to office in 2014.

World.title: Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia still on, organisers say, but golf tour postponed
World.content:
Share Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia still on, organisers say, but golf tour postponed on social media

The Asian Cup football tournament is on track to take place in Saudi Arabia early next year, local organisers say, but golf’s Asian Tour has postponed the Saudi International indefinitely in the aftermath of a series of attacks on Riyadh.

Yemen’s Houthi group claimed responsibility for the deadliest attack, which took place on Saturday on Riyadh’s international airport. It killed 14 people and ⁠wounded more than 300.

Australia also withdrew its team from the urban cycling World Championships on Friday, citing safety concerns over travelling to Riyadh, where the event is scheduled to take place in early November.

The Six Kings Slam exhibition tennis tournament in Riyadh has already been moved from October to December while FIFA on Thursday postponed the FIFAe Finals 2026 video game competition in ‌Jeddah until an unspecified future date.

In that environment, serious questions were being asked about whether the 24-team Asian Cup could still go ahead in Saudi Arabia from January 7 to February 5.

Three Saudi Pro League matches, including one featuring Cristiano Ronaldo’s Al-Nassr, were postponed this week while Al-Nassr’s Asian Football Confederation (AFC) Champions League game on Monday was delayed by an hour after Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence said it had intercepted a missile fired towards Riyadh.

AFC chief Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa said earlier this week that a postponement of the continental championships until 2028 was possible if necessary, but the local organising committee (LOC) said on Friday that it was sticking to the original schedule.



“Preparations across all organisational and operational areas are progressing according to the approved schedule, including work on venues, facilities ⁠and supporting services,” it said in a statement.

The LOC “will continue to monitor developments ⁠relevant to the tournament and ensure the appropriate conditions are in place for its successful delivery”.

Attacks in Saudi Arabia disrupt sport calendar

The $5m Saudi International, which is sponsored by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), is the flagship event on the Asian Tour and had been scheduled to take place at Riyadh ⁠Golf Club on November 18-21.

“The decision to postpone was taken following an assessment of the organisational and logistical challenges associated with hosting the tournament and ensuring the event is ⁠delivered to a standard befitting its international stature,” an Asian Tour statement ⁠said.

AusCycling said its decision to withdraw the Australian team from the urban World Championships was made “with the safety and wellbeing of our athletes and staff our highest priority”.

The Australian government is advising travellers to “reconsider” trips to Saudi Arabia in general and Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport in particular “due to recent ‌security incidents”.

The Saudi government has invested heavily in sport through the PIF in recent years, and the Asian Cup was pitched as an early rehearsal for hosting football’s FIFA World Cup in 2034.

World.title: Norway wealth fund urged to ease nuclear arms ban after Gaza investment row
World.content:
Review prompted by Gaza action calls for Norway’s sovereign wealth fund to lift ethical risk limitations on its investments.

A government-appointed committee has called for Norway’s sovereign wealth fund to lift limitations on its investments based on ethical risks, including those regarding nuclear weapons and Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.

In a report released on Thursday, the committee said the world’s largest sovereign wealth fund, which controls assets totalling nearly $2.3 trillion, should be allowed to invest in companies that produce nuclear weapons. With reference to Gaza, it also called for the fund to refrain from involvement in diplomatic issues.

Led by former Central Bank Governor Svein Gjedrem, the committee recommended easing the fund’s investment conditions as part of a broader overhaul that would give its manager, the central bank, greater discretion over how it addresses ethical risks.

The review was prompted in part by controversy over the fund’s disinvestment last year from United States construction giant Caterpillar. The fund said the move was prompted by Caterpillar’s purported involvement in rights violations perpetrated by Israel amid its genocidal war on Gaza and in the occupied West Bank. Washington has since pressured Oslo over the move.

“Parts of the rationale for the appointment of the Committee was the Fund’s management related to the war in Gaza,” the committee commissioned by the government said. In the report, it argued that decisions regarding “another state’s conduct” should not be made by the fund but “reserved for the ordinary diplomatic channels of the Norwegian authorities”.



The unanimous recommendations of the committee in the report, which was submitted to the Ministry of Finance, also called for a review of the fund’s exclusion of investment in companies involved in the production of nuclear weapons.

Citing Norway’s reliance on NATO’s nuclear deterrent and a worsening security environment, the report suggested that investments in companies based in the US, United Kingdom and France that are involved in the production of nuclear weapons should be allowed.

The proposals also extended to reshaping the role of the fund’s independent ethics watchdog, allowing some assessments of potential investments to remain confidential.

‘Pandora’s box’

The report has already provoked a backlash in Norway, with opposition politicians slamming the potential changes. Meanwhile, analysts suggested that weakening ethics considerations could have a wide impact.

“If the Norwegian sovereign wealth fund – often considered a global gold standard – changes its posture towards nuclear weapons, it will open Pandora’s box for many global investors to follow suit,” Lawrence Loh, director of the Centre for Governance and Sustainability at the National University of Singapore Business School, told Al Jazeera.

The committee framed the proposed change as an obligation to protect Norway’s national security, citing the country’s dependence on its allies’ nuclear umbrella.

“The global security situation has changed. Norway is building up its defence capabilities, and the protection provided by NATO’s nuclear umbrella has become increasingly important. The companies that would be reincluded produce weapons that Norway needs for its own defence”, the report argued.

Gareth Evans, former Australian foreign minister, told Al Jazeera the report was “an encouraging initiative in a world that has become alarmingly complacent about the risks of nuclear war, with every major nuclear arms control agreement dead, dying or on life support, and the longstanding taboo against threat or use eroding”.

Amid US President Donald Trump’s shake-up of NATO, European countries are increasingly looking to join France’s nuclear deterrent umbrella.

Trump said on Thursday that Washington is holding talks with Russia and China aimed at denuclearising the countries with the biggest stockpiles of nuclear weapons.

However, Loh warned that shifting the Norwegian fund’s investment conditions could encourage investment by others in nuclear companies “in scenarios different from the Norwegian’s condition of the invested companies being based in allied, nuclear-armed NATO countries”.

World.title: Tesla unveils car that can drive upside down and jump through the air
World.content:
Tesla unveils car that can drive upside down and jump through the air

NewsFeed Tesla unveils car that can drive upside down and jump through the air

Tesla has unveiled an electric sports car that can drive upside down and use rocket-like thrusters to jump and turn mid-air. Developed with Elon Musk’s SpaceX, it can reportedly accelerate to 97km/h in under a second. First promised in 2017, the car is now expected in 2028.

World.title: How Israel’s elections will affect Palestinians
World.content:
NewsFeed How Israel’s elections will affect Palestinians

How Israel votes this month will shape the future of over 5.5 million Palestinians who have no say in the election. Even if there’s a new government, Al Jazeera’s Nida Ibrahim says it’s unlikely to change the situation for Palestinians living under occupation.

World.title: Children aged 5, 8 and 11 killed in US school shooting before suspect shot by bystander
World.content:
"We are stunned and heartbroken by this senseless tragedy," Steven Cook, the top administrative official of the local school district, said in a statement.

"No words can adequately express the grief our community is experiencing."

Police said the attacker was a local 16-year-old boy, but they did not release any further details on him or the identity of the victims.

Police were alerted to an active shooter at Silver Rail Elementary at 12:59 local time (19:59 GMT), Bend Police Department spokeswoman Sheila Miller told reporters.

The first call came from a person who said that an unknown suspect was shooting into their car with a long gun, police said. Photos released from the scene show a red truck with bullet holes.

Minutes later, the local county dispatch received 911 calls reporting that the attacker had entered the school.

Police said he shot at locks on the doors in order to force his way inside.

Local media reports suggested the school received new classroom doors in 2022 which can be locked with the flip of a switch.

A bystander saw the shooting begin to unfold, pursued the attacker into the school and shot him dead, police explained.

Three minutes later, officers first arrived at the scene. They confirmed that the attacker had been killed, and then searched the school.

Oregon Governor Tina Kotek praised the bystander who "heroically intervened" to stop further loss of life.

"Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well," she told a media briefing alongside other officials.

World.title: 'It's really hard to believe' - How Oregon primary school shooting unfolded
World.content:
Four victims, including a teacher and three children aged 5, 8 and 11, were killed in a shooting at a primary school in the US state of Oregon, local police say.

A 16-year-old suspect forced his way into the school by firing at locked doors. He was also killed in the shooting by an armed member of the community who followed the suspect inside the school, police said at a press conference.

Two additional victims, a 7-year-old and another teacher, were hurt and transported to hospital in critical condition.

World.title: Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow
World.content:
The number of ships that have reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz has hit a record high, BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows.

Twelve vessels were attacked between 5 and 11 October - the largest number of weekly strikes reported to the UK's Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency since the US-Israeli war with Iran began. The previous week saw 10 ships reporting attacks.

Six of the vessels were struck last Sunday, according to the UKMTO - a one-day high. So far this week, there have been four reported attacks.

As the number of strikes has risen, the recovery in oil shipments through the strait seen last month has slowed, industry data suggests.

BBC Verify collated incident reports published by the UKMTO on its website and created a timeline based on the first date cited in each report. This is approximate because some incidents use the date of the attack and some the date on which it was reported.

World.title: Zelensky rallies EU support as Trump says Ukraine leader 'more difficult to deal with than Putin'
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has renewed his sharp criticism of Volodymyr Zelensky, saying the Ukrainian leader is "more difficult to deal with than [Russian President Vladimir] Putin".

Speaking to US media on Thursday evening, Trump also called Ukraine's fresh wave of strikes on Russian oil refineries a "disgrace".

Zelensky, who is in Brussels for a summit with EU leaders, had paused the attacks for three days at Trump's request for a ceasefire on energy targets, but said on Thursday the strikes would resume because Moscow had never stopped.

Meanwhile, deadly attacks on Ukraine continued overnight, with several people killed in a Russian drone strike in the north-eastern city of Kharkiv, the regional governor said.

At least 19 people were injured, Oleg Synegubov wrote on Telegram.

Zelensky has not commented on Trump's latest criticism. He arrived at the summit in Brussels flanked by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President AntÃ³nio Costa.

"Of course we supported President Trump's energy ceasefire but we've seen that Russia did not respect it, not a single minute," Von der Leyen told reporters. "Russia escalated and therefore we have to increase sanctions on Russia... We will not lift any sanctions unless Russia stops the war."

Moscow said it had never agreed to the energy ceasefire that Trump suddenly announced last week.

The EU summit's agenda will focus on funding for Ukraine, and helping it get through another cold winter - the fifth since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

"Russia is trying everything to destroy the energy and water infrastructure," Von der Leyen told Zelensky before the summit began, "but we stand by your side, we support you as we did in the other winters."

Zelensky said his country wants the war to end "as quick as possible", but added that Russia is not showing signals that it wants the same thing.

"That's why we have to prepare for the winter. A winter package is not only energy, it's also defence and fundings," he said.

World.title: China tells Israel to stop 'forced establishment' of West Bank settlements
World.content:
Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi has told Israel to stop its "forced establishment" of settlements in the West Bank and reverse its actions, his office said.

The "Palestinian question" is "the greatest historical injustice of this century", Wang told Israeli President Isaac Herzog in a face-to-face meeting on the sidelines of a conference in Azerbaijan on Thursday.

Beijing has been a longstanding supporter of the Palestinian cause and has maintained that a "two-state solution" is the "correct direction".

It has also been positioning itself as a mediator for conflicts in the Middle East.

In 2023 Beijing brokered a deal to restore diplomatic ties between Iran and Saudi Arabia after years of hostility. Earlier this year, it was part of efforts, along with Pakistan, to propose a ceasefire in the US-Israel war against Iran.

Beijing's efforts to tackle the war in Gaza have focused on Palestinian unity.

In 2024 Beijing got rival Palestinian factions to agree to form an interim "national reconciliation government" for the occupied West Bank and Gaza after the war with Israel, although it was never implemented.

Now, Wang says the "immediate priority" is to fully open access to Gaza and stop the continued spread of a "humanitarian catastrophe".

China is willing to work with the international community to get the parties to return to dialogue and "seek a political solution to the conflict", Wang said.

In a post on X, Herzog said he was "pleased" to meet Wang and their talk "focused on the relations between our countries and the situation in the Middle East".

"I emphasised Israel's desire for peace in the region, alongside the strategic threats to our security, first and foremost from Iran and its terror proxies," he wrote.

China maintains close ties with Iran and is the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, which had previously come under US sanctions because of Tehran's nuclear programme.

One year into the ceasefire, people in Gaza continue to live under the regular threat of Israeli strikes, displacement and food security challenges.

Although large-scale bombardment has stopped, Israel has continued strikes in Gaza almost every day. More than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli strikes there in the year since the ceasefire started in October 2025.

The US-brokered ceasefire was the first phase of a deal to end the war in Gaza, which had been triggered by a deadly Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.

But progress into the deal's next phase has been stalled, with both Israel and Hamas accusing each other of violating the terms of their agreement.

World.title: Dad fined after son, 2, died in Cyprus hotel fall
World.content:
A father whose two-year-old boy fell to his death at a five-star hotel in Cyprus has been fined 3,000 euro (Â£2,500).

Joshua Foster thought the window was closed when he placed his son on a sill to show him the view of a waterpark and "lost control" of him, Paphos District Court previously heard.

The toddler fell nearly 40ft (12.1m) from the fourth floor of the King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort on 12 July, the first day of the family's holiday in Chlorakas.

Foster, 37, from Essex, admitted causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act and was sentenced on Friday morning.

He told reporters afterwards: "Thank you for the support. I'm looking forward to going home and being with my wife and daughter."

The auditor, his wife, two children and in-laws had arrived in Cyprus in the early hours of the morning on the date of the incident.

They spent the day carrying out various activities, including visiting the pool, before getting ready for dinner in the evening.

At about 18:00, Foster, his father-in-law and son walked towards an elevator, and his lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, told the court he was in a "good mood" and was playing with his son.

World.title: Bus hits train stopped on French side of Channel Tunnel, with 19 injured
World.content:
"Two trains were on either side of the platform. One was being loaded by heavy goods vehicles ahead of a cross-Channel journey, and another train that had previously been loaded was departing," Cury said.

"For a reason that currently remains unknown, the minibus collided with the departing train.

"The bus did not overturn, it is still upright â but the shock and the collision caused injuries to the people involved."

The incident involved a minibus transporting workers who were about to board Le Shuttle. All were men of different nationalities, she added.

It is not clear whether any British nationals are among the injured.

Cury said it was "the first time an incident of this type has occurred" on an Eurotunnel loading platform.

The BBC's Evan Davis, who was travelling through the Eurotunnel to Calais at the time of the incident, witnessed blue light vehicles "concentrated on one of the platforms" as he entered France.

"There were plenty of cars queueing up at check-in when I drove past just now, and I saw some cars going through check-in, so despite the collision they weren't being held," he said from the scene.

Photos published by local French newspaper La Voix du Nord, external showed a small bus with damage to its front and side standing alongside a train, among a crowd of emergency workers.

Eurostar has released an update saying: "An incident occurred several kilometers away from the Channel Tunnel.

"This incident does not involved or impact Eurostar trains running from and to London. All of Eurostar trains will run as expected."

World.title: At least 33 pupils and teacher killed after school roof collapses in Pakistan
World.content:
At least 33 pupils and a teacher have been killed after a school roof collapsed in the north-western Pakistani city of Peshawar, according to hospital officials.

More than a dozen others are injured, with some in a critical condition.

Emergency services were called to the private Al-Khair school in Dir Colony at 08:48 (03:48 GMT) on Thursday after lessons had begun, rescue official Bilal Faizi told the BBC.

The roof of an upper-floor classroom had collapsed, he said, causing ceilings below to cave in and trap children beneath the debris.

Announcing the arrest of the school's owner, police chief Mian Saeed promised a thorough inquiry into "whether there were any violations of building codes".

Warning: This article contains distressing details

An English teacher from a nearby school said he immediately rushed to the site with other local residents when they heard sirens and the sound of ambulances.

Together, they pulled more than 20 children from the rubble, he said.

"I personally pulled out six children with my own hands. Most of them were alive and talking. But later it was found that they had passed away."

"There was a lot of blood," he said. "One child said he was in a lot of pain. His tongue had dried up in his mouth, [and he was] asking for water."

Sohail, another local resident, said he and others tried to remove children from under the rubble "using shovels".

World.title: 2027: Dickson urges INEC to restore omitted NDC candidates in final list
World.content:
The National Leader of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Seriake Dickson, has urged the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to “promptly” restore omitted names of NDC candidates in the final list of candidates for the 2027 general elections.

Mr Dickson, a former governor of Bayelsa State, appealed in a post on his Facebook page on Thursday night.

“We urge INEC to remedy this apparent omission promptly,” he appealed.

PREMIUM TIMES reports that the NDC governorship candidates in Kano, Kaduna and Cross River States were omitted from the final list of candidates for the 2027 election recently published by INEC on Saturday.

The NDC leadership had attributed the omission to an error.

‘We’re working diligently to correct the omission’

In the Facebook post, Mr Dickson, the Bayelsa West senator, said the NDC was working “diligently” to correct the omission.

“Our candidates and supporters are assured that the party has been working diligently and has taken adequate steps to address the cases of those whose names were not published by INEC a few days ago,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“All affected candidates registered with the party before the statutory 21-day period required by law.”

READ ALSO: Mbah speaks on shootings at NDC secretariat

The national leader said the NDC fielded qualified candidates, from the presidential candidate to those in state houses of assembly, who, he argued, “emerged through a rigorous and painstaking screening process.”

“We are confident that INEC will correct this omission without delay,” he stated.

Mr Dickson said consultations and campaigns would continue in all states while the NDC sustains ongoing engagements with INEC on the missing names of its candidates.

“We will continue lto fight without giving up until we are victorious,” he maintained.

World.title: Why Diri’s defence of Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway makes him a ‘local champion’ – Duke
World.content:
Former Cross River State Governor and presidential candidate for the Peoples Redemption Party in the 2027 general elections, Donald Duke has criticised Bayelsa State Governor Douye Diri’s defence of the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, describing the governor as a “local champion” for allegedly viewing the controversial project through a regional rather than national lens.

PREMIUM TIMES reported that Mr Diri had rejected Mr Duke’s claim that the coastal highway project is unbuildable because of Niger Delta’s swampy terrain, citing roads and bridges constructed in similar conditions in Bayelsa.

But during an interview on Arise TV Morning Show on Thursday, Mr Duke argued that the project was financially impractical. He questioned its necessity and accused the federal government of pursuing what he described as a land grab under the guise of coastal road construction.

“If the governor of Bayelsa did say so, I don’t know the fellow, but if he did say so, I think he is just being a local champion,” Mr Duke said.

“He is seeing within the ambit of his state…I am looking at the totality of Nigeria.”

Mr Duke argued that the federal government should assess the project against the country’s financial capacity and competing development needs rather than regional interests.

“We don’t have the kind of money to do it,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Duke questions highway’s feasibility

The former governor renewed his opposition to the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, insisting that the project’s proposed route through the Niger Delta raised questions about its affordability, necessity and eventual destination.

He argued the project should be called the Lagos Coastal Highway, saying its name implied a connection to Calabar that he doubted would materialise.

“It’s actually the Lagos Coastal Highway. Don’t call it Lagos-Calabar. And I’ve said that if I do that, it will not get there. And the minister has vindicated me. And he also talks about the terrain,” he said.

Mr Duke acknowledged that constructing a road across Bayelsa was technically possible but argued that the difficult terrain and financial implications made the project impractical.

“It’s not that you can’t build a road across Bayelsa, but it’s just not affordable. And it doesn’t make sense because there is a road going to Calabar, if that is it,” he said.

He also alleged the project could serve interests beyond transportation, pointing to land reclamation and sand-filling activities along the proposed route.

“To me, it’s a land grab. Let’s be honest with ourselves,” he said.

Mr Duke further questioned the reported decision to divert the proposed highway onto the East-West Road, asking why the existing route had not been adequately considered from the outset.

“They have now said that they’re going to divert the road onto the East-West Highway. Weren’t they aware of the East-West Highway from the get-go?” he asked.

Questions funding priorities

Mr Duke also faulted the federal government’s decision to pursue the project in the face of Nigeria’s financial constraints, saying the country was borrowing to finance sections of the highway.

“We’re literally borrowing even to fund the stretch, the Epe stretch. We’re borrowing. We can’t do it,” he said.

He questioned the government’s spending priorities, citing what he described as inadequate releases for healthcare despite the sector’s importance to governance.

“Look, this programme, I think even this morning, you said health, which is critical to governance. Only N36 million was released last year, from a budget of almost ₦300 billion. So what are our priorities?” he asked.

Mr Duke’s criticism centres on whether the coastal highway represents a sound use of public funds at a time when the government faces competing demands for investment in essential services.

World.title: National policing bill to reach National Assembly in a week – Gbajabiamila
World.content:
Femi Gbajabiamila, chief of staff to President Bola Tinubu and chairperson of the Presidential Working Group on the National Policing Bill, said the proposed framework would be presented to the National Assembly in “about a week or so,” after integrating input from state governors.

Mr Gbajabiamila disclosed this to journalists in Abuja after chairing the committee meeting at the State House on Thursday, presidential spokesperson Bayo Onanuga stated.

“The National Policing Bill is more or less ready for transmission to the National Assembly,” he said, adding that the committee will sit one more time to “make sure every area is covered.”

PREMIUM TIMES reported that the committee was created on 7 July after the National Assembly passed the state police bill to fulfil one of President Tinubu’s key security reforms. While the constitutional amendment changes the law to allow state police, it does not provide the practical rules on how to run them, necessitating the creation of the committee.

To kickstart its mandate, the committee launched a seven-week operational roadmap running from 27 July to 14 September. The roadmap was adopted to audit existing laws like the Police Act 2020 and write the initial draft of the new law.

During this phase, the committee opened a crucial two-week window for public consultation, inviting memoranda and policy proposals from security experts, civil society, and everyday Nigerians to ensure citizen-centred accountability. The committee subsequently received inputs from Nigerians.

While the committee engineered the bill’s operational standards in Abuja, the foundational constitutional amendment advanced concurrently across the country. To legally scale, the amendment requires ratification by 24 of the 36 State Houses of Assembly. Progress has steadily gained traction, with states like Edo, Osun, Oyo, Rivers, and Zamfara formally passing the ratification bill.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Governors’ undisclosed observations

“The governors have one or two observations,” Mr Gbajabiamila said, not giving details.

However, many Nigerians, including lawmakers and former police chiefs, have expressed worries over potential abuse of the system by governors.

Describing the bill as “the most consequential Bill of the administration,” Mr Gbajabiamila disputed rumoured pushbacks by states yet to pass the amendment bill

“I see no reason why anyone will want to have a rethink on it,” Mr Gbajabiamila was quoted as saying, noting that there was a “national consensus” among Nigerians on the matter.

World.title: ﻿Stakeholders seek unified framework for school safety in Nigeria
World.content:
Stakeholders at the 7th Annual Summit of the Education Writers Association of Nigeria (EWAN) have called for a unified national framework to coordinate efforts to protect schools from attacks and other security threats.

The stakeholders made the call on Wednesday at the summit in Lagos, themed “Schools Under Threat: From Reactive Responses to Sustainable Protection.”

The stakeholders highlighted that Nigeria had introduced several policies and initiatives to improve school safety. Still, weak coordination among government agencies, security authorities, state governments, schools, communities and civil society organisations continued to undermine their effectiveness.

The summit featured a diverse lineup of speakers and panellists, including the National Coordinator, Financing Safe Schools in Nigeria, Halima Iliya; Lagos Commissioner for Basic and Secondary Education, Jamiu Alli-Balogun; Executive Director of the Wole Soyinka Centre for Investigative Journalism (WSCIJ), Motunrayo Alaka; and other stakeholders in education and security.

Identified gaps

Representing the summit chairperson, Oluwatoyin Ogundipe, a professor and Dean of the Faculty of Education, University of Lagos, Joseph Awoyinka said fragmentation remained a major gap in Nigeria’s approach to school safety.

“Policy exists, but implementation is inconsistent,” said Mr Ogundipe, who is the Chairman of the Governing Board of the National Universities Commission (NUC).

He called for a unified national approach that would align federal, state and local efforts, clarify responsibilities and strengthen accountability.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Coordination should not depend on personality or political affiliation. It must be institutionalised,” he said.

Mr Ogundipe also said school safety should go beyond physical security measures such as perimeter fencing and surveillance cameras.

He called for functional emergency preparedness plans in schools, including evacuation procedures, communication protocols, safe rooms and trained personnel capable of responding during emergencies.

He said rural and conflict-prone schools require particular attention, while school safety should also be incorporated into government budgeting and planning.

“For too long, our responses have been largely reactive, mobilising security after an incident, issuing statements of condemnation, and providing temporary relief to affected communities. While these actions are necessary, they are not sufficient,” Mr Ogundipe said.

Existing interventions

Nigeria has had the Safe Schools Initiative since 2014, following the abduction of 276 schoolgirls from Chibok, Borno State.

The country also ratified the Safe Schools Declaration in 2019 and developed a National Plan on Financing Safe Schools for 2023-2026.

In her comments, Ms Iliya said the federal government had established a national response coordination centre and conducted needs assessments to identify vulnerable schools and communities.

She said the programme also involved training parents, teachers, students and community actors, while security agencies had been supported to improve their capacity to respond to threats.

According to her, states are expected to integrate the Safe Schools programme into their annual budgets.

Security agencies

In his keynote address, the Inspector-General of Police, Tunji Disu, represented by the Lagos State Commissioner of Police, Tijani Fatai, also called for stronger coordination between security agencies, schools and communities.

Mr Disu said protecting schools sustainably requires shifting from responding to attacks after they occur to identifying vulnerabilities, gathering intelligence, and preventing threats.

He urged school administrators, teachers, parents, students and community members to report credible security concerns through appropriate channels.

He also stressed the importance of trust between security agencies and communities, saying effective partnerships depend on professional conduct, accountability and public confidence.

Mr Disu said schools should have safety arrangements and emergency procedures suited to their locations, sizes and levels of vulnerability.

“The future of our nation depends, in no small measure, on the opportunities we create for our children today. Protecting those opportunities is a responsibility we must all take seriously,” he said.

READ ALSO: FG approves N15bn for 2026 Safe Schools programme

Role of journalists

Ms Alaka said education journalists also have a responsibility to identify vulnerabilities before they result in attacks.

She urged journalists to understand what safe-school standards should look like and to visit schools regularly rather than focusing only on crises, government announcements, or donations.

EWAN Chairperson Mojeed Alabi similarly urged journalists to move beyond reporting attacks after they happen and to investigate warning signs, funding, emergency preparedness, and whether authorities implement promised safety measures.

Mr Alabi said the effectiveness of school safety efforts should ultimately be measured by whether children can attend school without fear, teachers can teach safely and parents can confidently send their children to school.

World.title: APC proposes 12-state campaign tour for Tinubu ahead of 2027 elections
World.content:
The All Progressives Congress (APC) has proposed a nationwide campaign rally schedule covering the 36 states of the federation and the Federal Capital Territory ahead of the 2027 general elections.

The proposed campaign is scheduled to begin in Kaduna on 24 October 2026 and end with a grand rally in Lagos on 9 January 2027.

The itinerary lists 12 states where President Bola Tinubu is expected to appear for the APC’s presidential campaign rallies as the party seeks to mobilise support across the country ahead of the 2027 general elections.

Kaduna is listed as the starting point of the proposed nationwide campaign tour, with Mr Tinubu expected to attend the opening rally in the state on 24 October 2026.

From Kaduna, the President is expected to appear at the APC campaign rally in Port Harcourt, Rivers State, on 7 November, followed by Jos, Plateau State, on 14 November and Ibadan, Oyo State, on 21 November.

Mr Tinubu is then scheduled to appear at rallies in Maiduguri, Borno State, on 25 November, Enugu, Enugu State, on 28 November, and Bauchi, Bauchi State, on 29 November.

The President is also expected to campaign in Sokoto, Sokoto State, on 4 December, Asaba, Delta State, on 12 December, and Kano, Kano State, on 17 December.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

In January 2027, Mr Tinubu is expected to appear at the APC rally in Yola, Adamawa State, on 4 January before the proposed campaign tour concludes with a grand rally in Lagos on 9 January.

According to the APC, the proposed itinerary is designed to cover the country’s six geopolitical zones, with the party focusing on grassroots mobilisation, party unity and engagement with Nigerians.

“From North to South, East to West, the focus remains on grassroots mobilisation, party unity and meaningful engagement with Nigerians,” the party said.

However, the APC said the schedule is subject to adjustments.

World.title: NAHCON pushes sustainable Hajj fund management digital transformation at global forum
World.content:
The Chairman of the National Hajj Commission of Nigeria (NAHCON), Ismail Yusuf, has called for strategic investments and digital transformation to strengthen Hajj fund management, reduce pilgrimage costs and safeguard financial benefits for future generations of pilgrims.

Mr Yusuf made the call while serving as a prominent international panellist at the 8th International Hajj Fund Forum (IHFF) 2026, held on Thursday at the Jakarta International Convention Centre in Indonesia.

The global forum, hosted by Indonesia’s Hajj Financial Management Agency (Badan Pengelola Keuangan Haji – BPKH), brought together policymakers, Sharia finance experts and institutional leaders to explore sustainable approaches to managing Hajj funds amid rising economic uncertainties.

Digital transformation key to sustainable Hajj management

The forum, held under the theme “Sustainable Hajj Fund Management Through Strategic Synergy and Digital Transformation,” examined the growing macroeconomic challenges affecting pilgrimage operations, rising costs and the need to preserve the long-term financial benefits of Hajj funds.

According to a statement issued on Thursday by NAHCON’s Head of Information and Publications, Shafii Mohammed, Mr Yusuf shared Nigeria’s experience and perspectives during a high-level panel discussion alongside BPKH Executive Board Chief Fadlul Imansyah and other international dignitaries.

He emphasised the importance of coordination among relevant agencies, stronger institutional partnerships, and robust digital systems to protect Hajj operations from global financial volatility.

“The future of Hajj administration depends on our collective ability to innovate. Managing Hajj funds efficiently is no longer just about financing the immediate next pilgrimage; it is about protecting wealth and ensuring sustainable benefits for future generations of pilgrims.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

By leaning into technological transformations and cementing strategic ties with key global partners like Indonesia, NAHCON is positioning Nigeria at the forefront of transparent and economically sound Hajj operations in line with the interests of current and future generations of pilgrims,” Mr Yusuf said.

NAHCON eyes strategic investments to reduce costs

Beyond digital transformation, the NAHCON chairman highlighted the need to expand investments in high-yielding infrastructure projects across the Hajj value chain.

He identified hospitality and logistics as key areas where strategic investments could reduce pilgrim accommodation costs while generating sustainable returns for the Hajj fund.

He said such investments would strengthen the financial foundation of Hajj administration and reduce exposure to rising costs associated with pilgrimage operations.

The approach aligns with the broader objective of ensuring that Hajj funds are managed not only to meet immediate operational needs but also to create lasting economic value for future pilgrims.

Nigeria and Indonesia seek stronger financial cooperation

The forum also featured opening remarks from Indonesian dignitaries, including the Minister of Hajj and Umrah, K.H. Mochamad Yusuf, and the Vice Minister of Finance, Juda Agung.

Participants commended Nigeria’s active involvement in the discussions and its interest in strengthening strategic partnerships with other Muslim-majority countries.

The engagements focused on leveraging financial technologies, institutional cooperation, and sustainable investment models to modernise Hajj administration and improve pilgrimage fund management.

Step towards sustainable Hajj financing

NAHCON’s participation in the 8th International Hajj Fund Forum represents a significant step in Nigeria’s efforts to develop more autonomous, technology-driven and sustainable frameworks for managing Hajj funds.

The commission’s engagement with international partners is expected to strengthen knowledge-sharing and cooperation on financial innovation, investment strategies and institutional reforms aimed at improving Hajj operations.

The broader objective is to establish a financially sustainable system that can support present-day pilgrims while preserving wealth and delivering long-term benefits to future generations.

World.title: Why Tinubu will not campaign in all 36 states – Campaign Council
World.content:
A member of the media and strategic communications committee of the All Progressives Congress (APC) Presidential Campaign Council, Obafemi George, has defended President Bola Tinubu’s decision not to visit all 36 states during his re-election campaign, saying the president will prioritise governance while the party mobilises support for his second term.

Mr George said the president had assessed the country’s electoral map and decided that sustaining the gains of his administration was more important than embarking on a nationwide campaign tour.

He spoke on Arise TV’s Prime Time programme on Thursday, amid preparations by the APC for the 2027 presidential election.

“The president has looked at the electoral map of the country and decided that what is more important at this time is to sustain the gains for Nigerians,” he said.

Mr George argued that there was no constitutional requirement for a presidential candidate to visit every state during an election campaign.

He said Mr Tinubu would continue to promote his administration’s policies while ensuring that government business did not suffer during the campaign period.

Tinubu’s economic reforms

Mr George also defended the president’s economic policies, arguing that the reforms had restored investor confidence and created opportunities for economic growth, despite the hardship experienced by Nigerians.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He said investors had been leaving Nigeria before Mr Tinubu assumed office in May 2023 because of inflation, macroeconomic instability and difficulties accessing foreign exchange.

According to him, some international companies and financial institutions, including JPMorgan Chase and Shell, have since shown renewed interest in Nigeria because of the country’s economic outlook.

“They are coming to Nigeria to invest because of the growth trajectory,” he said.

Mr George cited the removal of petrol subsidy as one of the administration’s major economic decisions, noting that Nigeria had previously spent more than 90 per cent of its revenue on subsidy payments.

He also criticised opposition politicians who have promised to reverse some of the administration’s policies, saying all presidential candidates in 2023 had supported subsidy removal.

He argued that economic restructuring often comes with temporary hardship and said the administration’s reforms were intended to address longstanding structural problems.

Mr George maintained that economic indicators cited by institutions such as the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund supported the administration’s position that the economy was moving towards recovery.

NELFUND, healthcare reforms

Mr George also highlighted social intervention programmes introduced under Mr Tinubu, particularly the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND), which provides financial support to eligible students in tertiary institutions.

He said the scheme had expanded access to higher education for students who might otherwise struggle to pay their fees.

The official noted that the administration had also introduced healthcare interventions to support indigent women, including funding for medical procedures.

He further cited reforms intended to improve access to dialysis treatment, arguing that the measures would help people who previously struggled to afford the procedure.

Mr George said beneficiaries of these programmes and other government interventions would help communicate the administration’s achievements to voters ahead of the 2027 election.

Why governors are backing Tinubu

Mr George also rejected suggestions that the backing of 33 state governors for Mr Tinubu was driven solely by the advantages of incumbency.

He argued that the governors were supporting the president because they had benefited from the administration’s economic policies, which he said had increased the resources available to state and local governments.

“They are supporting the president because they are performing at the sub-national level, and that performance is only possible because of the macroeconomic policy at the centre. Allocation has tripled,” he said.

“That is why a local government can now build roads.”

Mr George said the administration would focus on consolidating its reforms rather than reversing key policies ahead of the election.

He ruled out a return to pre-2023 fuel prices or foreign exchange arrangements within 90 days, arguing that economic transformation could not happen overnight.

World.title: NBBF: Abdullahi wins presidency as court battle, protests cloud election
World.content:
Mustapha Abdullahi, Director-General of the Energy Commission of Nigeria, has been elected president of the Nigeria Basketball Federation (NBBF) after a disputed election in Abuja on Thursday, with his victory coming amid allegations of irregularities and protests by rival candidates.

Mr Abdullahi secured 40 of the 48 votes cast at the Bola Ahmed Tinubu International Conference Centre, defeating former D’Tigers captain Olumide Oyedeji, who received eight votes.

Former Nigerian international Ejike Ugboaja received no votes, while another presidential aspirant, Igoche Mark, withdrew from the contest a day before the election, citing concerns about the fairness and credibility of the process.

Mr Ugboaja also walked out of the proceedings after voting began, alleging that the process had been hijacked in favour of Mr Abdullahi. The election nevertheless continued, producing a new president for the federation.

The outcome followed a petition dated 12 October, in which Mr Mark, Mr Oyedeji and Mr Ugboaja asked President Bola Tinubu to direct the National Sports Commission (NSC) to halt the election and investigate alleged breaches of the NBBF constitution.

In the letter made available to PREMIUM TIMES, the three aspirants accused outgoing president Musa Kida of compromising the process to favour Mr Abdullahi. They also alleged that more than 15 state basketball association chairmen and representatives had been removed and replaced shortly before the election.

The allegations have not been independently established. Mr Kida and Mr Abdullahi have not responded to the claims made in the petition either.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Election proceeds amid legal challenge

The controversy surrounding the election extended beyond the withdrawals and allegations at the congress.

A Federal High Court in Abuja adjourned a suit challenging the legality of the NBBF elective congress until 3 November, allowing the election to proceed while the legal challenge remained pending.

The suit was filed by former D’Tigers coach Ayodele Bakare against the NBBF and the NSC. Mr Bakare, who was disqualified from contesting the presidency after submitting his nomination forms after the deadline, is challenging the validity of the extraordinary congress held in Yola, Adamawa State.

The election also followed a directive from the International Basketball Federation (FIBA) that the NBBF conclude its board election by 15 October. The deadline formed part of the process for ending Mr Kida’s tenure and installing a new administration.

Mr Kida, who led the federation from 2017, had earlier said he would not seek a third term, bringing his eight-year administration to an end.

At the congress, NSC Chairman Shehu Dikko urged candidates and other basketball officials to put their differences aside and work together after the election.

“Today is the day to show that we are for basketball. Whatever it is, let’s put the ball to a stop here and see how we can move forward together as one family,” Mr Dikko said.

Who is this new NBBF president?

According to his LinkedIn profile, Mr Abdullahi is a chartered engineer and a member of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers. He began doctoral research at the University of Manchester in 2016, initially enrolling for an MPhil before advancing to a PhD.

He holds a master’s degree from the University of Salford’s School of Computing, Science and Engineering and a bachelor’s degree in mechanical engineering from Kano University of Technology, Wudil.

His research interests include acoustic engineering, particularly computational and experimental studies of acoustic wave propagation and its applications. His professional experience also includes more than six years at Nigeria’s National Space Research and Development Agency, where he worked in space technology.

Personal milestones

Mr Abudullahi has described his election as the culmination of a longstanding personal connection with basketball, recalling that he once borrowed money to buy a pair of shoes to pursue the sport as a young boy growing up in northern Nigeria.

“As a young boy growing up in Northern Nigeria, my basketball journey began on grassroots courts, driven by a passion so strong that I once had to borrow money to buy a pair of basketball shoes,” he wrote in a Facebook post after his election.

He said the presidency represented a responsibility to develop the game and create opportunities for young people.

“This is more than a personal milestone; it is a call to serve and a commitment to the future of Nigerian basketball,” he added.

Mr Abdullahi has pledged to work with basketball officials and other groups to expand grassroots participation, improve facilities and strengthen domestic competitions. His administration is also expected to address concerns about player welfare, funding and the organisation of the domestic game.

Ugo Udezue was elected vice-president unopposed, having emerged as the sole candidate for the position.

Challenges ahead

The new president takes over a federation whose national teams have recorded notable international successes, particularly the women’s team, D’Tigress.

Unfortunately, the domestic basketball structure continues to face questions over funding, competitions and development pathways.

Improving on past performances will require consistent player development, effective administration and support for domestic competitions.

Mr Abdullahi’s immediate challenge, however, will also be to address the divisions exposed by the election and build confidence among officials and other members of the basketball community who questioned the process.

World.title: Elon Musk unveils Tesla’s ‘flying’ car
World.content:
Tesla CEO Elon Musk unveiled what he described as a “flying” car, equipped with thrusters, during a livestreamed event at his SpaceX rocket company’s facility on Thursday.

Technical and regulatory challenges have so far prevented the much-hyped flying car sector from getting off the ground.

Musk revealed his new Roadster sports car during a launch event at a SpaceX test facility in Texas.

During the demo, which was livestreamed on Tesla’s X account, the car launched from a steep ramp and landed on its wheels.

“Flying cars are real,” Musk said during the event.

He added that the vehicle’s “success is not guaranteed” but that “it will probably work.”

Musk said the car was equipped with “ultra high-pressure air tanks” to propel itself into the air.

The tech billionaire described the development as “what happens when you have a collaboration with the world’s best car company and the world’s best rocket company,” referring to Tesla and SpaceX.

The vehicle would go into production in 2028, he said.

American aviation pioneer Glenn Curtiss debuted the first flying car prototype in 1917.

But successful designs have become more seriously contemplated only in recent years as electric motors and high-performance batteries have advanced.

AFP

World.title: A saint has joined the angels – Tope Alabi mourns Toluwanisings
World.content:
Nigerian gospel singer Tope Alabi has expressed sadness over the passing of gospel artiste Olayemi Bolaji, popularly known as Toluwanisings, who died at age 41.

Alabi took to her social media platforms to pay tribute to the late singer and said she finds comfort in her faith in spite of the painful news.

She described the news as a major shock, admitting that she was still struggling to come to terms with the loss.

According to her, her Christian faith gives her hope and comfort, adding that she strongly believed that the departed singer is now with the Lord.

“This is such a big shock! I still can’t wrap my head around this. It hurts, but I will not sorrow as those who have no hope.

“I find comfort in knowing that a saint has joined the angels.

“Toluwanisings, rest on, dear one, in the bosom of your Lord.

“May God comfort and strengthen your family, friends, and colleagues. You will forever be remembered,” she wrote.

The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that Toluwanising’s sudden death was announced by his family on Wednesday night. (NAN)

World.title: AI is coming for every company, says Nvidia boss
World.content:
File image

Artificial intelligence will ultimately become a key aspect of all companies, the head of AI chip giant Nvidia said during a visit to Stockholm, where he urged Europe to ramp up its AI industry.

“Every single company will be an AI company eventually. Every single industry will be impacted by AI,” Jensen Huang told an event late Thursday, part of a European tour that includes a Nvidia-hosted conference in Berlin next week.

“The important thing for us is to recognise that Europe needs to build out the entire stack,” he said, referring to the AI technology chain from data centres to chatbots and other apps.

Speaking later to AFP, Huang said his company had invested $8 billion in Europe over the past year.

“We’ve strategically invested in different parts of that ecosystem, really high quality companies that we believe could help lift it, the whole ecosystem in Europe,” he said, citing the British data centre and AI cloud provider Nscale and the Dutch cloud provider Nebius as examples.

“In the last one year, we’ve invested $8 billion already. We have another couple of billion dollars in the pipeline,” he added. “We’re helping Europe create the AI ecosystem.”

Huang was in Stockholm for the launch of Sferical One, a Swedish supercomputer using Nvidia chips that will keep sensitive Swedish data and expertise in the country.

During his visit, Volvo Cars also announced it was expanding its partnership with Nvidia to improve safety technology in its planned self-driving vehicles.

World.title: 2027: Opposition fragmented; It’ll take magic to stop Tinubu -  Dan Ulasi
World.content:
Dan Ulasi.

A Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) chieftain, Chief Dan Ulasi, said the fragmentation of opposition parties ahead of the 2027 general election could make it difficult to stop President Bola Tinubu from securing a second term.

Ulasi stated this on Friday during an interview on Arise Television’s The Morning Show, where he discussed divisions among opposition leaders and reported disagreements within the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), the party of former Anambra State governor Peter Obi.

He said the opposition was more divided than it was before the 2023 presidential election, warning that underestimating Tinubu’s political strategy would be a mistake.

“In 2023, I said on this platform that if anybody takes President Tinubu for granted, you’re doing it at your own peril,” Ulasi said.

Describing Tinubu as one of Nigeria’s most strategic politicians, the PDP chieftain recalled an opposition meeting held before the 2023 election, where some attendees reportedly expressed confidence that former Vice President Atiku Abubakar would defeat Tinubu.
