World.title: UPDATE: Another delay in case of murder-accused club cricketer
World.content:
Tristan Perez – who stands accused of murdering girlfriend Elana Brooke – has been at the centre of ongoing postponements in recent court proceedings.

A few weeks ago, Perez appeared in the Wynberg Regional Court, but following a procedural issue relating to documentation provided to the defence, the case was postponed until 15 October.

Upon his latest appearance this week, the case was again postponed to 17 November, apparently to allow him a final opportunity to resolve outstanding legal fees which he owes his lawyer.



According to Brooke’s ex-husband and family spokesperson, David, the court warned that no further postponement would be granted for this reason.

His bail was extended.

“The continued delays are obviously frustrating but we welcome the court’s firm stance and remain focused on seeing this matter progress and getting justice for Elana,” David commented.



Tristan Perez stands accused of murder

Back in March, police first apprehended Perez after suspecting his involvement in the murder of Brooke after what was reportedly suspected to be a heated argument.

According to reports, police were granted permission to check Perez’s phone, where they found a recording of an escalating argument, and suspicions that it ended with the tragic killing of Brooke. She was 46.



Perez reportedly told officers that Brooke had died by suicide. With Perez having been released on bail, and after a series of court appearances and postponements, David said there is still hope that progress is being made.

“Thank you to everyone who continues to stand beside us,” he commented. “Your support means more than you know.”



Well-known former club cricketer now awaits his fate

Perez was a mainstay in Cape Town’s club cricket scene for several years, but Claremont Cricket Club had already abruptly ended his membership in mid-February due to “disciplinary matters arising from conduct deemed to be inconsistent with the ethos, values and spirit of the club.”

According to the Club Cricket website, just before his arrest, Perez had just recently scored a record-breaking double century for Claremont Cricket Club’s second XI, smashing 237 runs off 113 balls.

World.title: Iconic waterside restaurant returns to Durban after 20 years
World.content:
A beloved name in Durban’s hospitality scene will be returning soon, with Thirsty’s Dockside Tavern targeting a reopening next year.

After two years of searching for a suitable site, negotiating and changing plans, the team behind the iconic Durban name has finally signed a new lease. The reopening is still dependent on licensing, but co-owner Brett Michielin said the target is to have Thirsty’s back in business early next year.

Michielin said he first approached former owner Bob Humphreys about bringing the venue back.



“I asked him if I had his blessing and if he wanted to partner with me on this, and he said, ‘Yes, let’s go for it’,” Michielin revealed to IOL.

The pair then began looking for a new site, with Michielin making it clear that Thirsty’s needs to retain one of the features that helped make it famous: It has to be near water.

Bringing back a Durban institution

Thirsty’s Dockside Tavern first opened in September 1995 at the site of the old King’s Gun Battery near Durban harbour.

Humphreys had spotted a derelict building at the harbour mouth and saw its potential as an entertainment venue. Alongside business partners Tony Dickinson and Tony Bolt, he transformed it into a popular pub with a distinctive waterfront setting and views of the harbour.

The venue quickly became a favourite among locals and international visitors, offering patrons the chance to enjoy a drink while watching ships move through one of South Africa’s busiest ports.

Sadly, the hotspot closed its doors in January 2007, after the National Ports Authority (NPA) needed to demolish the building to widen the Durban Harbour mouth.



Now, almost three decades after it first opened, the name could once again become part of Durban’s hospitality landscape.

But for Michielin, the comeback is about more than reopening a restaurant.

“I want that soul again”

Announcing the news on Facebook, Michielin said he hopes Thirsty’s can play a small role in reviving the city’s restaurant and hospitality scene.

“There was a time when Durban had a restaurant industry that was impossible to ignore,” he said.

“It had characters. It had legends. It had chefs who were artists, restaurateurs who were larger than life and restaurants where people came together, celebrated, argued, laughed, fell in love and probably drank far more than they should have.”

“It had soul. And I want to see that soul again.”

A new chapter for Thirsty’s

For former regulars, the planned reopening offers a chance to see a familiar Durban institution return. But Michielin has bigger ambitions for the new Thirsty’s.

He wants the venue to encourage young chefs to open restaurants in Durban, inspire restaurateurs to take risks and help give people a reason to visit the city for its food and hospitality. He also hopes the return will bring together the old guard and a new generation.

“I want the old legends to come out and show the youngsters how it was done,” he said.

“And I want the youngsters to come along and show us old farts how it’s going to be done.” he added.

The ultimate goal, he said, is to bring back some of the swagger that once defined Durban’s restaurant scene.

The exact new location has not yet been revealed, but the team has signed its lease and is targeting March or April 2027, subject to licensing.

World.title: Suliman Carrim could face further charges over alleged municipal corruption
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - North West businessman Suliman Carrim could face further charges linked to alleged fraud and corruption involving the Ngaka Modiri Molema District Municipality.

Carrim was arrested at OR Tambo International Airport on Thursday by the Madlanga Commission’s Recommendations Task Team as he was about to board a flight to the United Arab Emirates (UAE).

He is expected to appear in the Pretoria Magistrate’s Court on Friday on a charge of failing to appear before the Madlanga Commission of Inquiry.

READ | Suliman Carrim nabbed at OR Tambo

The 49-year-old’s arrest followed his failure to appear before the commission, which subsequently laid a criminal complaint against him.

According to police, Carrim had a return ticket when he was arrested and was due to return to South Africa on 28 October.

He has also been implicated in alleged corruption and questionable dealings involving alleged underworld figure Vusimuzi “Cat” Matlala.



National police spokesperson Athlenda Mathe said Carrim had been flagged by the Cold Case Unit in connection with fraud and corruption allegations under investigation involving the Ngaka Modiri Molema District Municipality in North West.

The team was alerted that this individual was flying out of the country. They flagged him and alerted the Cold Case Unit, which then alerted the Commission’s Recommendations Task, as they have been working closely together,” Mathe said.

World.title: Brand SA banks on 'renewal' to attract investment to South Africa
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Brand South Africa says the country is experiencing a period of renewal as it seeks to attract investment at the Investing in Africa Conference in London.

The organisation aims to position South Africa as a premier investment destination, despite geopolitical tensions and rising oil prices that are prompting many countries to focus more on domestic priorities.

Brand South Africa’s Advocate Cawekazi Mahlati says the conference is more than a talk shop, describing it as a deal-making platform for which the organisation has prepared extensively in the hope of securing investment.

Mahlati says South Africa is highlighting opportunities in fintech, infrastructure, energy and tourism.

Brand South Africa is also pointing to developments it believes strengthen the country’s investment case, including its removal from the Financial Action Task Force’s grey list, the end of rolling blackouts and a credit rating upgrade -- the country’s first in nearly two decades.

World.title: Boxer murders: Minister urges public to stop sharing CCTV footage
World.content:
ESHOWE - Employment and Labour Minister Makhosazana Meth has appealed to the public to stop sharing CCTV footage of the killing of three female managers at a Boxer supermarket in Eshowe, KwaZulu-Natal, urging people to show empathy towards the victims’ grieving families.

The murders took place on 10 October, reportedly following a disciplinary process.

The footage circulating on social media shows a man dressed in black standing at the doorway of an office where the three managers were seated.

He then opens fire repeatedly, with all three women shot. The footage shows them attempting to take cover as the gunman continues firing.

In a statement, Boxer said it had extended its condolences to the families of the victims and was working with the South African Police Service (SAPS) and other authorities as the investigation continued.

Meth has called on law enforcement to leave no stone unturned in their efforts to bring those responsible to justice.

“No person should ever fear for their life or personal safety while carrying out their duties and responsibilities in the workplace,” she said.

The killings have sparked widespread reactions on social media. While many users have expressed horror and condemned the attack, others have voiced sympathy for the alleged gunman, claiming he may have worked in a toxic environment.

Some comments have been criticised for appearing to justify the killings.

“We cannot speculate,” said University of Johannesburg academic Professor Corne Buitendag, who focuses on gender-based violence and gender equality.

Buitendag said South Africans should not normalise violence or shift blame for the killings.

While crime, including violence against women, remains a serious concern, she warned against becoming desensitised to violent incidents, whether they receive widespread media coverage or not.

She also cautioned against arguments that frame the incident as three women against one man, saying such narratives can reinforce a sense of entitlement among some men.

“Even if you are disgruntled, you cannot kill,” Buitendag said.

She added that social media comments around the murders that excuse or justify the violence should be condemned.

World.title: ANC condemns killing of two members during KZN campaign
World.content:
DURBAN - KwaZulu-Natal police have launched a manhunt following the fatal shooting of two African National Congress (ANC) members in Umgababa, south of Durban.

Three other people were injured in the attack and are recovering in hospital.

The victims were part of an ANC campaign team conducting door-to-door campaigning, accompanied by two bodyguards, when a gunman opened fire from a bakkie.

The killings have raised fresh concerns about political violence ahead of the local government elections. The incident comes just days after two ANC Youth League members were murdered in Ekurhuleni.

READ | Umgababa shooting leaves ANC members fearful

ANC KwaZulu-Natal spokesperson Sifiso Sonjica condemned the killings, describing the attack as a serious concern for the country’s democracy.

“It’s a serious concern. The democracy we fought for is that we must fight elections using the ballot. We have seen a lot of these killings. This was brazen,” he said.

“We are a leader of the society as ANC, and we have full confidence that the police will crack this case. We generally will hope that this is not an attack to democracy itself.

“We have seen a lot of these killings, ANC members, but our view is that nobody must be killed for whatever reason.”

Police investigations are continuing as authorities work to identify and arrest those responsible.

World.title: Western Cape motorsport precinct targets 2031 Grand Prix
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Blue Mountain Racing CEO Bobby Hartslief says the prospect of Formula One returning to the African continent is encouraging for South African motorsport fans.

“I think South African motorsport fans should be encouraged by the development,” Hartslief said.

“It is a significant move away from what they have been doing across the world in the last years,” he added.

Rwanda is expected to host Africa’s first Formula One Grand Prix since 1993 in the early 2030s, following reports of a decade-long deal with the country.

Rwanda has been pursuing a race for several years, using sport to boost its international profile and attract investment.

World.title: The final lap? Two days on the campaign trail with Trump
World.content:
WASHINGTON - Donald Trump is crisscrossing America to drum up votes for Republican candidates facing tough midterm election races, but the US president's rallies are often hijacked by his basking in the adulation of fervent supporters.

AFP followed him on Tuesday and Wednesday during one such trip out West, a rapid succession of flights and rallies -- in a glacial valley in Alaska, on an arid plain in Arizona and in the forests of Montana.

The Republican leader is betting on his ability to mobilise voters despite polls predicting that his party will lose control of one or both chambers of Congress on November 3.

A Fox News poll released Thursday puts his approval rating at just 36 percent, a new low, largely because of growing dissatisfaction over the cost of living.

"Please pretend that I am on the ballot," the 80-year-old leader, wearing a red cap, told the crowd Wednesday in Bullhead City, Arizona.

— Nostalgia for 2024 —

In 2024, he got nearly 78 percent of the vote in the county where he was speaking in Arizona. The other two counties he visited, in Alaska and Montana, also gave him decisive victories over Democrat Kamala Harris.

Donald Trump makes no secret of his preference for travelling to friendly territory, telling reporters that he wants to "pay my respect" to supporters. "We brought back the spirit" of the 2024 presidential campaign, he declared.

It is difficult to judge.

World.title: 'Mixed feelings': AI cracks centuries-old ciphers
World.content:
TOKYO - Napoleon Bonaparte ordered the wartime missive written in code, creating a puzzle that went unsolved for more than 200 years -- until AI cracked it in a matter of hours.

Artificial intelligence is helping non-specialists unlock the secrets of historical sources, a trend described as a "turning point" in a field previously the preserve of scholars and dedicated hobbyists.

One new sleuth is Carter Church, a 27-year-old AI engineer who decrypted a 19th-century letter to one of Napoleon's generals.

Without digital tools, the task could have taken weeks, but the latest model from ChatGPT-maker OpenAI broke the cipher in just six hours.

"What AI mostly brings is persistence," Church told AFP, saying he felt "an unbelievable sense of satisfaction and excitement when I saw the result".

The message from 1809 -- detailing French and allied troops' positions in two dozen lines of symbols, numbers and letters -- had lain ignored in an online academic archive.

Because traditional, low-tech methods to crack ciphers are effective but time- and labour-intensive, historians "have more important problems to solve, so many ciphers like this often sit unattended", said Church.

To find the solution, Church, who works at US cybersecurity firm SentinelOne, needed to learn "very little" about code-breaking techniques or the historical period.

He spent some evenings going over it, then consulted Japanese patent engineer Satoshi Tomokiyo, who maintains an online list of unsolved ciphers, to verify it.

"2026 will be remembered as a turning point for codebreaking of historical ciphers," Tomokiyo wrote on his website Cryptiana, a go-to resource for the small but enthusiastic global community of amateur cryptographers.

- 'Mixed feelings' -

Researchers were already developing AI models to break ciphers, but the public release of state-of-the-art generalist tools has unleashed dozens of new solutions.

Although Church used OpenAI's most powerful model, GPT-6 Astra, other people have used top offerings from rival US lab Anthropic instead.

World.title: Le Pen looms large as Macron enters final months on EU stage
World.content:
PARIS - The spectre of far-right leader Marine Le Pen winning France's presidency with a pledge to go head-to-head with the European Union is already giving Brussels the jitters -- and looming large over Emmanuel Macron's final months in power.

France heads to the polls in April and May, after which Macron will exit as he can only serve two terms as president of the EU's second-largest economy.

But as Macron met his EU counterparts for a Brussels summit, a European diplomat said Le Pen was already "in the room" -- with the frontrunner's potential victory hanging over their talks Thursday and Friday on future spending and Ukraine.

Seeking to tighten the screws on the EU, Le Pen travelled to the Belgian capital on the eve of the leaders' meeting to address the media, vowing to slash France's contribution to the European Union budget and to cut short financial support to Ukraine.

European officials do not hide their concerns that Le Pen is trying to exert influence over EU affairs months before the vote.

"It was very cunning of her to hold her press conference" the day before, said a second European diplomat, speaking on condition of anonymity.

The National Rally leader also spoke at length to the Financial Times newspaper, read by policymakers in Brussels, warning of a potential showdown over the EU budget and difficult times for EU chief Ursula von der Leyen if she wins.

The interview was "quite scary" especially on Ukraine, said Francesco Nicoli, politics professor at Italy's Polytechnic University of Turin.

A senior European official admitted Brussels could barely imagine what the EU would look like with a French far-right government -- with no known formal contacts between Le Pen and the EU executive to date.

- 'Possible storm' -

For Macron, fears of a disruptive Le Pen presidency have sharpened focus on what he may yet achieve at EU level in his final few months in power.

The fervent European who has spent nine years pushing deeper EU integration maintains influence over his counterparts in Brussels, diplomats say, despite a pileup of crises at home from student protests to French debt turmoil.

"What is certain is that in Brussels there is the will to make the most of the fact he is still there, and to lock in whatever can be before a possible storm," said Sebastien Maillard, of the Jacques Delors Institute.

Observers note that no other current EU leader has managed to take on a leadership role in the bloc, with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz weaker than ever after the strongest far-right win in Germany since 1945.

"Macron understands what is happening around the (leaders') table. He's a very skilled negotiator and much more agile than Merz," the first EU diplomat said.

World.title: Inside conflicting accounts of Raila Odinga's death
World.content:
The most direct disagreement concerns a deeply personal question: who was with Raila when he took his last breath?. [File, Standard]

One year after Raila Odinga’s death, a fresh account by his longtime bodyguard has reopened questions about the former Prime Minister’s final moments, exposing striking differences between what he says happened and accounts from members of the Odinga family told Kenyans in October last year.

The most direct disagreement concerns a deeply personal question: who was with Raila when he took his last breath?

World.title: From 'Chogo' to senator? Winnie Odinga steps into her own political spotlight
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

From Raila Odinga’s shadow to her own political path, Winnie sets her sights on the Nairobi Senate seat in 2027. [Courtesy]

The hat was more than a hat. Literally.

As Raila Odinga’s body made its final journey home from India, his youngest daughter, Winnie, held tightly to his familiar cream-coloured fedora. It was one of the few things she could still protect, a small piece of a man whose presence had filled her life and Kenya’s political imagination for decades.

The image of Winnie carrying her father’s hat was deeply personal. The country was mourning a political giant, but she was mourning her father.

A year later, on the first anniversary of Raila’s death, Winnie has announced her intention to contest the Nairobi Senate seat in the 2027 General Election.

The timing is poignant. On a day devoted to remembering her father, she has declared her own political ambitions, signalling a shift from being one of the most recognisable faces of the Odinga family to a politician seeking a mandate in her own right.

“As Edwin Sifuna seeks a higher office, I see an opportunity in Nairobi, which is why I have decided I will vie for Senator of Nairobi County,” she said.

And just like that, the conversation shifted from the daughter who carried Baba’s hat to the politician who wants a seat of her own.

The last-born girl

To many Kenyans, Winnie is Chogo, the last-born child of Raila and Ida Odinga. The nickname carries the familiarity of family life, a reminder that behind the powerful surname is a daughter who grew up in a household where politics was never far from the conversation.

Her father was no ordinary political figure. His name could summon crowds, ignite debate and divide opinion. His decades-long career placed the Odinga family at the centre of Kenya’s political story.

Growing up as Raila’s youngest daughter meant sharing him with a country that claimed a piece of his time, energy and, eventually, his final goodbye.

Yet Winnie was not simply a spectator in her father’s political world. She worked around his campaigns and communications before stepping into politics herself, eventually winning a seat in the East African Legislative Assembly.

In November 2022, Parliament elected her to represent Kenya in the regional legislature, where she took office in December that year. Based in Arusha, Tanzania, she became part of the East African Community’s legislative institution, serving a five-year term running to 2027.

The EALA offered Winnie a political platform beyond her father’s immediate circle and an opportunity to participate in regional affairs. Her current tenure has also given her experience in legislative politics before her proposed move into elective politics at home.

The Nairobi Senate bid would take her into a different contest, one in which voters will have to decide whether her experience, ideas and political programme merit their support.

The hat she could not let go

For years, Raila’s trademark headgear had been part of his public identity, appearing at political rallies, meetings and public ceremonies. But in Winnie’s hands, it became something else: a personal possession tied to the final journey of a daughter and her father

She explained how protective she had been of it throughout the journey, describing it as one of the few things she could still hold on to.

The image captured a kind of helplessness that public figures’ families rarely get to show. Crowds could mourn Raila, politicians could speak of his legacy, and supporters could debate who would inherit his political movement. Winnie, however, had been left with the painful task of bringing her father home.

The symbolism of the hat has since acquired another layer. At a ceremony in Bondo earlier this month, elders placed a traditional hat on Winnie’s head in a symbolic gesture associated with the possibility of her carrying forward her father’s political mantle.

Winnie’s political journey has not started with this Senate announcement.

Her election to the East African Legislative Assembly placed her among Kenya’s representatives in a regional institution whose work concerns cooperation among East African Community partner states.

The role gave her a platform in regional legislation while her father remained a central figure in national politics.

The Senate is responsible for representing counties, participating in lawmaking on matters concerning counties and exercising oversight over revenue allocated to county governments. A Nairobi senator must therefore make a case on issues that touch residents directly, from public spending and service delivery to the accountability of county leadership.

The capital is also a demanding political terrain. Its electorate is diverse, its concerns immediate and its contests fiercely competitive.

A famous surname may open doors, but it cannot replace a convincing programme on jobs, housing, transport, healthcare and the management of public resources.

Winnie will have to demonstrate that she understands Nairobi beyond its place in her father’s national political story.

Can she translate the loyalty associated with Raila into support for her own agenda? Can she persuade voters that she is more than the daughter of a political icon?

Those questions will follow her into the campaign.

The Odingaism

Political inheritance can be both an advantage and a burden.

Raila’s name carries a formidable history of opposition politics, democratic reform and a loyal support base. It also invites comparisons that few politicians have to contend with.

Winnie’s challenge will be to honour that history without allowing it to become the entirety of her political identity.

Raila’s death left a space in the Orange Democratic Movement and among supporters who had looked to him for direction through decades of political contests. The question of who will carry his legacy has inevitably turned towards his family and the wider political movement he helped build.

Winnie’s Senate bid will require her to turn recognition into a political proposition that voters can interrogate. Her experience at EALA gives her a legislative starting point; the Nairobi contest will demand that she demonstrate how that experience can serve residents of the capital.

She must also navigate the expectations attached to her father’s name while making room for her own ideas, priorities and leadership style.

There is a temptation to see Winnie’s future entirely through the lens of inheritance. She is Raila’s daughter, the last-born known as Chogo, the woman who carried his hat and the politician whom some supporters hope will continue his legacy.

But she is also a woman making a decision about her own future.

The Senate bid offers her an opportunity to define what that future means, beyond the grief surrounding her father’s death and the weight of a name that has shaped Kenyan politics for decades.

The hat remains an unforgettable image from Raila’s final journey home. A daughter attempted to protect the last tangible thing she could hold on to.

The Senate will demand something different: a political vision, a campaign and the votes of Nairobi residents.

Chogo has announced her next move. Will Winnie Odinga turn the memory of Baba into a mandate of her own?

World.title: Motorists, households face fresh fuel price hikes
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

EPRA attributed the price increases to the escalating conflict in the Middle East. [FIle, Standard]

The Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority (EPRA) has increased fuel prices, raising the cost of super petrol by Sh12.93 per litre, diesel by Sh9.90, and kerosene by Sh28.49.

The new prices, effective from October 15 to November 14, 2026, will see motorists in Nairobi pay up to Sh226.96 per litre for super petrol, Sh227.76 for diesel, and Sh219.85 for kerosene.

EPRA Director-General Edward Mwirigi Kinyua attributed the price increases to the escalating conflict in the Middle East, which has disrupted petroleum supply chains and driven up the cost of importing fuel.

The rise in kerosene prices is likely to hit low-income households that rely on the fuel for cooking and lighting.

Meanwhile, higher diesel prices could raise the cost of transporting goods and operating public service vehicles, potentially driving up fares and commodity prices.

Diesel is a key fuel for the country's freight transport sector and a significant portion of public service vehicle operations, meaning the increase could have a ripple effect across the economy.

The latest review comes after EPRA maintained pump prices during the September 15 to October 14 pricing period, despite a decline in the cost of importing petrol.

World.title: Oburu Oginga to leave hospital soon - ODM
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

ODM SG Catherine Omanyo criticised bloggers spreading unverified information about the veteran politician.

ODM Secretary General Catherine Omanyo has dismissed social media reports about the health of party leader Oburu Oginga, saying he is recovering well and is expected to be discharged from hospital either today or tomorrow.

Omanyo criticised bloggers spreading unverified information about the veteran politician, accusing them of exploiting his health condition to attract online attention and increase engagement.

“It's unfortunate what I've been reading on social media. Those people who are seeking to have more likes or viewers, they will be disappointed because he's up, he's well, he's fine. In fact, he's headed home either today or tomorrow,” she said.

Omanyo insisted that the reports had exaggerated his situation, dismissing claims of his death and assuring the public that he was doing well.

She noted that health conditions could fluctuate, saying Oburu's position as ODM party leader had made his well-being a subject of heightened public interest.

“Everybody, everybody, including you and me, our health is not static. You can be under the weather any time. It's just that he's a party leader, and it makes breaking news,” Omanyo said.

She urged social media users to exercise restraint when discussing the health of public figures, warning against spreading unverified reports, particularly claims of death, before confirmation from credible sources.

Her remarks come amid growing speculation on social media about Oburu's health, with some users circulating unverified claims about his condition.

World.title: Kenya declares Ebola a formidable epidemic disease, sets new rules
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale, who declared Ebola caused by the Bundibugyo virus a formidable epidemic disease under the Public Health Act. [File,Standard]

Kenya has declared Ebola virus a formidable epidemic disease, introducing new rules governing screening, isolation, quarantine, contact tracing and the handling of bodies.

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale issued the declaration through a legal notice published in the Kenya Gazette on Monday, October 12, under Section 35 of the Public Health Act.

The declaration follows Kenya’s confirmation of its first imported case of Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease on October 6, after a Kenyan citizen who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo travelled through Uganda to Nairobi. The patient died despite receiving supportive treatment.

The case prompted health authorities to trace people who may have come into contact with the patient and strengthen screening at points of entry.

In an update on October 12, the World Health Organization (WHO) said Kenya had listed 127 contacts, with 94 in quarantine, and screened more than 665,000 travellers at points of entry.

WHO also supplied protective equipment and testing materials worth about US$70,000 to support the response.

The government published two legal notices on October 12. Legal Notice No. 203 declares the disease a formidable epidemic, while Legal Notice No. 204 establishes the Public Health (Ebola Disease) Rules, 2026.

The regulations provide for screening at points of entry, medical assessment, isolation, referral, quarantine and monitoring.

They also assign responsibilities to transport operators, health facilities, medical practitioners and laboratories.

Health authorities will conduct investigations and contact tracing, while designated health facilities will manage suspected and confirmed cases. The rules also provide for the inspection and decontamination of premises.

The regulations cover the safe and dignified disposal of bodies, burial procedures, record-keeping, transportation and repatriation. They also address public communication, media houses’ responsibilities in public sensitisation and assistance from enforcement agencies.

The rules provide for offences and penalties, although the Gazette extract does not specify the penalties for individual violations.

What the declaration means

Bundibugyo virus disease is a form of Ebola that spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person or contaminated materials.

Contact with the body of someone who has died from the disease can also expose people to infection during unsafe burial practices.

Symptoms can include fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headache and sore throat, followed by vomiting and diarrhoea. The incubation period ranges from two to 21 days.

WHO says no approved vaccine or specific treatment currently exists for the Bundibugyo strain, making early detection, isolation, supportive care and contact tracing central to controlling its spread.

The health agency has advised against travel or trade restrictions on Kenya, Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo based on the information available.

The new rules establish a legal framework for managing the disease, from identifying suspected infections and monitoring contacts to caring for patients and preventing exposure during burials.

World.title: Ruto wades into growing ODM-UDA conflict
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto marks Mazingira Day by planting trees in Elgon downs, Trans-Nzoia County. [PCS]

President William Ruto delved into the growing tension among Orange Democratic Movement (ODM) and United Democratic Alliance (UDA) contenders in the Coast and asked them to tone it down during his recent tour of the region.

Speaking hours before he wound up his eight-day tour, Ruto appeared to notice the widening cracks and told politicians within the two parties to embrace a ceasefire and unite against the opposition.

The head of state, who is facing a formidable challenge from the united opposition, warned that divisions in the ODM and UDA could weaken their team, whose union gives it a chance to win the 2027 general election.

“ODM and UDA are one team, and you should accommodate each other under a broad-based government. We should not allow divisions in ODM and UDA to undermine our unity of purpose,” he stated.

His statement appeared to be directed at the growing tensions among contenders, particularly in Kwale, Mombasa and Kilifi counties where prominent politicians face challengers within the ODM and UDA political union.

President Ruto’s earlier attempt to zone the region in favour of sitting governors is also blamed for the cracks in the broad-based team at the Coast.

In Mombasa County, UDA secretary general Mr Hassan Omar has already rejected a plan by the so-called broad-based team to support governor Abdulswamd Nassir’s re-election.

Omar, who is also a member of the East African Legislative Assembly (EALA) insisted that he will challenge Mr Nassir.

Already, businessman and EALA member Mr Suleiman Shahbal has quit ODM after he left he could not get the party ticket as the president's allies favour Nassir, a deputy party leader.

Shhabal has since aligned himself to former Laikipia governor Mr Murithi Nderitu’s Kenya Reform Party even as he insisted that he will be on the ballot.

In Mombasa, Mining, Blue Economy and Maritime Affairs Cabinet Secretary Mr Hassan Joho and governor Nassir appeared to be handing over Coast which was the ODM leader late Raila Odinga’s political turf, to President Ruto.

“This region stands with Ruto because he has dignified us with title deeds and many other development projects. We however expect him to support us when we seek the presidential seat in 2032,” Joho said.

Joho’s elder brother Abubakar Joho, who is a prominent businessman, has also joined the campaign for President Ruto.

While touring Kwale, Ruto addressed the growing noise among the main contenders, Governor Fatuma Achani (UDA), Prof Hamadi Boga and Engineer Lung’anzi Chai (ODM) after the broad-based leaders appeared to settle for Ms Achani who has the backing of Sports CS and former Kwale governor Salim Mvurya.

After witnessing the rising political tension, Ruto changed tone and told the three contenders to directly seek support from the voters rather than relying on external political backing.

In a complete change of heart and political tact, Ruto emphasised that the power to choose leaders ultimately belongs to the electorate, who will evaluate candidates based on their track record and development agenda for the region.

“You should all seek votes from the people and not rely on external backing. What I need from all of you is your support,” he stated.

For long, Governor Achani has enjoyed unwavering backing of President Ruto, Mvurya and recently Joho, who had preferred Kwale to be zoned in favour of the governor and UDA.

But Prof Boga, who has been Mr Joho’s ally, described the broad-based government’s zoning arrangement as undemocratic and a coercion to the Kwale electorate who he said should be allowed to choose their leaders without external interference.

Boga has been critical about the attempt to stop some aspirants from contesting seats in the broad-based government, noting that it was possible to zone candidates and difficult to do so for the voters.

In a statement, Boga noted that former Gender CS and Kilifi governor aspirant Ms Aisha Jumwa’s recent departure from UDA to Wiper Patriotic Front (WPF) reflected a growing sense among a segment of coastal leaders that decisions about their political future are increasingly being made elsewhere, then handed down as settled outcomes rather than negotiated realities.

“Zoning at the Coast is a fantasy: You can zone candidates but you cannot zone the voters,” Boga had warned.

“And if UDA and ODM are not paying attention to that signal, they may be underestimating the political consequences of their emerging arrangements at the Coast. “There is a dangerous assumption taking root in the broad-based arrangement: that coastal politics can be settled around a table in Nairobi and then delivered to voters as a finished political package. You take this seat, we take that one, and the voters will follow,” he added.

Boga, who came second in the 2022 governor poll, warned that if the Coast is mishandled, the problem will not necessarily be that voters have suddenly embraced another political formation, but the greater danger is that voters may decide that none of the established arrangements speak for them, creating either a rebellion or apathy.

In Kilifi County, the broad-based team publicly worked with Governor Gideon Mung’aro, forcing Ms Jumwa, his main challenger, to quit the government team in protest.

Kilifi Senate aspirant Mr Stephen Kahocho and Ganze parliamentary aspirant Ms Zawadi Kingi have publicly warned that they might be forced to quit UDA and vie as independent candidates or join other political formations.

This is after it emerged that the broad-based arrangement was behind Mung’aro (ODM), Kilifi senator Stewart Madzayo (ODM) and Ganze MP Kenneth Kazungu Tungule of Pamoja African Alliance (PAA), an affiliate of UDA.

World.title: Egypt halts Sudan truck transit following fatal shooting of two Egyptian drivers
World.content:
Egypt has indefinitely suspended the transit of trucks bound for Sudan via the Qustul land port after two Egyptian drivers were killed and a third was injured in a shooting at a market in southern Khartoum, the Sudanese capital, RT Arabic reported.

The management of Egypt’s Qustul Land Port, under the General Authority for Land and Dry Ports of the Ministry of Transport, issued directives to halt all trucks heading toward the port and prevent them from crossing on ferries to the Sudanese side until new instructions are issued, “against the backdrop of security developments in Sudan’s Northern State.”

The decision made an exception for passenger traffic, as buses, private cars, and microbuses—along with individual travelers—continue to be allowed to cross without being affected by the suspension of truck traffic.

An earlier decision by the Internal and International Land Transport Regulatory Authority had prohibited Egyptian trucks from entering conflict zones in Sudan, restricting commercial transport movements strictly to Wadi Halfa, Argeen, and the city of Dongola in Sudan as part of measures aimed at protecting drivers from security risks.

The authority emphasized the necessity for truck drivers to adhere to instructions regulating transport movement inside Sudan, exercise the utmost caution and vigilance, and refrain from crossing beyond designated areas under any circumstances.

These instructions are based on directives issued by the Ministry of Transport on May 11, 2025, which mandated avoiding conflict zones and limiting cargo offloading to safe areas within Sudan’s Northern State.

The suspension of border crossings comes at a time when overland transport between Egypt and Sudan faces heightened security risks associated with the armed conflict, following an incident where two Egyptian drivers were killed and a third was injured during a shooting at a market south of Khartoum.

World.title: Egypt expects rain and 3°C temperature drop on Friday
World.content:
The Egyptian Meteorological Authority disclosed the weather conditions across Cairo and Egyptian governorates.

Mildly warm weather is expected during the daytime along the northern coasts, Greater Cairo, Lower Egypt, and northern Upper Egypt, while remaining hot in southern Upper Egypt and South Sinai.

Nighttime weather will feel cool across most parts of the country, accompanied by a drop in temperatures of up to 3°C.

Weather phenomena

Weather maps warned today of morning fog forming on key roads leading to and from the north of the country down to Greater Cairo, the Canal cities, central Sinai, and northern Upper Egypt.

Scattered rainfall chances are expected, ranging from moderate to occasionally heavy (with a 40 percent probability) across parts of the northern coasts and northern Lower Egypt.

Light to moderate rain is expected over parts of central and southern Lower Egypt, the Canal cities, and may extend (with a 20 percent to 30 percent probability) to areas in Greater Cairo, northern Upper Egypt, and further south toward Halaib and Shalateen.

Active winds are also anticipated across parts of the northern coasts, Lower Egypt, Greater Cairo, and South Sinai.

World.title: Egyptian farmed fish approved for export by 27 EU nations
World.content:
In a major breakthrough for Egypt’s agricultural export ambitions, Egyptian farmed fish has officially cleared one of the world’s toughest regulatory hurdles: gaining full approval for export across all 27 European Union member states.

The decision, officially published in the EU’s Official Journal under Regulation (EU) 2021/405, marks the culmination of a grueling two-year overhaul of Egypt’s food safety and oversight architecture.

Overcoming Brussels’ regulatory wall

Reaching EU tables required Egypt to completely align its aquaculture safety protocols with European Union standards. Spearheaded by the National Food Safety Authority (NFSA) alongside marine resources, veterinary, and pharmaceutical regulators, the country executed a comprehensive revamp of its oversight systems.

Key upgrades that satisfied European regulators include:

Contaminant Surveillance: Strict monitoring of banned chemicals and residue levels.

Legislative Overhaul: Updating legal framework to mirror rigorous European quality standards.

Inter-Agency Coordination: Direct integration between regulatory bodies, commercial attache offices in Brussels, and private sector exporters.

Opening a lucrative market

With the EU seal of approval secured, Egyptian aquaculture producers now gain access to a premium market of over 400 million consumers.

Dr. Tariq Al-Hobi, Chairman of the NFSA, framed the achievement as a strategic shift for Egypt’s food export portfolio—transitioning local aquaculture into a high-value global trade driver aligned with the nation’s Vision 2030 economic strategy.

World.title: Jonglei Canal could double or triple Egypt and Sudan’s annual water share: Former Minister
World.content:
Mohamed Nasr El-Din Allam, former Minister of Water Resources and Irrigation, stated that Egypt’s per capita water share has dropped to approximately 500 cubic meters per year, amidst water resources that are no longer sufficient to keep pace with growing needs. He emphasized the necessity of linking water management to economic viability, enhancing cooperation among Nile Basin countries, and studying projects capable of increasing available resources.

Speaking during an interview on the program Red Line, hosted by journalist Mohamed Mousse on Al-Hadath Al-Youm TV channel, Allam explained that the Jonglei Canal project is one of the important initiatives to boost water resources for both Egypt and Sudan, as it could help tap into water lost in swampy areas. He noted that the quantities that could be saved through this project might equal two to three times the total annual water yield of both countries combined.

Jonglei Canal: A halted project despite its hydrological importance

Allam noted that efforts to increase Egypt’s water resources have been linked to projects and moves across successive presidential eras. He explained that the late President Gamal Abdel Nasser took steps regarding Egypt and Sudan’s share of Nile water, while the late President Anwar Sadat sought to increase water resources as the Egyptian citizen’s share declined due to population growth. He added that the Jonglei Canal project saw progress during Sadat’s era, with parts of the work executed before halting due to the civil war in South Sudan, keeping the project stalled to this day.

The former irrigation minister stressed that water cooperation projects among Nile Basin countries continue to face challenges despite efforts made across successive presidential terms, including the era of President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi. He underscored the importance of boosting cooperation among basin states to serve mutual interests and optimize the use of available water resources.

500 cubic meters per capita annually

Allam explained that the drop in per capita water share to around 500 cubic meters per year reflects Egypt entering a state of water scarcity. He pointed out that this amount equals half of the 1,000-cubic-meter annual per capita benchmark—which he noted is the standard limit set for desert countries like Egypt, according to World Bank thresholds.

He indicated that the standard limit for countries with normal hydrological conditions stands at around 1,500 cubic meters per capita annually, whereas it is around 1,000 cubic meters for desert nations.

He added that the repercussions of water scarcity are evident in Egypt’s reliance on importing a large portion of its food needs, alongside resorting to seawater desalination to provide drinking water, and treating and reusing water multiple times to meet rising demand.

He concluded by noting that the state bears heavy financial burdens to secure necessary food for the population, which calls for evaluating the sustainability of current policies and striking a balance between available resources and increasing demands.

Drinking water and industry first

Regarding the allocation of water resources across different sectors, Allam explained that the requirements for drinking water and existing industries cannot be easily reduced, as compromising drinking water supplies or lowering the water needed to sustain industrial activity would have direct repercussions.

He added that the water remaining after satisfying drinking and industrial needs represents the resource available for agriculture and other uses. He pointed out that these quantities are diminishing annually, making an increase in water resources a necessity to preserve Egypt’s limited arable land and satisfy the demands of various sectors.

The former irrigation minister stressed that agricultural expansion must be grounded in precise hydrological and economic calculations that factor in the cost of providing water per acre, the value of the resulting crops, and whether crop returns can cover water production costs. He noted that desalination costs can reach about US 0.75$ to US 1.00 per cubic meter, according to his figures, warning against using high-cost water to grow crops that do not generate economic yields proportional to the cost of supplying that water.

He emphasized that while agricultural expansion aims to enhance self-sufficiency and reduce reliance on food imports, achieving this goal requires selecting crops whose water requirements align with available resources—thereby ensuring genuine economic viability and reducing financial burdens on the state.

Rice, sugarcane, and reevaluating crop mapping

Allam linked water resource management directly to decisions regarding crop patterns, pointing out that rice and sugarcane are among the most water-intensive crops. Expanding their cultivation imposes additional burdens on Egyptian water resources, even when certain crops yield high economic returns.

He noted that rice and sugarcane are major crops cultivated in several Nile Basin countries, particularly in the Equatorial and Ethiopian plateaus, underscoring the need to review agricultural policies to match the state’s actual needs and water capacity.

He stressed the importance of placing water economics at the forefront of agricultural decision-making, ensuring that crop evaluations are not limited solely to economic yields, but also encompass the volume of water required for production and the cost of providing it—achieving a balance between agricultural output and water conservation.

Reuse and water treatment to expand available resources

Conversely, Allam indicated that Egypt has achieved an advanced level in optimizing its water resources through water reuse and maximizing the utility of various sources, including Nile water, groundwater, and agricultural drainage water.

He explained that agricultural drainage water represents a key source for reuse, alongside water that seeps from canals and drainage systems into the subsoil. He added that discharging a portion of agricultural drainage water is also necessary to flush out accumulated salts from the soil.

He stated that water resource use efficiency in Egypt reaches approximately 70 percent, according to his figures, comparing it to levels achieved in the United States, while stressing the importance of continuing to develop the water management system and raise the efficiency of available resources.

He added that Egypt has relied for decades on water treatment and multiple reuse cycles, alongside blending certain water sources to meet diverse needs. He noted that recent technological advancements in treatment processes have enabled higher standards, allowing water to be reused for various purposes in compliance with required quality parameters.

He cited the Bahr El-Baqar Drainage Water Treatment Plant as a prominent project in this field, noting that it reflects the capacity to execute advanced water projects despite their high cost.

Allam concluded by emphasizing that evaluating water treatment and reuse projects should not rely on technical capabilities alone; rather, it must encompass the total cost compared to the economic yield and final product. He explained that any project failing to generate a return proportional to its cost risks becoming an economic burden, regardless of its technical importance.

World.title: Gift for Putin as fears grow that Trump is turning the screws on Ukraine
World.content:
Ultimately, you have to wonder what it is that Vladimir Putin says to Donald Trump when they are on the phone.

A week ago, a call between the US president and his Russian counterpart seemed to be about an urgent clarification over a possible outbreak of plague in Siberia. Instead, a controversial deal to buy Russian diesel emerged, prompting fury from Ukrainians, and then Trump demanding they get a new president. For days, fears grew across Europe this may spill into the real world of the US limiting military aid and intelligence for Ukraine, and in the past 48 hours, that might be spilling into reality.

Twice now, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky has declared Kyiv was not given the usual warning about Russian ballistic missile attacks from its partners.

The US, whose satellites and other methods are the early warning mechanisms for Russian launches, normally provide Ukrainians a vital few minutes to run to the shelter before the missiles hit. Thirty-nine slammed into Ukraine last night. President Trump has openly rejected the idea he has stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine, saying Tuesday: “We are helping them, and we are sharing intel.” But that does not preclude the possibility less intelligence is being shared, or it is less in real time.

With the dead from Russian strikes often in the dozens, as Moscow seeks to yet further widen the envelope of what civilian carnage it will impose, a sudden withdrawal of these early warnings would mean many Ukrainians will likely die. It is possible there is another reason for Zelensky’s messaging – that he is pre-emptively posturing, or that poor weather or technical issues prompted the lack of warnings.

The second withdrawal of assistance that appeared to beset Ukraine Wednesday also suggests Trump is squeezing them harder.

Ukrainians watch over an apartment building damaged by a Russian attack in Kyiv on Wednesday. Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters

Starlink space-based internet antennae – assisting Ukrainian medium and longer-range drones to hit their targets, and interceptors to tackle Russian loitering drones – have had significant speed limits imposed on them. This may amount to the removal of a bonus capability negotiated by the former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov with Space X’s owner, Elon Musk. It is important to note it is not comparable to Musk’s decision to entirely stop Starlink functioning inside Russia, which significantly hampered Moscow’s frontline operations in the summer of last year. But it is a palpable snub with operational significance, and one that Ukrainian officials have said would only have occurred at the behest of the White House.

For days, European and Ukrainian officials have warned the US was threatening to limit intelligence and other cooperation if Kyiv did not stop hitting Russian diesel facilities. Trump has – somewhat misleadingly – stated Ukrainian targeting of Moscow’s oil facilities is behind a surge in pump prices in the United States, choosing to ignore the role the Strait of Hormuz has played in this global economic calamity. It is possible the Starlink slowdown and lack of ballistic warnings shows this threat coming to life.

Smoke rises over Russian oil producer Gazprom Neft’s oil refinery near Moscow on June 18. Russian and Ukrainian forces have increased attacks on each other’s energy infrastructure. AFP/Getty Images

President Trump has denied this is the case, but that is not in of itself definitive proof it is not happening. Trump has also – since he spoke to Putin – again swung from deciding to finally allow Ukraine to build its own Patriot interceptors, a high-profile and vital move long-prevaricated over, to deciding the true obstacle to peace is Zelensky, the president of the invaded country, who has been asking for an immediate ceasefire for over a year.

It does not appear to influence Trump’s thought process when Putin attacks Ukrainian energy facilities in the middle of Trump’s self-declared “energy ceasefire.” Or when Putin’s operatives plot to murder a dissident in Washington DC. Or when US businesses are relentlessly hit in Ukraine. There are moments when Trump simply appears bent on hurting Ukraine and damaging its position. We may never learn why, or what it is that Putin says to him to cause this relatively frequent flip in Trump’s worldview.

Conjecture might revive the old trope that Trump the real-estate dealmaker seeks to pressure his subcontractors (here, Ukraine) to get the deal to go through or forge a price more palatable to his end consumer (Putin), who he has correctly assessed is in the driving seat of the war and therefore any peace deal. But the timing of this pressure rarely comes when a deal is close, or appears supported by logic. Trump’s decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel, by most analysis, won’t impact prices at the American pump before the mid-terms, but will likely flood the Kremlin’s coffers with badly needed cash.

Zelensky and his European allies have seen this vacillation enough times to be inured to its emotional impact, and perhaps even relaxed about how long it might sustain. Perhaps more Trump-whispering by France’s Macron, or another call from NATO’s Rutte, or visit from Italy’s Meloni, will see the US president flip back again. Indeed, Zelensky was in London Wednesday, and the topic has surely come up.

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky (left) and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz (right) inspect a damaged building in Kyiv on October 4. Tetiana Dzhafarova/AFP/Getty Images

But Trump’s persistent sympathy for Russia’s position remains a mystery of our time. Critics say it is unlikely to achieve his apparent goal of a peace deal, incompatible with the long-term security interests of the United States, and oblivious to Moscow’s role in assisting Iran , which continues to embarrass Trump and injure American servicemen.

There is an inherent risk in the current state of affairs, however, to both Trump and Putin.

First, Trump might create such acrimony in his transatlantic relationships, that his allies simply zone him out for the 18 months after the mid-terms, and wait for him to depart. That could leave Trump further hamstrung when dealing with an intractable conflict, spreading in the Middle East.

There is risk for Putin too.

Europe and Ukraine being forced to forge ahead without the United States, fashion resilience, find new methods, and surge funding into their defense, does not leave the Kremlin in a dominant position. The more Moscow antagonizes Europe, the more it arms up, and the greater, in the long-term, the (defensive) threat Europe’s armies pose to Russia.

Ukraine has shown extraordinary inventiveness and capability. That is unlikely to stop, and likely to again reshape the landscape of warfare in the coming years. Similarly, Russia’s capacity to absorb pain is immense. Yet its breaking point is rarely publicly visible, and tends to surge menacingly from the deep without warning, as when the frustrated chief of Russia’s infamous Wagner mercenary force launched a short-lived rebellion in 2023.

In the immediate term however, the risk of this current strategy is born entirely by Ukraine. Its children and mothers are dying from nightly strikes. Its cities are sleepless. And its military aid is prey to two powerful men’s curious bromance.

World.title: Inside the Kenyan manufacturer betting on Africa’s industrial future
World.content:
In a central Nairobi factory, a steady stream of household, hair and skincare products rolls off the production line.

HACO Industries makes around 90 products designed for African consumers. Its brands reach more than 3 million families across the continent, while raw materials are sourced from more than 500 farmers in Africa.

For Mary-Ann Musangi, whose family launched HACO more than 50 years ago, the opportunity lies in making products on the continent for people whose needs the business recognizes.

“How do we reach African consumers with products that they want and need, manufactured by a company that understands them — understands African skin, African hair and African needs?” she said.

HACO currently exports to eight African countries. Kenya is its largest market, but it also has a presence in Uganda, Rwanda, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Zambia. “Distances can be a challenge and African logistics is one of the key challenges in terms of penetrating across the continent,” Musangi said.

The company’s plastics plant, which produces the packaging for its products, has the capacity to produce 5 million components a month, according to its manufacturing director, Peter Ndichu. A separate plant has the capacity to process and pack 1,365 metric tons of products monthly.

HACO is trying to strengthen its supply chain by buying more ingredients within Africa. The company works with small and medium-sized suppliers of natural oils, offering technical support to help them meet its quality standards.

Shea butter is now sourced from Uganda or Ghana. Ndichu said HACO previously imported it from the United States for 5,000 Kenyan shillings ($38.50) per kilogram, compared with 1,000 shillings ($7.70) per kilogram from Uganda.

HACO is now looking to automate more of its operations. “In terms of packing, we are currently achieving 3,000 pieces in an hour,” said Ndichu. Automated machinery could quadruple that to roughly 12,000 items an hour, he said, adding that HACO plans to build a new factory to accommodate the upgrades.

Hubs and partnerships

To support its goal of exporting to 30 African countries by 2030, HACO plans to establish five regional hubs across Africa. Ghana is set to become its West African manufacturing base, from which products can be exported to neighboring markets.

Musangi said collaborating with local companies will be essential for expansion.

“Africa is so fragmented in many ways: the countries, the boundaries, our taxation laws, our policies, our culture, our language, our money, currency. We’ve got to see, how do we reduce these points of fragmentation?” she explained. “The only way I see we can do it is through these partnerships, working with local people.”

HACO Industries makes around 90 household, hair and skincare products. CNN

In Ghana, HACO is partnering with Ayewa Labs, a product development and manufacturing firm specializing in making goods from African ingredients. Founder Nanayaa Bates said the African Continental Free Trade Area — which came into effect in 2019 and is the world’s largest free-trade area by number of countries — is helping the company attract clients from other African countries.

HACO supplies raw materials for Ayewa, which then manufactures products for other companies beyond Ghana. Bates said the partnership had increased Ayewa’s manufacturing output tenfold.

Making more in Africa

Manufacturing is seen as an important route to economic growth and job creation across Africa, yet in many countries it accounted for less than 15% of gross domestic product in 2023.

Musangi argues that African countries should retain more of the value generated by their raw materials. “It is unacceptable that we continue to simply extract raw materials from Africa and send them out to the West for them to manufacture and send us the finished product to consume at much higher prices,” she said.

“We have the technical skills,” Musangi added. “Our youth are highly skilled and highly educated. We need to make sure that we develop and continue developing the manufacturing sector so that we can add value to these raw materials.”

World.title: OpenAI accuses former employee of leaking intel on AI device to Apple
World.content:
OpenAI is accusing a former employee of stealing intellectual property related to an unreleased device and later sharing some of the information with Apple.

The employee, OpenAI alleges, had previously worked at Apple, then joined OpenAI for six months, before going back to Apple, according to a court filing from OpenAI on Wednesday.

The company said the employee downloaded over 100 highly confidential files to his personal accounts before rejoining Apple. The transferred files include “detailed images of the unreleased device(s), as well as highly confidential engineering and manufacturing data about the device(s),” according to the filing. The last file was sent in June on the employee’s final day, OpenAI alleges.

OpenAI went on to claim the former employee, who it did not name, “made a presentation about OpenAI’s product plans to Apple’s senior leadership, including Apple’s vice president of operations in Asia.”

“That presentation appears to have happened months ago—and now, armed with that information, Apple is making a new push into AI-enabled products,” OpenAI wrote in the filing.

Apple told CNN it has found no evidence to support the allegations and that it has strict policies in place to make sure new employees don’t use confidential information from previous workplaces. The company also said it would work with OpenAI to remediate any of OpenAI’s information found on Apple’s systems.

Apple accused OpenAI of trying to create a distraction from the original claims of their case. The allegations came as part of a filing in an ongoing lawsuit that Apple brought against OpenAI in July, alleging the AI company stole the iPhone maker’s trade secrets to develop its own gadgets. Apple alleged in its original filing that former employees who went to work for OpenAI downloaded confidential files, and urged job candidates to bring Apple parts to interviews at OpenAI. OpenAI has denied the claims, saying Apple hasn’t been able to identify any stolen trade secrets and has sought to dismiss the case.

Both companies are racing to create AI-enabled devices. This week, Apple announced HomeView, its biggest push into the smart home market in nearly a decade with a revamped version of Siri, making it a critical piece of Apple’s AI strategy. OpenAI is working on an AI-enabled device, reported to be a small screen-free smart speaker. Last year, OpenAI brought on former Apple product design chief Jonny Ive and his company, io, to take over design and creative responsibilities across the company.

While engineers and researchers regularly switch companies in Silicon Valley, Apple said in a court filing that OpenAI has hired more than 400 of its former employees.

CNN’s Lisa Eadicicco contributed to this report.

World.title: Harry and Meghan make first joint appearance since returning to the UK
World.content:
London —

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have made their first joint public appearance in Britain since moving back to the country.

Prince Harry and Meghan were greeted by well-wishers as they arrived at the Community Recording Studio (CRS) in Nottingham on Thursday morning.

Crowds gave the couple balloons and flowers, Britain’s PA Media news agency reported, with Harry and Meghan stopping to greet onlookers and pose for selfies. Meghan told one woman in the crowd: “It’s great to be back.”

The CRS, which Harry has visited before, is a charity that teaches film, video and music skills to young people. Inside the studio, Meghan joined a group of girls for a confidence-building and bracelet-making workshop.

When asked what makes them feel most like themselves, one participant said she liked doing gymnastics, to which Meghan replied: “Our daughter is doing that too right now. She loves it,” according to PA Media.

The duchess, whose Netflix lifestyle “With Love, Meghan” show centered around hosting and cooking, added: “I feel most like myself when I’m with my family and also when I’m cooking. I love doing that. I love to cook.”

The couple’s second stop while in Nottingham on Thursday was at Himmah Hub, a food poverty community action group. While there, they participated in cooking classes and packed food parcels for donations.

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex during a visit to Himmah Hub in Nottingham on Thursday. Annabel Lee-Ellis/PA

A crowd of about 50 people gathered at the gates to try and catch a glimpse of the Sussexes, according to PA Media.

In a surprise announcement this summer, the couple revealed that they would be leaving their home in California to resettle in the UK, together with their two children Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5. The family landed in August, ahead of the start of the school year last month. They returned as private citizens and are not resuming any official duties on behalf of King Charles III.

The engagements in Nottingham come more than six years after the couple departed the United Kingdom for the United States and the years since have seen a public falling out with some members of the royal family.

Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, arrive at Himmah Hub in Nottingham on Thursday. Dominic Lipinski/Getty Images

Harry and Meghan had cited tabloid intrusion, racism in British institutions, online abuse and complex family dynamics as among the reasons behind their 2020 departure.

Harry and Meghan’s Nottingham visit is not an official royal engagement.

Last month, Harry’s father, King Charles, issued a letter in which he clarified that the couple should be treated as “private citizens.” The missive is said to have caught the Sussexes off guard.

According to the letter, sent by the UK’s Lord Chamberlain – the most senior officer of the British royal household – all charitable work carried out by Harry and Meghan is a “personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity.”

The letter also made clear that any operational issues involving them should be directed to the relevant police authorities. Harry has continued to push for the UK Home Office to reinstate his family’s taxpayer-funded security, which was downgraded when the family left for North America in 2020.

The last time the Sussexes appeared together in public in Britain was four years ago, at the funeral of Harry’s grandmother, the late Queen Elizabeth II, in September 2022.

While living in the US, Harry made several trips back to the UK, including for the funeral of his grandmother Queen Elizabeth II in 2022 and the coronation of his father King Charles III the following year.

CNN’s Lauren Said-Moorhouse and Max Foster contributed reporting.

World.title: Gov’t of Liberia Begins Validation of Draft Intellectual Property Policy and Strategy
World.content:
— As acting Commerce Minister describes the document as an essential instrument for enterprise development, investment promotion, industrial growth, and economic diversification.

Front row: Acting Minister of Commerce and Industry Hon. Stephen Yekeson (second from left), with Mr. Emmanuel Rugomboka, Counsellor in WIPO’s Division for Africa, and Hon. Garmai Koboi, Director General of the Liberia Intellectual Property Office.

The Government of Liberia has begun the validation of its draft National Intellectual Property Policy and Strategy (NIPPS) to guide short-, medium-, and long-term actions in the protection, administration and commercialization of intellectual property rights.



The ongoing validation exercise, which runs from October 15 to 16, comes as President Joseph Boakai’s administration has made intellectual property protection and development a key policy priority under Pillar One of the ARREST Agenda.

Opening the validation workshop, Acting Minister of Commerce and Industry Hon. Stephen Yekeson said the exercise represents a step toward a national framework that recognizes the economic value of knowledge and protects the legitimate interests of creators and innovators.

“In today’s increasingly knowledge-driven global economy, national competitiveness depends not only on the natural resources a country possesses or the goods it produces, but also on its ability to generate ideas, protect innovation, develop valuable brands, commercialize creative works, and transform knowledge into economic value,” Hon. Yekeson added.

Min. Yekeson further noted that the Ministry of Commerce and Industry sees the NIPPS as an important document that connects to Liberia’s wider trade, investment, and economic development priorities, as an effective intellectual property system is key to a more supportive business environment, encourages responsible investment, and reinforces Liberia’s broader efforts to improve trade competitiveness and private sector growth.

“Today’s validation workshop is particularly important because the success of a national policy depends not only on the quality of the document, but also on its relevance to national priorities, its responsiveness to practical challenges, and the commitment of the institutions and stakeholders responsible for its implementation,” the Minister also noted while stressing the importance of the validation exercise.

Acting Minister of Commerce and Industry Hon. Stephen Yekeson opens the validation workshop on Liberia’s draft National Intellectual Property Policy and Strategy.

The ongoing workshop, which brings together stakeholders from government circles, the creative industries, the business community, higher education institutions and civil society, is convened by the Liberia Intellectual Property Office (LIPO) in collaboration with the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, with technical assistance from the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO).

It comes after a national review of the IP Audit findings last year, which identified gaps in institutional capacity, infrastructure, coordination, and access to intellectual property services as constraints that continue to limit the use of the intellectual property system.

The draft NIPPS responds to these findings by seeking to strengthen the country’s intellectual property system and increase its usage and responsiveness. The document, which was developed by experts in intellectual property, aligns with the Government’s national development priorities in the ARREST Agenda and brings coherence to the work of LIPO and other government institutions, while positioning Liberia to take full advantage of regional and global opportunities.

Speaking earlier, LIPO Director General Hon. Garmai Koboi said the draft was made possible through high-level engagement with WIPO in order to align the country’s IP regime with international intellectual property standards and frameworks administered by WIPO, the African Regional Intellectual Property Organization (ARIPO), and others.

Hon. Koboi noted that the workshop gives stakeholders an opportunity to confirm that the draft reflects their experiences, challenge impractical measures and examine institutional responsibilities.

“We extend our profound appreciation to the World Intellectual Property Organization for its invaluable technical and financial support. This partnership reflects WIPO’s long-term commitment to helping member states build intellectual property systems that serve their development aspirations, and Liberia is proud to count WIPO among its steadfast partners,” Hon. Koboi added.

“I also recognize both the national and international consultants, whose expertise guided the preparation of this draft; the members of the Technical Steering Committee, who gave their time and recommendations; and the many institutions, enterprises, creators, and individuals who participated in the National IP Audit and the stakeholder consultations,” noted the Director General.

Also speaking, WIPO Representative Emmanuel Rugomboka, a Counsellor in the organization’s Division for Africa, said the document could help connect intellectual property protection with economic diversification, stronger local enterprises and opportunities for women and young entrepreneurs.

He illustrated this potential with a hypothetical Liberian cocoa or coffee cooperative. “Imagine a Liberian agricultural cooperative producing high-quality cocoa or coffee. With the right policy framework, the cooperative could receive support to develop a distinctive brand, protect its trademark, meet quality standards, and explore geographical indication protection where appropriate,” Mr. Rugomboka said.

“By combining intellectual property protection with improved production, processing, packaging and market access, the cooperative could differentiate its products, negotiate better prices and reach higher-value domestic and international markets,” he added. “The resulting benefits could include increased incomes for farmers, new opportunities for young entrepreneurs, and jobs in processing, packaging, marketing and distribution.”

According to Mr. Rugomboka, WIPO stood ready to support implementation of NIPPS in line with Liberia’s priorities and available resources, including efforts to help businesses build competitive brands, researchers bring discoveries to market and creators benefit from their work.
