World.title: Justice Dept. sues California, claims noncitizens were sent ballots
World.content:
Washington — The Justice Department sued California on Thursday, alleging that the federal government has identified more than 20,000 noncitizens who are unlawfully registered to vote.

The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, came after Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter sent letters to counties earlier this week, including Los Angeles, ordering them to review a list of names of suspected noncitizens who he alleged received mail-in ballots for the upcoming midterm elections.

"State-facilitated voter fraud is unacceptable in the United States of America," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement announcing the lawsuit.

"If found responsible in a court of law, the State of California will have seriously undermined confidence in our electoral system and violated laws that protect our nation's representative system of government."

In the letter that McCotter sent to the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk, he enclosed a password-protected thumb drive that he said contained names compiled by the Department of Homeland Security, and imposed a 48-hour deadline for the clerk's office to review the list.

Dean Logan, the registrar-recorder and clerk, said in a statement responding to McCotter's demands that the county would not be reviewing the materials on the thumb drive because doing so would conflict with "established data privacy and information security protocols." He said the device was not considered a "secure medium."

Secretary of State Shirley Weber, meanwhile, said the Justice Department had not provided the list of names and blasted the Trump administration for what it said were "unsubstantiated claims" that California had 190,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls.

In Thursday's lawsuit, the Justice Department accused the state of failing to work with the federal government to correct the alleged problems with its voter rolls.

"The Federal Government asked California to work collaboratively to identify any noncitizens registered to vote in the State. California made no serious effort to do so," the lawsuit said.

"The United States thus seeks commonplace election relief when a ballot is called into question. This Court should enjoin California from presently tabulating vote-by-mail ballots from likely noncitizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter's citizenship status can be determined," it added.

In a statement provided to CBS News, the California Secretary of State's office said, "Due to the pending litigation, we have no further information we can share regarding the matter." It directed CBS News to its news release on the situation and Weber's letter to McCotter.

CBS News has also reached out to the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk for comment.

The Justice Department's Civil Rights Division has filed 31 lawsuits in an effort to force states to hand over unredacted copies of their voter rolls. The division has said it wants to ensure states are keeping clean voter lists, but it has since acknowledged that it also intends to share the data with the Department of Homeland Security so that the lists can be screened for noncitizens.

Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general for the Civil Rights Division, sent letters to all 50 states in July threatening to take criminal action if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their voter rolls.

So far, the Justice Department has lost 26 of those cases, and has not achieved one legal victory to date.

It has resorted to using publicly available voter lists and other investigative means to try to identify noncitizens who may be registered in those states.

World.title: Why some Gen Z voters who backed Trump now regret their decision
World.content:
Why some Gen Z voters who backed Trump now regret their decision

toggle caption i Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images

Gen Z Americans were a key part of President Trump's winning coalition in 2024. Nearly two years later — and with early voting underway in multiple states for the midterms — some of that youth support has faded.

That sentiment was on display in a focus group, conducted last week, of eight Generation Z Trump voters, who reported varying degrees of unhappiness and disappointment over the state of politics, with some going as far as to say they regret supporting Trump in 2024.

The conversation was conducted virtually by Navigator Research, a left-leaning polling group. Participants ranged in age from 20 to 29 and spanned five states: Florida, Mississippi, Ohio, Texas and South Carolina — places Trump won by double digits in the last election. Two of those states, Texas and Ohio, are home to competitive races that could be key to control of the Senate.

Sponsor Message

For participants who now regret their vote for Trump, much of their frustration centers on what they see as a string of failed promises. When asked to give the president's job performance a letter grade, a majority of participants, 6 out of 8, assigned him a grade of either D or F, while two selected C.

"I just feel like nothing went correctly. I just feel like everything got worse," said John, a 29-year-old Black man from Florida. (Participants agreed to be part of the focus group on the condition that they be identified by only their first names.)

John, who identifies as a Republican and has voted for Trump since 2016, gave the president an F and said he now plans to support Democratic candidates this fall, in large part because of the strain he has felt from rising costs.

"I'm willing to give the other side a chance," he added. "I don't think they're going to make a total change. But things are just horrible right now for me. So I feel like even if they make one or two small changes, it will probably benefit me."

Though the focus group is not a nationally representative survey, the frustrations shared by participants echoed Navigator polling released in August, which found that nearly a third of Gen Zers — those under age 30 — regret voting for Trump, higher than older generations do.

Sponsor Message

Trump's rising unpopularity among young voters isn't in a vacuum. He has also lost ground with other key groups that shifted right in 2024, notably independents and Latino voters — and in a year when the Republican Party is facing political headwinds, it's unclear whether that expanded coalition from two years ago can show up at the same strength now.

Shifting toward Democrats — or not

While some voters, like John in Florida, do feel compelled to vote blue this cycle in response to Trump, 4 of the 8 who took part in the focus group said they still planned to back Republicans this year. Three said they'd vote for Democrats; one participant said she was still deciding.

Matthew, a 25-year-old Black man living in Texas, said he doesn't regret his support for the president and gave him a C grade.

"I feel like he's done a really good job closing the border," he said. "I also do appreciate his efforts in trying to end some of the conflicts that began under the last administration, besides the fact that the Iran conflict hasn't really worked the best, from my perspective."

He plans to vote in the midterm elections and argued that Trump will be able to carry out more of his agenda if Republicans can secure a larger majority in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, although national polls indicate that the GOP is more likely to lose seats.

But enthusiasm is a different question.

Courtney, a 20-year-old white woman based in South Carolina, said she doesn't regret her vote for Trump in 2024 and overall aligns with Republicans, but she did admit she has grown more distrustful of both major political parties, particularly on foreign policy.

"I just really do feel like we would be in this situation either way. … Education, the economy, everything else would be so much better if we weren't pumping money out into other countries that aren't ours," she said, referring to U.S. aid for Israel and the decision to go to war with Iran.

Sponsor Message

"I don't think it matters what side you vote on — that's why I voted red, because I agree with those policies more — but at the end of the day, what we do in the Middle East is going to be not at all up to [the] party [in power]," she said during the focus group.

That sense of political disaffection may underscore a growing challenge for both Republicans and Democrats moving forward as both try to repair ties with this generation.

"As we see people regret their vote for Trump, sour on the Republican Party and Republican policies, that doesn't necessarily mean that they're swinging right over to Democrats," said Melissa Toufanian, the managing director at Navigator.

Toufanian points to Navigator's own polling, which has found that even as the GOP has lost trust on economic issues, "it's not a one-for-one with Democrats gaining that trust."

"A lot of people are moving to this middle, this category that 'I don't trust either party,'" she said. "We are seeing people who are becoming increasingly pessimistic about our political parties and our political system, and they're not feeling strongly that either party can really deliver for them."

World.title: Do Americans own the president's papers? Appeals court to weigh in
World.content:
Do Americans own the president's papers? Appeals court to weigh in

toggle caption i Alon Skuy/Getty Images

President Trump has famously pushed the bounds of executive power since he returned to the White House.



In arguments Friday before a federal appeals court in Washington, administration lawyers will make an especially bold claim: that papers created in the White House belong to Donald Trump, not to the American people. The move comes amid a series of actions under Trump's second term to test the limits put in place after the Watergate scandal, and could be another case that ends up at the conservative-leaning Supreme Court.

Six months ago, the Justice Department moved to invalidate the Presidential Records Act, a federal law in place since 1978. Conservative lawyer Michael Edney cast the move in a long line of other attempts to pare back statutes from that era.

Sponsor Message

"This is a story about a post-Watergate, overbroad statutory incursion into the prerogatives of the executive branch," Edney said in a recent webinar sponsored by the Federalist Society.

For some 200 years, presidents could decide for themselves what to do with the papers they created in office, until disputes with Richard Nixon prompted Congress to weigh in. Every president since then has complied with the records law, until this year.

"The Presidential Records Act is unconstitutional and a clear violation of the separation of powers," said White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis.

The White House's reinterpretation of the act comes after Trump was indicted on obstruction of justice charges for allegedly stockpiling classified documents in a bathroom, ballroom and office at his Mar-a-Lago resort. A federal judge threw out the case for technical reasons, related to the appointment of the prosecutor, and the Justice Department ultimately dropped the case after Trump won reelection.

Question about the public's right to papers

Nikhel Sus is chief counsel for Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a watchdog group that sued over the Trump move.

"If the courts were to accept it, and we are hopeful that they will not, it would mean the people really have no right of access to the president's papers and that would be a major loss for archivists, historians and to the American people writ large," Sus said.

Senior U.S. District Judge John Bates, an appointee of former President George W. Bush, ruled against the Trump White House this year, in a decision that opened with a passage from George Orwell's dystopian novel 1984: "Who controls the past controls the future; who controls the present controls the past," the judge wrote.

Sponsor Message

Three judges from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit will consider the issue on Friday.

The Trump administration said in court papers that keeping all those records imposes a burden on the White House and that it could chill advisers from having honest conversations with the president.

Continuity of government

But former government officials say being able to consult these papers is essential.

"Access to the records on national security issues of former presidents is really vital for the continuity of our government," said John Bellinger, who served as legal adviser to the National Security Council under George W. Bush.

Bellinger said he and other members of Bush's staff sometimes requested the papers of President Bill Clinton, to understand conversations Clinton had with world leaders and members of Congress.

"Often the only record of what a president has said to a foreign leader — or perhaps even more important, what a foreign leader, friend or foe, has said to the president of the United States — is in a written document," Bellinger said.

To not be able to see those papers, he said, will leave future presidents at a "terrible disadvantage."

Edney, who also worked for Bush's National Security Council and Justice Department, said he believed that Congress could probably pass a "thoughtful" records preservation statute. He said parts of the current Presidential Records Act that provide Congress with automatic access and presume the records will be publicly disclosed are "constitutionally problematic."

Edney said he has some doubts about whether the watchdog groups suing to challenge Trump's move actually have legal standing to proceed.

But the Trump administration appears to have breezed past those concerns, because they have a higher goal in mind.

"They want this to go to the Supreme Court," Edney said. "I think they want this resolved at a time of their choosing, with arguments of their choosing, and a court of their choosing, and with the Solicitor General's office that's making their arguments, as opposed to a subsequent administration."

World.title: A rare family of barn owls moved into Manhattan's Upper West Side. New Yorkers are captivated
World.content:
A rare family of barn owls moved into Manhattan's Upper West Side. New Yorkers are captivated

toggle caption i Yuki Iwamura/AP

NEW YORK — Manhattan's Upper West Side has been reveling in the company of its latest celebrities: A family of barn owls nested in a water tower atop a building near Central Park.

This is the first documented instance of barn owls nesting in Manhattan in modern history, according to one expert, and the owls have attracted nightly crowds of people in the street eager to get a glimpse of the elusive birds.

"It was, like, totally shocking," Andrew Farnsworth, a migration ecologist at the Cornell Lab of Ornithology, said of the barn owls. "To the best of our knowledge, like the collective birding knowledge, there hasn't been a nest in, you know, in Manhattan, at least in recorded history."

toggle caption i Yuki Iwamura/AP

Word of the barn owl family didn't get around until last week, when Elisabeth Williams, an Upper West Side resident, notified a local news outlet on Oct. 6 that she and her husband saw multiple owls at the water tower atop a building on West 75th Street close to Central Park West.

Sponsor Message

The couple had previously seen a single owl on an apartment windowsill a few days earlier and were shocked even then, Williams recalled.

"In a place like Manhattan, you normally really have to go out of your way to encounter nature," she said. "And here it was, just sort of right outside our window."

Barn owl sightings are rare in New York City

It's not the first time that birds have captivated New Yorkers. Residents have fallen in love with American woodcocks, who are known to stop in Midtown Manhattan's Bryant Park every year as they migrate north in early spring.

After Flaco the Eurasian eagle-owl died in 2024, dozens of mournful fans gathered to say goodbye to the beloved creature who flew around Manhattan and became a joy to many after someone let him out of his zoo enclosure the previous year. Then there was Pale Male, a red-tailed hawk who nested above Fifth Avenue for three decades before dying in 2023.

But barn owl sightings in New York City parks are very rare, according to the New York City Department of Parks & Recreation. New York is at the northern fringe of the barn owl's range and the barn owl population has declined "at an alarming rate" over time, according to the state Department of Environmental Conservation.

Sponsor Message

"There's lots of excitement among New Yorkers, both birders and non-birders alike, about these owls because owls really capture the attention," said Jessica Wilson, executive director of NYC Bird Alliance. "They're magical, they're nocturnal, they are secretive, they're not commonly seen, especially on the Upper West Side of Manhattan. And to have this chance to see these birds is really thrilling."

Photographers and casual onlookers have gathered on the street on a nightly basis to spot the owls.

toggle caption i Yuki Iwamura/AP

"I've only seen one barn owl ever, and that was in California," said Val Coleman, a retired New York City resident who was on the Upper West Side earlier this week trying to spot the owls. "At dusk, we hope they will come out to hunt. We hope they don't eat poisoned rats with rodenticide in 'em."

David Barrett, a Manhattan-based birder who runs the popular social media account, Manhattan Bird Alert, said he's observed at least one adult barn owl and five fledglings at the water tower. He's also seen an adult owl carrying rodents back to the water tower. There are believed to be two adult owls, and some photographers have claimed to have seen six fledglings, Barrett added.

"Having one barn owl is a rarity, but it's not national news. Having a family, for the first time ever, breeding in Manhattan in recorded history, that's special news," Barrett said.

Screeching was heard by residents

Before the recent barn owl sightings, Williams and her husband heard periodic screeching noises outside going back to early September. They initially assumed it was a bird of some kind but were skeptical when a phone app indicated the noise was from a barn owl.

Thomas Obersteiner said that he first heard bizarre screeching and wailing noises from outside one evening in mid-September. It sounded like someone was "being murdered outside," he said.

Sponsor Message

"That lasted for two or three weeks, every night, sometimes more, sometimes less, coming from different directions," Obersteiner added. "But I had no idea what that was."

toggle caption i Yuki Iwamura/AP

On multiple occasions, Obersteiner or his wife ran into their children's bedroom after mistaking the owls' screech for a child in pain, he said. It wasn't until he saw a news report that he realized that owls were making the sounds.

Farnsworth said the screech is typical of barn owls, who use it to communicate with one another. The screech is like a "horror movie kind of experience," he said.

Obersteiner, who said his roof deck is "probably the best location in town right now" to watch the owls, has been letting nature photographers access that perch to observe the owls "almost every night" since news of the barn owls spread. On one night last week, 20 people had gathered.

"We can't say no because it's so much fun and these people are so serious," Obersteiner added. "It's beautiful."

Williams and her husband were not bird watchers before the barn owl family moved in to the water tower. But that may change soon after their "delightful" experience.

"I think we're about to become birders," Williams said.

World.title: Brewers sweep the Dodgers to reach the World Series for the first time since 1982
World.content:
Brewers sweep the Dodgers to reach the World Series for the first time since 1982

toggle caption i Ashley Landis/AP

LOS ANGELES — After 44 years, the Milwaukee Brewers are finally going back to the World Series.

Propelled by a lockdown bullpen and repeated comebacks, the young and fearless Brewers swept the two-time defending champion Los Angeles Dodgers out of the playoffs Thursday with a 6-4 victory in Game 4 of the National League Championship Series.

"We weren't coming in to play patty-cake," manager Pat Murphy said. "We were hungry, and as long as it's an even playing field, we're going to come in and give it our best shot to win. That's exactly what we did."

Garrett Mitchell hit a go-ahead homer in the sixth inning and Milwaukee's brilliant relievers slammed the door late, giving a vocal contingent of Brewers fans their chance to celebrate in the Dodger Stadium stands.

Now, the Brewers get an opportunity to win their first title after topping the majors with 103 wins during the regular season. Milwaukee has a week off before hosting Cleveland or Tampa Bay in the World Series opener on Oct. 23.

Sponsor Message

"I'm excited that we've got a few more games to play and get to go home with the fans and celebrate there, too," Mitchell said.

Shohei Ohtani's first home run this postseason helped put the Dodgers ahead 4-0 in the second inning before the Brewers came back to complete a four-game sweep.

No. 9 hitter David Hamilton's two-out solo shot off Edwin Díaz gave Milwaukee a two-run cushion in the ninth. Hamilton had just four homers in the regular season.

"We got down early tonight and we were like, it's going to be a great story," Brewers captain Christian Yelich said. "We're going to come back and win this. Like, stay together, start chipping away. And that's exactly what they did."

Aaron Ashby pitched three scoreless innings for a save as the Brewers won their first NL pennant and second overall. Milwaukee was in the American League when the franchise made its only previous World Series appearance in 1982, a seven-game loss to the St. Louis Cardinals.

The Dodgers' goal of a three-peat — not done since the New York Yankees from 1998-2000 and never by a National League team — died with their anemic offense and injuries to Ohtani and others on their aging roster.

Sponsor Message

"I'm not used to those consolation speeches," manager Dave Roberts said. "Those guys played flawless. You got to sometimes tip your cap."

Milwaukee became the first major league club to finish a postseason sweep after getting swept by that same opponent in the previous postseason. Los Angeles took all four NLCS games against Milwaukee last season.

"They may have a bunch of Hall of Famers, but we've got a bunch of gamers — and the gamers won this week," Murphy said.

"I think the Dodgers figured out that we came in here with a little different attitude this year."

The Brewers also are the first team to sweep a best-of-seven postseason series in which it trailed in every game.

"There was never a doubt in that dugout what was going to happen tonight. We knew we were going to win that game," said first baseman Jake Bauers, the NLCS MVP.

toggle caption i Ashley Landis/AP

With the score tied 4-all, Mitchell fell behind 0-2 before reliever Tanner Scott threw three straight balls for a full count. Mitchell's 409-foot leadoff drive to center field — the first homer of his career on an 0-2 count — put the Brewers ahead for the first time. Mitchell also homered in their 6-2 victory Wednesday.

"It's absolutely surreal," Mitchell said. "You talk about the battle-tested Brewers. We went down early and the belief in that dugout got stronger and stronger."

The Brewers' bullpen coolly turned away multiple threats when the Dodgers had the potential tying run on base.

Winning pitcher JoJo Romero struck out Max Muncy with Kyle Tucker at third to end the sixth.

With one out in the seventh and a runner on third, Ashby struck out Ohtani swinging before Mookie Betts grounded out to end the inning. Will Smith doubled to right with one out in the eighth and was safe at third when the ball got away from Sal Frelick for an error before Ashby got Tucker to fly out and Teoscar Hernández to strike out.

Sponsor Message

"Playing with that chip on our shoulder," Ashby said. "You don't ever know what to expect going into a series like that last year (against the Dodgers). You don't know how bad it can be, and then it was as bad as it was. And we came out and we survived, and we came back this year, and those guys played their tails off."

The Brewers tied it in the fifth, when the Dodgers bullpen issued four walks and Milwaukee stole two bases. Hamilton's single chased starter Tyler Glasnow and scored Frelick, who walked and stole second, to pull Milwaukee to 4-3.

Alex Vesia came in and promptly walked Brice Turang and William Contreras to load the bases. Vesia then walked Bauers with two outs to force in Hamilton with the tying run.

Glasnow retired his first 10 batters — six on strikeouts — before the Brewers got to him in the fourth. Turang walked, Contreras hit a ground-rule double and Bauers followed with another ground-rule double that closed Milwaukee to 4-2.

Ohtani broke out of his postseason slump with a three-run homer after Andy Pages' RBI single in the second. The four-time MVP released weeks of pent-up frustration by raising his arms and yelling and the crowd of 49,104 joined him in celebration.

But the Brewers wouldn't be denied. And when it was over, owner Mark Attanasio thought of Milwaukee's longtime owner and beloved late broadcaster.

"It's so important for the community, the entire state of Wisconsin," Attanasio said. "We're standing on shoulders of Bud Selig and Bob Uecker."

World.title: Hit a midlife wall? This test identifies your strengths and what matters to you
World.content:
Hit a midlife wall? This test identifies your strengths and what matters to you

toggle caption i Westend61/Getty Images

When's the last time you asked yourself: What do I love to do? What makes me feel alive?

Earlier this year, as Ailsa Chang planned her 50th birthday party, I welcomed her to this side of life. Ailsa and I pick up that conversation on All Things Considered as I launch a new podcast, Your Turn with Allison Aubrey , aimed at navigating the twists and turns of midlife.

If you've been focused on work deadlines and family obligations, without much time to focus on yourself, you're in good company. And in midlife, a lot can shift: Kids launch. Careers and relationships change. These transitions can be tough, but they also open the door to what's next.

Sponsor Message

So, I went in search of tools to help me find my way. I invite you to join the Your Turn newsletter journey - starting with this survey that ranks your character strengths.

Start with a strengths survey

The VIA Character Strengths Survey is a free online questionnaire developed by researchers in positive psychology, the scientific study of what helps people flourish. The question behind it: How do we go from feeling just OK to thriving?

"Character Strengths are the positive parts of your personality that impact how you think, feel and behave," explains the VIA Institute on Character. After you answer a series of questions, the survey rank-orders 24 strengths, from creativity, humor and teamwork to curiosity, bravery and spirituality.

Research suggests that applying your strengths in daily life can help boost wellbeing and reduce stress. And a study of women 50 and older, found those who used a signature strength in a new way, had increased levels of happiness and less depression.

The survey takes about 15 to 20 minutes to complete. You can take it on your own or with a facilitator. I took it at a retreat at the Modern Elder Academy with Christine Carter, Ph.D. , a wellness and lifestyle coach, and a senior fellow at UC Berkeley's Greater Good Science Center.

Sponsor Message

Your strengths are a compass

Carter says there's value in reflecting on the results.

"What I really like people to do is take it and then look at their top strengths and remember how you feel when you're engaging that strength," she told me. "I think that it can be a real compass for the types of intrinsic motivation that we're looking for in finding our purpose."

Carter has an art degree and used to be a painter. Appreciation of beauty and excellence ranks near the top of her list, along with gratitude and zest. When she's absorbed in a work of art or a great piece of writing, she says, she feels part of something bigger than herself.

One of my top strengths is a love of learning, a good match for a career in journalism. I get to learn something new every day.

What if your results don't resonate?

This happens a lot. Your top strengths can reflect where you've been and how you've been spending your time. The good news: They aren't fixed. "Your character strengths can evolve," Carter says. Shift your focus, or how you spend your time, and your results can shift too.

3 questions to ask as you review your strengths

Which strengths do I want to cultivate? Look for a strength you value but haven't made time for. If creativity ranks lower than you'd expect, that's a sign of where to invest a little time. "Humans are meaning makers," Carter says. As your roles shift, so can your sense of purpose. A new project or hobby doesn't need to be big. It just needs to be true to you. What brought me joy as a kid? Think back to what absorbed you before life got busy, whether it was exploring the woods, drawing or singing in a choir. Then look for the strengths behind it. If appreciation of beauty ranks high, more time in nature or at a concert may be what feeds you. What do I want to leave behind? Notice the habits and expectations that no longer serve you. Change takes courage, especially when it means letting go of something to make room for what's next. But many people who've made big midlife changes describe it as freeing.

Sponsor Message

If you have a half hour this week, take the survey. Then pick one strength you'd like to make more room for, and invite it into your life. You don't need to overhaul your life to start; one small step can set you on a new course.

World.title: He followed a debunked conspiracy theory to claim a tax refund. So why did the CRA agree to a $40M payout?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In the summer of 2023, northern Ontario ironworker Jonathon Pearce filed bogus tax returns to the Canada Revenue Agency, falsely claiming he was owed refunds going back several years totalling more than $40 million.

Internal records obtained by CBC's the fifth estate show the agen cy did not check the veracity of the returns and two weeks later began sending out the refunds in instalments to Pearce's bank account, including a $10-million deposit on Aug. 8, 2023.

Pearce, a longtime resident of Temiskaming Shores, 500 kilometres north of Toronto, initially declined an interview.

But when fifth estate co-host Steven D'Souza knocked on his door recently, Pearce said he was as surprised as anyone when the millions landed in his personal bank account.

"I thought [the CRA] would turn around and say, 'I'm sorry, sir, this doesn't work that way.' Next thing you know, [I was] getting a refund," he said. "Well, this is an easy way to create money."

WATCH | Explaining his perspective: CBC interviews man who received more than $10M in CRA refund | Duration closed caption 1:28 When the fifth estate knocked on his door, Jonathon Pearce was initially reluctant to talk but spent more than an hour explaining his perspective as hidden cameras rolled.

A fifth estate investigation has found that Pearce is one of a growing movement of so-called "sovereign s" who believe Canada as a country does not exist. Following debunked online conspiracy theories, they have successfully duped the CRA into repeatedly handing over millions in bogus refunds, taking advantage of massive gaps in the agency's fraud detection systems.

A CRA affidavit obtained by the fifth estate shows that Pearce himself contacted the agency's call centre 10 days before he got the refund. An agency investigator who later listened to the recording stated that Pearce outlined the tax "scheme" and his conspiracy beliefs.

Despite Pearce's phone call, the agency still deposited millions in his bank account.

Watch the full documentary, "The Sovereign Swindle," from the fifth estate on YouTube or CBC-TV on Friday at 9 p.m .

After the agency looked into how Pearce got his refund, leaked records show it identified that between May 2023 and January 2024, nearly $300 million in bogus claims were linked to the same tax scheme as Pearce. It is unclear how much was paid out.

One auditor later wrote there was no validation process in place to "verify the legitimacy" of the requested refunds before they go out.

Heather Evans was appointed commissioner of the Canada Revenue Agency on July 13, 2026. Evans declined an interview with the fifth estate. (Canadian Revenue Agency)

In a recent stateme nt to the fifth estate, the CRA said it is "unable" to know how much money in total the agency has paid out in bogus returns to sovereign citizen groups, also known as "tax protesters," because it does not track fraudulent returns by "personal views or intent."

The commissioner of the Canada Revenue Agency, Heather Evans, declined an interview.

The minister responsible for the agency, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, told the fifth estate he was unaware of the specific allegations.

"We have a robust process to make sure of the integrity of what we do at the CRA, but we'll be looking into that," he told co-host Steven D'Souza outside a recent cabinet meeting.

An in-depth review of Pearce's Facebook profile shows he follows a debunked online conspiracy theory falsely claiming that every Canadian has a secret trust set up for them when they are born worth millions. According to the fallacy circulating online, only people with specialized knowledge are able to unlock the funds.

Former CRA investigator Shawna Roy says the theory is ludicrous and that there is no pot of money assigned at birth.

"That is not a thing," she said.

The government does "not have a trust assigned to you" when you are born, Roy told the fifth estate.

Former Canada Revenue Agency investigator Shawna Roy thinks there needs to be more checks and balances at the CRA to stop bogus refunds from being sent out. (Ousama Farag/CBC)

Pearce, however, said he believes more strongly in the debunked conspiracy theory than ever because the CRA did, in fact, give him the money.

"If the CRA gives me money, who are you to f–king question it?" Pearce told D'Souza.

"As far as I'm concerned, it was between me and CRA. If CRA had a problem, they wouldn't have given me the money."

In his return, Pearce filed T4A slips, which are typically used to report extra income. In his case, Pearce did not report any income, but erroneously stated he had paid millions in taxes since 2016 and wanted it refunded.

CRA's conduct 'enraging,' says former investigator

Roy told the fifth estate Pearce's views are not based on fact or law and that he clearly filed a bogus tax return at the expense of the public purse. She said it is concerning that three years later he appears not to have been charged with tax fraud.

"I can't comprehend it, I can't make sense of it."

Roy said if the agency had done even a little due diligence, it would have known that a factory worker requesting a $40-million refund would probably not qualify for one.

"I think it's enraging."

If you have tips on this topic please email, in confidence, Harvey.Cashore@cbc.ca or fifthtips@cbc.ca or call or text 416-526-4704.

During an hour-long interview on his front porch, Pearce remained unapologetic about getting the refund, echoing anti-government and anti-tax videos he frequently reposts on his public Facebook page, including conspiracies that Western democracies are illegitimate.

The conversation took place only a few metres from Pearce's Ford F-250 truck, which he says he purchased after receiving the CRA refunds and which he then made his profile picture on Facebook.

Pearce said everyone could do what he did if they just knew how.

"If you really want to know this stuff, you really got to dig deep."

Pearce said he learned those secrets through online "sovereign" gurus who provide seminars on how not to pay tax and still get a refund from the CRA.

The CRA alleges in court documents that Teresa Wallace, left, Angela Bowolin, Bernard Yankson and Pearce are linked to bogus tax refunds. (Daniel Rofusz)

In a statement, Dave Conabree, the CRA's assistant commissioner of security, said that while he could not comment on specific cases, they were aware of schemes "promoted by individuals who reject or challenge Canada's tax system."

"The CRA takes these activities very seriously and has measures in place to detect, prevent and address fraud and non-compliance."

Still, those public court documents obtained by the fifth estate detail how the agency was aware of the ironworker's conspiracy beliefs in advance of paying the bogus refunds.

An affidavit filed in early September 2024 by the CRA in Ontario Court of Justice states that Pearce contacted the agency's call centre on July 21, 2023 — more than a week before the CRA began sending Pearce the money.

According to the affidavit, Pearce discussed "matters relating to the alleged scheme for a majority of the [July 21] call" and told the call centre "he shouldn't be paying taxes."

Yet 10 days later, on July 31, the CRA deposited the first instalment of refunds into Pearce's account for slightly less than $500,000.

Instalments stopped after bank alert

On Aug. 8, Pearce received a further $10 million. Two more scheduled instalments of $10 and $20 million for later in August were stopped after Pearce's bank alerted the agency to the unusual payments, according to internal CRA documents.

In a followup email to the fifth estate, the agency said it would not answer questions about why it began depositing millions into Pearce's account despite knowing about his conspiracy beliefs beforehand.

Despite having filed a lengthy affidavit in public court about Pearce's tax details, the media office said that the CRA itself cannot disclose individual taxpayer information and would therefore also not provide the fifth estate with recordings of Pearce's conversations with the agency's call centre.

Former CRA investigator Roy said the whole story is discouraging for honest Canadians who pay their fair share of taxes and that the $10 million-plus refund should never have been paid in the first place.

"We're paying what we're supposed to pay and then you have people who can make a complete mockery and joke out of the system and then still get away with it."

Canada is a 'corporation'

According to Carmen Celestini, a lecturer at the University of Waterloo in Waterloo, Ont., who studies conspiracy theories and disinformation, so-called sovereigns believe Canada is not a country, but rather a "corporation" — and that they can opt out.

A sovereign is "somebody who sees themselves separate from society," she told the fifth estate. "They are not part of our nation. They can create their own nation. They are not beholden to our laws."

WATCH | An inadvertent effect: Carmen Celestini responds to what the fifth estate uncovered | Duration closed caption 0:17 University of Waterloo lecturer Carmen Celestini says bogus payouts by the CRA inadvertently validate anti-democratic conspiracy theories.

Leaked internal CRA records say that, in addition to Pearce, there were 19 social insurance numbers representing other individuals involved with the specific scheme he used.

Facebook conspiracy theories

The fifth estate has learned there are networks of "sovereign" online forums, websites and social media apps, many of which sprang up after the 2020 COVID-19 lockdowns. For a fee, some of them actively instruct followers how to become "sovereign" and claim tax refunds from the CRA.

One "sovereign" website promising tax refunds is run by Angela Albright Bowolin in Kaslo, in B.C.'s southern Interior.

In her online videos, she promises to unlock sovereign secrets to members who make a "donation." On her personal Facebook page, she said "not paying taxes" is possible, and that she is "leaving that system" and that "You can, too!"

The fifth estate has learned that one of her followers is Teresa Wallace, from Silverton in B.C.'s Interior, who the CRA now alleges received a bogus $5-million tax refund in 2024. Court records show the agency is attempting to get the money back.

In an audio recording posted on Bowolin's website, Wallace and her partner, Peter Gay, who also goes by Peter Carson, credit Bowolin and her colleague, Bernard Yankson, with helping them out.

Wallace and Gay did not respond to calls and emails from the fifth estate.

Pearce, however, credits Vancouver-based sovereign guru AJ DeSwart for helping him achieve his refund fr om the CRA.

DeSwart, who has their own public Telegram channel, posted voice memos in June that there are "billions and billions" available. "I knew about this shit a long time ago."

WATCH | Following a sovereign guru: Following a Vancouver-based sovereign guru | Duration closed caption 0:13 Jonathon Pearce says AJ Deswart looked over his CRA documents before he sent them in.

Raids 'across the country'

The fifth estate has learned that after paying out tens of millions in bogus refunds, the CRA is scrambling to undo the damage — and has launched criminal investigations into at least two sovereign gurus in the Vancouver area.

DeSwart has raised concerns about those CRA investigations on Telegram.

"There are raids happening across the country with 16-plus f–king agents and a bunch of RCMP officers," DeSwart said in a Telegram voice note in June.

DeSwart declined an on-camera interview, but told the fifth estate they did not help Pearce.

Still, court records obtained by the fifth estate back up their claims about criminal investigations.

A search warrant dated May 23, 2026, authorized a CRA search of Yankson's home, alleging he and Bowolin had engaged in tax fraud by counselling "others to make false statements … on tax returns" and to "obtain refunds that they are not entitled to."

According to internal records, the CRA scrambled to recover the millions it paid Pearce, but was still searching for more than $1 million that had been spent or gone missing. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

The fifth estate reached out to both Bowolin and Yankson.

Bowolin declined to speak to the fifth estate. In an e-mail to the CBC, Bolowin says she hasn't been charged with any offence and denies any criminal wrongdoing.

In an email, Yankson said he "categorically rejects any allegation" that associates him with fraud, unlawful activities or anti-government movements, or hostility towards government institutions, including allegations made by the CRA.

Yankson has filed a lawsuit concerning the raids in Federal Court, arguing his Charter rights were violated. No court date has been scheduled.

Back in Ontario, Pearce told the fifth estate the CRA searched his home two years ago and is garnishing his wages, but believes he will never be charged.

According to internal agency records, the CRA scrambled to recover the millions it paid Pearce, but was still searching for more than $1 million that had been spent or gone missing.

"I know I haven't done anything wrong," Pearce said.

World.title: Former student says someone hid a webcam in her Royal Military College dorm. No one was ever charged
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Kelly Stewart was plugging in her phone in her dorm room, planning to let it charge while she was in class at the Royal Military College of Canada (RMC), when she found a cord she didn't recognize — one she would later trace to a web camera hidden inside the heater in her wall.

"My whole body just went completely cold," she said during a recent interview at her home in Kingston, N.S.

Documents obtained by Stewart through Access to Information legislation, and shared with CBC News, show the Canadian Forces Military Police launched an investigation into voyeurism and breaking and entering offences on Oct. 31, 2018 — the same day Stewart discovered the webcam in her Kingston, Ont., dorm room and reported it to her superiors.

The following day, the National Investigation Service — a specialized unit that investigates serious matters — took over her case. According to the documents, no charges were ever laid due to insufficient evidence.

Eight years after the alarming discovery — and five years after a firestorm of sexual misconduct allegations in the Canadian Armed Forces prompted a federal review — Stewart is sharing her story publicly for the first time, emboldened by the support for a woman who alleges she was gang raped at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y.

Stewart posted on social media on Oct. 3, writing that recent events out of Cornell had brought back painful memories.

"For 8 years I have carried the weight of other people's disgusting actions, failures and systemic sexism. I owe it to my 20-year-old self to pass that weight off to the men who failed."

WATCH | The moment Stewart found the camera: Woman describes the moment she discovered the hidden webcam | Duration closed caption 1:39 Kelly Stewart was plugging in her phone in her dorm room, planning to let it charge while she was in class at the Royal Military College of Canada, when she found a cord she didn’t recognize — one she would later trace to a web camera hidden inside the heater in her wall.

Stewart files official complaint

Stewart, now 28, believes the investigation into her case was flawed, and though she believes the webcam was put in her room by another student, she says her superiors didn't support her, told her to "toughen up" and suggested her career could be affected by accessing mental health support.

She says her health suffered so much that she ultimately requested a voluntary release, which was granted in September 2019 on compassionate grounds, meaning she was not required to reimburse the government for the cost of her schooling.

In her social media post, Stewart named four people: her former superiors and a military police investigator. CBC News is choosing not to name them as there is no suggestion of any legal wrongdoing on their part.

The Department of National Defence (DND) has confirmed to CBC News that two of the four individuals have since retired. DND declined an interview, but in a statement said it is aware of claims, but for privacy and legal reasons it doesn't comment on matters involving identifiable individuals.

Stewart also filed a formal complaint on May 11, 2025, about the investigating officer. The Military Police Complaints Commission confirmed to CBC News that the complaint is being processed.

The 2018 RMC investigation

The 335-page military police report is heavily redacted but contains photos of the webcam, handwritten police notes and officer activity logs that shed some light on the investigation.

Stewart said she initially thought the investigation would reach a successful conclusion quickly. She felt her immediate, lower-level superiors took her seriously and there was a physical piece of evidence, the camera.

"I found myself a year later with nothing having been actioned," she said.

The documents show it took a month to access surveillance footage from the hallway outside Stewart's room, and that there was some confusion around whether an officer had even requested it.

Stewart said it took more than four months for the police to seize the suspect's laptop, which she said she witnessed herself. She believes it was the first time his laptop was taken.

Investigative photos that show the inside of Stewart’s dorm room at the RMC. Stewart says she found the webcam in the heater. (Canadian Forces National Investigation Service)

The documents show the investigation was formally closed on Aug 14, 2020 because it did not yield enough information to substantiate the elements of the offence.

The documents list one "person of interest." All the information about them is redacted.

Stewart said around three months after she discovered the webcam, and after she had moved back into her dorm, a staff member at the college told her that her superiors knew who the suspect was and that he was living a few doors down from her. She said the staff member told her he had been told not to give her this information.

Having to continue living alongside the man she believed violated her was incredibly difficult, she said.

She said she repeatedly asked her superiors to move the suspect to another building but was told it was not possible — that she could move instead. She felt that was unfair.

WATCH | How Canadian Forces investigate: Rare look at how Canadian Forces investigates sexual assault allegations | Duration 9:14 Documents obtained by CBC News reveal details of military investigations into two separate, alleged sexual misconduct incidents, giving a rare look into Canada's military justice system and how that system could be failing victims of sexual assault.

Stewart said she quit going to class, was afraid to go to the dining hall for fear of running into the suspect and lost a lot of weight.

She said a superior told her: "If you want a career in the military, you'll have to get used to being uncomfortable and not getting along with everybody."

Stewart's release records, which she provided to CBC News, state she performed well in all aspects at the college, up until her last semester, when she failed three courses.

Her release records state she was a victim of harmful and inappropriate sexual behaviour and that her release was directly related to that incident.

Sexual harassment not uncommon: former RMC student

CBC News has spoken with a male friend of Stewart's, who lived in the same dorm.

CBC News is withholding his name because he remains a serving member of the military and fears disciplinary repercussions that could affect his career progression.

He said he believes it was possible for RMC to move the suspect to another building to make things easier for Stewart.

"I just don't think they were thinking hard enough because they could have just moved a handful of people into different positions at the beginning of the next year."

He also said all of his female friends from the RMC have told him they've experienced some level of sexual harassment or assault during their time there.

"I don't think I know a single one that didn't have something happen."

A friend of Stewart's said all of his female friends from the RMC have told him they've experienced some level of sexual harassment or assault during their time there. (Dan Taekema/CBC)

During her interview with CBC News, Stewart also disclosed that she had previously been sexually assaulted while she was a student at the French military college in Saint-Jean-sur-Richelieu, Que., before transferring to RMC.

She said she did not include that incident in her social media post because she did not report it. "At the end of the day, nobody failed me because I didn't do anything about it."

A 2023 survey of women attending Canadian military colleges, administered by the colleges, found that five per cent of women canvassed said they were sexually attacked during the previous 12 months.

Everyone deserves 'dignity and respect,' DND says

DND declined an interview, but called Stewart's assault allegations "very concerning," in a statement, stressing there is no time limit for making a report.

"Every Defence Team member has the right to serve in an environment where they are safe and treated with dignity and respect," the statement reads. "We know this standard has not always been met."

The statement goes on to say that in recent years DND and the CAF have taken steps to strengthen support for those affected by sexual misconduct, improve how incidents are reported, reinforce leadership accountability and create a safer culture.

On June 18, the Military Justice System Modernization Act received Royal Assent.

The new law means cases of sexual misconduct in the military will be transferred to the civilian justice system. It includes prohibiting military police from investigating voyeurism. There will be a mandatory external review in three years to determine whether the law should be repealed.

WATCH | The federal government's apology in 2024: Anand issues apology to victims of sexual assault in Canadian Armed Forces | Duration 2:35 Canada's Minister of National Defence Anita Anand said the government acknowledges the pain and trauma members of the Canadian Armed Forces experienced.

Only the passage of time will tell whether there has been meaningful change, said Megan MacKenzie, an expert in gender and the military at Simon Fraser University in B.C.

"We definitely have seen a commitment from many leaders, from many senior people to make changes," she said.

"Whether that is executed on a day-to-day basis for individual leaders and the people that they are responsible for, it's hard to know."

Stewart said she has been diagnosed with generalized anxiety disorder, major depressive disorder and complex post traumatic stress as a result of her experience.

She wants the higher chain of command to know her story.

"I want the colonels, the generals to hear this," she said. "I want them to wake up in the morning and go, 'What can I do differently to protect my subordinates?'"

World.title: Trudeau government advised it would be expected to carry out ICC arrest warrants, including for Netanyahu
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

An internal memo told Justin Trudeau's government that it was expected to pursue the arrests of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, his then defence minister and Hamas leaders if the International Criminal Court were to issue the warrants being prepared by one of its prosecutors.

Trudeau and his successor Mark Carney both later said they would act on the warrants. But the document — dated months before the warrants were ultimately issued — offers a rare glimpse at internal advice the government received from a non-partisan source.

"The International Criminal Court is a designated extradition partner under Canada's Extradition Act," Trudeau's national security adviser at the time, Nathalie Drouin, wrote in a memo dated June 10, 2024.

"Upon a request to co-operate, should one ever be received, Canada would be expected to seek an arrest warrant in a Canadian court," wrote Drouin, who is now Canada's ambassador to France.

CBC News asked the ICC and the federal government if Canada had received a request to co-operate related these warrants, but did not get an answer by deadline.

A protester holds a placard depicting an arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Berlin on Oct. 10, 2026. (Christian Mang/Reuters)

The heavily redacted document, obtained by CBC News through an access to information request, is dated less than a month after ICC prosecutor Karim Khan sought applications for the arrests of Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant, along with senior Hamas figures Yahya Sinwar, Ismail Haniyeh and Mohammed Diab Ibrahim al-Masri.

Israel rejects the charges against Netanyahu and Gallant. The three Hamas leaders have all since been killed by the Israeli Defence Forces.

Immediately after the issuance of Khan's applications, Trudeau publicly said he was troubled by false equivalencies being drawn between Israel's democratically elected government and Hamas, which Canada lists as a terrorist organization.

Similarly, Trudeau's foreign affairs minister, Mélanie Joly, declined to answer journalists' questions about what the Canadian government would do if Netanyahu or Gallant ever came to Canada, calling such a scenario "hypothetical" as no warrants had yet been issued.

"The ICC may request that Canada, as a state party to the Rome Statute, co-operate in the provisional arrest or (if the subject is on the way or in Canada) in the arrest and surrender of that person," Drouin wrote.

Canada's Ambassador to France Nathalie Drouin speaks to reporters during the G7 summit in June. In her previous role, Drouin wrote a memo stating Canada has obligations to the International Criminal Court to enforce arrest warrants. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

"For example, Canada has received a request for provisional arrest following the issuance of a warrant against [Russian] President [Vladimir] Putin."

While the ICC issued its arrest warrant for Putin in March 2023, over a year after Canada prohibited Russian planes from entering its airspace, it is unclear in the memo when that provisional arrest request was received by Canada. CBC News requested more details from Global Affairs Canada but did not receive them by deadline.

The unredacted portions of the memo do not make clear whether Drouin's advice also applied to Canadian airspace.

Once the ICC warrants related to the war in Gaza were issued in November 2024, Trudeau said Canada would "abide by all the regulations and rulings of the international courts, this is just who we are as Canadians."

Joly reiterated Trudeau's stance, though neither explicitly used the word arrest nor named any individuals in their answers.

Carney has been slightly more explicit, saying "yes" in an interview with Bloomberg in October 2025, when he was asked about whether he would arrest Netanyahu should the latter enter Canada.

Netanyahu's government airplane, the Wing of Zion, has flown over Canadian airspace a number of times since the warrants were issued, with the federal government declining to turn the flights away.

On the latest occasion, during the Israeli prime minister's visit to the United Nations General Assembly in New York, a spokesperson for Global Affairs Canada said "authorization to pass through Canadian airspace should not be interpreted as an endorsement of the policies or actions of any particular government," adding that overflight request was related "to the United Nations General Assembly, a critical forum for diplomatic engagement."

Whether or not flying over sovereign airspace would require state parties to the Rome Statute to enforce ICC arrest warrants is a matter of debate. France has said its ICC treaty obligations do not extend to its airspace, while some international law experts argue that Canada and others failing to do so weakens the court.

World.title: Reid returns! 45 days on, he's a little lighter, but even more adored — if possible
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

What did he eat? Where did he sleep? What, or who, did he meet along the way?

How Reid, the large Bernadoodle, a cross between a Bernese mountain dog and a poodle, spent 45 days in and around the forests of Gander, N.L., will never be known — and that’s OK with his owner.

"He's a warrior," said Carmel Reid. "He took care of himself. And he figured out a way … to keep himself alive."

The three-year-old dog, who had never been off-leash, fled from a single-vehicle collision mid-afternoon on Aug. 21. While Carmel’s husband, Lorenzo, was being taken to hospital, people passing by said they saw Reid go into the nearby forest.

"Lorenzo left in an ambulance and I wasn't there," said Carmel. "By the time I got to Gander and went back up to look for Reid, there was no sign of him anywhere."

Reid the bernedoodle poses with his housemate Piper prior to getting lost in August. (Submitted by Carmel Reid)

The following morning, someone spotted a dog on the Gander Golf Course, which is located on the Trans-Canada Highway.

After that, no sightings for nearly three weeks. Nineteen days after the crash, he showed up on a surveillance camera around the Twin Ponds area, not even a kilometre away from the site, Carmel said.

"That was the first time that I guess we had seen him since he went missing," she said.

"So we were delighted to know that he was still alive."

The morning after that sighting, Reid showed up in Joe Batt’s Pond, a popular cabin area on the opposite side of the highway as Twin Ponds, and a few kilometres west of the crash site.

"Several people saw him there. They had him on video again. It was definitely him."

But then nothing again — for three whole weeks.

Social media pages such as "Help find Reid the dog" were abuzz with activity during the bernedoodle's 45-day disappearance. (Facebook screengrab)

During that time, the Reid family never gave up hope on their family pet. They searched every day and others were helping.

"There was times where it started to creep in, but then we were like, 'No, until somebody can come to me and say he's no longer alive, we're not giving up on him.'"

How moose meat played a role

Then, a breakthrough: Reid showed up in Gander. Along with the dozens of people who had come out to help search for him, now people’s home security systems aided the search exponentially.

They set up three traps to see if he could be lured in. They were baited with moose meat.

"We knew that the only way we were going to catch him was with the trap … he was running from everybody."

WATCH | Reid went into ‘survival mode,’ owner says: Return of Reid: Missing dog found 6 weeks after escape | Duration closed caption 3:43 The owners of a dog lost for 45 days in and around Gander are relieved he’s back, and thankful for the strangers who helped bring the three-year-old bernedoodle home. The CBC’s Troy Turner has the story.

A text woke her up at 3:30 a.m. The dog was spotted near one of the traps. Carmel turned on the trail camera she had set up to view the trap. After some shuffling around the perimeter, the moose meat drew Reid into the trap.

"We took off over there and I went in by myself," Carmel said. "It was dark ... I walked up to him. As soon as I started to walk up to him, he started to growl because he was afraid. So I just sat down, probably like six feet away from him on the pavement and just talked to him for a little bit.

"He was trying to smell [me]. As soon as he was able to do that his tail started to wag. And I could see that he recognized me. So just like that, he was back to Reid our pet. We took him out of the cage, he was perfect. And he's been perfect ever since."

In the 45 days he was missing, Reid shed more than 30 pounds. But, besides some cuts on his paws and bruising on the chest, he was given a clean bill of health. A trip to the groomer's to get the cement-like mud cut from his fur was a help.

His personality is also slowly getting back to normal too, she said.

"It wasn't too long after he left that we had a big thunder and lightning storm, and I was like, where is he to, he must be so scared. But since he's been back, we had a thunder and lightning storm and he went on outside and didn't even bother him.

"I think it'll be a while before he settles back down entirely. But we're not in a hurry. We have lots of time."

The family has been moved by the outpouring of support for Reid, as well as the generosity of those helping in the search.

"Strangers that we didn't even know existed, or didn't know we existed, were coming out of nowhere and saying, ‘What can I do to help you?

The family is looking forward to a long life ahead for Reid. And they’re hoping his first time being off leash — for a whopping 45 days — will be his last.

She says that when a pet is missing, it's important to heed any instructions from the owner not to approach the animal, especially one that was traumatized from an accident like Reid, as it might drive them farther away.

"He's not processing things the way he should. He can't use his senses the way that he should. So he's not able to recognize that you're a friendly person, that you're trying to help him."

United again, Reid and Piper are getting along well, says owner Carmel Reid. (Troy Turner/CBC)

World.title: Think you'll win the $90M Lotto Max? Here's a primer on your odds
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

May the odds be ever in your favour (even though, statistically, they're very much not).

Friday's $90 million Lotto Max draw will be the largest lottery jackpot prize ever available to win in Canada.

Draws take place every Tuesday and Friday at 10:30 p.m. ET. Tuesday's previously record-setting $85-million jackpot went unclaimed and rolled over, which allowed the prize pool to keep growing.

Lotto Max, a national lottery, announced in April that it was increasing its jackpot cap from $80 million to $90 million — and its play price from $5 to $6 — but this is the first time it's actually happened.

So, how does this compare to past jackpots? And what are the odds of winning?

Let's break it down.

Previously, Canada's biggest lottery prize was $80.4 million, won by a pair of long-time friends in London, Ont., last December. At the time, Greg S. and Krys P. said they're still overcoming the shock. (OLG)

What are the odds of winning?

Don't quit your job in anticipation just yet.

The odds of winning the main jackpot are one in 33 million per $6 play, according to OLG. You're almost exactly as likely to flip a coin 25 times in a row and have it land on "heads" each time.

To put all that in perspective, the odds of being struck by lightning in Canada are less than one in a million, according to the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety.

You're actually far more likely to be struck and killed by an asteroid on your way to buy the ticket than you are of winning the $90-million jackpot. We're sorry.

How does the $90M compare?

Yes, despite the odds, people do win the lottery. And the prizes keep growing.

Previously, Canada's biggest lottery prize was $80.4 million, won by a pair of long-time friends in London, Ont., last December. They won the $80-million Lotto Max jackpot and the $403,285.40 second prize for in the combination play option.

At the time, the men, identified only as Greg S. and Krys P., said they weren't sure how they would spend the money.

Before that, the top prize was claimed by a B.C. man who won the $80 million Lotto Max jackpot in May 2025. Justin Simporios of Surrey quit his job hours before the news conference where he claimed his cheque.

Lotto Max's first $80-million draw in Sept., 2024, was split between two winning tickets sold in Ontario and Quebec. The first $70-million prize was in 2020, and the first $65-million draw was in 2019. (It was actually the second time the $65-million winner, a family in Montreal, had won the lottery).

The first Lotto Max draw for $60 million was in 2015, after they had changed the rules previously capping the jackpot at $50 million. Two years before that, however, a record-breaking $63.4 million Lotto 649 prize was split between four tickets.

Some of us may also recall when 17 oil and gas workers from Alberta split Canada's biggest jackpot-to-date in 2005, a whopping $54 million. Before that, the previous lottery record was $37.8 million, offered in a Super 7 draw in 2002.

Canada's first national lottery, however, dates back to 1974, when nine women from Quebec City split the prize of $1 million. The lottery had been to raise money for the Montreal Olympics.

World.title: CREA revises down 2026 home sales forecast again as September transactions fall 7.7% over same month last year
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA) has revised down its projection for 2026 home sales again, while monthly data shows sales across Canada fell in September.

CREA previously expected home sales to tick up slightly in 2026, but now expects 5.2 per cent fewer homes will change hands this year compared to last. The adjustment follows similar downward revisions in April and July .

Oil prices have soared since the spring, which had a knock-on effect on bond yields and thus fixed mortgage rates, which CREA says weighed on the market .

While monthly activity ticked up slightly over the summer , CREA senior economist Shaun Cathcart says once-again rising oil costs and growing anxieties that the Bank of Canada will have to raise interest rates to combat inflation are expected to keep more potential homebuyers on the sidelines in the last months of the year.

"We've been on this roller-coaster for two years now," Cathcart said, referring to hurdles presented by U.S. tariffs and rising lending rates. "Now it's the uncertainty, and I think a lot of people are going to resist jumping in this fall because of that."

WATCH | Toronto's condo market shows signs of recovery: Toronto's condo market shows signs of recovery. Here's what you need to know | Duration closed caption 2:42 After a year of sluggish sales and cancelled projects, Toronto's condo market is showing signs of recovery. CBC's Philippe de Montigny breaks down what you need to know.

Real estate company Royal LePage says it's hearing the same message from potential homebuyers. President and CEO Phil Soper says the fall housing market has proven softer than expected as prospective buyers remain cautious about making such a massive purchase amid so much global uncertainty.

"The chaotic nature of language coming out of Washington is directly impacting people's willingness to make large financial decisions like buying a home," said Soper.

September home sales slide

Those economic factors were already showing up in more sluggish September sales figures, according to the CREA.

Home sales for the month were down 2.3 per cent compared to August, and down 7.7 per cent compared to September of last year.

Are you in the housing market, either as a prospective buyer or seller? We want to hear from you — email us at askcbc.ca

The number of newly listed properties also fell by 1.8 per cent on a month-over-month basis. New supply has generally been falling since September 2025, according to CREA.

The average home price across the country was $666,538, also down compared to a year before, by 1.6 per cent.

On a regional basis, Cathcart says markets in Vancouver and Toronto were particularly weak in September. But markets in the Prairies, Quebec and on the East Coast — which have been hot for quite some time now — have started to cool off, too.

"Now everyone's going to have to take a breather, I think, until we find out what interests are going to do next year," Cathcart said.

Despite the downgrade in the forecast, CREA is predicting that home sales will pick up next year. Based on an optimistic outlook where the Bank of Canada makes limited rate changes and borrowers get more certainty about lending rates, CREA predicts home sales will tick up by 4.4 per cent in 2027.

World.title: New Sense and Sensibility movie delves deep into the sisterly bond at the heart of Austen's classic
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Stars Daisy Edgar-Jones (Elinor) and Esmé Creed-Miles (Marianne) discuss how their longtime friendship helped shape the bond between the Dashwood sisters.

The sisterhood at the heart of Sense and Sensibility

It is the eternal question of the prestige drama. Do we really need another period piece? Do we really need another Jane Austen adaptation? More specifically, do we need another version of Sense and Sensibility?

For audiences familiar with director Ang Lee's 1995 Sense and Sensibility, the question might feel pointed. All of Austen's works have been adapted for the screen, and Sense and Sensibility alone has had at least five earlier adaptations.

Now comes director Georgia Oakley's Sense and Sensibility, which hits theatres Oct. 16. Starring Daisy Edgar-Jones as Elinor Dashwood and Esmé Creed-Miles as her sister, Marianne, and written by Diana Reid, this version doesn't try to out-romance the 1995 film.

Instead, it delves deeper into their sisterly bond and the financial insecurity that limits their choices.

WATCH | The official trailer for the 2026 film:

A new lens on the Dashwood sisters

After their father's death, the Dashwood estate passes to their half-brother, leaving the women with limited financial security and forcing them to move to a more modest home. In Austen's time, women's prospects depended heavily on the goodwill of male relatives or the security of marriage, making this sudden loss of status and stability especially precarious.

The film's visual world moves with them: away from the controlled elegance of the drawing room and out into the open countryside, amid weather, mud and unkempt fields.

They garden, go on long walks, run on the beach and wade through ponds. While Elinor finds peace in sketching and skipping rocks, Marianne is often seen lying in fields, watching the clouds.

Esmé Creed-Miles as Marianne Dashwood, left, and Daisy Edgar-Jones as her older sister Elinor sort through their belongings as they prepare to leave their family home. (Universal Pictures)

That rougher setting makes their vulnerability physical as well as financial — and brings their shared experience into view.

Elinor's restraint can conceal how deeply she feels and Marianne's openness leaves her more exposed to heartbreak. Throughout the film, circumstances bring each of them to see the other's perspective.

'The sisters are the constant'

"They really wanted to centralize the love story as being the two girls," Edgar-Jones said of Oakley and Reid's approach.

She also told CBC News that working with her longtime friend Creed-Miles felt effortless.

"I had an idea of who I thought Elinor was, but it wasn't until I really started acting those scenes with Esmé's Marianne that I really understood her," she said.

Creed-Miles says their friendship quickly helped them find a "familial, sisterly, best friend sort of energy." She says she "couldn't have gotten through the project" without Edgar-Jones's support.

WATCH | Sense and Sensibility's modern take: Why Sense and Sensibility still resonates | Duration closed caption 3:36 The cast discuss how the new adaptation of Sense and Sensibility makes Jane Austen's story feel fresh, from its focus on sisterhood to modern parallels like ghosting and love bombing.

The sisters are each other's confidantes, critics and support system.

Canadian author Natalie Jenner, whose novel, The Jane Austen Society, draws on Austen's work and life, sees that connection as one reason the book continues to resonate.

"If your family relationships are strong, you feel emboldened to take on anything," Jenner said. "The sisters are the constant. And that sense of constancy and a North Star is something that you can always go back to. I think that taps into a modern need for community and stability," she told CBC News.

A different kind of Brandon and Willoughby

Marianne’s love interests are John Willoughby, played by Frank Dillane, left, and Colonel Brandon, played by Herbert Nordrum. (Universal Pictures)

The new film's male characters offer a departure from the archetypes established in Ang Lee's 1995 adaptation.

In an interview with CBC News, Herbert Nordrum explains that he played Colonel Brandon as awkward and difficult to read, focusing on the character's internal struggle to express his feelings. This contrasts with Alan Rickman’s 1995 performance, which gave Brandon a sense of gravitas and a devotion to Marianne expressed through quiet, powerful gestures.

In the 1995 adaptation, Greg Wise portrays Willoughby as a dashing romantic hero, making his betrayal all the more shocking. In the 2026 version, Frank Dillane told CBC News he wanted to emphasize Willoughby’s sweeter qualities — "his joy, his exuberance, his lust for life, poetry and romance" — while still letting his questionable actions speak for themselves. He aimed to portray him as a rounded young man who makes mistakes and falls in love.

He jokes that Willoughby's grand romantic gestures would now be called "love bombing," while his habit of ignoring Marianne's letters is the period-drama equivalent of "ghosting."

In Ang Lee’s 1995 adaptation of Sense and Sensibility, Colonel Brandon (Alan Rickman) carries Marianne Dashwood (Kate Winslet) through the rain after finding her gravely ill. (Sony Pictures Releasing)

What Austen means to audiences now

While Lee's film is lush and sweeping, Oakley's is quieter and more grounded. It doesn't try to replace the older version; it's asking what these stories can mean to audiences now.

Jenner says Austen's characters endure because they're trying to find happiness without losing themselves. "You've got to know what makes you happy," she told CBC News, "and stay true to that."

She introduced her own daughter to Austen's books and films when she was seven or eight. Jenner wanted her to meet characters who were "strong-spirited" and full of "intellect, brightness, vivacity, kindness, curiosity."

Jenner says she believes younger audiences are craving more naturalistic depictions — a shift she noticed through conversations with her daughter, now in her mid-20s.

Elinor (Edgar-Jones) and Marianne (Creed-Miles) share a quiet moment in a field of tall grass. (Universal Pictures)

She says that coming out of the pandemic, there's been a longing for a return to nature and the simple warmth of picnics, books and blankets, which has seeped into the visual style of modern adaptations.

Jenner believes that Austen doesn't belong to one decade or one aesthetic. Her stories offer romance, but also friendship, family, community and the difficult work of figuring out what kind of life will make you happy.

The question of whether the world really needs another Sense and Sensibility remains.

Audiences may well find that it does, not because of a desire to surpass previous versions, but because Austen's story is timeless enough to invite a completely new interpretation.
