World.title: Man accused of burglarizing YWCA and Divine Mercy Church, acting as his own attorney, asks Magistrate to recuse herself after she previously convicted him in case overturned by High Court
World.content:
Man accused of burglarizing YWCA and Divine Mercy Church, acting as his own attorney, asks Magistrate to recuse herself after she previously convicted him in case overturned by High Court

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A burglary trial involving Denfield Lemott has been left in limbo after he requested that the Magistrate hearing his case recuse herself because she had previously convicted him of burglary in a separate matter, a conviction that was later overturned on appeal.

Lemott, who is representing himself, appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Thursday, October 15, where his case was adjourned to November 17, 2026, as the court considers how to proceed.

The trial had already commenced in Court #4, with evidence taken from the complainant, when Lemott raised concerns about the Magistrate’s involvement and requested her recusal. The matter was subsequently transferred to Court #5, leaving unresolved questions about how the partially heard trial should continue.

The dispute follows Lemott’s successful appeal of a 2025 burglary conviction for which he had received an eight-year prison sentence. High Court Justice Candace Nanton subsequently quashed the conviction and set aside the sentence, allowing him to regain his freedom.

As previously reported by Breaking Belize News, Lemott later faced two additional burglary charges involving the alleged theft of $130 from a program officer and $350 from a teacher at the YMCA building in Belize City. He pleaded not guilty to those allegations.

In another case, Lemott was charged with allegedly stealing $2,000 from Divine Mercy Church in July 2026. He also pleaded not guilty in that matter and was denied bail.

During Thursday’s appearance, Lemott informed the court that he had misplaced his original disclosure documents and requested another copy.

The Magistrate adjourned the current burglary case to November 17 for mention, when the prosecution is expected to clarify its position on how the trial should proceed following the transfer between courts.

World.title: Jamie Young’s murder trial delayed again, rescheduled for Friday
World.content:
Jamie Young’s murder trial delayed again, rescheduled for Friday

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The murder trial of Jamie Caesar Young, accused of fatally shooting his former girlfriend’s new partner during a high-speed pursuit along the Philip Goldson Highway in 2024, has been postponed yet again.

Young was scheduled to stand trial before High Court Justice Candace Nanton on Thursday, October 15, but the proceedings could not begin due to unforeseen circumstances. The matter was adjourned to Friday, October 16, at 9:00 a.m.

Young, who is represented by attorney Dr. Lynden Jones, is charged with the March 16, 2024 murder of 30-year-old former Belize Defence Force soldier and bus driver Damion Dominique Baptist of Burrell Boom.

According to police, Baptist was travelling with Young’s former girlfriend when Young allegedly pursued them in a grey pickup truck along the highway near Ladyville.

Investigators allege that Young repeatedly pulled alongside their vehicle and fired shots, eventually striking Baptist in the head and causing him to lose control of his red Ford Fusion, which crashed into a lamppost near Our Lady of the Way RC School.

Baptist was transported to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where he was pronounced dead.

Young was subsequently arrested and charged with murder and aggravated assault against the woman.

The latest adjournment follows an earlier postponement on October 5, when the trial could not proceed because Young’s attorney was reportedly ill. BBN previously reported on that delay.

The case is now expected to proceed on Friday morning.

World.title: Belize City teen takes rap and gets 2 years in jail for unlicensed Glock 17 so his sister can go free
World.content:
Belize City teen takes rap and gets 2 years in jail for unlicensed Glock 17 so his sister can go free

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 19-year-old Belize City man who pleaded guilty to possessing an unlicensed Glock pistol, resulting in the withdrawal of a firearm charge against his older sister, has been sentenced to two years in prison.

Aaron Ayren Pitter, of Pitter Street, was sentenced on Thursday, October 15, before a Magistrate in Court #5 at the Belize City Magistrate’s Court. His sentence was ordered to take effect from August 18, 2026, the date he pleaded guilty.

The conviction stems from a police search conducted on August 17 at a residence on Pitter Street, where officers from the Violence Prevention and Enforcement Team discovered a Glock 17 Gen 4 9mm pistol wrapped inside a pair of blue short pants hidden in a hole beside a bathtub.

The firearm was fitted with a black magazine and red extension, but police confirmed that the gun and magazine contained no ammunition.

According to police, Pitter arrived home while officers were conducting the search and admitted that the firearm belonged to him, telling officers, “Da feh me, big man. I have knowledge that was there.”

Pitter and his 20-year-old sister, Gregoria Veronica Pitter, were initially jointly charged with keeping a firearm without a gun licence. However, after Aaron accepted responsibility and pleaded guilty, prosecutors withdrew the charge against his sister, allowing her to walk free.

As previously reported by Breaking Belize News, the Magistrate initially encouraged Pitter to seek legal advice before accepting his guilty plea, but the teenager insisted on taking responsibility for the weapon so his sister could go free.

During Thursday’s sentencing, Pitter offered no mitigation. Although he had initially faced a possible five-year prison term, the Magistrate imposed a two-year sentence, retroactive to August 18.

World.title: “I just want to be your mother-in-law”: Daughter-in-law drops harm charge against ‘ma-lee’
World.content:
“I just want to be your mother-in-law”: Daughter-in-law drops harm charge against ‘ma-lee’

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City woman who was arrested on a bench warrant after repeatedly missing court appearances has been spared further legal trouble after her daughter-in-law, who accused her of causing harm more than two years ago, asked the court to withdraw the charge.

Angela Copious appeared before a Senior Magistrate in Court #2 on Wednesday, October 14, after being detained over the holiday weekend for failing to attend previous court hearings.

Copious was charged with causing harm to her daughter-in-law following an alleged altercation on July 26, 2024.

In court, Copious explained that she had been seriously ill and claimed her daughter had emailed medical documents to explain her absences. However, the court had no record of receiving those documents.

The matter took an unexpected turn when the daughter-in-law appeared and informed the Magistrate that she had forgiven her mother-in-law and no longer wished to pursue the case. She requested that the charge be withdrawn so both women could move on with their lives.

Faber also asked that they be bound over to keep the peace, but the Magistrate did not impose such an order.

With the charge withdrawn and her bail not revoked, Copious was allowed to leave court.

Before departing, a relieved Copious turned to her daughter-in-law and told her, “I just want to be your mother-in-law.”

The emotional exchange brought an end to a criminal complaint that had been pending since July 2024.

World.title: Belize participates in U.S.-Caribbean Dialogue hosted by U.S. Deputy Secretary of State
World.content:
Belize participates in U.S.-Caribbean Dialogue hosted by U.S. Deputy Secretary of State

By Zoila Palma: Today, Oscar Arnold, Chief Executive Officer for Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade, is participating in the U.S.-Caribbean Dialogue, hosted by U.S. Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau.

The Ministry says that the high-level dialogue provides an important platform to strengthen regional partnerships and advance shared priorities in security and defense coordination, strategic economic growth, disaster response, and regional health cooperation.

CEO Arnold is joined by the Ambassador of Belize to the U.S., Nestor Mendez, and Counsellor, Alexya Perez.

“Belize remains committed to constructive engagement and regional collaboration with the Caribbean and its partners,” the Ministry said.

World.title: Belize City man fined $55 for riding bicycle up-stop on his own street
World.content:
Belize City man fined $55 for riding bicycle up-stop on his own street

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 26-year-old Belize City man found himself in trouble with the law after police caught him riding his bicycle against the flow of traffic on the very street where he lives.

Jermaine Lewis, a resident of King Street, was detained on Saturday, October 10, 2026, after police observed him riding his bicycle in the wrong direction along the one-way street.

Lewis was escorted to the nearby Precinct 1 Police Station, also located on King Street, where he was charged with causing a bicycle to proceed up a one-way street.

He appeared before the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Tuesday, October 13, and pleaded guilty to the traffic offence.

The Magistrate imposed a fine of $50 plus $5 court costs, giving Lewis until November 30, 2026, to pay or face one week in prison.

Riding a bicycle against the designated flow of traffic is an offence under Belize’s traffic laws, and similar violations have resulted in fines and, in some cases, imprisonment for unpaid penalties.

World.title: International News: Strong El Niño raises global concerns over wildfires, food security and power shortages
World.content:
International News: Strong El Niño raises global concerns over wildfires, food security and power shortages

By Zoila Palma: An exceptionally strong El Niño weather cycle is contributing to drought, wildfires, power shortages and growing food security concerns in several parts of the world, with scientists warning that its effects could intensify as the phenomenon approaches its expected peak in December.

In Indonesia, prolonged dry conditions have contributed to fires in forests and plantations in Borneo and South Sumatra, triggering a regional haze crisis that has affected neighbouring Malaysia and Singapore.

Authorities and conservation groups have rescued dozens of orangutans from the fires. Meanwhile, Brazil’s Amazon region has also experienced widespread fires, with Amazonas state recording nearly four times as many fire hotspots in September as in the same month last year.

In Myanmar, authorities have warned of possible electricity outages as unusually high temperatures increase power demand, while the Philippines is preparing for higher energy consumption and potential declines in hydropower production. The impacts are also raising concerns about food security, with International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva expressing concern about the global consequences and saying the IMF is preparing to support countries that may struggle to cope.

The World Meteorological Organization has warned that El Niño is likely to bring above-average temperatures to much of the world and alter rainfall patterns, increasing the risk of droughts and floods.

World.title: Wrong And Strong: ‘Dads’, 61, fined $110 for riding bicycle up-stop and upstarting police
World.content:
Wrong And Strong: ‘Dads’, 61, fined $110 for riding bicycle up-stop and upstarting police

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 61-year-old Belize City man who was caught riding his bicycle against traffic on a one-way street ended up facing two charges after allegedly refusing to cooperate with a police officer.

Jose Augustine August appeared unrepresented before the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Wednesday, October 14, where he pleaded guilty to causing a bicycle to proceed against the designated direction of a one-way street and obstructing a police officer.

According to police, the incident occurred on Sunday, October 11, on Cemetery Road, where August was intercepted for riding his bicycle in the wrong direction. He subsequently obstructed a female corporal while she was executing her duties.

August admitted both offences and did not dispute the prosecution’s allegations. When given an opportunity to offer mitigating circumstances, he remained silent.

The Magistrate imposed a fine of $50 for each offence, along with $5 court costs on each charge, bringing his total penalty to $110.

August was given until November 30, 2026, to pay the fines or face one week in prison for each offence.

World.title: DOMESTIC DISPUTE TURNS FATAL
World.content:
Nesta Anderson, a window maker and disc jockey who reportedly committed suicide after stabbing his wife who was taken hospital where she is said to be battling for life.

SAVANNA-LA-MAR, Westmoreland — The usually quiet community of New Market Oval in Savanna- la-Mar has been left in shock following a violent family dispute that left a nurse battling for life in hospital and her husband dead.

The husband, Nesta Anderson, a window maker and disc jockey, was from a neighbouring community. Police report that the couple had been involved in a dispute at their home when the woman was allegedly stabbed by Anderson.

Following the attack, Anderson used a ratchet knife to inflict stab wounds to his abdomen about 10:30 am Thursday.

He was rushed to hospital where he was pronounced dead. The Jamaica Observer was told that the couple, who had been together for more than a decade, has three young children.

Unconfirmed reports suggest the children witnessed the incident. When the Observer visited the community, police were processing the scene, while residents shied away from speaking publicly about the matter.

President of the Cooke Street Benevolent Society Bishop O’Neil Russell said he spoke with Anderson just a few days ago and that the incident came as a complete shock as the family was known to be quiet.

“We had a conversation because, you know, there were some things that the benevolent society was supposed to do for him.

We are always in constant dialogue, but he had not shown any sign of depression. It is so shocking. It comes as a shock to see really what took place,” stated Russell.

Councillor Julian Chang (Jamaica Labour Party, Savanna-la-Mar Division), who visited the scene, expressed sadness over the tragedy.

“It’s not anything to rejoice over. We all have issues, and we all have problems. We all go through things,” stated Chang.

She noted that the community, which was devastated by Hurricane Melissa last October, is already under stress and attempting to rebuild.

“We understand the constraints, but you know, we have to deal with our problems better than this, instead of taking our own lives or taking the lives of others,” stated Chang, who joined Russell in calling on people having problems to seek help.

Domestic violence, it can affect anyone regardless of our income, education, or social status. It stretches across all socio-economic backgrounds. We just have to understand that it is right in our midst and we should not be ashamed of it.

We should seek help. And I implore the persons in the Savanna-la-Mar Division, or anywhere for that matter in Jamaica, to seek help because I’m sure there are telltale signs even before it occurs,” Chang said.

She also emphasised the need for community sensitisation to stop judging victims and instead offer support, “because we all deserve to be safe in our own homes”.

World.title: Protecting Palisadoes
World.content:
An overhead shot of the Palisadoes Peninsula.

SPURRED into action by the warning from Hurricane Melissa which lashed sections of the island last year, the Cabinet has approved a US$56-million ($8.9 billion) coastal protection system for Palisadoes main road in Kingston which leads to Norman Manley International Airport and Port Royal.

The Category 5 storm, which hit Jamaica on October 28, 2025, reached wind speed of up to 190 miles per hour and devastated sections of the island’s southand north-western coasts, leaving several communities inaccessible.

With the pain from Melissa still fresh in Jamaicans’ minds, Minister of Energy, Telecommunications and Transport Daryl Vaz on Wednesday told a post-Cabinet media briefing that the Government is moving to provide even more protection for Palisadoes, the narrow approximately 14.2-kilometre strip of land that serves as a protective barrier for Kingston Harbour.

“The Government is advancing efforts to strengthen coastal protection along the Palisadoes Peninsula and Port Royal, safeguarding the Norman Manley International Airport, the main road that links from Harbour View to Port Royal, and surrounding communities against coastal erosion and storm surges,” Vaz said.

“The initiative represents a coordinated effort to protect critical transportation infrastructure, preserve access to Port Royal, and strengthen Jamaica’s resilience to coastal hazards.

So this is a far-reaching project that is going to once and for all protect the airport and access all the way to Port Royal,” added Vaz.

He underscored that over the last few years the Government has made efforts to protect the strip, which included approximately 4,500 metres of revetment work.

“We started back in 2007 when we did all of those boulders on the stretch.

As a result of Melissa and realising that, had Melissa come closer to Kingston, the access to the airport and, of course all the way to Port Royal, would be non-existent…

and seeing the work that has been done and what needs to be done, the Government has completed a comprehensive shoreline protection project [study] covering approximately 14.2 kilometres,” added Vaz.

He explained that proposed works will include strengthening revetments, rehabilitating dunes and mangroves, revegetation, and 12.1 kilometres of dunes [while] improving vulnerable road sections and installing coastal monitoring systems.

Underscoring that the country’s airports must also be built with resilience, Vaz noted that this project will be undertaken by the National Reconstruction and Resilience Authorities (NaRRA) under its work programme, with funding expected from its designated project pool.

He said with the project being under NaRRA, the Government will ensure that the procurement process is fast-tracked, which will result in it being completed in a timely manner.

“I just want to impress again, with all the noise that is being said about NaRRA, here is a project out of my ministry which has been approved by Cabinet as a NaRRA project.

Just to indicate that the noise is not always what you must listen to; you must watch the sale.

Here is a good sale.

Money that is going to be well spent [so] that if we have another catastrophe, God forbid, and it comes closer to Kingston, we will be able to respond how we responded to Melissa to get all the flights in with relief within hours,” Vaz told the media briefing.

The revetment work on Palisadoes came after Hurricane Ivan passed close to Jamaica’s south coast on September 10, 2024, leaving behind a trail of destruction not seen in the island since the passage of Hurricane Gilbert in 1988.

Ivan generated storm surge that caused the sea level to rise pushing mountains of sand and stones on the Palisadoes, leaving the vital roadway impassable.

The sand had also formed what was later referred to as the Palisadoes New Beach, essentially strips of land on the Kingston Harbour side up to 50 metres wide.

In 2007, sea water from storm surges associated with Hurricane Felix, which passed south of the island on September 3, flooded a section of the Palisadoes, making it impassable for several hours.

World.title: Insurers set to gain investment flexibility
World.content:
WILLIAMS... announced during the 2026/27 Budget Debate that the Government intended to simplify Regulation 47 to make it easier for life insurance companies to invest in corporate debt

Insurance companies could gain access to a wider range of investment opportunities under proposed changes to rules governing the sector, with the Senate’s Regulations Committee raising no objections to a measure that would remove a requirement for four conditions to be met simultaneously before certain investments qualify.

Deputy executive director of supervision at the Financial Services Commission (FSC) Nicolette Jenez told the committee on Thursday, during a virtual sitting, that the amendment to Regulation 47 of the Insurance Regulations is intended to widen insurers’ investment choices, which she said have been restricted by the existing rules.

Under the proposed change, insurers would be able to invest in certain obligations issued by solvent institutions if they satisfy any one of four conditions rather than having to meet all four at the same time.

The criteria include investments secured by adequate collateral and meeting prescribed fixed-interest requirements; investments rated as investment grade by an agency recognised by the FSC; obligations meeting prescribed earnings-coverage requirements; or obligations listed on the Jamaica Stock Exchange or another stock exchange recognised by the commission.

Jenez said the existing requirements, introduced through amendments in 2022, had limited insurers’ ability to diversify their portfolios, invest in corporate debt, and support infrastructure financing.

“While intended as prudential safeguards, this cumulative application of requirements has significantly restricted the range of investments available to insurers, limiting diversification opportunities, asset liability matching, participation in corporate debt markets, and infrastructure financing,” she said.

Asset-liability matching refers to ensuring that an insurer’s investments can provide the money needed to meet future claims and other financial obligations.

The FSC expects the amendment to broaden investment opportunities, support the development of Jamaica’s capital markets and make it easier for insurers to direct funds towards productive sectors of the economy.

The proposed change also forms part of the commission’s regulatory modernisation programme and its efforts to align Jamaica’s insurance supervisory framework with international standards.

Jenez stressed that the reform would not weaken the FSC’s oversight of the industry.

“What this amendment will not do is to reduce the FSC supervisory authority or existing prudential safeguards,” she said.

She pointed to other provisions in the Insurance Regulations, including 72(B), 72(G), 72(J), and 72(K), which set out requirements relating to insurers’ investment management and the handling of risk.

The amendment follows concerns that the existing rules have made it difficult for insurers to invest in some otherwise eligible corporate obligations because those investments must satisfy several conditions at once.

Finance Minister Fayval Williams announced in March, during the 2026/27 Budget Debate, that the Government intended to simplify Regulation 47 to make it easier for life insurance companies to invest in corporate debt.

The Government has argued that the existing requirements restrict investment choices and limit the development of the domestic corporate debt market.

World.title: Prison officials deny reported fight between P Diddy and Dudus
World.content:
American rapper P Diddy and Jamaican drug lord Christopher 'Dudus' Coke a

Prison officials are reportedly denying a reported physical altercation between American music mogul Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs and convicted Jamaican drug lord Christopher ‘Dudus’ Coke, which resulted in the rapper being rushed to hospital on Wednesday.

A TMZ report on Wednesday said the confrontation reportedly erupted after Combs allegedly caused trouble that resulted in disciplinary action against fellow inmates. The Bad Boy for Life singer reportedly sustained a head injury and was subsequently transported to an outside medical facility for treatment.

But the Federal Bureau of Prisons is denying that the fight took place.

“While, for privacy, safety, and security reasons, we do not comment on the conditions of confinement for any individual in our custody, we can tell you that the story you are referring to is false and did not happen. Sean Combs is in the custody of the Federal Bureau of Prisons and is incarcerated at the Federal Correctional Institution Fort Dix. Beyond this, we have no additional information to provide,” a spokesman for the Federal Bureau of Prisons was quoted as saying in a statement to The Daily Mail.

Combs was sentenced last year to just over four years in federal prison after being convicted on prostitution-related charges involving two of his former girlfriends.

World.title: JC appeals ISSA sanctions over Jamone Lyle, says procedure was unfair
World.content:
Jamaica College forward Jamone Lyle. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Jamaica College (JC) has appealed sanctions imposed by the Inter-Secondary Schools Sports Association (ISSA) over the eligibility of footballer Jamone Lyle, with the school’s Board of Management Chairman Lance Hylton describing the penalties as “unsupportable, extreme and excessive”.

In an update to the school community, seen by Observer Online on Thursday, Hylton said JC lodged its appeal within 24 hours of the disciplinary hearing on October 13 and is awaiting the outcome ahead of Friday’s Walker Cup final.

The sanctions followed a ruling that JC fielded an ineligible player after Lyle was found to have a professional contract with Waterhouse Football Club, making him ineligible for schoolboy football under ISSA regulations.

JC was subsequently removed from the Walker Cup, banned from next year’s competition and ordered to forfeit its Manning Cup second-round match against St Catherine, which it had won 3-2. The result was reversed to a 3-0 victory for St Catherine.

READ: JC booted from Walker Cup for fielding ineligible player Jamone Lyle

The decision also paved the way for Kingston College (KC) to face Mona High in Friday’s Walker Cup final, after Mona lost to JC in the semi-final on penalties.

Hylton said the school received a letter from ISSA on October 12 informing Principal Wayne Robinson that a complaint had been made concerning Lyle’s eligibility. The hearing was scheduled for the following day at 2:00 pm.

According to Hylton, the letter provided no prior notification of the complaint and did not identify the complainant or provide further particulars of the charge.

He said the school’s leadership, football management and coaching staff immediately mobilised to prepare written submissions for the hearing, with assistance from the Jamaica College Public Relations Committee.

Hylton added that ISSA’s rules did not permit the school to have a lawyer or anyone other than the coach or his replacement to accompany the principal to provide representation or support.

“ISSA’s harsh ruling followed with blinding speed…We consider the sanctions unsupportable, extreme and excessive,” he said.

Hylton said the school intends to address aspects of the hearing as part of its appeal, although he did not disclose the details of its submissions.

JC is challenging both the application of ISSA’s rules and whether Lyle’s purported contract with Waterhouse constitutes a valid and enforceable agreement.

Hylton said the school’s interpretation of the relevant rule is that it prohibits players from being under contract with clubs, whether through professional agreements or other contractual arrangements. However, he argued that the rules have not been consistently enforced over the years, pointing to what he described as widespread contractual arrangements involving schoolboy footballers.

He also said JC does not concede that a valid contract exists in Lyle’s case and intends to pursue that argument on appeal.

“We regard the treatment of JC as unfair,” the board chairman said. “In our view, the treatment of both the school and the player, who appears to have entered into the purported contract without independent representation, is particularly harsh when many well-known contractual arrangements have attracted no sanctions.”

He said JC had lodged complaints concerning other contractual arrangements.

A central part of the school’s position is that it was never informed by Waterhouse that Lyle had signed a professional contract or that the club was restricting him from playing for JC.

The dispute follows a disciplinary letter from Waterhouse dated October 9, in which the club said it had fined Lyle $60,000 for unauthorised participation in a Manning Cup match on October 7. Waterhouse alleged that Lyle ignored instructions from head coach Donovan Duckie and General Secretary Richard McCallum not to play for JC, in breach of his professional contract and the club’s rules.

Hylton said JC was particularly concerned that a professional club would have a minor sign an agreement purporting to prevent him from continuing to play for his school.

Lyle, who turned 17 in July, has represented JC since he was 12 and was at a significant stage of his schoolboy football career, Hylton said.

The chairman added that the school had seen no indication that Lyle received independent legal representation during the process. He also said information available to JC suggested that the player did not have a parent or guardian in Jamaica supporting him through the process, including a disciplinary hearing with Waterhouse.

Hylton stressed that the school had received no written communication informing it of the purported restriction or instructing it to stop the player from participating.

He further questioned whether the restriction could be enforced against a minor, citing legal precedents concerning contracts entered into by minors, including a case involving former England footballer Wayne Rooney.

JC intends to pursue that issue as part of its appeal.

Hylton has called on Waterhouse president Donovan White to withdraw and retract a statement that the school had been informed about Lyle’s contractual status. He said the principal was adamant that he had received no telephone call or other communication from White on the matter.

Hylton also called on the Waterhouse president to identify whom he claimed to have informed, when the communication took place and how it was delivered.

According to Hylton, the school has received no response to that request.

The chairman also addressed questions from stakeholders about why the school had not sought an injunction to challenge ISSA’s ruling.

He said the disciplinary letter referred to ISSA’s rule against members taking the association to court, adding that the school had previously been warned that seeking an injunction could result in a ban from all sporting activities under ISSA’s jurisdiction.

Hylton described the restriction as constitutionally objectionable and cited the cases of Butler v KSAFA and Royale Lakes Football Club Limited v St Catherine Football Association in support of the school’s position on access to the courts.

Quoting from Chief Justice Bryan Sykes’ judgment in Butler v KSAFA, Hylton argued that membership of an association should not require individuals to surrender their fundamental right to seek judicial redress.

He said, however, that the school faces a difficult decision because court action could trigger an immediate ban while proceedings continue, potentially affecting students across all its sporting programmes.

“For now, we have decided that it is not a risk worth taking at this stage,” Hylton said in the update, while making clear that court action remains an option.

Hylton said the immediate priority is the appeal lodged within 24 hours of the October 13 hearing, with the school awaiting a decision ahead of Friday’s final.

The chairman maintained that JC had been treated unfairly and expressed regret that the controversy had overshadowed the school’s football achievements.

He thanked members of the school community for their research, assistance and support, while urging stakeholders to continue submitting questions and suggestions.

World.title: Guilty by report?
World.content:
CHUCK... questioned whether the Integrity Commission’s practice of publicly identifying categories of people whose matters have been referred to it could fuel perceptions of corruption

JUSTICE Minister Delroy Chuck has questioned whether the Integrity Commission’s (IC’s) practice of publicly identifying categories of people whose matters have been referred to it could fuel perceptions of corruption, even when those matters do not result in findings of wrongdoing.

Speaking at Wednesday’s meeting of Parliament’s Integrity Commission Oversight Committee, Chuck argued that reporting such figures could create an impression of widespread corruption even when investigations might not lead to charges.

“You must say how many investigations you have started and so on, but when you start, if you see in your report that you’re investigating permanent secretaries, you have… 18 or so permanent secretaries, even if you have three where you’re investigating, all of them come under scrutiny, and so when you say you’re investigating six, nine parliamentarians, every single one of us come under scrutiny,” he expressed.

The minister questioned whether the commission’s reporting approach was helping or hurting Jamaica’s efforts to fight corruption, arguing that the public needed to see clear results from investigations, rather than repeated references to matters still being examined.

He also questioned whether the country was getting value for money from the anti-corruption body, given the resources spent on its work and the need to demonstrate progress in tackling corruption.

“Because all I’m really saying is, yes, if there is corruption, expose it, find it, but… far too many of your reports are actually saying you are investigating, and at the end of the day nothing comes of it, or you don’t hear about it, and I am concerned, because when people speak about corruption, they should at least be able to say we have investigated these, we have charged so many for failing to report,” Chuck said.

However, Opposition spokesman on finance Julian Robinson rejected the suggestion that the commission should be blamed for the effects of its reporting, arguing that public accountability required it to explain the work it was doing and the progress of its investigations.

Robinson said the commission had to report on the nature of matters referred to it, while the public should also question why so many matters were being brought to its attention.

“As far as I know, you get to an investigation, having gone through a process, and you have met a particular threshold to determine that somebody

should be investigated. Part of your accountability mandate must be to report where you are in a process, which means whether it is public officials, parliamentarians, you must indicate of the number, how many have reached so-and-so, so I don’t share the view that the issue is with the Integrity Commission. If there are a lot of people under investigation, then the issue must be why are there so many people under investigation?” Robinson questioned.

The debate prompted director of investigation at the Integrity Commission Kevon Stephenson to explain the distinction between matters referred to the commission and cases that proceed to a formal investigation.

Stephenson said not every complaint or referral led to an investigation, as each matter had to be assessed before a decision was made. He told the committee that only a small fraction of matters referred to the commission proceeded to investigation.

“I think the public could appreciate that when matters are reported to the commission as under [Section] One of the Second Schedule, there is no guarantee that those complaints will be investigated, because an assessment has to be done on each of those complaints for a decision to be made under Section 47 of the legislation as to whether an investigation will be conducted,” Stephenson said.

He added that investigations could also be discontinued if the evidence did not provide a sufficient basis to continue. In those circumstances, the director of investigation was required to issue findings to the commission, but those findings were not made public.

Stephenson said reports reached Parliament when a completed investigation found a breach of a code, policy or law. He also explained that the annual report’s description of matters referred to the commission should not be interpreted as a list of cases actively under investigation.

Stephenson suggested that if Parliament is dissatisfied with what the law required the commission to include in its annual report, any change in policy would need to be reflected in legislation.

In the meantime, committee Chairman Pearnel Charles Jr said the concerns about reputational damage had to be considered without restricting the commission’s work.

“The commission must fearlessly carry out its work. But fear perhaps can be spelled in two ways, F-E-A-R and F-A-I-R. So as you fearlessly carry it out, it must be fair to the persons who you may have thoughts of, but not established evidence about,” Charles Jr said.

Furthermore, director of information and complaints at the commission Joeth Jones also criticised the media for what she described as a failure to give sufficient attention to positive compliance findings in the commission’s reports.

Jones said parliamentarians had performed relatively well in meeting their statutory obligations, but argued that this aspect of the commission’s work was not receiving adequate coverage.

“The media does not pick up that,” Jones told the committee, referring to the group’s compliance performance.

World.title: Secret location
World.content:
CHANG... we handed them over to The International Organisation for Migration and they made arrangements for them as to where they are to stay (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

THE location of the first batch of 22 third-country nationals (TCNs) that arrived in the island on Monday will remain concealed says National Security Minister Dr Horace Chang.

Responding to questions posed by journalists at a post-Cabinet media briefing at Jamaica House Wednesday, Chang maintained that though he is aware of where the TCNs are being housed, it’s not his “privilege” to announce where they are.

“I cannot give you their housing. We handed them over to International Organisation for Migration (IOM) and they made arrangements for them as to where they are to stay. The officers were in Jamaica and they looked at a number of hotels; they now have the responsibility of where they are to stay. In fact, they can move them at anytime,” said Chang.

The group, which arrived under an agreement signed between the Jamaican and United States (US) governments in June this year, comprises of 15 males and seven females, representing seven nationalities.

According to the Government, under the agreement, up to 25 asylum seekers who have unresolved migration cases in the US will temporarily transit through Jamaica en route to their home countries every two weeks.

But Chang on Tuesday shared that he is unaware of when the next batch of TCNs will arrive.

“I cannot tell you when others will arrive. We have a 14-day gap. As I’ve indicated, we can get another trip after 14 days, but there’s no guarantee. It’s not like these are designated numbers as we have with the involuntary returned migrants that we receive — our own citizens. Every two weeks, we know we get a batch, a flight, anywhere from 50 to 75 individuals. The TCNs depend on the number which might penetrate the barrier getting into the United States, as well as where they are from and what the State Department will decide or Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) will decide where they’re sending them and to which country,” he said.

According to Chang, no limitations will be placed on the TCNs during their stay in the country.

“They are individuals from different cultures, and what they do is up to them. They are here as visitors and they are working closely with the IOM in terms of conveying relevant information. The IOM will extract the information they require to prepare them for transit to their home country. They are free to do as they wish, like any visitor to Jamaica.

“They are individuals, who just like you in this room are regular working people who have sought to migrate, but done so illegally to the United States. The ones we accept, there are no criminals in there. They’re just families looking for a better life and we are accommodating their transition back home,” Chang reiterated.

Responding to concerns about the number of people who may want to seek asylum, Chang told journalists that the issue is not one of the Government but that of the institution which deals with the applications.

“The commissioner that deals with asylum or refugee status is a public body. It’s like a court. The documents are available. And I’m not saying we’ll not say how many…It’s their right to do so. And if they do so, it will be established. The asylum committee will sit, and the public will have access to it,” he said adding that the process can be lengthy, but the Government will notify the public as the numbers are available.

“They may ask to stay without going to asylum. It’s their freedom to do so. They are here as visitors, and if they have a skill set that is in high demand, they may. Doesn’t mean we have to accept it, but they can apply for that as well as apply for refugee status. They have a number of options,” he said.

According to Chang, their options will be discussed with them by the IOM.

“The IOM will interrogate and not only make arrangements for their movement, if they seek other alternative arrangements, then the IOM will inform us and we take it from there. But that is an important part of the nature of the IOM. As indicated, the United Nations body, they do this kind of activity globally as a trusted organisation in humanitarian relief activity. And, therefore, we allow them to proceed without any interference,” he said.

World.title: Infantino apologizes to FIFA Council for World Cup sell-off plan
World.content:
The football chief said he was sorry “for the mistakes that we made,” but reminded that his project was only a proposal and “in no way a done deal.”

FIFA President Gianni Infantino expressed regret to the organization’s board on Thursday regarding his plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

“I apologized for the mistakes that we made in relation to the communication and consultation process related to the … project, which then led to many consequences,” said Infantino after the meeting, adding that his proposal had dominated discussions.

“But what is important to remember is that it was a proposal — so in no way a done deal — just a proposal that actually intended to enable FIFA to invest more in our member associations, as opposed to replacing support from existing resources,” he added.

World.title: Deutsch-Französische Einigung zu „Made in Europe“ und Autoabgasen verzögert sich – SPD erhebt Einwände
World.content:
Anfang dieser Woche hatte der französische Präsident Emmanuel Macron angedeutet, dass nun Deutschland am Zug sei. „Auf der anderen Seite des Rheins gibt es politische Zwänge, und ich respektiere die Koalitionsgespräche voll und ganz“, sagte Macron am Montag am Rande des Pariser Autosalons.

Gemäß den Bedingungen des vorgeschlagenen Abkommens würde Deutschland strengere „Made in Europe“-Kriterien für den Automobilsektor im „Industrial Accelerator Act“ akzeptieren, auf die Frankreich gedrängt hat, im Gegenzug für eine Abschwächung des Verbots von Verbrennungsmotoren, einer der langfristigen Forderungen Berlins.

„Angesichts der erheblichen technologischen, wirtschaftlichen und geopolitischen Veränderungen seit der Einführung des bestehenden Rechtsrahmens sollte das Automobilpaket ein besseres Gleichgewicht zwischen Klimazielen, industrieller Wettbewerbsfähigkeit, technologischer Entwicklung und der Stärkung der europäischen Wertschöpfung herstellen“, schrieben die beiden Länder in einem POLITICO vorliegenden Vertragsentwurf.

„Auf der Grundlage der deutsch-französischen Ministerräte in den Jahren 2025 und 2026 schlagen Deutschland und Frankreich daher ein ausgewogenes Verhandlungspaket vor, das ehrgeizige CO2-Reduktionsziele mit zusätzlicher Flexibilität und gezielten Anreizen für die europäische Wertschöpfung verbindet“, heißt es in der Vereinbarung weiter.

Derzeit sieht das Ziel der EU vor, dass Unternehmen die Emissionen von Verbrennungsmotoren bis 2035 um 100 Prozent gegenüber dem Niveau von 2021 senken, wobei sie die Möglichkeit haben, sich durch Initiativen wie Ausgleichsmaßnahmen und Investitionen einen Spielraum von 10 Prozent bei den Emissionen zu „erwerben“.

Im Rahmen des vorgeschlagenen Abkommens wollen Frankreich und Deutschland das Ziel für 2035 auf 90 Prozent absenken und im Gegenzug für Investitionen in alternative Kraftstoffe einen zusätzlichen Spielraum von 10 Prozent einräumen (was insgesamt 80 Prozent ergibt).

World.title: EU leaders resume talks as Ukraine is ‘running out of money’
World.content:
After 14 hours of talks dominated by splits on energy and the EU budget, leaders are turning to migration and aid for Kyiv.

EU leaders returned Friday for their second day of marathon talks, where Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will make a direct pitch for more help amid a crisis of faith among allies over Donald Trump’s latest steps favoring Russia.

“Ukraine is running out of money now,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said on her way into the meeting.

Leaders are expected to turn to the question of how to protect the bloc from Russian hybrid attacks, maritime security and the Middle East — as well how to tackle migration, with the stage set for a showdown over whether to push for tougher controls.

On Thursday, a three-hour argument over taxing car emissions derailed Antonio Costa’s carefully laid plans to tackle the biggest challenges facing the bloc: fixing its economy and sorting out its spending priorities, drawing ire from some diplomats.

As leaders piled into their motorcades around midnight after 14 hours of talks, they seemed as far away as ever on negotiations over the bloc’s next long-term budget — with the next serious round of talks slipping to November.

World.title: Fonds publics détournés : pourquoi la Cour des comptes européenne pourrait avoir plus de mal à les repérer
World.content:
Cet avertissement intervient alors que l'épineux débat du montant du budget 2028-2034 de l'UE est au menu du sommet des dirigeants européens à Bruxelles cette semaine, et que la Cour a constaté une augmentation des irrégularités dans l'utilisation des fonds publics.

Outre le montant total des moyens, se pose la question de leur répartition. Après un cycle budgétaire marqué par la pandémie, les guerres et les conséquences du changement climatique, la Commission souhaite rendre le prochain budget plus agile. Pour ce faire, elle prévoit d'en affecter environ la moitié — soit près de 1 000 milliards d’euros sur sept ans — à une enveloppe unique dans laquelle les pays pourront puiser pour remplir leurs objectifs dans des domaines comme l'immigration, l’agriculture ou le développement régional.

Ces fonds destinés à l'agriculture et au développement régional — souvent octroyés sous forme de subventions aux exploitations agricoles et aux projets locaux — sont depuis longtemps exposés à la fraude et aux détournements.

Selon Tony Murphy, accorder aux gouvernements nationaux une plus grande marge de manœuvre pour réorienter leurs dépenses rendrait le suivi de ces dernières encore plus difficile.

"Il y aura une certaine flexibilité, mais à quel prix ?", a-t-il soulevé lors d'une interview. Une grande partie du contrôle dépendra des mesures de surveillance que chaque pays a déjà mises en place.

D'autant que les irrégularités dans l'utilisation des fonds du budget de l'UE sont en hausse. Les erreurs de versement se sont élevées à 5 milliards d'euros l'année dernière, selon le dernier rapport de la Cour des comptes européenne.

World.title: EU summit runs out of gas
World.content:
It’s been a packed agenda at the European Council summit, with little sign of progress on key issues. EU leaders continued to argue over the bloc’s long-term budget, with energy supply and security taking up much of the discussion … including questions over strategic gas reserves and the future of the Emissions Trading System.

The war in Ukraine looms large over the summit. Earlier this week, President Trump alarmed European leaders and horrified Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy by announcing a deal to release Russian diesel onto the U.S. market, apparently in an attempt to lower fuel costs for American consumers.

Host Sarah Wheaton unpacks developments late into the night with colleagues who have been reporting on the summit. She’s joined by Chief EU Correspondent Zoya Sheftalovich, Chief Political Correspondent in Europe and the U.K. Tim Ross and Gregorio Sorgi, financial services reporter.

World.title: Are the Brexit wars back?
World.content:
Customs union, single market, rejoin, second referendum. It’s all feeling a little Ground Hog day in Westminster after Andy Burnham reopened the Europe question at Labour Party conference.

Hosts Sascha O’Sullivan and Pat Baker find out how the row over Europe will play out in the next few years, with Reform MP Danny Kruger and Labour MP Stella Creasy.

Sascha speaks to Cecilia Malmström, former EU Trade Commissioner during the Brexit negotiations, who says any new deal with the EU would need to be “Nigel Farage-proofed” in case Reform wound up in Downing Street.

UK-EU reporter Jon Stone explains what Burnham is hoping to gain from the EU summit next month, and whether Britain’s friends in Brussels care about Westminster looking again at Britain’s relationship with the trading bloc.

World.title: Britain’s Lib Dems are having a mini-meltdown. Here’s what’s going on.
World.content:
The botched coup comes as the Liberal Democrats try to answer a more existential question: what are they actually for and how do they make an impact in Britain’s fragmented political landscape?

POLITICO’s Poll of Polls shows the Lib Dems coasting along. After getting 12.2% in the 2024 general election — and bagging a record 72 members of parliament as a result — the party has slipped down, polling between 9% and 11% since Andy Burnham became prime minister.

POLITICO explains why Lib Dems are now openly discussing Davey’s future; how much danger he is in; and exactly how the man known for a cheery demeanor and eye-catching paddle-board stunts could be capsized.

1) Why is Davey’s future in the headlines?

The surprise resignation of the Lib Dems’ Treasury spokesperson Charlie Maynard a week ago triggered the latest round of soul-searching about the leader’s future — but the grumbling goes back a bit further.

Maynard’s resignation followed costly tax-cutting pledges from Davey at the party’s conference in September and came hot on the heels of sharp responses — including from 2024-intake Lib Dem MPs Tom Gordon and Vikki Slade — to the way Davey defended an existing guarantee on state pensions. Some MPs believe the party isn’t adequately representing younger voters by opposing changes to the so-called triple lock, now targeted for reform by Burnham.

The immediate threat looks to have receded. Maynard’s resignation has gone down badly among a host of colleagues.

World.title: Marine Le Pen’s EU dream is a nightmare for Brussels
World.content:
Other buildings in the EU Quarter of Brussels (or, as it’s now known, the 21st arrondissement) have not been so lucky. Most have been razed to the ground. Some have been occupied by disgruntled former EU staff, who are refusing to leave and have set up a working group to discuss a future roadmap that will feed into a discussion on how to bring back a European Union that Le Pen has largely destroyed.

Largely, but not completely. There is still an official EU office; the corner table in the branch of sandwich shop Exki near the Schuman roundabout (ironically, Le Pen used some of the money saved from dismantling the EU to finish the roundabout as planned). It is staffed 24/7 by Maroš Šefčovič, and he has a plentiful supply of leaflets.

Le Pen had more in store for the EU after her crushing 2027 presidential election win over Kylian Mbappé (who won a primary against Raphaël Glucksmann to be the unity centrist candidate, which was decided by who could do the most keepie-uppies).

The phrases “non-paper,” “stakeholder” and “trilogue” have been consigned to la poubelle de l’histoire. The European Committee of the Regions and the European Economic and Social Committee were closed down within weeks of Le Pen taking office, which shocked millions of Europeans who had no idea they ever existed. The European Parliament building is still there but is now occupied by a strange breed of zombie-like creatures wandering aimlessly through the corridors in search of something to do. No one can tell the difference.

Von der Leyen was, as Le Pen promised would happen, sent back to Germany where — in a somewhat unexpected move — she has become chancellor, succeeding Angela Merkel, who herself came out of retirement and orchestrated a coup to bring down current Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

Anyway, back to 2026 and an EU reeling from a Le Pen speech in which she pledged to turn the Commission into a “secretariat” in the service of its member countries, and scrap some institutions altogether.

World.title: Putin seizes five more European firms, continuing Russia's hostile asset crackdown
World.content:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has signed a decree ordering the compulsory seizure of Russian assets belonging to French flooring manufacturer Tarkett and four other European companies, whose combined annual revenue exceeds 50 billion roubles (€532 million).

 

The assets have been placed under the interim control of a management company called Centre Capital, registered in February 2026.

Its chief executive is listed as Marat Mirkhaydarov, former head of the administration of the regional governor of Zabaykalsky, who stood down in 2025 following an injury sustained in Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine.

The decree also covers paper packaging producer Kappa Rus, formerly part of Ireland's Smurfit Kappa, hygiene product maker Ontex RU, part of the Belgian Ontex group, metal packaging manufacturer Eviosys Packaging Kuban, part of US-based Sonoco Products Company, and Menshen Packaging CIS, owned by German plastics producer Menshen.

All five companies continued operating in Russia after the country's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Tarkett, which ranks third globally by floor covering sales and leads the market in vinyl flooring according to its 2024 annual report, kept two plants in Russia out of its 34 production sites worldwide and continued paying taxes to the Russian budget.

The latest seizures follow a series of similar moves in September, when Putin placed the Russian assets of Swiss food giant Nestlé, German hypermarket chain Metro, French retailer Auchan and home improvement chain Leroy Merlin under temporary administration.

Those assets were transferred to a company called LEV Management, established shortly before the decision and reported by Russian media to have links to the country's security services. A manufacturer of plastic dispensing systems owned by French holding Aptar Europe Holding was also placed under temporary administration shortly afterwards.

A presidential decree signed in April 2023 established the mechanism for such seizures, authorising the imposition of temporary administration over certain Russian assets of foreign companies.

Western governments and international legal experts have described the move as unlawful expropriation. Companies whose assets are seized can, in principle, pursue compensation through international arbitration under bilateral investment treaties Russia has signed with EU member states, although enforcing judgments against the Kremlin and its entities is nearly impossible.

The first targets under that decree were Danish brewer Carlsberg and French dairy group Danone.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov directly linked the transfer of Nestlé's and Auchan's assets to the fact that they are companies from what Moscow terms "unfriendly countries".

“Unfriendly countries” is an official Russian government designation applied to all EU member states, the US, the UK and other states that imposed sanctions following the 2022 full-scale invasion, in an attempt to dissuade them from aiding Kyiv.

Russia has framed the asset seizures in part as a response to the EU’s decision to freeze approximately €300 billion in Russian sovereign assets following the all-out invasion.

World.title: Social media favourites, Pompeii's cats star in new photo book
World.content:
After charming thousands of visitors and turning into genuine social media celebrities, the cats that live inside the archaeological area of Pompeii have now become the stars of a photographic book dedicated to them.

 

The book, entitled Cats of Pompeii, is published by Giunti Editore in collaboration with the Pompeii Archaeological Park. Richly illustrated, it tells the stories of the everyday life of the feline colony that inhabits the UNESCO World Heritage site.

The volume grew out of photographs donated to the Park by archaeologist and photographer Silvia Vacca and offers a journey into the most unusual and captivating side of the ancient city. The shots capture the cats as they roam among domus, gardens and Roman streets, providing an original perspective on a presence that has long since become an integral part of the Pompeian landscape.

Cats of Pompeii Parco Archeologico di Pompei

The Park’s feline colony numbers between forty and fifty animals, and their presence is constantly monitored through a management and protection system that makes it possible to combine animal welfare with the conservation of the archaeological heritage and the safety of visitors. The Park has also introduced a video surveillance system to prevent animals being abandoned.

Thanks to cooperation with the charity Archeogatti Onlus, chaired by Antonella Carotenuto, the Archaeological Park also ensures sterilisation campaigns, health checks, measures to prevent abandonment, and the management of feeding the colony and arranging adoptions for some of the "archaeologist" cats.

Cats in ancient Pompeii

The presence of cats in Pompeii is a symbolic feature of life at the site. Ongoing archaeological research sheds light on the relationship between humans and felines in the ancient world, while today these animals remain a familiar sight and are much appreciated by visitors from all over the globe.

Cats of Pompeii Parco Archeologico di Pompei

The camera lens reveals intimate, evocative images taken during the Park’s quietest moments, when the streets of the ancient city fall silent once more. Out of this comes a portrait of a different Pompeii, where safeguarding cultural heritage goes hand in hand with protecting the animals that have inhabited its spaces for years.

"Cats of Pompeii" is available at sales points in the Pompeii Archaeological Park and through Giunti’s distribution channels.

World.title: Latest news bulletin | October 16th, 2026 – Midday
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: Dinosaur fossil hidden in London’s Natural History Museum for 100 years identified as new species
World.content:
A dinosaur fossil that spent almost a century in the collections of London’s Natural History Museum has been identified as a new species.

 

The skull fragment belonged to Invictibellatrix amberina, a previously unknown carnivorous dinosaur that lived around 120 million years ago. It’s also the first confirmed evidence of a megaraptoran dinosaur in Europe.

The fossil was originally discovered at the foot of a cliff on the southwest coast of the Isle of Wight by amateur fossil hunter Reginald Walter Tooley. After his death in 1924, the Natural History Museum acquired more than 1,000 specimens from his collection, including the fragment.

Although scientists knew it belonged to a dinosaur, exactly which one remained a mystery for decades.

Now, researchers have taken another look at the fossil using CT scanning technology, allowing them to examine its internal structure and create a 3D model. Their full findings were published in the journal Royal Society Open Science.

"More dangerous than a T.rex"

Professor Paul Barrett, the study’s senior author from the Natural History Museum, says, "Despite over 200 years of collecting, the Isle of Wight continues to surprise us with new dinosaur species, and finds of carnivorous dinosaurs, such as Invictibellatrix, have been particularly elusive."

"Work like this shows the exceptional value of working with historical museum collections where there are still many discoveries to be made," he added.

Despite their name, megaraptorans were not the small, bird-like dinosaurs we commonly associate with the word "raptor". They were larger predators, more closely related to tyrannosaurs, with "slender heads", "large arms" and "giant curved claws", according to the Natural History Museum.

Invictibellatrix amberina is estimated to have measured between 3 and 4 metres (10 and 13 feet) in length and stood around 1.5 metres (5 feet) tall. It lived during the Early Cretaceous period, when dinosaurs dominated terrestrial ecosystems.

Researchers have also suggested that it may have had feathers, although its exact appearance still remains uncertain.

According to Dr Cassius Morrison, a researcher at the University College London's (UCL) Earth Sciences department, the species would have eaten small dinosaurs, lizards and mammals - similar to the role in the food chain a hyena holds today.

"It was not the apex predator of its time, but for humans this dinosaur would have been more dangerous than a T. rex. We would have been perfectly sized prey, about a third of their body weight. They definitely would have chased us. A T. rex would not have bothered, as we would have been too small," explains Dr Cassius Morrison, who led the study.

The discovery is particularly exciting because megaraptorans have previously been identified in Asia, Australia and South America, but never conclusively in Europe.

World.title: The world’s best countries to live in for 2026 – and six of the top 10 are in Europe
World.content:
Been dreaming of a life abroad, but haven’t decided on where to go yet? Then you might just want to take a look at this new ranking.

 

Produced by Nomad Capitalist, the Nomad Lifestyle Index evaluated 63 destinations against five pillars: Nature and climate; tax; residence and access; safety and freedom; and quality of life and infrastructure.

Within these pillars, the ranking looked at things like air quality, extreme weather risk, routes to legal residence and citizenship, the Global Peace Index, life expectancy, cost of living and broadband speed, among others.

After crunching the numbers, the top 10 is filled with European countries, including the number one spot: Monaco.

Every destination was given a score out of 100 for each of the five pillars, which were then used to calculate an overall score.

The three top destinations – Monaco, Andorra and the United Arab Emirates – were separated by just 0.74 points.

The best places to live in Europe

Monaco claimed the top spot as it was the only country to receive a perfect 100 score under the quality of life and infrastructure pillar, but it also ranked highly for its safety and freedom score.

In second place, Andorra leads in the safety and freedom pillar while also having the fourth-best nature score, with the cleanest air of any European country included in the Nomad Lifestyle Index. It was pipped to the top spot because of its route to citizenship, which takes 20 years of residence and requires a language and history test.

Malta took fourth place, with praise for its strong passport and route to naturalisation within five years. It also ranked highly in the nature pillar, but was held back by its tax score and quality of life and infrastructure rating.

Portugal, a long-time favourite of digital nomads, came fifth, ranking highly for its safety and freedom, residence and access, and tax scores, but was let down by its nature score as it is exposed to extreme weather conditions as a result of climate change.

Cyprus placed sixth, coming second in the residence and access pillar, with a strong passport and seven years to naturalisation. Its quality of life and infrastructure score held it back, as well as the air quality.

Rounding out the top 10 is Switzerland, which performed well in the safety and freedom pillar.
