World.title: How Will Croatia Actually Benefit From the €50 billion Data Centre?
World.content:
October the 15th, 2026 – In what way will Croatia actually concretely benefit from the giant €50 billion data centre in Topusko that has many deeply concerned about the environment and water?

The previously announced construction of the huge and very controversial Pantheon data centre in Topusko, whose value is estimated at as much as €50 billion, raises a series of questions about the real benefits Croatia could gain from such an investment. Vedran Salvia reports for Index that this gigantic project recently took another step towards realisation. Sisak-Moslavina County has initiated amendments to the spatial plan in order to create the conditions for the construction of the centre and the accompanying infrastructure.

Although a series of procedures and the obtaining of the necessary permits still lie ahead before construction can begin, below we provide answers to some of the key questions about the project, its possible benefits and costs. For the purposes of this text we also received an expert comment from Tomislav Vazdar, an expert in cybersecurity and artificial intelligence.

intended for large tech companies with little care for anyone else

According to Ryan Rich, executive partner of Pantheon AI, who wrote about the project for the Wall Street Journal, the centre is intended for large technology companies that need enormous computing capacity for continuous operation and the development of artificial intelligence. Rich also stated that the infrastructure would be available to European defence, intelligence and commercial users.

Pantheon representatives were asked about who specifically will use the future data centre and whether there are already agreed tenants, but we had not received a reply by the time this text was published. Project manager Mario Gudelj explained to Večernji list in July that the final value of the investment will depend on the requirements of future users, whom he described as large technology companies developing artificial intelligence. According to the announcements at the time, the first users should start using the centre’s capacities at the beginning of 2029.

Vazdar explained to us who the most common users of such data centres are. “The largest users are global cloud service providers, companies developing large artificial intelligence models, and increasingly the defence and security sector. In a centre of this scale, AI models would primarily be trained and run. Money is earned by renting out capacity, most often through long-term contracts with a few large clients,” Vazdar commented for Index.

is there any benefit to anyone outside of big tech?

Part of the investment will relate to construction works and infrastructure, and a significant part to the purchase of computer and other technological equipment. The value of the campus construction is estimated at up to €12 billion, while the total investment, including IT equipment, should exceed €50 billion. One of the possible long-term benefits is the construction of electricity infrastructure. In addition to the construction of a 500-megawatt solar power plant, for which cooperation with the international energy group Greenvolt has been announced, according to project representatives’ announcements, the construction of approximately 280 kilometres of power lines and a new substation is planned, and the investment would be financed by the investor.

The built infrastructure should then pass into the ownership of the Croatian Transmission System Operator. “The benefits won’t come by themselves; all of that has to be contracted in advance. So, a share of capacity for domestic companies, universities and the public sector, engagement of domestic contractors and investment in the network that remains with the state. Equally important is control over the data. If data is processed in Croatia but control over it remains outside the European legal framework, the state bears the risk and does not gain digital sovereignty,” Vazdar said.

are there any benefits for croatian companies?

One of the concrete opportunities for Croatian companies is linked precisely to the construction of the mentioned electricity infrastructure. At the end of April, Končar signed a non-binding letter of intent on cooperation on the Pantheon project, which envisages the participation of several companies from its group, including Dalekovod. One of the investors, entrepreneur Jako Andabak, claimed on HRT back in April that the majority of the works during the construction and equipping of the centre should be carried out by Croatian companies, using domestic knowledge and workforce.

what about new employment opportunities?

As announced at the project presentation, more than 3,000 workers should be engaged during construction, around 1,500 people employed after the centre starts operating, while the project could indirectly contribute to the creation of a further 6,000 jobs. Andabak stated that approximately half of the 1,500 permanently employed should have higher education qualifications. That would mean around 750 highly qualified jobs, primarily linked to the operation and maintenance of complex technological infrastructure.

It is not yet known how many of the employees will be from Croatia, and especially how many jobs could go to residents of Topusko and the surrounding area. “The most jobs are created during construction, and once the centre is up and running there are few permanent employees, although these are highly qualified positions. Realistic expectations should be based on signed commitments, not on announcements,” Vazdar said.

how will pantheon help croatia’s own tech sector?

One of the potentially greatest long-term benefits of the project could be the development of Croatia’s technology sector, especially companies dealing with artificial intelligence. Large computing capacities are needed for the development and training of advanced artificial intelligence models, and access to such infrastructure could open new opportunities for domestic companies, universities and research institutions.

Project manager Mario Gudelj spoke to N1 in May about the ambition for Pantheon to bring the industry of the future to Croatia and position it among the leading countries in digital transformation. Vazdar said more about the importance of Pantheon for the development of artificial intelligence and the domestic technology sector. “The significance is potentially great, but only with clear access conditions for domestic companies and scientists. Without that, the centre can operate at full capacity for foreign clients, while the domestic sector gets almost nothing from it,” he added.

how much will the state and the local community benefit financially?

In addition to employment and the engagement of domestic companies, one of the more important potential benefits of the Pantheon project relates to tax and other public revenues. The Municipality of Topusko has particularly high expectations. Its mayor Ivica Kuzmić stated on HRT in May that the realisation of the project could increase the municipality’s revenues three to four times. He emphasised that the additional funds would primarily be used to improve communal infrastructure.

However, a detailed financial projection showing how much the state and the Municipality of Topusko would earn annually from the centre’s operations has not yet been publicly presented. The amount of tax revenues will depend, among other things, on the centre’s business results, the number and salaries of employees, and the way in which the business of the companies involved in the project is organised.

will electricity prices shoot up?

One of the more important questions relates to the high consumption of electricity and water and the possible consequences for the general public, for whom a giant data centre represents little but a deep worry. As Gudelj announced, Pantheon in full operation would consume around five terawatt-hours of electricity per year, 1.5 times more than Zagreb and a little more than a quarter of Croatia’s consumption.

However, he stated that electricity would not become more expensive for citizens because of the centre. According to his announcements, the centre would primarily be supplied from renewable sources, and the investor would also finance the necessary electricity infrastructure. “A data centre of this scale consumes as much electricity as a large city, and continuously. That means great pressure on the electricity system and a risk that the cost of adapting the network will spill over onto all users if the rules are not set in advance,” Vazdar adds.

“Cooling data centres down also requires significant amounts of water, so it is necessary to transparently determine how that will affect local sources. All of this must be publicly and independently assessed before any decision,” Vazdar says.

data centres and their devastating environmental impact

The impact of Pantheon on the environment is a separate and extremely important topic that deserves an analysis of its own. We have already written about this in detail on Index, and here we will only recall that part of the public is mainly concerned about the high water consumption, noise, waste heat, interventions in the space and potential consequences for the local ecosystem.

Vazdar warns for Index that cooling a data centre requires significant amounts of water, which is why it is necessary to transparently determine the possible impact on local sources and to assess everything publicly and independently before any decision is made. Gudelj says that the final solution has not yet been chosen. Pantheon, as he emphasised, will not connect to the public water supply or use water from rivers and streams, and hydrogeological research is being carried out. Earlier, the investors claimed to Index that the impact on the environment would be negligible or non-existent. In any case, the strategic environmental impact assessment and the assessment of acceptability for the ecological network are only part of the procedures that must precede construction. Therefore it still remains to be determined what consequences the project could have for the environment and what protection measures will be necessary.

World.title: Split High on Quality of Life in Relation to Costs Ranking – But Should It Be?
World.content:
October the 15th, 2026 – Split has occupied a high position in terms of quality of life in relation to costs of living, being above Stockholm and and Copenhagen, but should it rank this highly?

Two of Croatia’s largest cities also made it into the aforementioned quality of life ranking. Slobodan Mufic reports for Index that according to this research, Zagreb and Split are cities with above-average, even high, quality of life, but at the same time they are extremely expensive relative to the median salary.

does split really offer a better life than 94% of other european cities?

The analysis shows that Split offers a better life than 94 percent of other European cities, including Copenhagen, Prague, Stockholm and Madrid, but in order to enjoy its benefits and advantages one needs to earn 29 percent more than the net median salary, which in Croatia back in July amounted to 1,346 euros. The median salary means that half of employees received a net salary lower than 1,346 euros, and half received at least that much or more.

Zagreb fared somewhat worse, or better, depending on which parameter on the chart you look at. In the capital, the chart says, the quality of life is significantly lower than in Split: Zagreb is better than 64 percent of other European cities (for example Graz, Rome, Berlin and Milan). On the other hand, the mentioned standard is also significantly more accessible and one needs to earn only three percent more than the net median salary.

the worst quality of life is in belgrade

The best and most affordable life, according to the research, is lived in Vienna, Helsinki and the Dutch cities of The Hague and Eindhoven. And the worst and most expensive in Skopje, Belgrade, Sofia and Bucharest. That is at least how it was calculated by Alessandro Palombo, an Italian entrepreneur and doctor of legal sciences, who published the research in the form of several charts on social networks and his website.

Of course, what immediately catches the eye on the chart is the paradox that Skopje is more expensive than Paris and London, and that Oslo and Geneva are cheaper than Zagreb. However, Palombo did not take into account absolute living costs, according to which the largest European cities are certainly expensive, but the ratio of costs to the median salary in those cities. The contradiction is nevertheless only apparent: a city can be very expensive, but the local median salary can be sufficient for an excellent standard of living. Likewise, a city with relatively low prices can be difficult to afford for local residents with low salaries.

numbeo deemed “an unreliable data source”

The fundamental problem that largely calls into question the validity of the research is the source of the data. As usual when it comes to such analyses, Palombo uses data from Numbeo, an online database that, based on user inputs, collects and compares information on living costs, prices, salaries, safety, quality of life and other indicators in cities and countries around the world.

Numbeo is often quite unreliable as a source because anyone can enter data in a certain category. Although there are automatic filters for suspicious values, its data and analyses should generally be taken with a large dose of caution. For this reason, Palombo himself does not present his comparisons as infallible. In a discussion on X he admitted that he considers the quality of such data limited and that some components of quality of life are inevitably subjective.

Specifically, according to the October data on prices on Numbeo, for Split in the previous 12 months data was submitted by 37 different participants, and for Zagreb by 156. Dozens of voluntary participants are not a representative sample for a display on a map with seemingly precise coordinates. Numbeo’s standard quality-of-life index includes eight factors: purchasing power, safety, healthcare, property prices relative to income, cost of living, commute time, pollution and climate.

Palombo states that he calculated quality of life without Numbeo’s price-related indicators. What remains are the criteria of safety, healthcare, traffic, pollution and climate, which at Numbeo to a large extent rest on the perception of the website’s users rather than on official statistics. Financial affordability is shown separately by Palombo on the horizontal axis.

croatia’s housing structure makes a major difference

However, quality of life in this research does not take into account other important criteria at all, such as the quality of education, employment opportunities, availability of kindergartens, cultural offer, social protection and the real possibility of finding long-term housing.

It should also be borne in mind that the research is based on a single person who earns the median salary and lives in a rented one-bedroom apartment outside the city centre. That in no way corresponds to the financial status of the majority of the population. For Croatia specifically, this difference is particularly important. According to Eurostat data, in 2024 91 percent of Croatia’s inhabitants lived in their own property. A person living in their own paid-off apartment, a young tenant, a married couple with two salaries, a four-member family and a pensioner have completely different relationships between income and living costs. This clearly shows how much the author’s model differs from reality.

It is also not explained by what criterion these particular 79 cities were selected. It is not entirely clear whether the author of the research took into account the median net salary in the entire country, the region or only in the specific city.

osijek finds itself (surprisingly) on the list

Interestingly, Palombo also offers another interactive map that, according to the same criteria, compares 322 world cities. Among Croatian cities, Osijek is the biggest surprise. It is at approximately the 99.7th percentile of quality of life, which places it among the highest-rated cities, even slightly ahead of Vienna, Helsinki, Split and Rijeka. The only problem is that the basic (and entirely bizarre) assumption is an annual gross income of 86,000 US dollars, which is deeply unrealistically high for Croatian standards. Only a few thousand employees in Croatia receive such a salary.

World.title: Expert: Trump does not have the power to force Ukraine to capitulate
World.content:
While Donald Trump's unpredictable behavior and disruptions to Starlink are complicating the situation in Ukraine, the U.S. president does not have the power to force Ukraine to surrender, security expert Ilmar Raag finds.

Security expert Ilmar Raag shared his view on social media that U.S. President Donald Trump is not Estonia's ally. Raag explained on ETV's "Ringvaade" that Trump and the United States should not be equated.

"We have American allied troops here in Estonia and when our military personnel interact with them, they are doing their own jobs. I also hear about what is happening in Washington. Following Trump's latest statements, there are senators in the Republican camp who say they disagree with him. I have to say that if there are Americans anywhere whom I consider my Americans, they are the Republicans who are currently standing up to Trump."

Trump, who has recently been pressuring Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to make peace, signed a diesel fuel deal with Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin last week in an attempt to regain popularity in the United States ahead of the midterm elections. In recent days, he has also threatened to stop sharing U.S. intelligence with Ukraine and has partially restricted the war-torn country's access to the Starlink satellite communications system. During a visit to the United Kingdom, Zelenskyy told journalist Piers Morgan on his show that he felt betrayed by Trump.

"First of all, we can say that no major catastrophe is going to happen immediately, for two reasons. First, although American intelligence is very important, it does not do everything. When we talk about Starlink, it serves many different functions in drone warfare, but not all of them. For example, units can still communicate with one another via Starlink and headquarters can communicate with teams on the front line operating these drones. That accounts for half of what Starlink does. The problem is that the most effective drones the Ukrainians have will naturally be affected if Starlink's more important functions — those provided by Starshield — are not working," Raag said.

According to Raag, it is impossible to say for certain whether the Starlink disruptions were accidental or deliberate, but the coincidences are significant enough to suggest that something else may be behind them.

"It appears to be some kind of unilateral action by a smaller group. You can see that Ukrainians are receiving warnings about incoming missiles too late after Starlink actually stops working for them. The Americans are not speaking with one voice, saying they made a decision and acted accordingly. Some are saying one thing, while Trump is already saying it never happened. This shows that the head does not know what the tail is doing, or vice versa. That brings us to the second argument that describes the current situation: Trump, being as unpredictable as he is, could change his mind yet again," Raag explained, adding that this was a sign that Europe needed to take responsibility for its own affairs.

European leaders have responded to Trump's statements and decisions. While many have condemned the U.S. president's rhetoric, others believe Trump should be approached more calmly to avoid provoking him further.

"It is true that Trump is a very emotional man and in some ways he thrives on conflict — he can always escalate things further. In that respect, European leaders have already realized that if they keep their heads down and wait a little, perhaps the midterm elections will come around and Trump will lose much of the power he currently holds. That is what many are hoping for," the security expert said.

According to Raag, surveys conducted in the United States show that most Americans consider Putin the aggressor and support Ukraine, raising hopes that if Trump suffers a defeat in the midterm elections, Congress may adopt a more supportive position toward Ukraine.

"Ukraine cannot afford a situation in which people are losing their lives while Trump is allowed to play games, shifting back and forth. People are dying in the meantime. In that respect, Trump is influenced most by his approval ratings in the United States, fuel prices and, ultimately, European leaders as well. He has now demonstrated several times that when Europe says a very clear 'no,' Trump returns to his previous positions," Raag said in response to the host's question about whether diplomatic exchanges had become too heated.

There are also concerns that if Trump stops receiving praise from Europe and Ukraine, he may become more interested in holding talks and making deals with Putin.

"But what can he really agree on? Trump can conclude various economic agreements with the Russians and do business with them. But Trump does not actually have the power to force Ukraine to capitulate. That is not going to happen and Trump has realized that as well. Perhaps that is also one of the sources of his frustration — that he simply cannot do it, just as he cannot impose on the Iranians the peace terms he has been announcing for quite some time," Raag said.

According to Raag, the war has escalated since August, but the Ukrainians are holding out and have already learned how to deal with the challenges they face.

"The escalation began in August when it became clear that the Ukrainians currently lack sufficiently effective air defenses against ballistic missiles and therefore face a very difficult winter. However, they have spent several years learning and the Ukrainians themselves say that although they curse Trump and Putin, they will survive this," Raag said.

World.title: Platform workers' grueling hours raising health and safety concerns
World.content:
Many food couriers and ride-hailing drivers in Estonia work exhausting hours that put their health and road safety at risk, but the government has no plans to intervene.

A recent study by the Foresight Center and the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications (MKM) found that a quarter of food couriers and ride-hailing drivers work more than 50 hours a week, well above Estonia's standard 40-hour workweek.

"The study also found that many couriers and drivers were working more than 100 hours a week," said Olavi Miller, an expert at the Foresight Center.

Such workloads can harm workers' health and raise concerns about road safety. But while the MKM doesn't condone excessive workloads, Hedi Arukase, the ministry's deputy secretary general for labor and equality, says platform workers are independent contractors, not traditional employees, and thus are free to set their own hours.

"Unfortunately, there isn't much we can do about it," she said.

Money is a major reason workers put in such long hours. About 90 percent earn additional income elsewhere, while platform work is the sole source of income for roughly 2,000 people. Two-thirds earn less than €1,200 a month.

Social protections are another concern. Not all platform workers contribute to pensions, and most rely on other jobs or educational institutions to qualify for Estonian Health Insurance Fund (EHIF) coverage. Fourteen percent have no health insurance at all.

Ex-minister: They chose this job

MP Signe Riisalo (Reform), chair of the Riigikogu's Social Affairs Committee and former minister of social protection, said platform workers are all independent, capable adults who have chosen this form of employment, but did also acknowledge a broader problem.

"Is this a broader problem for society? Yes, it is," Riisalo said. "And do we need to look for solutions? Yes, we do."

One option would be for platform workers to unionize, she said, "because social protections can be provided by an employer, which in their case is the platform."

A new EU directive aims to make platform work more transparent, and legislation to implement it in Estonia is currently pending in the Riigikogu. Arukase said the bill should help workers better understand their employment conditions and figure out how to earn more in less time.

World.title: Experts: French grocery store cyberattack a warning sign for Estonia
World.content:
A cyberattack on French grocery stores Sunday that resulted in large quantities of food being destroyed is also a warning sign for Estonia, cybersecurity experts say.

Hundreds of grocery stores in France were hit by a cyberattack on Sunday when hackers raised the temperature of refrigerators to as high as 50 degrees Celsius. As a result, large quantities of food were spoiled, causing financial losses for the stores. Estonia must also be prepared for a similar threat.

"Things like this can happen and the threat is very real. Fortunately, Estonia has not experienced a problem like the one in France, at least to my knowledge. But that does not mean something similar could not happen at some point because of mistakes or poor cyber hygiene," said Toomas Lepik, a cybersecurity analyst at Tallinn University of Technology (TalTech).

Minister of Justice and Digital Affairs Liisa Pakosta, who is attending a cybersecurity conference in Singapore, described the incident in France as shocking. She said society must adapt to the reality that cyberattacks are no longer limited to computers and information systems. At the same time, Pakosta said Estonia has some of the strictest cybersecurity requirements in the world.

"We have particularly strict cybersecurity requirements for companies providing vital services, including those responsible for food security, and these requirements must be met. Companies need to ensure their software is up to date, that systems are properly connected and that they are not accessible to just anyone passing by. As for how much companies in Estonia, such as grocery stores, have done to mitigate this risk, all I can say is that larger companies responsible for food security are required to undergo audits," Pakosta said.

However, these requirements do not apply to all grocery stores. Pakosta added that both the government and businesses need to invest more in cybersecurity to ensure their systems are secure.

"On the one hand, we face financially motivated cyberattacks, but we also face attacks directed against our country or society as a whole. As a digital nation, we all need to pay much more attention to this," she said.

Estonian supermarket chain Selver is also closely monitoring the incident in France to prevent a similar situation at its stores. It remains unclear who was behind the cyberattack in France and whether a ransom demand will follow.

"I can confirm that Selver has not experienced any incidents of this kind. We are doing everything we can to ensure that it never happens. I believe every company and every retail chain has its own strict rules and systems governing how these things work. Overall, I believe we are well protected against this kind of threat," said Selver communications manager Mariann Järvela.

Järvela added that the consequences of the incident in France are not significantly different from those of a power outage, a scenario for which the supermarket chain already conducts emergency preparedness exercises.

World.title: Estonia gets €32m EU funding for 'free world's first line of defense' surveillance
World.content:
The European Commission has given preliminary approval for nearly €32 million toward Estonia's eastern border drone surveillance system, a project already partly built.

The funding is the latest installment in a program announced in March, with the first fixed systems installed on the south-eastern border in May and the full system due by the end of 2029.

The Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) will continue building the multi-layered integrated drone detection and air surveillance system on the EU's external border in cooperation with the Estonian Defense Forces (EDF).

"In cooperation with the Defense Forces, we can buy and install radars and cameras, equipment needed for drone detection, and the IT system supporting them, for a shared situational picture," said Interior Minister Igor Taro (Eesti 200).

"This will improve our ability to detect and assess potential threats so we can respond quickly. Our aim is to prevent threats before they reach the point of affecting the security of Estonian people," the minister went on.

Taro said Estonia's eastern border is currently the free world's first line of defense. "The European Union's support for strengthening drone surveillance here says that we have done good work so far, have been on the right path, and shows trust in our skills and capability to protect the EU's external border."

Veiko Kommusaar, deputy director general of the PPA for border management, said the Commission's decision was a clear sign of trust in Estonia and confirmed that the EU sees strengthening the external border as a shared security question.

"With this support, we can, over the next three years together with the Defense Forces, take air and land surveillance on the eastern border to the next level, create a more complete situational picture and improve our ability to detect and assess potential threats on land, on the Narva River and in the airspace," Kommusaar said.

He added that the investment's greatest value is not its individual radars or drones, but the ability to see what is happening on the eastern border as a whole, and to be able to respond to potential threats faster and more precisely than ever before.

The funding comes through the EU's border management and visa policy fund, with 10 percent national co-financing.

The system was announced by Prime Minister Kristen Michal in March, with over €200 million earmarked for drone defense and around €214 million for drone surveillance and countermeasures over four years. The first fixed counter-drone systems were installed on three sections of the south-eastern land border in May, and the PPA says full coverage of the Russian border should follow. The first phase — the external border and Estonia's four largest cities — is due by the end of 2027, with the full system complete by the end of 2029.

World.title: Ralf Tribuntsov takes third at World Cup,sets Estonian record
World.content:
Swimmer Ralf Tribuntsov set a new domestic record in the 100-meter backstroke at the World Cup stage in Astana, Kazakhstan, finishing third in 49.88 seconds.

It was the second time in his career he has swum under 50 seconds, improving last year's record by 0.04. Pieter Coetze won in 48.40, with Pavel Samusenko second in 49.29.

Tribuntsov qualified fifth from the morning heats in 50.70, then set the national record in the final.

The 32-year-old said he was especially pleased with the second half of the race, usually his weaker suit.

"[Estonian swimmer] Daniel [Zaitsev] and [coach] Toni [Meijel] are my lucky charms! As soon as they arrived, I got a medal! I'm incredibly happy, especially that I managed to swim the second half of the race faster, which is usually my weaker side. Today I managed to beat the other men precisely with the second half of the race," Tribuntsov said after the event.

"In the last 25 meters, when I came up from under the water, I already understood that there was still strength left, that I could fight and that this would be a decent swim. I managed to do exactly what I wanted, and that doesn't happen often in sport! The feeling in the water is quite good, so I'm expecting good results in other events too," he added.

Coach Meijel said a different competition schedule played a part too. At the previous two stages the 100m backstroke was on the third day, but in Astana, Tribuntsov could start his primary event on day one.

"A very decent swim! This time the 100m backstroke was on the schedule on the first day, and the Estonian record came fresh as well!" was Meijel's evaluation of his charge's performance.

Meijel said there is still room for improvement, noting some errors but highlighting Tribuntsov's strong final 25 meters.

Tribuntsov has improved his 100m backstroke time at every World Cup stage this year: Fifth in Baku in 50.12, fourth in Tashkent in 50.05, and third in Astana in 49.88. The final World Cup stage continues on Friday and Saturday, with Tribuntsov and Zaitsev down to swim the 50m freestyle on Friday.

World.title: Museums fear research funding shuffle threatens key projects
World.content:
Museums are concerned that the loss of research funding will jeopardize their projects and hope the decision will be reversed.

Under a government decision, the Ministry of Culture's research and development funding, totaling approximately €900,000, will be transferred to the Ministry of Education and Research's budget starting in 2028.

The transfer means that, starting in 2028, the Ministry of Culture will no longer hold funding rounds for creative research, nor will it have research and development funding in its budget to support museum research projects.

The decision stems from a proposal by Minister of Education and Research Kristina Kallas (Eesti 200) to channel ministries' research and development funding through the Ministry of Education and Research's strategic research program.

The explanatory memorandum accompanying the regulation indicates that although the funding will formally pass through the Ministry of Education and Research's budget, the Ministry of Culture will retain its own "quota" and decision-making authority to support strategic objectives and research projects within its area of responsibility, including museums. Nevertheless, the transfer of research funding to the Ministry of Education and Research has sparked discontent, particularly among Estonian museums, which have been among the main beneficiaries of these funds.

"This is incredibly bad news and the wording is utterly hopeless. This research funding has been absolutely vital to the Art Museum of Estonia in recent years, supporting virtually all the more substantial parts of our exhibition and publication programs. Now we're supposed to maneuver our way back under the umbrella of universities and convince them that exhibitions and creative research also count as research," Kumu Director Kadi Polli wrote on social media.

Mariann Raisma, director of the University of Tartu Museum, is also unhappy with the plan but remains hopeful that an exception will be made for the Ministry of Culture's area of responsibility when research funding is allocated.

"I still very much hope that this decision is not final. We have a regular meeting of the Museum Council coming up at the end of the month where we will meet with the minister of culture and I sincerely hope that there is still some way to reverse this decision," Raisma told ERR.

According to Raisma, the regulation's entry into force would be very bad news for Estonian museums, which fear that this much-needed funding will effectively disappear for them in the future. One major concern is that the new funding scheme sets a relatively high minimum grant of €150,000 per year for projects lasting two to four years, while museums need grants roughly one-tenth that size.

"Another thing I would highlight about this funding, which was particularly good, is that the amounts awarded were not very large. We weren't distributing hundreds of thousands of euros; instead, the grants made it possible to carry out smaller projects. That suits museums particularly well. Of course, the total amount of funding wasn't very large either, but it has certainly been extremely important for museums," Raisma told ERR.

"We carried out several very important research projects that enabled museums and research institutions to work together on topics for which funding would otherwise not have been available," Raisma said.

Ministry adviser: We'll lose flexibility and some projects will be discontinued

Viivian Jõemets, research adviser at the Ministry of Culture, is also concerned about several aspects of the new funding allocation system. She likewise noted that the program requires projects that are too large for the cultural sector's current capacity.

"The annual budget of €150,000 per project required under the new rules — amounting to at least €300,000 over two years — is unreasonably large for a museum. Current projects at our museums with nationwide responsibilities and research obligations, as well as the National Library, range from €40,000 to €70,000, depending on whether it is a large or small museum," Jõemets said.

According to Jõemets, building research capacity on this scale takes time and cannot be accomplished in a single year. "In the cultural sector, it is simply not possible to immediately develop projects with budgets this large in several important research areas," she added.

"Another concern is that the Ministry of Culture's total sector-specific research funding amounts to approximately €800,000. If we distribute it among smaller groups, each museum can develop something — activities take place and progress is made. But if we allocate very large sums to just three projects across our entire area of responsibility, what happens to all the other important areas of research?" Jõemets asked.

"What will happen to the research areas we have developed so far, such as efforts to advance research at the Art Museum of Estonia and the study of musical heritage? Under the strategic research regulation, it is unclear how we can continue developing our fields in these circumstances," she added.

Jõemets noted that other questions also remain unanswered. For example, if no applications are submitted for a particular research area simply because there are no potential applicants, it is unclear what will happen to that funding within the Ministry of Education and Research's budget.

"But if those funds remained in the Ministry of Culture's budget, we could flexibly reallocate them to other important activities," she added.

Jõemets emphasized that the government's decision to channel sector-specific research funding through the strategic research program affects all ministries and that the Ministry of Culture was granted a one-year extension compared with the others.

"I hope that in the near future there will be an assessment of the successes and shortcomings of the reform of sector-specific research funding, weighing its advantages and disadvantages. Perhaps a new government will want to revisit this decision. For now, however, transferring sector-specific research funding from the Ministry of Culture's budget to that of the Ministry of Education and Research remains the current government's decision," Jõemets said.

Jõemets does not have to worry about losing her position.

"My position at the Ministry of Culture will not be eliminated as part of this reform. Even now, funding rounds for the Ministry of Culture's research programs are administered by the Estonian Research Council under regulations issued by the minister of culture and there will be no significant change in that regard. The only change concerns where and how flexibly we can allocate sector-specific research funding and we will have to operate under a regulation issued by the minister of education and research," she said.

"Not all of the Ministry of Culture's current research activities will be able to continue under this regulation," Jõemets concluded.

World.title: Estonia plans to bring back its blue passports from 2030
World.content:
The Interior Ministry plans to redesign Estonian passports and add new security features, with blue covers returning for citizen passports from 2030.

Security updates come sooner than that — those on "gray passport"-holders documents in January 2027, with those found on citizens' passports to follow in July. Existing passports remain valid until they expire.

The blue passport covers had been in use following the restoration of independence in 1991, but with accession to the EU in 2004 the familiar burgundy colored covers – an EU recommendation but not mandatory – came in.

Interior Minister Igor Taro (Eesti 200) said the idea of changing the cover color came up while preparing the updated passport.

"We had to review the design of the entire new generation of Estonian passports, and from there came the idea that, since the Estonian passport is a representative link between the state and its citizen in international communication and the main identity document when traveling, its visual form should also reflect the colors of the Estonian state," Taro told ERR.

Blue covers were first used on Estonian passports during the interwar period, when Estonia was first an independent state.

The security updates include a boulder-shaped, partly transparent window containing an oak-leaf-shaped chip antenna. The holder's signature image moves from the second page to the third.

Example of the new color scheme for Estonian passports over the burgundy EU-style cover currently in use. Source: ERR

Taro explained why the changes are being phased in rather than being done all at once:"This is because we have a so-called physical passport production contract valid until 2030. So that no additional cost or additional steps would need to be taken in connection with the color switch, it simply changes over naturally."

Personal data in the passport will not change, and applicants will not need to do anything extra. Existing passports remain valid until their original expiry date; the blue ones will enter circulation through natural renewal.

Opposition politicians: A cosmetic act ahead of elections

Some leading opposition politicians were critical of the changes.

Former interior minister Lauri Läänemets (SDE) said they were focusing on the wrong thing.

"Considering that we have to deal with preventing Russian hybrid attacks more and more, considering the challenges related to the staffing of the police and rescue services, considering the situation with migration, the interior minister's focus is in completely the wrong place," he told Postimees.

MEP Jüri Ratas (Isamaa), a former prime minister, said that while blue is a beautiful color and the EU's common color scheme is a recommendation rather than an obligation, the timing of dealing with passport color inevitably seems to him like pre-election distraction ahead of the Riigikogu election next March.

World.title: China protests Estonian politicians attending a Taiwanese event in Tallinn
World.content:
The Embassy of the People's Republic of China in Estonia submitted a formal diplomatic note to the Riigikogu over lawmakers' attendance at an event celebrating Taiwan's National Day in Tallinn.

In the note, the embassy expressed concern that Riigikogu members Marko Mihkelson (Reform), Peeter Tali (Eesti 200), Kristo Enn Vaga (Reform), Kalle Laanet (Reform), Jüri Jaanson (Reform), Riina Sikkut (SDE), Anti Poolamets (EKRE) and Evelin Poolamets (EKRE) attended a reception marking the National Day of the Republic of China (Taiwan) in Tallinn on September 29, organized by the Taipei Representative Office in Latvia.

The embassy recalled that Estonia has made a clear commitment to recognize the government of the People's Republic of China as the sole legitimate government of China and Taiwan as an inalienable part of Chinese territory.

"The government of the Republic of Estonia has undertaken not to establish formal or official relations with Taiwan in any form," the Chinese Embassy said.

"Members of the Riigikogu are officials of an Estonian state institution. The attendance of the aforementioned Riigikogu members at the 'reception' can be regarded as a form of official interaction with Taiwan, which violates the commitments made and undermines China's sovereignty and territorial integrity," the note said.

The embassy called on the Riigikogu members in question to adhere to the one-China principle and exercise caution in their words and actions concerning Taiwan to avoid further damage to bilateral relations.

The Chinese Embassy has also sent diplomatic notes in previous years over Riigikogu members' contacts with Taiwan. The most recent such note was sent last summer, following a visit to Taiwan by the Riigikogu's Estonia-Taiwan Parliamentary Friendship Group.

The parliamentary group plans to continue attending events

According to Kristo Enn Vaga, chairman of the Riigikogu Estonia-Taiwan Parliamentary Friendship Group, it has become something of a tradition for the Chinese Embassy to send diplomatic notes whenever the group attends Taiwan-related events.

"When communist China writes that I or other Riigikogu members are doing something wrong, I take it as a compliment because it must mean I'm doing something right," Vaga said.

He noted that although Estonia has diplomatic relations with China, no foreign country can dictate what members of the Riigikogu may or may not do.

"Estonia does not recognize Taiwan as a state and there are no plans to change that. But from a pragmatic perspective, we see Taiwan, with the world's fastest-growing economy, as a potential partner," Vaga said.

Vaga emphasized that Estonia and Taiwan have cooperated on several projects. For example, the Taiwanese government has made financial contributions in cooperation with Estonia to support Ukraine.

"Thanks to these donations, a family home was opened in Zhytomyr Oblast at the end of the summer. It was built entirely with funding from the Taiwanese government and the project was carried out by ESTDEV, the Estonian government agency responsible for humanitarian aid."

According to Vaga, economic cooperation with China is being scaled back.

"This has also been highlighted in the Estonian Foreign Intelligence Service's annual reports, which say that reducing dependence on China would be advisable, particularly in the technology sector, as it could become a security threat. Even now, the use of Chinese technology in certain critical sectors may pose a security threat to Estonia," Vaga said.

The Estonia-Taiwan Parliamentary Friendship Group has no intention of yielding to Chinese criticism.

"I personally, along with many of my colleagues, intend to continue engaging with Taiwan just as actively as we have in the past and Chinese criticism or diplomatic notes certainly won't change that," Vaga said.
