Bago City held a groundbreaking ceremony on June 10 for phase 1 of the project, which has a capacity of 150 MW.

Both the Cauayan and Bago projects are onshore wind farms.

The last project scheduled for development is Haraya Wind Energy’s 1,215-MW Haraya IV-Negros Wind Project, which is expected to begin commercial operations in May 2030.

The DOE has yet to identify a specific site within the province for the project.

Rafael Coscolluela, a former Negros Occidental governor who now serves as a provincial consultant on energy and environmental issues, said the 11 projects would comprise both onshore and offshore wind farms.

Offshore development poses significant challenges, he said.

The DOE has yet to determine which cities and municipalities will host the onshore and offshore projects.

Coscolluela said proponents would face lengthy procedures to secure an environmental impact assessment (EIA) and an environmental compliance certificate (ECC) from the Department of Environment and Natural Resources.

The DOE Visayas office said energy projects with capitalization of at least P3.5 billion may qualify for a Certificate of Energy Project of National Significance (CEPNS), which can help streamline and expedite permitting.

On concerns about the projects’ proximity to the Guimaras Strait bird migration route, Coscolluela said an initial agreement with proponents called for painting turbine blades in bright colors to make them more visible to birds.

Coscolluela welcomed the wind farm developments, noting that Negros Occidental was declared coal-free on March 6, 2019, when then-governor Alfredo Marañón Jr. signed Executive Order No. 19-08.

The order has not been repealed and remains in effect, he said.

“The only hurdle is, can Negros Occidental benefit from the power to be produced by wind farms?” Coscolluela said.

He said the province’s three distribution utilities could be encouraged to prioritize contracts with solar and wind power producers as their existing power supply agreements (PSAs) expire.

Wind farms would also contribute to the province’s goal of gradually shifting from fossil fuels to renewable energy as part of its energy transition and decarbonization efforts, he said.

The national target is for renewable energy to account for 35% of the country’s energy mix by 2030, Coscolluela said.

“SecuRE Negros,” an energy program backed by PEDC, aims to contribute to that national goal, he added. – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: Plane with drugs not same aircraft used to fly Duterte to The Hague
World.content:
The tail number of the aircraft used to transport former president Rodrigo Duterte to The Hague does not match that of the jet carrying suspected illegal drugs from Laos, contrary to claims in social media posts

Claim: The post claimed that the plane found to be carrying illegal drugs from Laos is the same one used in bringing former president Rodrigo Duterte to The Hague.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: Amid recent reports of an aircraft from Laos allegedly carrying illegal drugs bound for the Philippines, a Facebook post by Tinood Politiko, which has garnered nearly 1,000 shares, claimed that the aircraft was the same one used to transport former president Rodrigo Duterte to The Hague, the Netherlands.

The post also used AI-generated photo showing an aircraft and Duterte with the overlay text: “SAME AIRPLANE LEARJET 55B N73GP” and “KATAPATAN BA ITO O MALALIM NA KONEKSYON?”

(Same airplane Learjet 55B N73GP. Is this right or there is a deeper connection?)

The facts: Upon verification, the jet plane flagged in Laos has a tail number showing “N73GP,”a 1986 model of Gates Learjet 55B, which is different from the plane that carried Duterte to The Hague, Netherlands on March 11, 2025.

Reports show that the plane used to to fly Duterte was Gulfstream G550 with tail number “RP-C5219” contrary to the fake post.

The jet plane with alleged illegal drugs was reported by a Malaysian media site, containing 521 kilograms of suspected shabu worth P3.1 million, and is allegedly bound for the Philippines.

One of the plane’s passengers is a Filipino citizen, who reportedly booked the aircraft supposedly to move vape products.

Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA) spokesperson Joseph Frederick Calulut shared on October 11 that full details have not been received from the Malaysian authorities.

Ongoing trial: Last October 13, Duterte attended a status conference at the International Criminal Court, prior to his full trial on November 30. The prosecution has presented further evidence against the former president and emphasized their relevance to the drug war campaign.

Duterte will be tried in connection with his crimes against humanity case resulting from his bloody war on drugs. — Axel Cainglet/Rappler.com

Axel John Cainglet is a political science student at the University of the Philippines Manila. An Aries Rufo Journalism Fellow for 2026, he is also the editor-in-chief of The Manila Collegian.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: China’s Shrinking Politburo Has a Diversity Problem
World.content:
China’s Communist Party chose 24 men for its Politburo in October 2022, all of them Han Chinese. It was the first Politburo without a woman in 25 years, and it included nobody from any of China’s 55 officially recognized ethnic minority groups. After four years, the group is even more exclusive.

In October 2025, the party expelled Central Military Commission Vice Chairman He Weidong. Former Xinjiang Party Secretary Ma Xingrui followed in July 2026, and top general Zhang Youxia last month. Official notices accused all three of serious violations; the notice on Zhang also alleged disloyalty, “faction-building” and a remarkably large number of bribes. Their removal leaves an active Politburo of 21—a concentration that tells us something important about power under Xi Jinping. Diversity exists farther down the political system, often through quotas and administrative rules. It disappears where the most consequential decisions are made.

A narrowing funnel

The contrast starts with the membership. At the end of 2025, women accounted for 31.5 percent of the Communist Party of China’s 101.3 million members, while ethnic minority members made up 7.8 percent. Among people admitted in 2025, women made up 46.5 percent and ethnic minorities 10.2 percent, according to the Central Organization Department.

Representation was also visible at the 20th Party Congress. Its 2,296 delegates included 619 women or 27 percent, and 264 ethnic minority members or 11.5 percent, drawn from 40 minority groups. Then the funnel thins. Only 11 of the 205 full members elected to the 20th Central Committee were women, while nine came from ethnic minority groups. At the Politburo level, both figures fell to zero.

This isn’t a simple story of too few qualified candidates. Shen Yiqin, an ethnic Bai woman, had served as Guizhou governor and provincial party secretary before the 2022 congress. She became a state councilor in 2023 and later president of the All-China Women’s Federation, yet never entered the Politburo. Her current brief covers civil affairs, human resources, social security, veterans, sports and liaison with the ethnic affairs bureaucracy. Those duties matter, but a state councilor ranks below the Politburo members.

Rules stop below the top

China has spent decades building representation requirements. A 2001 party directive called for at least one woman in provincial and prefectural party, government, legislature and political advisory leadership teams, as well as in county party and government teams. It gave early priority to women in education, culture, health, family planning, civil affairs and similar departments. The 2021-2030 national program for women calls for more women in local government leadership, more female principal officials and better access to training, rotation and key posts.

Yet many targets use the phrase “gradually increase” without a numerical floor for the Central Committee, Politburo or its Standing Committee. The result is presence without a reliable route to the top.

A peer-reviewed study of every prefectural mayor and party secretary serving between 2003 and 2020 found that women followed faster but more restricted careers. Female officials were younger and better educated, but more often came through the Women’s Federation, Communist Youth League and other less powerful portfolios. Men had greater access to finance, development and core party offices. Women held only 135 of 1,987 mayoral posts and 88 of 1,694 party secretary posts.

The study also found a revealing pattern: about 20 percent of women mayors were ethnic minority members, compared with 13 percent of male mayors. One appointment could therefore satisfy expectations for both gender and ethnic representation, while leaving more positions open for Han Chinese men. The evidence supports this “tandem quota” effect at the prefectural mayor level, but it doesn’t establish that top leaders consciously use the same calculation when selecting the Politburo.

Ethnic glass ceiling

Ethnic minority cadres face a parallel divide. China’s ethnic autonomy law reserves the head-of-government in autonomous areas for a member of the relevant minority, but the more powerful party secretary post has generally gone to a Han Chinese official. For decades, minorities held roughly 10 percent to 11 percent of full and alternate Central Committee seats, yet most sat in the alternate tier.

No ethnic minority official has ever joined the Politburo Standing Committee. A handful reached the wider Politburo: Zhuang general Wei Guoqing and Mongolian leader Ulanhu served there during the Mao and early reform years; Hui Liangyu later served in the body and became a vice premier. Those cases show the barrier isn’t formal, but they also highlight how rarely it has been crossed.

Under Xi, official ethnic policy increasingly centers on “forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation.” At the 2021 Central Ethnic Work Conference, Xi linked good cadre standards to firm support for centralized party leadership and commitment to his national community project. The policy stresses political unity, shared identity and security more than representation by distinct groups.

Perhaps this policy did not directly cause the all-Han Politburo. Public records don’t reveal the bargaining, vetting or rejected candidates behind elite appointments. Still, the roster fits a system where minority identity can warrant representation in congresses and autonomous governments but offers little access to the center.

Diversity and decision quality

An all-male, all-Han Chinese Politburo doesn’t mean every member thinks alike. Nor does adding women or minority officials guarantee different policies. Officials who rise through the same selection system may share its priorities. But there is evidence that representation can affect what institutions do. Women held about one-fifth of the seats in China’s 12th National People’s Congress but sponsored 44 percent of legislative bill proposals and more than half of proposals concerning women’s rights and interests. That finding comes from the first systematic study of female legislators’ behaviour in the national legislature.

The useful question isn’t whether one woman or minority official would transform policy but whether the leadership is drawing on the country’s full pool of political experience. The body, after all, makes decisions on birthrates, employment, Xinjiang, Tibet and social welfare.

The practical tests are clear. Party authorities could publish measurable targets for women and ethnic minority officials at each rung of the promotion ladder, report compliance and place more candidates in finance, security, organization and provincial party secretary jobs that feed Politburo selection. They could also stop treating one minority woman as sufficient evidence that two representation goals have been met.

Watch the 21st Party Congress, expected in 2027. Count who enters the full Central Committee, who receives powerful provincial and central portfolios, and who reaches the Politburo. Speeches about equality are easy to issue. Twenty-one occupied seats provide the harder evidence.

Chandu Doddi is an Assistant Professor at the Centre for Chinese Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi.

World.title: New ID Rules Tighten Regime’s Grip on Migrant Remittances From Thailand
World.content:
Desperate for revenue, the Min Aung Hlaing regime is again using the Certificate of Identity (CI) process to extract money from undocumented Myanmar migrants in Thailand, forcing them to shoulder even greater financial hardship.

The regime recently added new rules to the CI process, requiring migrants to use the regime’s official channels for 25 percent of their remittances before applying for the certificate.

The CI is a temporary document intermittently issued by Myanmar that serves as an alternative to a passport for migrant workers in Thailand, allowing them to secure a legal work permit.

Regime Labor Minister Maung Myint told Parliament on Thursday that five centers issuing CIs started operating on Wednesday in Thailand’s Samut Sakhon, Samut Prakan, Chiang Mai, Chon Buri and Surat Thani.

The new order requires workers to provide proof of remitting 6,000 baht (about US$180) through official channels, equivalent to 25 percent of three months’ wages calculated on a fixed monthly salary of 8,000 baht, as well as proof of payment of 2 percent income tax. Newly appointed regime Labor Minister Maung Myint said remittances are a matter of “national interest,” and workers should consider them “a donation” to the country.

The move is part of the regime’s longstanding effort to extract foreign currency from overseas workers, including through the income tax and mandatory 25-percent remittance rule introduced in 2023.

Groups assisting migrant workers said the new requirements would complicate the employment process, potentially leading to higher costs for workers.

“Many workers do not have stable jobs,” a member of a migrant assistance group told The Irrawaddy. “How can they transfer the money, when they are already struggling with the cost?”

Complicating the process by requiring more documents would create space for service providers to charge more money, he said.

The CI application costs around 3,600 baht, but workers must rely on service providers or agents, who normally charge between 7,000 and 15,000 baht, including service fees, though precise costs under the latest rules remain unclear.

A migrant worker in Thailand told The Irrawaddy that the agent who managed his CI application process charged around 15,000 baht.

The amount is paid in installments to his employer through deductions from his monthly wages, reducing the amount he could send home.

“I send less money to my family. Everyone around me has to do the same thing,” he said.

Meanwhile, service providers said families of some workers in Myanmar do not have access to the banking system, making it more difficult to obtain proof of remittance transfers.

“Some workers’ families live in remote areas. It is not easy for them to withdraw the money,” a service provider told The Irrawaddy. He added that the regime was also likely to introduce stricter checks on applicants and their supporting documents.

U Set Aung, an economist and former deputy minister of planning and finance under the ousted civilian government led by Aung San Suu Kyi, wrote on his Facebook page on Thursday that low-wage Myanmar workers in Thailand were struggling to cover their living expenses and could not afford to remit 25 percent of their wages.

“The amount workers send home should be their own decision,” he said.

He added that the policy was designed solely to benefit the regime, rather than to support families and formal banking use.

“When remittances are converted at exchange rates below prevailing market rates, workers and their families suffer additional financial losses,” he said. “It raises serious concerns about freedom of movement, the right to pursue a livelihood, and fundamental labor rights.”

As the Myanmar regime steps up efforts to squeeze remittances from overseas workers, workers in Thailand are a prime target. Thailand hosted nearly 3 million Myanmar workers as of November 2025, according to official Thai figures. But the real number is likely to be much higher as many workers are undocumented.

Labor Minister Maung Myint said on Thursday that remittances from Myanmar migrant workers abroad totaled $5.6 billion in 2025. Experts say the regime’s remittance controls have cut a vital financial lifeline for the Myanmar population, which has been badly affected by conflict and economic collapse triggered by the 2021 coup that brought the regime to power.

World.title: Kyat Slides Again as Regime Wins Approval for 2.1 Trillion-Kyat Borrowing Plan
World.content:
The kyat lost value again this week after the regime-backed parliament on Wednesday approved borrowing of up to 2.1 trillion kyats (approximately US$1 billion at the fixed official rate) for a junta struggling with ballooning defense costs.

The kyat has weakened drastically since the 2021 coup plunged Myanmar into a dollar crisis, with economic sanctions, the withdrawal of foreign investment, declining exports and fighting in border trade zones taking a toll on the regime’s coffers.

On Wednesday, the rubber-stamp parliament approved the regime’s proposal to “borrow” up to 2.1 trillion kyats from the Central Bank of Myanmar to fill its budget deficit for fiscal year 2026-27. The legislature has already approved the regime’s plan to borrow money from major arms supplier Belarus, which will be used to import goods from Minsk.

Prior to Wednesday’s parliamentary approval, the regime had already raised nearly 14 trillion kyats through multiple treasury bill and bond auctions to finance its budget deficit for fiscal year 2026–27, according to Central Bank Deputy Governor Thet Htun Aung. He admitted the regime had also relied on treasury bond issuances and borrowing from the Central Bank to address budget shortfalls in previous years.

Analysts warn that borrowing from the Central Bank will accelerate inflation and the kyat’s depreciation. Currency traders report the dollar rose to 4,670 kyats in the unofficial market on Thursday, up from 4,450 kyats earlier this month, while the baht has risen from 129 to 139 kyats. Before the coup, the kyat was trading at less than 1,300 to the dollar.

“This surge is linked to the new loans. The market jumped from 4,400 to nearly 4,700 within days. Whether it will continue to increase, or decline—or if the regime will make arrests—remains to be seen,” one trader told The Irrawaddy. The regime has repeatedly arrested foreign exchange traders during currency spikes, accusing them of speculation and market manipulation.

The loan proposal has triggered fears that the revenue-deprived regime will simply print more banknotes to address the shortfall.

Deputy Finance and Revenue Minister Kyaw Htin explained that the regime has other plans to address the shortfall, apart from borrowing money. “We are working to reduce reliance on Central Bank financing to boost state revenue. We are developing taxation policies,” he told the parliament.

Recently, the regime has escalated its efforts to enforce remittance rules requiring Myanmar migrant workers to send at least 25 percent of their salaries back home at the official exchange rate of 2,100 kyats per dollar.

Officially, the Central Bank pegs the dollar at 2,100 kyats, while the trading rate between banks is 3,660 kyats and the market rate currently hovers at around 4,670 kyats. Meanwhile, the regime has restricted imports to reduce dollar spending, which has proved counterproductive for a war-ravaged economy heavily reliant on imports ranging from cooking oil and pharmaceuticals to fuel and fertilizer.

Rising dollar rates are expected to push up the cost of imported fuel, medicines, food, consumer goods and machinery, with knock-on effects for transport and production costs. Domestic industries face mounting pressure as expenses rise.

Meanwhile, the Belarus loan package, arranged through the Development Bank of the Republic of Belarus (DBRB) and Belinvestbank JSC, carries interest rates of between 2.25 and 9.33 percent. The loans will be used to import goods including capital goods from Minsk, but the total amount was not revealed.

Myanmar can receive loans in five currencies—the dollar, euro, Russian ruble, Belarusian ruble and Chinese yuan—said Kyaw Htin, who admitted exchange rate fluctuations would affect the amount of money Myanmar will actually receive.

Unlike concessional loans from Japan’s aid agency JICA—which carry a 40‑year repayment term at just 0.01 percent interest—analysts note that the Belarusian loan is a “tied” arrangement, warning the regime is locking itself into costly debt that will further deepen Myanmar’s economic crisis.

International organizations and Japan suspended development aid to Myanmar following the coup.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Launches ‘ASEAN Affairs’ Panel to Clinch Full Reintegration
World.content:
Myanmar coup leader Min Aung Hlaing has formed a new ASEAN Affairs Committee to “regain the country’s original role and rights” in the regional bloc, which continues to bar his regime from summits months after it rebranded as an “elected” government.

The committee’s inaugural meeting on Tuesday was chaired by Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe, with representatives from the President’s Office and ministries of Defense, Home Affairs, Information, and Social Welfare also in attendance.

While the Foreign Ministry normally serves as the focal point for international relations, the new body includes the defense and home affairs ministries, underscoring the junta’s bid to institutionalize its efforts to reintegrate into the regional bloc.

Reintegration is crucial for coup leader Min Aung Hlaing, who is seeking international legitimacy after installing himself as president in April following an election widely denounced as a sham by Western nations and rights groups.

While individual members including Thailand have recognized Min Aung Hlaing’s presidency, ASEAN as a whole remains divided, prompting continuous regime demands for full integration as a “legitimate elected government.”

Tin Maung Swe told the meeting that Myanmar had suffered “discriminatory treatment” since 2021, when ASEAN excluded Min Aung Hlaing from top-level meetings for ignoring its Five‑Point Consensus agreed in Jakarta. The bloc’s peace plan calls for an immediate end to violence, dialogue among all parties, and humanitarian access—conditions the junta has refused to meet.

Tuesday’s meeting came just weeks ahead of the next ASEAN Summit in Manila. Since assuming the presidency, Min Aung Hlaing has made official visits to five bloc members, securing support for Myanmar’s reintegration from Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam, and Malaysia. Analysts say the committee was formed in an effort to win over the remaining five members.

“The regime is attempting to win a majority consensus through bilateral engagement with individual member states,” said political analyst Htin Kyaw Aye.

“The committee is designed for this purpose. But it remains difficult for ASEAN to allow Myanmar’s return while there is no visible progress on the Five-Point Consensus.”

Since assuming office in April, the pseudo-civilian regime has dismissed the Five-Point Consensus as a non-binding declaration, before formally rejecting the peace deal through its rubber-stamp parliament.

The regime said Tuesday’s meeting tabled “Myanmar‑led approaches” to restore the country’s role in ASEAN—a statement reiterating defiance of the Five-Point Consensus spearheaded by an ongoing military campaign that has killed over 8,500 civilians since the coup.

While rights groups warn that countries hosting Min Aung Hlaing risk legitimizing a regime still committing atrocities, others have different views after more than five years of isolation has delivered no results.

Former Japanese prime minister Fumio Kishida told Nikkei Asia on October 12 that Japan should help Myanmar rejoin ASEAN. Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. recently hailed Min Aung Hlaing’s visits to fellow ASEAN countries as part of a “new approach” to resolving the country’s crisis. Meanwhile, Brunei and Indonesia plan to invite Min Aung Hlaing for official visits, according to junta spokeswoman Khaing Khaing Soe, leaving only Timor-Leste and Singapore standing firm against the regime.

As the bloc’s newest member, Timor-Leste has backed Myanmar’s pro-democracy movement while initiating legal action against the military regime in February over alleged war crimes. Meanwhile Singapore, which will take over the rotating chairmanship at year-end, recently affirmed that there can be “no political representation” for Myanmar at ASEAN meets.

Mon Mon Myat, a lecturer in the Department of Peace Studies at Thailand’s Payap University, said: “It appears that the Philippines wants to reintegrate Myanmar into the bloc before Singapore takes the chair next year. ASEAN countries that are stepping up their diplomatic engagement with Myanmar regime must exercise extra caution to avoid legitimizing war criminals.”

She added that ASEAN must set clear rules for accountability if the regime refuses to obey the Five-Point Consensus.

“Otherwise, the regime may secure full legitimacy as a leader of an ASEAN nation.”

World.title: Myanmar Regime Denies Drafting College Students Into Army
World.content:
Myanmar’s military regime has denied reports that university students must suspend their studies for two years to serve in the army, but fears persist among students and parents.

Earlier this month, a panic broke out when rumors said that young men selected in conscription lotteries must serve in the army even if they are registered university students, and those drawing numbers under 100 would be called up within three months.

Conscripts are selected randomly at ward levels by drawing lots from a box. Those with smaller numbers are drafted first, and those with larger numbers later.

In Mandalay, even high school students who just turned 18 were forced to participate in the conscription lottery last month, according to parents.

“High school students were also told to draw lots. I drew on my son’s behalf and got a large number, over 500,” said a mother from Mandalay. “But we are still really scared because of reports that university students would be called up.”

In denying the rumors, the regime’s central conscription committee this week cited Article 15 (a)(3) of the Conscription Law, which allows deferment for students in education. It said official newspapers “repeatedly stressed this point.”

But concerns persist as township administrative offices in regime-controlled areas including major cities like Naypyitaw, Yangon and Mandalay have called in lists of university and high school students, apparently separating out those with spectacles, health problems, disabilities or on long‑term medication.

In August, the regime centralized the draft, with regional and district authorities taking over management from township and lower-level conscription offices. Since early September, a new wave of lotteries have been held in wards and villages across Mandalay but not yet in Yangon.

“Ward offices summon us according to lists from the Population Department,” one young man said. “Everyone aged 18 to 35 including students must draw. In our ward alone, over 40 students were included. One 12th grader drew a number under 100, but officials said high school students would be granted temporary deferment.”

Previously, families with eligible young men could pay a monthly fee to the authorities for deferment, in theory so someone else could be paid to take their place. But the regime abolished the substitution fee in September, declaring that all those selected must serve in order of their lottery numbers.

The department also denied reports that ward offices are confiscating ID cards and smart cards of selected youths, requiring monthly check‑ins, and demanding parents sign pledges to prevent their sons’ escape.

A Mandalay conscription official told The Irrawaddy that the process strictly follows laws and regulations.

“Students who can prove they are genuinely enrolled, with proper documents and forms, are granted temporary deferment,” the official said.

According to the 2019 census, nearly 13 million people are eligible for conscription under the Conscription Law—6.3 million men and 7.7 million women. So far, about 140,000 men have been called up by the regime, assuming that around 5,000 recruits are drafted per batch.

When the long-dormant Conscription Law was revived in 2024, it forced a mass exodus of young people, and the regime has since been struggling to meet its quotas despite barring eligible men from working abroad and even snatching young men from streets and homes.

In Yangon, an eerie quiet descends after 8 p.m. as regime-backed thugs prowl the streets on the hunt for eligible young men to abduct, a practice that has swiftly degenerated into a black economy of kidnappings for ransom.

World.title: Myanmar’s Opposition Leadership Is Holding Back the Resistance
World.content:
Myanmar’s resistance coalition has lost the political and diplomatic war but not the military campaign. The main reason lies less in the junta’s strength than in what I call an “insurgency-industrial complex” that has grown around the opposition.

This international ecosystem of diaspora communities, exiles, dissidents, donors, rights-based organizations and Western governments, with the National Unity Government (NUG) at its center outside the country, is geared towards fighting a military dictatorship rather than defeating it and governing Myanmar in a different way.

Unless the resistance regroups around leaders inside the country and mounts a convincing battlefield turnaround, perhaps led by drone warfare, Min Aung Hlaing will keep consolidating his grip even as the fighting goes on.

It is critical to separate Myanmar’s two wars. After staging elections last December and January, Min Aung Hlaing has reinvented himself as a pseudo-civilian president. Since assuming the presidency in April, he has made eight foreign trips. China, India and Russia have received him, as have four Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) member states in three months, namely Laos in July, Thailand in August, Vietnam and Cambodia in September, and this month in Malaysia.

Counting Myanmar itself, nearly half of ASEAN now deals with him at the top level. Each visit lowers the diplomatic cost of the next. ASEAN, which has kept him out of its leaders’ summits since the 2021 coup, is now under pressure to readmit him. Once in motion, political engagement generates its own momentum towards normalization and eventual recognition. The political war more or less has been lost.

The military war, on the other hand, is not lost. The armed forces do not control most of the country. Ethnic armed organizations remain strong and continue to take the fight to the military in borderland states, while People’s Defense Force (PDF) units are still holding on in the central dry zone. Neither side has clearly won on the battlefield.

Yet the resistance had its chance and missed it. By mid-2024, resistance forces held more than half of Myanmar’s territory. The military was pinned down in Yangon, Mandalay and Naypyitaw and appeared close to being toppled. But the coalition of ethnic armies, PDFs and the NUG lacked the cohesion and bold thrust to take over. Its battlefield tenacity was not matched by political capability.

When Beijing saw that the resistance did not have what it took to seize control, it backed the junta, leaned on the ethnic armies along its border to stand down, and endorsed the election roadmap. The tide turned, and here we are.

Why did the resistance falter when it mattered most? The NUG has been weak and ineffective, but the deeper reason is structural. Donations, aid and grants flow into the insurgency-industrial complex.

These funds sustain offices, salaries, jobs, scholarships, residencies abroad and a way of life. Its currency is opposition and its output is advocacy. A resistance victory would end its funding model and require some of its leaders to return home to govern a broken country of 55 million people, with all the risks that entails.

Put this way, the insurgency complex almost needs a military dictatorship to fight against. For many in the diaspora and among critics who live outside the country, it is not about winning and taking over the country but about keeping a four-decade struggle going. To be sure, many exiles and dissidents are authentic and sincere and have paid a heavy personal price.

At issue are incentives, not intentions. And these incentives work squarely in Min Aung Hlaing’s favor. An opposition led from abroad keeps the contest outward-facing and predictable, and it allows the regime to portray its enemies as foreign-funded “terrorists” detached from the people.

It does not help that global standards on human rights and democracy have sagged, and international aid has been slashed systematically, from the dismantling of American aid programs to deep cuts by the United Kingdom and European donors. The moral pressure that once isolated Myanmar’s generals has weakened.

The only way to change this narrative and shift direction is a resistance counteroffensive, led mainly by the PDF and the ethnic armies still willing to topple the regime. The battlefield is where the resistance still holds cards, and the decisive weapon is the first-person-view (FPV) drone. FPV drones have already allowed small, motivated units to hit armor, outposts and supply lines. Scaled up and coordinated, a drone-led campaign against strategic towns and corridors could deliver the key victories needed to convince Beijing and ASEAN that Min Aung Hlaing is not a safe bet for them because he cannot control the country in the long run.

But a counteroffensive requires a different leadership. The resistance needs to regroup away from the NUG and towards those who are actually fighting inside the country. The Arakan Army, which now controls most of Rakhine State, has been the most successful fighting force in the civil war. Its commander-in-chief, Major General Tun Myat Naing, has the battlefield record and standing to serve as the resistance’s overall military commander. Meanwhile, PDF commanders must be brought into the top leadership, not treated as foot soldiers for exiled politicians.

Their fighters came of age during the decade of opening from 2011 to 2021, with mobile phones, jobs, travel, foreign investment and elections that counted. They want that country back. Their objective is to retake Myanmar, while the insurgency-industrial complex’s goal is to oppose the regime and keep fighting the military dictatorship to no end.

A leadership rooted inside the country would also be the kind of interlocutor that Beijing and ASEAN could take seriously, one with control over territory and troops rather than offices and press releases. That is precisely what was missing in mid-2024.

Unless there is a clear and convincing military turnaround in the resistance’s favor that is accompanied by a more capable leadership from inside the country, Min Aung Hlaing will continue to consolidate politically and diplomatically. Neighbors and major powers will deal with whoever looks set to last—right now that is Min Aung Hlaing.

Until the fighters inside lead the leaders outside, the resistance may win more battles but will keep losing the regional and international politics of the civil war.

Thitinan Pongsudhirak is a professor of comparative and international politics at Chulalongkorn University’s Faculty Of Political Science and a non-resident associate with the Southeast Asia Centre at the London School of Economics.

This article first appeared in the Bangkok Post.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Escalates Assault on Free Press Critical of Its Rule
World.content:
Myanmar’s military regime has intensified its threats against independent media critical of its rule, vowing to eliminate outlets and journalists regardless of their location.

An editorial in the junta’s mouthpiece Kyemon on Monday urged the “elimination of any destructive element inside or outside the country,” echoing the Home Affairs Ministry’s threats last week.

On October 6, Deputy Home Affairs Minister Major‑General Min Thu told parliament the regime has opened cases against independent media outlets The Irrawaddy, Mizzima, DVB, Myanmar Now, and Khit Thit under the Counter‑Terrorism Law, Telecommunications Law, and Penal Code. He claimed the regime was coordinating with international law enforcement including Interpol and Aseanapol to detain staff working for these organizations.

Interpol bans any interventions on political grounds while Aseanapol’s focus is limited to transnational crimes.

The Kyemon editorial stated that anyone inside or outside the country who “disrupts peace, stability, and development, undermines national sovereignty, prestige, and unity, or obstructs the administrative mechanism must be eliminated.”

Junta leader Min Aung Hlaing branded outlets reporting his military’s mass-killing of civilians as “nation‑destroying media” during his October 13 trip to Dawei, claiming they were misleading the public. “Those outlets do not want to see national development,” said the president, whose February 2021 coup plunged the country into turmoil.

The putsch was followed by a brutal crackdown, targeting not only peaceful protesters but also media documenting the military’s abuses. The regime revoked licenses, raided offices, and arrested scores of journalists, forcing independent outlets into exile. After establishing itself as one of the world’s worst jailers of journalists, it is now seeking to target exiled media.

Independent media groups emphasize that journalism is not a crime and note that Interpol does not act on political requests. “Interpol does not intervene in political or religious cases. Only genuine criminal matters are considered,” said Toe Zaw Latt, secretary of the Independent Press Council of Myanmar. He added that while the regime may attempt to link reporting with criminal activities, such requests are weeded out by Interpol. “So, there is no need to worry, but we should still monitor the situation carefully.”

Lower House Speaker Khin Yi—who as former dictator Than Shwe’s police chief led deadly crackdowns on pro-democracy demonstrators—has advised the Home Affairs Ministry that criminal cases must be concocted to pursue arrests abroad.

The junta’s warning comes as its propaganda apparatus struggles to discredit the resistance movement while concealing its own war crimes. Circulation of regime newspapers has sharply declined since the coup, and junta news outlets have been barred from multiple social media platforms.

A Yangon street vendor said demand for state‑owned newspapers is practically non-existent, except for once a month when lottery results are printed.

The junta’s threats come as it faces ongoing international isolation. ASEAN has barred Min Aung Hlaing from summits since the coup for failing to implement its peace plan, while he is wanted on an international arrest warrant issued by Argentina over the Rohingya genocide. Rights groups have repeatedly called on Interpol to arrest the coup leader during his overseas trips.

On Wednesday, the International Federation of Journalists (IFJ) and its affiliate, the Exiled Myanmar Journalists Network (Exiled-MJN), condemned the regime’s threats as a blatant abuse of international policing mechanisms.

“Myanmar’s junta will stop at nothing to try to legitimize itself in the world’s eyes and to expand its repression against the brave and determined media and journalists who continue to expose its gross violations against its own people,” IFJ stated.

According to MJN records, at least seven journalists have been killed by the regime since the coup. The International Centre for Not-for-Profit Law has documented at least 227 journalists detained by the junta, with at least 20 still in jail.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Forces Burn Church in Bhamo, KIA Says
World.content:
Myanmar military forces burned a Christian church near Bhamo on Monday evening as the regime continues its campaign to recapture the Kachin State town, according to Colonel Naw Bu, a spokesperson for the Kachin Independence Army (KIA).

“They [the regime] burned a Christian church in Three Mile Village on the way to Momauk,” Naw Bu told The Irrawaddy. “There have been periodic clashes in that area.”

He added that there has been frequent fighting between regime troops and KIA-led forces around Light Infantry Battalion 47 and near Bhamo University.

The KIA and its allies launched an attack on Bhamo in late 2024 and captured the majority of the town in 2025. This year, however, it has lost some ground there to the regime, which has been reinforcing its troops in preparation for a counteroffensive.

Naw Bu claimed resistance groups still control a large part of the town. The Irrawaddy could not independently verify the claim.

Citing residents, local media reported that the arson attack on the Kachin Baptist Convention-run church followed heavy regime casualties in the face of fierce resistance defense.

Human rights activists condemned the torching of the church.

“This is a violation of freedom of religion; we condemn it,” Jacob from Kachin Human Rights Watch told The Irrawaddy. “The regime does not respect international laws and continues to violate them.”

He said the regime and allied militias have used religious sites for military purposes, carried out drone attacks on churches, and detained religious leaders. “Religious rights in Kachin State are being increasingly violated,” he said.

Mervyn Thomas, founder president of Church World Service, an international Christian human rights group, said the attack was a “grave crime” and a “clear violation” of international laws and freedom of belief, while calling on the international community to cut off the regime’s access to aviation fuel and military equipment.

In September, the regime-allied Shanni Nationalities Army used the compounds of a Baptist church and a Catholic church in Indaw as a military training ground and an office, sparking criticism from ethnic Kachin residents.

The regime and its allies conducted a suicide drone attack on another church in Mohnyin Township in October.

The regime’s attacks on places of worship do not discriminate by faith, however. Myanmar Witness in April said it documented over 300 airstrikes on religious sites, including churches, monasteries and mosques, between January 2024 and December 2025. Nearly 90 percent of them were conducted by the regime’s air force, with Sagaing Region and Shan State the worst-affected areas.

In August, 14 civilians were killed in Sagaing Region’s Myaung Township when the regime launched an airstrike on a Buddhist temple that was hosting around 100 people for a meditation retreat.

World.title: Kazakhstan Joins World Bank Initiative to Attract $20 Billion in Minerals Investment
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has become the first country in Central Asia to join the World Bank Group’s Metals and Minerals Compact, a partnership aimed at attracting around $20 billion in investment by 2031 and expanding the country’s mineral resource base and processing capacity.

The official accession ceremony took place on Oct. 16 on the sidelines of the Annual Meetings of the World Bank Group and the International Monetary Fund in Thailand. Kazakhstan was represented by Yerlan Galiyev, chairman of the board of the National Geological Service under the Ministry of Industry and Construction, reported the Prime Minister’s press service.

Developed by Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Industry and Construction, the Agency for Strategic Planning and Reforms, and the World Bank Group, the country compact establishes a framework for cooperation in the metals and minerals sector for 2026-2030. It brings together the World Bank Group’s financial, analytical and technical support to advance the country’s industrial and investment priorities.

The compact builds on Kazakhstan’s existing development strategies, including the National Development Plan through 2029, the Concept for the Development of the Geological Industry for 2023-2027, and the Comprehensive Plan for the Development of the Rare and Rare Earth Metals Industry for 2024-2028.

The targeted investment of approximately $20 billion by 2031 is expected to support the expansion of mineral exploration, the development of mining and processing facilities, the adoption of modern technologies and the construction of supporting infrastructure.

The partnership focuses on three areas.

The first is improving public policy and regulatory frameworks for the mining and metallurgical complex to strengthen transparency, regulatory predictability and the investment climate, while promoting international environmental and social standards.

The second involves developing geological exploration, infrastructure and workforce capacity. Priorities include digitizing geological data, improving energy and transport infrastructure, introducing advanced metal-processing technologies and training qualified specialists.

The third focuses on attracting private investment into mineral extraction and downstream processing. The World Bank Group will support investment projects through financial and guarantee instruments, with an emphasis on higher-value-added production and international investor participation.

“Kazakhstan is committed to the principles of responsible and sustainable development of the mineral resource sector. Cooperation with the World Bank Group supports the implementation of national priorities in raw material processing and the expansion of higher-value-added production,” said Minister of Industry and Construction Yersaiyn Nagaspayev.

He added that Kazakhstan expects the partnership to strengthen the sector’s competitiveness and resilience, diversify the economy and improve the use of the country’s natural resource potential.

Implementation of the compact is expected to promote deeper processing of raw materials, create new jobs and strengthen Kazakhstan’s position in global production chains.

World.title: Kazakhstan Calls for Restraint, Diplomacy to Prevent Further Escalation in Middle East
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan called on all parties in the Middle East to exercise maximum restraint and prioritize dialogue and diplomacy, reaffirming its support for a two-state solution and the need to prevent further escalation.

Kazakhstan’s position was presented by Permanent Representative to the United Nations Kairat Umarov during the UN Security Council’s quarterly open debate on the situation in the Middle East, including the Palestinian question, held at UN Headquarters under the Presidency of Greece, reported the Foreign Ministry’s press service on Oct. 16.

The meeting featured 70 speakers, with Ramiz Alakbarov, acting UN Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, delivering the main briefing.

In his statement, Umarov expressed concern over continued tensions in the Middle East and stressed the need for political and diplomatic settlement to conflicts and the prevention of further escalation.

Kazakhstan reaffirmed its principled support for the Two-State solution and the New York Declaration as a framework for concrete steps towards this objective. Particular emphasis was placed on unhindered humanitarian assistance, the protection of civilians and the recovery of Gaza, as well as the central role of the United Nations, including the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA).

Kazakhstan also expressed its readiness to make a practical contribution to the stabilization and recovery of Gaza, including through civilian reconstruction, food security and digitalization. In this context, partners were encouraged to utilize the potential of the Astana-based Islamic Organization for Food Security.

The statement also highlighted Kazakhstan’s intention to join the Abraham Accords, which are viewed as an additional platform to support the UN-led political process towards the Two-State solution.

Kazakhstan confirmed its readiness to continue constructive engagement in support of peace and stability in the Middle East.

World.title: Middle Corridor Could Add $58 Billion to Regional GDP by 2040, World Bank Says
World.content:
ASTANA – The Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor could increase the combined gross domestic product of countries along the route by 3.3% and generate around two million jobs by 2040 if governments invest in infrastructure and improve cross-border coordination, according to a World Bank report presented in Astana on Oct. 15.

“The Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor, also known as the Middle Corridor, is more than a transit route. It can help Central Asian countries connect with global markets, attract investment, diversify their economies and create business opportunities,” said Andrei Mikhnev, World Bank country manager for Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan.

Speaking at the New Silk Way business forum, Mikhnev noted that Central Asia’s strategic location between Europe and Asia creates opportunities, but geography alone is not enough to deliver economic benefits.

“The European Union has even nailed the term ‘Global Gateway,’ of which this transport corridor is an important part. But geography alone does not create opportunities. The challenge is to turn connectivity into economic value, and transit flows into broader development,” he said.

Countries along the corridor have invested in railways, roads, ports, logistics facilities and border crossings, while pursuing reforms to facilitate trade and strengthen regional cooperation

According to Mikhnev, further progress will depend on more closely coordinated operations, streamlined border procedures, digitalization and greater private sector participation.

Trade volumes expected to grow

Luis Blancas, World Bank’s senior transport and logistics specialist, presented the report’s findings, describing the corridor as a platform for private investment, job creation and economic growth.

He noted that the route offers distinct benefits depending on countries’ geographic locations and trade needs.

“For the five Central Asian countries, the corridor provides access to global markets and helps diversify trade routes. For the South Caucasus and Türkiye, it offers a more direct connection to Europe, Central Asia and East Asia. For China and Western Europe, it provides an alternative for containerized freight,” Blancas said.

The corridor is also complementary to other Eurasian trade routes, rather than necessarily competing with them, because each route has different costs, operating conditions and advantages for particular types of cargo.

According to the Middle Corridor Association, total freight volumes on the route grew at an average annual rate of 34% between 2021 and 2025. Containerized freight volumes increased by an average of 32% annually over the same period.

The World Bank projects that total freight volumes could rise from about 9 million metric tons in 2023 to nearly 24 million metric tons by 2040, even without additional infrastructure investment beyond projects and facilities in place at the end of 2025.

With further infrastructure investment, volumes could reach 32 million metric tons by 2040. Non-oil freight volumes could increase to about 16 million metric tons, approximately 4.5 times the 2023 level.

Without additional investment, the corridor could miss out on 33% of potential total freight volumes and nearly 90% of potential non-oil freight volumes, according to the report.

The report estimates that infrastructure investment could boost the combined GDP of corridor countries by 3.3%, equivalent to $58 billion at current prices, through increased imports and exports by 2040. The estimate does not include the potential impact of transit trade.

Infrastructure is not the only challenge

Blancas noted that although infrastructure investment remains important, the corridor’s main challenge is likely to be operational performance rather than a lack of physical capacity.

The World Bank identified 16 critical bottlenecks along the corridor, with an estimated cost of around $25 billion to address them. According to the report, 75% of the identified bottlenecks, accounting for 85% of the estimated investment cost, were being addressed.

“The remaining 25% of the projects have not yet entered the implementation phase but are firmly included in government plans and are expected to proceed,” Blancas said.

Investments have already improved capacity on key sections of the network. In Kazakhstan, for example, the double-tracking of the Dostyk-Moiynty railway line reduced its estimated capacity utilization from 100% in 2023 to about 40%, according to the report.

However, infrastructure improvements alone will not necessarily make the corridor competitive with alternative routes for containerized freight between China and Europe.

For a shipment from Chongqing, China, to Budapest, Hungary, average delivery times on the Middle Corridor currently range from 47 to 50 days, compared with about 45 days by sea and 18 days via the Northern Corridor, according to the World Bank’s analysis.

Blancas highlighted that additional infrastructure investment could reduce delivery times on the fastest Middle Corridor route to around 26-27 days by 2040, while the Northern Corridor could offer delivery in around 19 days.

“According to our modeling projections, combining infrastructure investment with improvements in trade facilitation, service delivery and cross-border collaboration would allow the fastest route along the Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor to close the performance gap with the Northern Corridor by 2040,” he said.

Call for closer regional cooperation

The report proposes a framework called the TCTC Assessment and Response Structure, or TARS, to improve cross-border cooperation. It includes a shared system for measuring corridor performance, a public-private advisory committee and a platform for intergovernmental decision-making.

Blancas said inconsistent data and fragmented coordination make it difficult for governments and businesses to plan effectively. A common evidence base would help participating countries identify bottlenecks, assess progress and coordinate investment decisions.

The report also calls for simplifying transport documentation.

“Moving a container between China and Europe along the corridor currently requires around 15 documents, many of which contain overlapping information,” Blancas said.

The World Bank proposes introducing a single digital Transport, Transit and Trade document, known as T3, alongside a decentralized digital system that would allow national platforms to exchange information while preserving data sovereignty.

Another recommendation is to establish a joint railway and shipping undertaking involving the corridor’s main railway operators and shipping lines. The initiative could improve coordination across rail and maritime segments and support more reliable, time-specific freight services.

World.title: Satellite Solutions for Food Security
World.content:
Global food security faces a number of pressures, including conflict, climate change, pollution and overexploitation. North and Central Asia is a region at risk, with human activity contributing to significant levels of desertification in drylands and other fragile biomes. Agriculture is a major source of employment in the region, accounting for more than 40 per cent of the working population in Tajikistan, more than 30 per cent in Azerbaijan and Georgia and more than 20 per cent in Armenia, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan. Agriculture underpins the livelihoods of rural populations, which are often among the poorest sectors of society.

With greater efficiency and optimization, the agricultural sector can save water and resources, increase yields and adapt to new climatic realities. That kind of innovation is the theme of this year’s World Food Day (16 October) “Innovate today. Nourish tomorrow.” Across North and Central Asia, geospatial technology is already helping both farmers and policymakers. Making the most of it, however, depends as much on skills and on institutions working together as on the technology itself.

Geospatial technology can support farmers in decision-making processes through online platforms and applications. In Kazakhstan, the application AgroData integrates data from 226 agrometeorological stations, giving farmers real-time information on weather, soil moisture and crop health. Farmer App in Azerbaijan and KosmosAgro in the Russian Federation offer similar tools, from monitoring vegetation growth to estimating yields and spotting pests.

Kyrgyzstan has partnered with the World Food Programme in a project that equipped around 5,000 rural community members and farmers to interpret and apply climate information from new portable equipment deployed across 13 sites. Kyrgyzstan is also building AgroMap, a free application for farmers which will provide real-time information on environmental and agronomic conditions

Satellite technology can also help guide policy at the local and national levels. In Turkmenistan, geographic information system technology has been employed around Lake Altyn Asyr to identify suitable areas for agriculture. In Kazakhstan, the AgroSpace platform provides geospatial data on agricultural land to justify subsidy applications by the mapping and verification of field borders, crop history and current crop conditions.

Putting these tools to work also depends on skills. In 2024, ESCAP – with funding from the Russian Federation – launched a project to strengthen the capacity of Central Asian countries to use Earth observation (EO) and geospatial technologies for monitoring agricultural conditions and the impacts of drought. By July 2026, its training activities had engaged over 140 technical staff and experts from space agencies, hydrometeorological services, research institutions and universities.

The project, which spans Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan, draws on technical support from Regional Drought Mechanism service nodes in China, India and the Russian Federation. It has also supported countries in operationalizing national drought monitoring systems, including the demonstration of a prototype national portal, led by Uzbekspace, for accessing, visualizing and analysing EO-derived drought and crop information. Cloud-based EO platforms have also helped address digital infrastructure and connectivity constraints in Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan.

Institutions matter too. For satellite data to consistently guide food and agriculture policy, it needs to find its way into official statistics. That depends on two sets of institutions that have not always worked together. National statistical offices hold census and survey data and the mandate to produce and publish official figures; geospatial and cadastral agencies hold the maps, imagery and land records that tie those figures to a place. The Global Statistical Geospatial Framework (GSGF), developed jointly by the global statistical and geospatial communities, sets out how the two can be linked.

Uzbekistan is putting the GSGF into practice. Alongside its first population and agricultural census since independence, the National Statistics Committee of the Republic of Uzbekistan is using satellite imagery for land-cover mapping, starting with the Tashkent region. The approach combines satellite imagery and machine learning with cadastral parcel boundaries, so that land cover and cropland can be measured field-by-field rather than pixel-by-pixel. This matters where farmland is divided into many small plots and fields are often cropped twice a year. Field validation will check the model’s accuracy. The aim is to apply the method nationally and lay the groundwork for estimating crop area and production.

Neighbouring Kyrgyzstan shows where such collaboration can lead. With support from ESCAP’s project on Big Data for Official Statistics, the National Statistical Committee of the Kyrgyz Republic and Kyrgyzgiprozem, the national land management institute, geocoded the 2022 population census and used geospatial data to produce SDG indicators on rural road access and land consumption, which informed the country’s 2025 Voluntary National Review. The Committee has since adopted a national roadmap to extend the approach to further indicators.

As extreme weather events become more frequent and as slow-onset environmental crises unfold, the need for adaptation and resource management is clear, and geospatial innovation, backed by the right skills and institutions, can help meet it. The challenges North and Central Asia face are representative of those faced by the world, and its successes can serve as inspiration to us all. Many of the examples above feature in ESCAP’s forthcoming Geospatial Practices for Sustainable Development in North and Central Asia 2026: A Compendium, which showcases 100 practices from across the subregion.

The authors are Kareff May Rafisura, Chief of the Disaster Risk Reduction Section, ESCAP; Richard Pearce Tonkin, Statistician, ESCAP and Ladislav Charouz, Former Contractor, ICT and Disaster Risk Reduction Division.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan Launch 380-Kilometer Trans-Caspian Fiber-Optic Cable
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan have launched a 380-kilometer fiber-optic communication line across the Caspian Sea, creating a new digital link intended to connect Central Asia and China with Europe and strengthen the region’s telecommunications infrastructure.

Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev took part in the launch ceremony on Oct. 15. The project was implemented jointly by Kazakhtelecom, Kazakhstan’s telecommunications operator, and Azerbaijan’s AzerTelecom, according to the presidential press service.

Tokayev described the cable as a new form of regional connectivity that complements the development of the Middle Corridor, a major trade and transport route linking Asia and Europe.

“We have launched a very important project that will have international significance. Most importantly, this is a new type of corridor. It is not a transport corridor, but something new that fits into the modern era, the era of digitalization,” Tokayev said.

New digital route between Asia and Europe

The Trans-Caspian fiber-optic line will form part of a new communications route linking Kazakhstan, other Central Asian countries and China with Europe. It could also connect with submarine cable systems in the Mediterranean and Black seas, expanding international data transmission options.

The project is expected to strengthen Kazakhstan’s international digital connectivity and create conditions for attracting global technology companies, developing cloud services and expanding artificial intelligence infrastructure.

Aliyev described the launch as another step toward closer cooperation between Azerbaijan and Central Asia, noting that the cable would serve countries across Central Asia, the South Caucasus and neighboring regions.

“Today, we have launched a global project,” Aliyev said.

Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan strengthen Middle Corridor cooperation

The launch coincided with the exchange of a signed agreement between the governments of Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan on cooperation to develop the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, also known as the Middle Corridor.

The agreement establishes a common legal framework for the route’s continued operation and comprehensive development as global trade and logistics networks change.

It provides for coordinated expansion of infrastructure capacity and measures to address bottlenecks across railway, road and port sections. The countries also plan to cooperate on developing dredging fleets and maritime shipping on the Caspian Sea.

A major part of the agreement focuses on digitalizing transportation and logistics. Measures include integrating information systems, introducing a single-window mechanism, enabling end-to-end cargo tracking and preparing a separate agreement on mutual recognition of electronic digital signatures.

The document also envisages simplifying administrative, border and customs procedures through advance information-sharing, reducing inspections and mutually recognizing the status of authorized economic operators.

Together, the fiber-optic cable and the transport agreement are intended to strengthen connectivity between Central Asia and the South Caucasus across both physical and digital infrastructure.

World.title: Kazakhstan Puts Forward New Initiatives on Security, Energy and Digital Cooperation at CICA Summit in Baku
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan proposes expanding the agenda of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) to include artificial intelligence (AI), preventive diplomacy, water cooperation and regional transport connectivity, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said at the seventh CICA summit in Baku on Oct. 15.

Speaking at the summit, Tokayev also called for transforming CICA into a full-fledged international organization, proposed establishing new partnerships in water and human capital development, and highlighted Kazakhstan’s cooperation with Azerbaijan and other regional partners on energy and digital infrastructure.

“For Kazakhstan, the conference is of particular importance. More than three decades ago, our country initiated the creation of this forum to strengthen mutual trust and promote security in our vast region,” Tokayev said.

He noted that CICA member states cover nearly 90% of Asia’s territory and represent more than half of the world’s population. He also welcomed Laos as a new full member of the forum.

CICA urged to move from declarations to action

Tokayev said the summit was taking place amid mounting pressure on the international security system, with military force increasingly taking precedence over the rule of law.

“In essence, the very foundations of the international security architecture are gradually eroding, accompanied by a dangerous shift in priorities in favor of force and to the detriment of the rule of law,” he said.

Citing figures on armed conflicts, civilian deaths, displacement and food insecurity, President Tokayev argued that the scale of current challenges required stronger international institutions and more practical cooperation.

“The era of declarations of intent is coming to an end,” Tokayev said.

He recalled that participants at the sixth CICA summit in Astana in 2022 agreed to transform the forum into a full-fledged international organization. Kazakhstan expects the adoption of CICA’s charter to provide a roadmap for its future activities.

As a practical measure, he proposed launching a CICA Mechanism for Preventive Diplomacy to help member states address emerging disputes before they escalate.

“Peacebuilding must precede crises. Preventing a conflict is far more effective and less costly than settling an already raging confrontation,” he said.

He added that CICA should work more actively with the United Nations, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, the Commonwealth of Independent States and other international institutions to help resolve disputes in Asia and beyond.

AI and cybersecurity added to security agenda

Tokayev also called for adapting CICA’s agenda to rapid technological change, proposing that artificial intelligence become a sixth dimension of the organization’s existing five areas of cooperation.

He warned that AI capabilities were advancing faster than international legal frameworks and pointed to the risks posed by cyberattacks and AI systems that bypass safeguards or gain unauthorized access to external systems.

“AI development must not outpace humanity’s ability to maintain effective control over it. Therefore, confidence-building measures should also extend to the digital sphere,” he said.

In a related initiative, Kazakhstan will host the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific’s Asia-Pacific Center for Digital Solutions for Sustainable Development in Almaty. Tokayev invited CICA member states to participate in the center’s work.

Digital cooperation is also advancing through infrastructure projects. Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan are launching a project to build a Trans-Caspian fiber-optic communication line along the seabed of the Caspian Sea.

“This unique Digital Silk Road project will ensure faster and more secure data transmission across Eurasia, strengthen Asia’s digital potential and open up new opportunities for cooperation,” Tokayev said.

Kazakhstan seeks stronger transport and energy links

Regional connectivity was another focus of Tokayev’s address. He welcomed the reconciliation process between Azerbaijan and Armenia, saying developments in the South Caucasus demonstrated the potential of political leadership to overcome long-standing disagreements.

Against this backdrop, he proposed developing a CICA Strategy for Transport Connectivity to assess the potential of major international routes, including the Belt and Road Initiative, the North-South International Transport Corridor, the Middle Corridor and the TRIPP initiative.

Tokayev also highlighted cooperation with Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan on energy security, noting that the three countries had signed an agreement on strategic partnership in green energy supplies. The initiative lays the groundwork for a Caspian Green Energy Corridor intended to connect their power systems and eventually link them with European markets through the Black Sea.

New proposals on water and human capital

Tokayev identified water scarcity and ecosystem degradation as major challenges for Asia. He noted that Asia and the Pacific are home to 60% of the world’s population but account for only 35% of global freshwater resources.

To strengthen regional cooperation, Kazakhstan proposed establishing a CICA Water Partnership focused on technological exchange, joint research and the adoption of water-saving solutions.

Tokayev also reiterated Kazakhstan’s proposal to establish an International Water Organization within the United Nations system to improve coordination of the global water agenda. He suggested that Central Asian countries and Azerbaijan could jointly advance the initiative while keeping it open to other CICA members.

As part of the proposal, Kazakhstan is prepared to launch a research fellowship program on security and confidence-building in 2027 and provide scholarships to students from all 28 CICA member states. The country is also ready to offer research grants to scholars from participating states.

Tokayev concluded by wishing Azerbaijan success in continuing its CICA chairmanship and expressing confidence that the Baku Declaration adopted at the summit would provide a solid foundation for the organization’s future work.

World.title: Kazakhstan Pledges $25 Million to Extend Partnership With IMF Regional Center
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has pledged $25 million to extend its partnership with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) through the Caucasus, Central Asia, and Mongolia Regional Capacity Development Center, based in Almaty, IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva announced on LinkedIn.

“With the new pledge of $25 million, Kazakhstan shows its leadership and commitment to supporting stronger institutions and more resilient economies across the region. We are grateful for this partnership and excited for what we can achieve together,” she wrote.

The center provides support to nine countries: Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, Mongolia, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan. It is part of the IMF’s global network and serves a region with a combined population of nearly 100 million people.

The center was officially opened in Almaty in June 2023 with Georgieva’s participation. Its work focuses on strengthening regional expertise and institutional capacity, including improving professional qualifications, budget planning, statistical systems and economic forecasting, as well as supporting financial stability.

Since beginning operations, the center has hosted more than 615 events and provided training to over 4,670 participants from across the region, including 1,370 from Kazakhstan. The initiative is also expected to support Almaty’s business and educational tourism sectors and create opportunities for small and medium-sized enterprises.

World.title: Trust Emerges as Journalism’s Defining Asset in Age of AI, Media Leaders Say
World.content:
ASTANA – As artificial intelligence reshapes news production and digital platforms fragment audiences, media organizations must strengthen editorial accountability, provide context and build trust to remain relevant, international media representatives said at the 10th Astana Media Week, which opened in the Kazakh capital on Oct. 14.

The three-day forum brings together government officials, journalists, technology companies and international media organizations to discuss the future of journalism.

Opening the event’s plenary session, First Deputy Minister of Culture and Information Kanat Iskakov called for shared principles governing the use of artificial intelligence in newsrooms.

“The more opportunities any technology gives us, the higher the price of responsibility for its use,” he said.

Iskakov identified strong editorial teams, journalists’ accountability and technologies that improve information reliability as three pillars of trust. He also proposed developing ethical principles for AI use in consultation with the media community and supported labeling AI-generated content so audiences can understand how material was produced.

“An algorithm can write a text, we all understand that, but it cannot take responsibility for its words. Responsibility always rests with the journalist and the editorial team as a whole,” he said.

Trust becomes journalism’s most valuable asset

The question of responsibility was central to a panel discussion among representatives of international and regional media organizations.

Bojan Brkić, head of the Euronews Bureau in Astana, argued that professional reputation would become increasingly important as AI makes content production faster and cheaper.

“The only thing that we will have left that we will be able to sell is our reputation and our trustworthiness – our word that what we publish for you is true,” he said.

The discussion also highlighted the risks posed by algorithms that reinforce existing beliefs and keep audiences within information bubbles. As AI-generated images, videos and text become increasingly convincing, independent reporting and fact-checking are becoming more important.

Central Asia needs to tell its own stories

The panel also explored how Kazakhstan and Central Asia can strengthen their presence in international media.

Zhanna Shayakhmetova, editor-in-chief of The Astana Times, said international audiences need explanations of events, not just news.

“Our audience is no longer looking only for the news or what is happening. They are much more interested in why this news matters – in terms of geopolitical shifts and regional dynamics,” she said.

English-language journalism also carries a responsibility to provide historical and political context, she added, since international readers cannot be expected to know the background to every development in Kazakhstan.

Alyona Gorbacheva, editorial director of Qalam Global, a history-focused media outlet, said specialized media can help meet this need by exploring the historical roots of current events and building distinctive relationships with audiences.

“Journalism is answering the question of what is happening now. And we are answering the question of how we got here,” she said, describing the role of history-focused journalism.

Gorbachyova said Qalam Global’s history content reaches 10 million to 12 million people across platforms in three languages, demonstrating that a specialized editorial focus does not necessarily limit a publication’s reach.

Zahir Beyoglu, Türkiye correspondent for the Qatari newspaper Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, also stressed the importance of sharing Central Asia’s distinctive perspective with the world while maintaining regional languages and cultural identity.

The panel also featured Nadiya Dermanska, deputy editor-in-chief of AnewZ TV, Yergali Ramazanuly, editor-in-chief of the Silk Way international TV channel and was moderated by Lyazzat Shatayeva, a journalist, TV presenter and digital editor at Qalam Global.

Astana Media Week runs through Oct. 16. Subsequent sessions addressed information policy, regional media development, domestic content production and advertising, alongside practical workshops on AI, information verification and digital platforms. The forum will conclude with the Qazaqstan Media Awards ceremony.

World.title: Russia seeks to retain Armenian railway concession as Yerevan avoids confrontation
World.content:
Russia seeks to keep Armenia railway concession

“Armenia is not fixated on taking the concession away from Russia. The issue is ensuring that the railway operates to an adequate standard,” Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said in response to a question about whether the authorities might strip South Caucasus Railway of its rights to operate Armenia’s railway network.

Since 2008, South Caucasus Railway has operated Armenia’s railways under a concession agreement. The company is a wholly owned subsidiary of Russian Railways. The concession runs for 30 years. Since the Russian company took over, freight traffic has halved, some routes have ceased operating, and the company has yet to deliver on its mandatory investment commitments.

Pashinyan said Western companies were ready to invest, but they saw the existing Russian concession as an obstacle. Russia, meanwhile, considers further investment “economically unviable”.

“We say: fine, if it is economically unviable, then sell or transfer the concession rights to those who consider it viable. Alternatively, we will find ways to solve our problems ourselves,” the prime minister told journalists.

Pashinyan also said he had agreed with Russian Railways CEO Oleg Belozerov to set up a joint working group. The group will have three months to answer all the Armenian government’s questions, including whether the Russian side is willing to invest in developing Armenia’s railway network. Yerevan will decide on its next steps only after that.

The prime minister believes the scale of any potential Russian investment could put an end to all “political debate”. In particular, he was referring to concerns that Western countries might refuse to use a railway network under Russian control.
