“If Russia, for example, says, ‘I will invest $3 billion’, that means it has no concerns that the countries we mentioned might choose alternative routes. It would mean Russia is confident that these countries will use these railway lines and that its investment will pay off,” he stressed.

Political analyst Samvel Meliksetyan told JAMnews that Yerevan’s concerns had political rather than economic or investment-related roots from the outset.

For some time, people have been saying that international partners are unwilling to use a railway network under a Russian concession. This, in turn, prevents Armenia from becoming a transit country. Meliksetyan believes Armenia has “made concessions” compared with its original position.

“By deciding to set up a working group, Armenia is trying to postpone the serious and painful consequences that could follow if Russia decides to use its leverage,” he said.

The political analyst recalled that Moscow had hinted at a possible increase in gas prices and was already applying economic pressure by banning Armenian exports.

In the expert’s view, the creation of an Armenian-Russian working group effectively turns the concession dispute into a “negotiation process”.

“Three months from now, another issue could emerge and take a further three months to discuss. The problem would remain unresolved, but this approach would help avoid further deterioration in relations with Russia,” he said.

Pashinyan: “We have no problem with the Russian concession”

The prime minister recalled discussions with the Russian side in April 2026. At the time, Russian partners said investment in Armenia’s railways was economically unviable and that investment from other countries would be unacceptable.

“During the blockade, we might have said, ‘Fine, we’ll manage somehow.’ But now, as the region opens up, we cannot accept leaving our railway in its current condition. It needs investment, and we are talking about substantial sums,” he said.

Pashinyan stressed that investment was essential if Armenia’s railway network was to compete with the Kars–Dilucu line that Turkey is building. At the same time, he noted that competition might not even become an issue, given the expected growth in freight traffic across the region.

Speaking about his talks with Belozerov, Pashinyan said he had made it clear to his Russian counterpart that Armenia did not object to Russian management under the concession agreement. However, Yerevan expected the railway to become competitive.

“Our analysis of how to achieve this goal shows that a change in the concession management model would be a rational approach, particularly by involving third countries in the process,” the prime minister said.

He added that Russian partners could put forward their own proposals if they knew how to resolve the issue.

Moscow has yet to offer any concrete solutions. However, Russian partners assured Armenia that sanctions would not obstruct railway operations.

Nikol Pashinyan outlined the strategic priorities that the Armenian government expects to address now that the region anticipates the reopening of all borders:

Reopening the Ijevan–Hrazdan railway section;

Building a facility in Akhurik to change wheelsets, as Turkish railways use a different track gauge;

Connecting the Ijevan–Hrazdan railway line to the Vanadzor–Gyumri line.

“We understand that this is an extremely difficult task, both in terms of investment and from a technical and organisational perspective. But we cannot simply say, ‘You know, there are difficulties, so we will not pursue this.’ We will approach our friends in the most friendly manner possible, but these issues must be resolved,” he stressed.

What Armenia’s prime minister and the head of Russian Railways discussed

The previous day, Pashinyan received a delegation led by Russian Railways CEO Oleg Belozerov.

According to the Armenian prime minister’s office, Pashinyan stressed that his government aims to integrate Armenia’s railway network with those of neighbouring countries. The meeting covered:

Opportunities arising from regional developments;

Measures to improve the competitiveness of Armenia’s railways and integrate them into international transport routes;

Railway reconstruction projects, particularly the Gyumri–Akhurik–Turkish border line and the Yeraskh–Nakhchivan line, as well as the opportunities these projects would create;

Infrastructure development carried out by South Caucasus Railway under the concession agreement;

Management efficiency, existing problems and possible solutions.

Comment

Political analyst Samvel Meliksetyan believes Russia proposed setting up an Armenian-Russian working group on the railway issue to delay the process and buy time.

In his view, Russia intends to maintain its presence in Armenia’s railway network. He explains that Moscow wants to take advantage of the expected reopening of regional transport links and secure a political role in the process.

“This matters to Russia economically, in terms of its image and in terms of its geopolitical presence in Armenia. Moscow does not want to lose a very important lever of influence as the region’s transport links reopen.”

Meliksetyan believes the Armenian authorities are trying to act constructively and avoid escalating tensions with Russia. In this context, he recalled the “instruments of blackmail” that Russia openly uses.

At the same time, the political analyst does not rule out the possibility of Russian investment in Armenia’s railways.

“The scale of this investment would not pose a significant problem for Russia. We are talking about just tens of millions of dollars. Even amid Russia’s current crisis, that is a very small sum. Its daily military spending runs into billions of dollars.”

According to Meliksetyan, three months of work by the Armenian working group are unlikely to persuade Russia to relinquish the concession.

“Formal decisions or partial amendments to the concession agreement in Armenia’s favour are possible. However, this is a political issue. In the near future, I do not see a political solution that would not lead to a further deterioration in Armenian-Russian relations.”

Russia seeks to keep Armenia railway concession

World.title: Fidan says ‘everything is fine’ in Baku, but relations remain strained
World.content:
Strained relations between Turkey and Azerbaijan

Turkey’s Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan arrived in Baku on the evening of 14 October. The official reason for his visit was the seventh summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia (CICA), where Fidan represented Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. However, the visit came amid worsening relations between the two countries in recent weeks, putting every detail under close scrutiny.

Azerbaijan’s Youth and Sports Minister Farid Gayibov greeted Fidan at Heydar Aliyev International Airport. The decision to assign him to welcome the Turkish foreign minister prompted mixed reactions on social media in both Azerbaijan and Turkey. On 15 October, Fidan met Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev. Later that day, during the summit, he left the hall along with representatives of several other delegations when Israeli President Isaac Herzog began his speech.

After his meeting with Aliyev, Fidan said relations between the two countries remained strong and unbreakable. However, his remarks also acknowledged that disagreements existed between Baku and Ankara.

One of the main factors behind the deterioration in relations has been the de facto ban on wearing the hijab in Azerbaijani schools. JAMnews examined the issue in detail in an earlier article. This time, however, the focus is on a different question:

What is happening in relations between Baku and Ankara, and how serious is the growing chill between them?

Fidan’s message: “There are disagreements, but…”

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan at a dinner hosted by Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev in Baku to mark the seventh CICA summit. Photo: president.az

Speaking to journalists in Baku, Fidan said relations between the two countries had stood the test of wars and crises, while their leaders shared an “unbreakable friendship and brotherhood”. He added that Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan had given him special instructions before the trip.

At the same time, the minister openly acknowledged that the two countries might hold different positions on certain issues. Fidan stressed that neither side should allow these disagreements to damage their strategic relationship:

“We are a people with an ancient history. We must resolve our problems as befits a people with such a past: by sitting down at the negotiating table and discussing them in a civilised manner.”

The minister also said the two sides should not turn their differences into a propaganda tool on social media. He said his conversation with Aliyev had followed this approach, with the Turkish side hearing the Azerbaijani president’s position and his assessment of the situation.

Fidan did not explicitly mention the hijab issue, Israel or Aliyev’s speech on 2 October. However, his references to “our problems”, “differences in approach” and the “use of disagreements” suggest that Ankara acknowledges the existence of tensions but prefers to address them through diplomatic channels rather than in public.

Meanwhile, photographs from the visit attracted the most attention on social media. Some users analysed Fidan’s body language, noting that he appeared relaxed both at the airport and during his meeting with the president, as though relations between the two countries faced no problems. Although such assessments are subjective, they show how closely the public watches every gesture by representatives of Baku and Ankara.

However, the most notable moment of the visit came during Israeli President Isaac Herzog’s speech. At the summit in Baku, Fidan refused to listen to Herzog and left the hall. Just a month earlier, the decision by an Azerbaijani representative to remain in the hall during Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s speech at the UN General Assembly had drawn sharp criticism in Turkey.

What triggered the tensions?

A series of events over the past three weeks has heightened tensions between Baku and Ankara:

23 September — Speaking at the UN General Assembly, Erdoğan described bans on headscarves in schools in “some countries” as an infringement of women’s rights. During the same session, Azerbaijan’s representative remained in the hall while Netanyahu delivered a speech in which he called Erdoğan a “tyrant”.

— Speaking at the UN General Assembly, Erdoğan described bans on headscarves in schools in “some countries” as an infringement of women’s rights. During the same session, Azerbaijan’s representative remained in the hall while Netanyahu delivered a speech in which he called Erdoğan a “tyrant”. 2 October — Speaking at a congress of the ruling New Azerbaijan Party (YAP), Aliyev said, without naming anyone in particular, that everyone should “know their place” and that nobody had the right to interfere in the Azerbaijani people’s way of life. He stressed that Azerbaijan had achieved its military victories without foreign patronage and had bought weapons with its own money (JAMnews).

— Speaking at a congress of the ruling New Azerbaijan Party (YAP), Aliyev said, without naming anyone in particular, that everyone should “know their place” and that nobody had the right to interfere in the Azerbaijani people’s way of life. He stressed that Azerbaijan had achieved its military victories without foreign patronage and had bought weapons with its own money (JAMnews). 9–12 October — Azerbaijani schools began inspections during which officials barred female pupils and teachers wearing hijabs from attending classes. The measures sparked protests and led to the detention of 37 people (JAMnews).

— Azerbaijani schools began inspections during which officials barred female pupils and teachers wearing hijabs from attending classes. The measures sparked protests and led to the detention of 37 people (JAMnews). 12 October — Erdoğan’s chief adviser Oktay Saral called on Azerbaijan to “correct this mistake” as soon as possible. Leyla Şahin Usta, deputy chair of the parliamentary group of the Justice and Development Party (AKP), made a similar statement.

— Erdoğan’s chief adviser Oktay Saral called on Azerbaijan to “correct this mistake” as soon as possible. Leyla Şahin Usta, deputy chair of the parliamentary group of the Justice and Development Party (AKP), made a similar statement. 13 October — YAP’s press service criticised Saral and AKP MPs, naming them individually. Its statement called on the AKP to abandon its “harmful policy” and also referred to “hegemonic ambitions” (Yeni Azerbaijan).

— YAP’s press service criticised Saral and AKP MPs, naming them individually. Its statement called on the AKP to abandon its “harmful policy” and also referred to “hegemonic ambitions” (Yeni Azerbaijan). 14–15 October — Fidan arrived in Baku and met Aliyev.

Against this backdrop, AKP spokesperson Ömer Çelik limited his response to saying that the two countries’ leaders shared a “genuinely brotherly relationship”.

Why relations are cooling: Israel, Russia and claims to the role of “big brother”

All the experts JAMnews interviewed before Fidan’s visit believe the hijab issue represents just one manifestation of deeper problems in relations between Azerbaijan and Turkey.

“The need to choose between two rivals”

Araz Aliyev | Photo: Third Republic Platform

Politician Araz Aliyev, one of the founders of the Third Republic Platform, told JAMnews that he linked the current tensions to Azerbaijan’s foreign policy.

In his view, Baku has begun to see itself as “a major geopolitical player”. However, unlike the US or China, Azerbaijan lacks the capacity to maintain close relations with two rival states at the same time:

“Over the next ten years, Turkey and Israel will be the two main rivals in the Middle East. At the same time, Azerbaijan is a strategic ally of both countries. When Netanyahu speaks, the Turkish delegation leaves the hall, while the Azerbaijani delegation cannot do the same, even if it wants to. Israel also invests in Azerbaijan and supports it. Naturally, this causes resentment in Turkey.”

Araz Aliyev notes that Azerbaijan first felt the negative consequences of its “multi-vector policy” after it backed Pakistan in its confrontation with India. According to the politician, India blocked Azerbaijan’s accession to the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, while trade between the two countries — worth as much as $2 billion — suffered a setback.

Aliyev identifies Russia as a second factor. In his view, Baku has been pursuing closer relations with Moscow since August. He sees the resolution of disagreements over the crash of an AZAL aircraft as one sign of this rapprochement. Historically, he notes, closer ties between Azerbaijan and Russia have gone hand in hand with a degree of distancing from Turkey.

Araz Aliyev also links these changes to the domestic political situation in the US. In his view, Baku’s foreign policy strategy, which has largely relied on Donald Trump’s administration, could come under threat if Republicans lose the US midterm elections in November. The politician believes concerns about this scenario are pushing the Azerbaijani authorities to seek alternative foreign policy partners.

“I don’t depend on you”

Ömer Faruk Gergerlioğlu | Photo: Grand National Assembly of Turkey

Ömer Faruk Gergerlioğlu, a member of Turkey’s parliament representing Kocaeli province and the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM), told JAMnews that he sees Aliyev’s 2 October speech as a rejection of Turkey’s claim to the role of “big brother”.

“Turkey has always seen itself as the big brother of Central Asian countries and Azerbaijan. Aliyev, however, disagrees. His message is: I don’t depend on you; I need you only as much as you need me. We have mutual interests, but ours is not a relationship between an older and a younger brother.”

In the MP’s view, Baku sees cooperation with Israel as a “lifeline” that helps it preserve its authoritarian system of government, and it has no intention of making concessions on this issue.

Gergerlioğlu also points to what he sees as contradictions in Erdoğan’s position. The Turkish president sharply criticises Israel but turns a blind eye to oil shipments from the Turkish port of Ceyhan to Israel. The oil reaches the port through the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline. The MP claims he has repeatedly presented the government with documentary evidence of these shipments.

“If tensions between Turkey and Israel escalate, I think Aliyev will openly side with Israel. For him, the principle of ‘one nation, two states’ takes a back seat. He views the world primarily through the lens of preserving his own power.”

Against this backdrop, Fidan’s decision to walk out rather than listen to Israeli President Isaac Herzog’s speech in Baku takes on particular significance. This time, Ankara demonstrated its differences with Azerbaijan over Israel directly in the Azerbaijani capital.

Growing discontent in Turkish society

Джавид Ага | Фото: личный архив

Journalist and analyst Javid Agha notes that discontent with Azerbaijan in Turkish society extends beyond the hijab issue.

According to him, Turkish businesspeople have complained for years about the difficulties of doing business in Azerbaijan, demands for unofficial payments by tax authorities and deliberate delays affecting lorries at the Georgian-Azerbaijani border.

“Turkish society has accumulated numerous grievances against Azerbaijan. However, people have only begun expressing them more openly and actively since the summer. Previously, Erdoğan’s inner circle kept this discontent in check through groups it funded, which fell silent at the president’s first signal. Now I see posts supporting protests in Azerbaijan on Instagram, TikTok and even platforms where I would never have imagined seeing such things before.”

The hijab factor: a sensitive issue for Turkey

The de facto ban on wearing the hijab in Azerbaijani schools has provoked a particularly strong reaction in Turkey. According to Gergerlioğlu, bans on headscarves remained one of the most hotly debated issues in Turkish society from the 1980s until the 2010s. Today, even voters who support the secular Republican People’s Party (CHP) consider the issue “a thing of the past”.

“Footage showing girls in headscarves being turned away from school brings back painful memories for Turkish society. Supporters of the ban argued that without it, Turkey would become a state governed by Sharia law. But the ban was lifted, and Turkey still did not become a Sharia state.”

The MP also clashed with Azerbaijani lawmakers over the issue. He said that during an online meeting of the Parliamentary Assembly of Turkic States (TURKPA), he criticised the ban. Azerbaijani MP Hikmet Mammadov then claimed that no such ban existed in the country and accused him of lying. However, according to Gergerlioğlu, a lawmaker from Turkey’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP), who attended the meeting, chose to remain silent.

Araz Aliyev believes Ankara’s reaction was inevitable. In his view, under Erdoğan, Turkey presents itself as a defender of “moderate Islam” and Muslims, while religious voters form one of the ruling party’s main support bases. “In this situation, Baku’s decision could not go unanswered,” he says.

Javid Agha, meanwhile, points out that Leyla Şahin Usta was among those whom Azerbaijan’s ruling New Azerbaijan Party (YAP) criticised in its statement. In the late 1990s, a headscarf ban prevented her from continuing her studies in Istanbul. Şahin Usta later lost her case against Turkey at the European Court of Human Rights and completed her education in Vienna.

“These bans did not stop her. Today, she is among those who govern Turkey. The authors of the statement should at least have familiarised themselves with her biography,” Agha says.

Sheikh-ul-Islam: “Consultations could have taken place, but they did not”

Allahshukur Pashazade, chairman of the Caucasus Muslims Board, has also commented on the situation. In an interview with Real TV, he acknowledged that the authorities had not consulted the religious organisation he heads before making the decision:

“I deeply regret that consultations could have taken place on this issue in advance, but they did not.”

At the same time, Pashazade supported the government’s position. He said the school uniform regulations do not mention the word “hijab” and that the country has no ban on wearing it. Children can study in hijabs at madrasas, he added, “but a different decision was taken regarding state schools”.

The Sheikh-ul-Islam stressed that “religion is separate from the state, and school is separate from religion”. He also accused certain “internal and external forces” of politicising the issue and trying to turn citizens against the state.

Araz Aliyev sees Pashazade’s statement as evidence that the authorities made the decision hastily:

“If the decision had been carefully considered and prepared over many years, the authorities should have consulted someone. It appears they made the decision in haste.”

For more on the legal aspects of the hijab ban, protests at schools and detentions, see JAMnews’ earlier report.

How will relations develop?

None of the experts interviewed expects Azerbaijan and Turkey to break off their alliance. However, they all believe the chill between the two countries will persist for some time.

Araz Aliyev believes the tensions will remain at the political level and gradually ease:

“Turkey needs Azerbaijan, while Azerbaijan needs Turkey even more in terms of national security, the economy and defence. Companies close to the leadership in both countries may face pressure from one another, but I do not believe their alliance will be threatened. After some time, we will hear declarations of brotherhood again.”

He notes that the two countries have weathered similar crises in the past. In particular, tensions in the late 2000s, when Turkey and Armenia were discussing protocols to normalise relations, led to Turkish flags being taken down in Baku. Aliyev believes the summit of the Organisation of Turkic States, which is expected to take place in Turkey at the end of the month, could indicate the direction in which relations between Baku and Ankara will develop.

Gergerlioğlu also does not expect Erdoğan to distance himself from Baku solely over the hijab issue. He says Ankara places much greater importance on revenue from the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline, Turkey’s ambition to play a leading role in the “Turkic world” and the support of its nationalist-conservative electorate.

“Behind closed doors, they will probably say politely: ‘Wouldn’t it have been better not to introduce such a ban?’ However, if Aliyev begins openly supporting Israel, Turkey will also start signalling its discontent with the relationship more openly.”

The MP also points to declining electoral support for the ruling party. He claims that some voters dissatisfied with the AKP’s “two-faced” policy towards Israel backed the New Welfare Party in the last election. In his view, the hijab issue could deepen this discontent further.

Javid Agha reaches a similar conclusion. He believes that no matter how often Erdoğan repeats the slogan “one nation, two states”, he will have to take into account the views of the religious-conservative electorate that forms the foundation of his political support and adjust his position accordingly.

Fidan’s statements in Baku also offer insight into this diplomatic strategy. Ankara does not deny that problems exist, but seeks to move discussions about them out of the public arena and into closed-door diplomatic channels. So far, however, there are no signs that Baku intends to make concessions either on the hijab issue or on its relations with Israel.

Strained relations between Turkey and Azerbaijan

World.title: Millions spent on Patriarch’s funeral: scandal involving Georgia’s former culture minister Tinatin Rukhadze
World.content:
Scandal involving former officials in Georgia

On 14 October 2026, Davit Okitashvili, a supporter of the Georgian Dream party, publicly accused former Culture Minister Tinatin Rukhadze of misusing funds allocated for the funeral of the Patriarch of Georgia and called on the prosecutor’s office to launch an investigation. Okitashvili also criticised former State Security Service chief Mamuka Mdinaradze, whom he described as Rukhadze’s political patron.

Other Georgian Dream supporters also responded to Okitashvili’s allegations. Opposition figures believe such attacks on former senior officials may be intended to pave the way for their arrests.

How much did the Patriarch’s funeral cost?

Patriarch Ilia II was buried on 22 March 2026. The government allocated a total of 5.59 million lari to organise the funeral, distributing the funds among six government agencies. The largest share — 3 million lari — went to the Ministry of Culture, which Tinatin Rukhadze headed at the time.

It later emerged that the authorities had not spent more than half of the allocated funds. On 8 May, the government revised the funding to reflect actual expenditure, reducing the total to 2.56 million lari.

Georgian minister quits politics shortly after ex-PM’s accusations

From ‘crown prince’ to prisoner: Irakli Garibashvili’s break with Georgia’s ruling party

Patriarch’s funeral: farewell ceremony of unprecedented scale in Tbilisi. Photos/videos

The Ministry of Culture spent just 722,600 lari of the 3 million lari originally allocated to it. The remaining 2.28 million lari went unspent.

However, it remains unclear exactly how the ministry spent the 722,600 lari: who received the money, what services they provided and how transparently the ministry selected contractors.

September: first questions and the prime minister’s response

Questions about spending on the Patriarch’s funeral emerged in September, following an investigative report by the Pirveli television channel.

Acting Culture Minister Mikheil Kiknadze initially said that the audit documents reflected the shortcomings investigators had identified. However, he later added: “I did not say that there had been any violations.”

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze also commented on the issue on 14 September. He said the Ministry of Culture had spent only 722,000 lari of the 3 million lari allocated to it.

“If anyone had wanted to steal the money, they could easily have taken all three million,” Kobakhidze said.

He also made the following promise:

“This is preliminary information. I will examine the matter in greater detail and provide the public with a detailed account.”

The Patriarchate defends Rukhadze

On 16 September, Archpriest Andria Jaghmaidze, head of the Patriarchate’s public relations service, issued a statement.

He said the Patriarchate had known from the outset that a significant portion of the money allocated for the funeral would remain unspent.

“During that period, we were in frequent contact with Ms Tika Rukhadze, and we knew from her that most organisations and individuals who provided various services had declined any remuneration or payment,” Jaghmaidze wrote.

He expressed hope that people would stop using the Patriarch’s name as a pretext for unfounded accusations and slander.

What links Tika Rukhadze to Tikhart?

According to Transparency International Georgia, Tinatin Rukhadze earned 410,000 lari as a consultant for Tikhart, an event management company, in the two years before she became culture minister.

The organisation also reports that Tikhart secured government contracts worth a total of 3.8 million lari through direct procurement, bypassing competitive tenders.

These circumstances raise questions about whether the company also received payment for organising the Patriarch’s funeral. However, no publicly available information confirms that it did.

Transparency International Georgia has called on the Ministry of Culture to disclose who received the 722,600 lari spent on the funeral and specify which services they provided.

Another problem is that the government does not have to disclose procurement information for purchases financed through the government’s reserve fund. This makes it harder for the public to scrutinise how the authorities spend public money.

The minister’s resignation and a new political climate

Tinatin Rukhadze became culture minister in October 2024. On 28 July 2026, she left the post, citing health reasons. No evidence has established a link between her resignation and the allegations concerning funeral expenditure.

On 15 September, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze appointed Maia Bitadze, a Georgian Dream MP, as culture minister, specifically praising her integrity.

Around the same time, Mamuka Mdinaradze also left his political post as head of the State Security Service. Rukhadze and Mdinaradze subsequently became targets of coordinated public attacks.

October: accusations from a Georgian Dream supporter

On 14 October, Davit Okitashvili, president of the Georgian Chamber of Culture and an active Georgian Dream supporter, publicly accused Tinatin Rukhadze of obstructing his projects and damaging his reputation. He also described Mamuka Mdinaradze as the former minister’s patron.

Okitashvili raised questions about the cost of the Patriarch’s funeral and called on the prosecutor’s office and the State Audit Office to investigate the spending. In a post, he asked Rukhadze:

“Ms Tika, where did the millions go?!”

Other Georgian Dream representatives supported Okitashvili’s post, including party activist and MP Dimitri Samkharadze.

What does Mamuka Mdinaradze have to do with it?

Okitashvili did not limit his attacks to the former culture minister.

He claimed that Mamuka Mdinaradze had acted as Rukhadze’s political patron. According to Okitashvili, Mdinaradze helped secure her appointment as minister, and she subsequently acted under his influence.

In an interview with Palitranews on 15 October, Okitashvili repeated these allegations. He also claimed that both Rukhadze and Mdinaradze had betrayed Georgian Dream.

However, he noted that the prosecutor’s office had not contacted him.

Georgian Dream representatives also responded to Okitashvili’s accusations.

MP Tengiz Sharmanashvili said the prosecutor’s office should ask Okitashvili what evidence he had. If his claims proved credible, investigators should question those involved, including Rukhadze and Mdinaradze.

Opposition warns of possible arrests

The opposition also reacted to the October developments.

Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the Coalition for Change, said Okitashvili’s statements might be intended to prepare the public for the possible arrests of Tinatin Rukhadze and Mamuka Mdinaradze.

Gvaramia suggested that Bidzina Ivanishvili could be behind the process.

Ana Tsitlidze, a representative of the United National Movement, accused Rukhadze and Bakur Bakuradze, the former director general of Rustavi 2, of embezzling funds allocated for the Patriarch’s funeral. She also suggested that authorities might arrest Mamuka Mdinaradze.

Former MP Eka Beselia suspected that Okitashvili’s statement might form part of a pre-planned process. She said that if an investigation began immediately after his statement, it would confirm her suspicions.

Scandal involving former officials in Georgia

World.title: ‘Deadly consequences’: How lack of proper prison in Abkhazia leads to further crimes
World.content:
The recent murder of a Russian tourist has exposed problems with prison sentences in Abkhazia. Edgar Abukhba, who stands accused of murdering Amina Bikbova, received a nine-year sentence for a previous serious crime. In practice, however, he served only half that time. This proved fatal for his next victim.

Amina’s murder prompted Abkhazian society to take a closer look at how courts enforce their rulings. It emerged that in Abkhazia, a sentence tells you very little about how long someone will actually spend in prison. The republic has no proper prison, and a complicated system of “penitentiary arithmetic” determines how much time a person spends behind bars. Even those who apply the rules struggle to make sense of them.

One last coffee

Amina Bikbova’s family had a rule: call her mother every evening. The 26-year-old followed it without fail when she travelled to Abkhazia with her friend Adila for a holiday in September 2026. But one evening, she did not call and failed to answer her phone either. The next day, her phone remained silent. Her family then realised that something serious had happened.

Amina Bikbova

The circumstances surrounding Amina’s final day are known from accounts given by her family and witness testimony reported by Abkhazian and Russian media. Amina and Adila met Edgar Abukhba, a 25-year-old fruit seller. A couple of days later, he invited Amina for coffee. Adila says she tried to talk her friend out of going, but failed. Amina went to meet Edgar and never returned.

During his initial questioning, he denied any wrongdoing. He claimed that he and Amina had simply had coffee, after which she got into someone’s car and drove away. Investigators quickly disproved this account, and Edgar admitted that they had argued, that he had strangled Amina and left her body in bushes beside the road.

A familiar name

Edgar Abukhba

For Abkhazians who follow local crime reports, the surname Abukhba sounded familiar. In July 2019, a 24-year-old Russian tourist suffered a brutal attack in central Sukhum. Her assailants beat, raped and robbed her. Everyone familiar with the case said they had rarely encountered such brutality. Authorities arrested Edgar Abukhba on suspicion of the crime. The case took more than two years to reach court, and in 2021 a judge sentenced him to nine years in prison.

If the nine-year sentence is counted from 2019, when Abukhba entered pre-trial detention, he should not have been released before 2028. Yet by the summer of 2026, he was already selling fruit in Gagra.

Sentences without a prison

Court rulings specify the regime under which a convicted person must serve their sentence, and this affects the time they spend in prison. But Abkhazia has no prison colony with different security regimes, which creates confusion. Officials recalculate sentences differently depending on how much time a prisoner has spent under various conditions. The final figure depends on the coefficient they apply and can differ significantly from the court’s verdict.

Got that? No, of course not. For anyone unfamiliar with the system, it is almost impossible to understand. Even staff at the relevant institutions struggle to explain on the spot how they calculate a particular sentence, how long a specific prisoner will serve and when they will be released.

Perhaps this explains why a man who, on paper, received a nine-year prison sentence attacked another woman long before that term had expired.

Leniency vs prudence

There is another legal complication in Edgar Abukhba’s case. He was still a minor when he committed his first crime, and under Abkhazian law, courts must not take juvenile convictions into account in the future.

There are two opposing views on this rule.

The logic of juvenile justice holds that a teenager’s actions should not determine the rest of their life. But this approach conflicts with public safety concerns, which suggest that authorities cannot simply ignore a proven threat posed by an individual.

Many countries face this dilemma, but they also assess risks before releasing offenders and supervise them afterwards. They may also restrict where former prisoners can work or live and impose other measures. Abkhazia, however, has no such safeguards in place.

A tarnished reputation

Cynical as it may sound, Abkhazia’s tourism sector — and, consequently, its budget — can also be counted among the “victims” of this tragedy.

Abkhazia effectively lives off Russian tourists, who provide the republic’s main source of income. Its reputation as a safe holiday destination is vital to its survival. Now, Amina Bikbova’s murder has left a major black mark on that reputation. This is particularly troubling because it is not the first attack on tourists.

Tourists may forgive reckless taxi drivers or poor service. But they are unlikely to accept the idea that killers who have not served their full sentences can freely walk the streets in search of new victims.

Many Abkhazian lawyers believe the authorities should publish a breakdown of Edgar Abukhba’s first sentence, including the coefficients they applied and his release date. In other words, they should at least explain why he regained his freedom so quickly. Perhaps the authorities should also review the system for calculating prison sentences. Better still, they should finally build a proper prison colony so that no one has to perform these calculations in the first place.

The public, meanwhile, wants an open trial in this case. People are waiting for an explanation of how this mysterious coefficient can allow rapists and murderers to walk free earlier than petty thieves.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

What the lack of a proper prison in Abkhazia leads to

World.title: ‘Whether we should ‘marry’ the EU is question for future’, Armenia’s foreign minister says about EU membership
World.content:
Armenia’s foreign minister at the Warsaw Security Forum

The Armenian parliament approved a law launching the country’s EU accession process in spring 2025. However, only now has Armenian society begun to hold “serious, in-depth” discussions about membership. Foreign Minister and Minister of International Trade Ararat Mirzoyan made the remarks on the sidelines of the Warsaw Security Forum.

During a panel discussion entitled “Half-Readiness or a Gradual Approach: Rethinking EU Enlargement”, Mirzoyan was asked where the train taking Armenia towards Europe would ultimately stop. The minister replied that nobody knew — neither Armenia, nor the EU, nor its member states.

He said the good news was that both Armenia and the European Union were enjoying their current process of engagement.

“So let us enjoy these warm relations, discover new opportunities and explore new dimensions of cooperation. At some point in the future, we can sit down together and discuss whether we should ‘get married’,” Mirzoyan said.

During the panel discussion, the minister also addressed the reopening of the Armenian-Turkish border and the peace process with Azerbaijan.

He stressed that Armenia’s efforts to improve relations with its neighbours do not stem from its desire to integrate with European institutions.

Moreover, he assured the audience that this process would continue regardless of other factors.

“On the other hand, we should acknowledge that if our goal is to become a full member of the European Union, problems or conflicts with our neighbours are likely to become an obstacle along the way,” Ararat Mirzoyan noted.

Armenia and the EU are pursuing more than just political dialogue

“Our relations with the European Union have reached an unprecedented depth, covering a wide range of areas and forms of cooperation. We are holding a dialogue on visa liberalisation. The EU has established a monitoring mission in Armenia, which continues to operate and monitor the situation along the border with Azerbaijan. We recently welcomed a second mission. Although temporary, it operates on a permanent basis and helps us counter hybrid threats.

Although we are not an EU candidate country, the Union has granted us preferential trade access with its member states.

This is the latest development. The EU has approved autonomous trade measures to help Armenia diversify its export markets. We have also signed an agreement with the Union that will allow us to take part in various EU missions around the world.

Moreover, although we are not a candidate country, we have received a Resilience and Growth Plan and assistance from the EU, including support through the European Peace Facility.

Our cooperation therefore extends beyond support for political dialogue, the economy and trade. It also covers security, foreign policy and other areas.

Together with the European Union, we continue to explore new opportunities as we seek to strengthen our ties even further.”

On unblocking transport links, the interests of major powers align

“In my country, and probably across the entire South Caucasus region, the interests of the US and the EU do not conflict. On the contrary, they work together very well.

The United States is actively involved in the South Caucasus. In particular, it is taking part in efforts to open and unblock transport links between Armenia and Azerbaijan.

This will provide a vital transport connection, for example between Portugal and China, linking the West and the East.

I believe the EU and its member states will also benefit from this process.

Thus, many countries and major powers around the world share an interest in unblocking the South Caucasus.”

Opening the Armenian-Turkish border is entirely possible

“We are normalising relations with Turkey. The border remains closed, but I believe the process has already reached a significant level of maturity.

It is entirely possible that tomorrow morning we will wake up and see this headline in the news: ‘Armenia-Turkey border opens’.”

Peace with Azerbaijan and the situation in neighbouring countries

“In our case, Armenia’s neighbours are a critically important factor. Let us look at them.

Azerbaijan. We recently established peace and began bilateral trade. We are opening our territories to transport and transit, and unblocking regional communications. However, several sensitive issues still need to be resolved.

To the west lies Turkey, with which we are engaged in intensive dialogue. We are normalising relations, but the border remains closed.

To the south lies Iran, with its complex regional situation, specific conditions and challenges.

To the north lie Georgia and Russia […].

**As for Georgia, imagine how much easier the situation would be if it continued on its path towards EU integration. That would bring about significant changes.”

Moscow’s reaction must be managed carefully

“As for Russia, you can imagine how it might react to Armenia joining the EU, given the specific nature of our relationship with that country.

Historically, we have had very close ties, and we continue to maintain close relations to this day. However, we must manage any potential reaction carefully.

Nobody wants to make new enemies. Nor are we interested in harming any third party.”

Armenia’s foreign minister at the Warsaw Security Forum

World.title: Azerbaijani government websites hit by cyberattack allegedly originating in Turkey
World.content:
Cyberattack on Azerbaijani government websites

More than 100 government domains in Azerbaijan were targeted in a cyberattack that disrupted access to several government agencies’ websites. According to the State Service for Special Communications and Information Security, the attacks began at around 22:00 Baku time on 13 October. The agency said a foreign hacking group was behind them.

The agency said technical measures had helped limit the impact of the cyberattack and keep the websites running reliably. However, it has not disclosed detailed information about how the attack was carried out, who organised it or what motivated it.

As Meydan TV reports, one theory under discussion is that the cyberattack may have links to Turkey.

The incident has prompted debate about the resilience of the country’s digital government infrastructure and the possible political motives behind the attack. Available information confirms that the websites experienced disruptions, but it is not yet possible to assess the full scale of the cyberattack or its consequences.

Clarify the agency’s responseTighten the final paragraphUse more cautious attribution

Which websites were targeted?

According to initial reports in local media, users experienced access problems with the websites of the Cabinet of Ministers, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the Ministry of Emergency Situations, the Ministry of Health and the State Examination Centre. An official statement confirming a cyberattack followed simultaneous disruptions affecting several government websites.

According to official figures, the attack targeted more than 100 domains. However, this does not mean that the attackers managed to disrupt all these websites or gain unauthorised access to their systems. The number of resources targeted must be distinguished from the number of systems that actually suffered damage.

The official statement does not specify which websites became unavailable or how long the disruptions lasted. It is also unclear whether the outages affected only information pages or disrupted electronic services as well. The State Service for Special Communications and Information Security says it is continuing its cybersecurity measures.

The nature of the cyberattack remains unclear

Disrupting a website and gaining unauthorised access to its database are two different types of cybersecurity incident. In the first case, users lose access to the resource. In the second, the confidentiality and integrity of data may be at risk.

One common method of disrupting websites is a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack. This involves sending a large volume of requests to a server simultaneously from different sources. The resulting traffic overloads the servers or network infrastructure, leaving legitimate users’ requests unanswered. Such an attack can disrupt a website without anyone gaining unauthorised access to its database.

There is no official confirmation that the latest cyberattack in Azerbaijan used this particular method. Authorities have also published no findings from checks for possible data leaks. The available information therefore does not establish either that personal data belonging to citizens were stolen or that the authorities have fully resolved all the consequences of the attack.

The restoration of websites indicates that users have regained access to them. However, determining whether the attackers gained unauthorised access to the systems or whether any data leaked requires a separate technical investigation.

Possible motives and speculation about links to Turkey

Cyberattacks on government websites may aim not only to disrupt online services but also to express political views, attract public attention or undermine trust in state institutions. In its report on denial-of-service attacks, the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) lists political and ideological objectives, as well as financial interests, among the possible motives behind such attacks.

The specific motives behind the latest cyberattack on Azerbaijani government websites remain unknown. The fact that the incident occurred amid political tensions has prompted speculation about a possible link between the events. However, further evidence is needed to substantiate such claims.

According to Meydan TV, social media users are discussing a possible link between the cyberattack and Turkey. The outlet examines this speculation against the backdrop of protests by members of some religiously conservative groups in Turkey against restrictions on wearing the hijab in Azerbaijani schools, as well as Baku’s relations with Israel. Protesters gathered outside the Azerbaijani embassy in Ankara and the country’s consulate general in Istanbul.

However, no evidence has established a link between the cyberattack and these protests or any groups in Turkey. The Azerbaijani authorities have also refrained from naming specific countries or organisations in their official statement.

The phrase “foreign hacking group” used in the official statement does not, in itself, indicate that any foreign state was involved. Identifying those who organised and carried out the attack, establishing their motives and determining whether they have links to state institutions will require a separate investigation.

Warning about cyber threats issued five days before the attack

On 8 October, five days before the cyberattack, Azerbaijan’s Electronic Security Service published a warning about active cyber threats targeting several information systems. The statement noted that some attacks involved outdated database management software and default login credentials that administrators had failed to change.

The warning also said that attackers who gained access to inadequately protected systems could use them to launch attacks against other resources. The service advised administrators to update their software, change default passwords, restrict access to systems and monitor suspicious activity.

The service did not report any possible connection between this warning and the cyberattack that began on 13 October. There is currently no evidence to suggest that the two incidents formed part of the same operation. Nevertheless, the warning highlights that cybersecurity depends not only on responding to attacks but also on regularly updating software and controlling access to systems.

Questions left unanswered after services were restored

One of the key criteria for assessing the impact of a cyberattack is the extent to which it disrupts government electronic services. The temporary unavailability of an informational website can have very different consequences for users from disruptions to systems for submitting documents, registering applications and processing requests.

No specific data has yet been published on whether the latest cyberattack interrupted users’ transactions, caused people to miss deadlines for submitting documents or applications, or resulted in data loss. Without this information, it is difficult to assess the actual damage caused by the incident based solely on the number of domains targeted.

Future official statements will be particularly important in clarifying which services were affected, whether the attackers gained unauthorised access to internal systems, and what the security checks found regarding personal data.

The restoration of the websites demonstrates that the authorities have taken steps to respond to the cyberattack. However, a fuller assessment of how resilient the country’s digital government infrastructure proved to be against such threats will only be possible once more detailed information becomes available.

Cyberattack on Azerbaijani government websites

World.title: Škoda plant to open in Baku: Project progress so far
World.content:
Škoda Group plans rail vehicle production plant in Baku

Czech company Škoda Group plans to establish a rail vehicle production and maintenance facility in Baku.

The project could boost local industry, create jobs and facilitate technology transfer. However, investment figures, production capacity and a timeline have yet to be announced.

Czech transport equipment manufacturer Škoda Group has announced plans to establish a production facility and maintenance centre in Azerbaijan. The company aims to eventually use the facility to serve customers not only in Azerbaijan but also across the South Caucasus and Central Asia.

The plans emerged on 12 October during a meeting between Czech Transport Minister Ivan Bednárik and representatives of Azerbaijan Transport and Communication Holding (AZCON). The meeting was attended by AZCON head Shahin Babayev, Baku Metro chairman Vusal Aslanov and Azerbaijan Railways chairman Rovshan Rustamov.

Škoda Group vice-chairman Tomáš Ignačák said the company intended to establish a joint venture with a local partner in Azerbaijan and gradually expand production.

The proposal covers not only the supply of finished rolling stock but also maintenance services, training for local specialists, the involvement of Azerbaijani companies in component supply chains and the transfer of European manufacturing technologies.

However, the project remains at the proposal stage, with no investment agreement signed so far.

What is Škoda Group planning in Azerbaijan?

Škoda Group is one of Europe’s rail transport manufacturers. The company produces metro trains, trams, suburban electric trains, trolleybuses, as well as vehicle control and drive systems.

Škoda Group should not be confused with carmaker Škoda Auto. The latter is owned by Volkswagen Group, while Škoda Group, which specialises in rail transport, is part of Czech investment group PPF.

According to the company, it has production facilities in the Czech Republic, Finland and Turkey. In 2025, the group’s revenue, including figures from Turkish manufacturer TEMSA, reached €1.45bn.

Škoda Group’s proposal to Azerbaijan focuses primarily on modernising the metro and suburban rail networks. The planned joint venture would gradually develop local production and maintenance capabilities, using local resources and facilities.

One potential benefit would be reduced dependence on foreign manufacturers for maintenance, spare parts and repairs throughout the service life of rail vehicles.

Training local engineers and technicians could also become an important part of long-term industrial cooperation. However, the extent of these benefits will depend on which production and maintenance operations are carried out at the new facility.

Baku Metro expansion creates new opportunities

Škoda Group’s interest in the Azerbaijani market coincides with the country’s plans to expand its public transport infrastructure. Under a state programme approved in January 2025, Baku plans to build 10 new metro stations, modernise existing lines and purchase 299 new carriages by 2030.

In addition to new stations, the programme includes expanding train depots, upgrading power supply systems and increasing the metro network’s capacity. According to AZCON, around $2.5bn is earmarked for the expansion.

In June 2026, Baku Metro and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank signed loan agreements worth a total of $180m to finance the first phase of the expansion. The funds will primarily support ongoing work at the Darnagul and Khojasan train depots, as well as upgrades to existing metro stations.

Azerbaijan has therefore already approved a metro modernisation programme and secured funding for several projects. The Czech company’s proposal aims to meet potential demand for equipment, maintenance services and industrial cooperation arising from these plans.

How much production will take place locally?

One of the key factors determining the project’s economic significance will be the scale of production established in Azerbaijan.

Rail vehicle manufacturing involves various levels of localisation. Some facilities specialise in assembling components imported from abroad and testing finished vehicles. Others also manufacture metal structures and electrical equipment, and carry out engineering and design work. Each model requires different levels of investment, technical infrastructure and skilled personnel.

Azerbaijan already has experience assembling metro carriages at local facilities. In 2024, Baku Metro began assembling new-generation carriages using existing infrastructure. According to official figures, under a contract to supply 65 carriages between 2024 and 2026, specialists from the manufacturer also took part in assembling, commissioning and testing rolling stock in Azerbaijan.

This experience demonstrates that existing infrastructure can be used for final assembly and technical testing. However, it remains unclear how Škoda Group’s proposed model would differ from current practices.

The company has yet to disclose which stages of production would take place in Azerbaijan, what proportion of components would be locally manufactured, the terms of technology transfer or the facility’s annual production capacity. These indicators will help assess how much added value the project could generate for local industry.

Even if the facility initially focuses only on assembly and maintenance, the project could help train skilled workers and expand rolling stock repair capabilities. However, manufacturing more complex components in Azerbaijan would require additional investment and a steady flow of orders.

Škoda Group is not the only contender

Azerbaijan’s talks on purchasing new metro carriages and introducing modern technologies are not limited to the Czech company. In January 2026, Baku Metro officials met representatives of Swiss company Stadler Rail Group. They discussed the possible purchase of up to 300 new carriages, reducing operating costs and introducing modern signalling systems.

In February, a Škoda Group delegation led by CEO Petr Novotný also held talks with Baku Metro officials. Discussions focused on purchasing new carriages and prospects for long-term technological cooperation. Potential cooperation between AZCON and Škoda Group had also been discussed in May 2025.

These meetings indicate that Azerbaijan is exploring opportunities to involve international suppliers in modernising Baku Metro. However, Škoda Group’s proposal to establish a facility in Baku does not mean the company has secured orders for the carriages envisaged under the state programme.

Key criteria for selecting suppliers will include compliance with technical requirements, purchase price, energy consumption, maintenance costs and long-term operating conditions.

Localising production in Azerbaijan could bring additional economic benefits. However, its impact on procurement costs and competition will depend on the specific commercial proposals.

What does Uzbekistan’s experience show?

Škoda Group already has experience of a similar cooperation model in Central Asia. In April 2026, the company signed a strategic cooperation agreement covering the supply of 10 electric trains to Uzbekistan and their maintenance.

The project, worth more than €120m, also includes establishing a joint venture, localising maintenance services and training specialists. The company also plans to launch a Škoda Academy educational programme in Uzbekistan.

This example shows that Škoda Group’s cooperation model goes beyond supplying rolling stock to include developing local maintenance infrastructure and transferring technology. However, its projects in Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan are at different stages.

In Uzbekistan, the number of trains and project cost have already been agreed, and a strategic cooperation agreement has been signed. In Azerbaijan, the company has so far only announced plans to establish a production and maintenance facility.

The proposed Baku facility’s potential to serve regional markets will also depend on commercial prospects. This would require orders from neighbouring countries, compliance with technical standards and competitive production costs.

World.title: Progress or disaster? Armenia begins operations at Amulsar mine
World.content:
Operations begin at Amulsar mine

The Amulsar gold mine has begun operations in Armenia. Guests attending the official opening ceremony were shown the mining process and the production of the first gold bar. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan also attended the ceremony.

The Armenian government expects the project to generate $130m annually in tax revenue and other income for the state budget.

Environmental campaigners, who have warned about the risks associated with the project for years, condemned the government’s decision. More than 60 organisations issued a statement warning that mining at Amulsar would lead to an “irreversible environmental catastrophe”.

However, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan maintains that concerns about environmental risks have been comprehensively addressed. He insists that all questions raised by environmentalists have received thorough and conclusive answers, dispelling their fears.

“There were alarming statements and concerns, including about the possible poisoning of Lake Sevan and so on. And we are here today because we are convinced that none of these risks actually exist,” Pashinyan said.

Economist Suren Parsyan expects the development of the Amulsar deposit to bring significant economic and social benefits.

He also believes that the launch of the mine will demonstrate to investors that Armenia continues to operate in accordance with international standards and is ready to implement new projects.



$750m already invested in the project

The Amulsar mining project is being implemented as part of a strategic partnership between Lydian Armenia and the Armenian government.

According to the government, Lydian Armenia has:

introduced international best practices and standards at Amulsar;

adopted the principles of modern, responsible mining;

promoted a new culture of occupational safety, environmental management, social responsibility and the use of modern technologies.

The company has already invested around $750m in the project.

The Amulsar mine is expected to produce approximately 210,000 ounces (around 6.5 tonnes) of gold annually.

“According to expert estimates, the annual taxes and other contributions paid by Lydian Armenia to the state budget as a result of the mine’s operation will amount to approximately $130m, contributing an estimated 1.5–2% to Armenia’s GDP,” the government said in a statement.

The project is also expected to create more than 4,000 direct and indirect jobs.

Under an agreement between the government and Lydian Armenia, the company will allocate 7m–9m annually to socio-economic development programmes in nearby communities throughout the mine’s operational lifespan.

Pashinyan: ‘Country is entering a new stage of development’

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan described the launch of operations at the Amulsar mine not only as a successful investment project but also as a new stage in the country’s development and an important milestone in the history of Armenia’s mining industry and economic development.

“In the context of Armenia’s history, this is a major step forward. But I hope and firmly believe that in the near future, such steps will become routine and part of our everyday practice. And what we consider a major step in the future will involve projects on an even larger scale.”

According to Pashinyan, the project will provide Armenia with greater opportunities to invest in the security and well-being of its citizens.

He stressed that the country’s mineral resources belong to the Armenian people and that the government’s key responsibility is to ensure that this wealth “serves the development and prosperity” of every citizen.

Nikol Pashinyan inspected the facilities and infrastructure developed for the operation of the mine.

The prime minister said that Lydian Armenia had imported modern equipment to develop the deposit. In his view, Armenia can now boast a high-quality mining industry:

“For any developed country, mining of this calibre, carried out in compliance with environmental and social standards, is a key driver of national development.“

‘Ignoring the risks is unacceptable’: Environmental NGOs’ statement

According to civil society representatives, they have still not received information about realistic and well-founded measures to address the environmental and socio-economic risks associated with the project.

They described the ceremonial opening of the mine just days before the 17th Conference of the Parties to the UN Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17), due to take place in Yerevan, as “a very bold and irresponsible step”.

“By hosting COP17, Armenia is seeking to demonstrate its commitment to the green agenda to the international community, while an environmental catastrophe is unfolding within the country. Armenia’s natural environment, water resources and the future of local communities cannot be put at risk without proper public accountability and evidence that the project is safe. We consider it unacceptable to ignore these risks,” the statement said.

Expert commentary

According to economist Suren Parsyan, Amulsar is the largest investment project in Armenia’s modern history.

In an interview with Armenpress, he said the Amulsar deposit had sufficient reserves to sustain mining operations for at least 20–25 years. He therefore believes that the mine will have a significant economic impact not only on nearby communities but also on the country as a whole.

Parsyan said the company’s turnover or exports would amount to around $930m, meaning that Armenia would gain a new “industrial giant” comparable to the Zangezur Copper and Molybdenum Combine.

“We now have the second-largest mining company, which will have a direct impact of around 2% on the economy. Its indirect impact could amount to another 1.5–2%.”

He stressed that the company would become a customer for more than 200 small and medium-sized enterprises, serving as a “driving force for regional businesses”.

The economist also believes that the mine’s operation will bring significant social benefits. Around 1,000 direct jobs are expected to be created, alongside 4,000–6,000 indirect jobs.

“Salaries here are quite high, averaging 900,000 drams ($2,356) or more. This is a fairly high figure, even exceeding the average salary at other mining companies in Armenia,” he explained.

Suren Parsyan pointed out that Vayots Dzor is one of Armenia’s poorest regions, with a poverty rate of around 25%, above the national average.

He also noted that, in addition to creating jobs, the project includes a social component aimed at supporting nearby communities.

“The poverty rate could fall significantly, by around two to three times. In Vayots Dzor, where the population is small and employment opportunities are limited, this could provide a long-term solution to the problem,” he concluded.

World.title: Azerbaijan discusses CICA development with secretary-general (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 16. The work being carried out to promote the institutional development of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia (CICA) during Azerbaijan’s chairmanship in 2024–2026, including efforts to expand cooperation among member states and enhance the practical effectiveness of the organization’s activities, was discussed.

This was stated in a press release regarding the meeting between Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov and CICA Secretary-General Kairat Sarybay, published on October 16.

During the meeting, the parties exchanged views on the outcomes of the 7th CICA Summit, held on October 15 in Baku; activities carried out under Azerbaijan’s chairmanship; the organization’s priorities for the coming period; and its institutional development.

The importance of the successful holding of the 7th Summit under Azerbaijan’s chairmanship for strengthening dialogue, mutual understanding, and trust in Asia was emphasized. Confidence was expressed that the summit’s outcomes will contribute to strengthening the CICA’s activities, expanding cooperation among member states, and promoting joint approaches to addressing common challenges.

The parties noted the importance of the agreements reached in the summit’s final documents in defining the organization’s future directions and enhancing its practical effectiveness.

The meeting also highlighted Azerbaijan’s experience in multilateral diplomacy and its successful chairmanship of international organizations. It was noted that the country’s chairmanship of CICA is aimed at enhancing the organization’s international role and prestige, expanding opportunities for cooperation among member states, and promoting confidence-building measures.

The discussion touched on the work carried out during Azerbaijan’s chairmanship to accelerate CICA’s institutional development, improve the effectiveness of its activities, and expand its practical benefits for member states. Particular attention was paid to developing cooperation in the fields of education, the empowerment of women, youth, the media, and transportation links, as well as to the platforms established in these areas.

In addition, it was noted that the initiatives being implemented contribute to the exchange of experiences among member states, the strengthening of mutual understanding, and the creation of concrete opportunities for cooperation.

Kairat Sarybay expressed his gratitude to the Azerbaijani side for organizing the 7th CICA High-Level Summit and for its contribution to the organization’s activities during Azerbaijan’s Chairmanship. He also thanked Azerbaijan for the support it has provided over the past six years of his tenure as Secretary General.

The Secretary General emphasized the importance of Azerbaijan’s chairmanship for the development of the CICA, the expansion of cooperation within the organization, and the strengthening of trust among member states. He expressed confidence that efforts to strengthen the organization’s activities would continue in the coming period and wished the new Secretary General, Sultan Hajiyev, success in his future endeavors.

Jeyhun Bayramov, in turn, thanked Kairat Sarybay for his work and wished him success in his future professional endeavors.

The meeting also included an exchange of views on other issues of mutual interest.

World.title: Uzbekistan, Slovakia seek to raise trade turnover to $300M
World.content:
Photo: The Ministry of Investment, Industry, and Trade of Uzbekistan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 16. Uzbekistan and Slovakia have discussed increasing bilateral trade to $300 million and expanding investment and industrial cooperation during the second meeting of the Uzbekistan-Slovakia Intergovernmental Commission on Economic Cooperation in Bratislava on October 15.

This was reflected in the statement by Uzbekistan's Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade. The meeting was co-chaired by Akram Aliyev, Uzbekistan’s deputy minister of investment, industry and trade, and Vladimír Šimoňák, state secretary of Slovakia’s Ministry of Economy.

The parties discussed opportunities to develop joint projects in the automotive industry, energy, pharmaceuticals, transport infrastructure and digitalization.

As part of the meeting, the Uzbek and Slovak sides additionally held negotiations with representatives of Matador Holding, DATAPAC, Betamont, Saneca Pharmaceuticals, MicroStep-MIS and SOITRON to identify promising areas for cooperation.

The discussions focused on expanding business ties, attracting investment and strengthening industrial partnerships between the two countries.

Following the meeting, the parties signed a protocol formalizing the agreements reached during the negotiations.

They also agreed to hold the third meeting of the Uzbekistan-Slovakia Intergovernmental Commission on Economic Cooperation in Tashkent in June 2027.

"At the end of the meeting, a Memorandum was signed to solidify the agreements reached. It was agreed to hold the next meeting of the Commission in June 2027 in Tashkent," the ministry said in the statement.

World.title: Heydar Aliyev International Airport to switch to autumn-winter flight schedule on 25 October
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 16. Heydar Aliyev International Airport will switch to its autumn-winter flight schedule on 25 October 2026. The seasonal program, which will remain in effect until 27 March 2027, covers international flights to destinations across Europe, Türkiye, the Middle East, Central, South and East Asia, as well as other regions.

The European route network includes London, Paris, Berlin, Frankfurt, Rome, Milan, Vienna, Barcelona, Budapest, Warsaw, Prague, Belgrade and Chisinau. According to the current schedule, flights to Bratislava are planned to commence on 28 October.

Flights to Türkiye will serve Istanbul Airport and Sabiha Gökçen International Airport, as well as Ankara, Antalya, Izmir and Trabzon.

Middle Eastern destinations include Dubai, Sharjah, Abu Dhabi, Doha, Kuwait City, Riyadh and Jeddah. The schedule also includes flights to Sharm El Sheikh and Malé for passengers planning winter holidays.

In Central Asia, flights are planned to Almaty, Astana, Aktau, Tashkent, Samarkand, Bishkek and Dushanbe. The South and East Asian network includes Delhi, Mumbai, Islamabad, Lahore, Beijing and Urumqi.

Flights under the autumn-winter schedule will be operated by Azerbaijan Airlines, Air Arabia, Air Astana, China Southern Airlines, flydubai, IndiGo, Lufthansa, Pegasus Airlines, Qatar Airways, Turkish Airlines, Uzbekistan Airways, Wizz Air and other carriers.

Operating days and flight frequencies may vary depending on the destination and the period of the season. World.title: FAO develops program for liberated territories – Nasar Hayat (Exclusive Interview)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 16. The United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) is working with Azerbaijan's Ministry of Agriculture to develop a strategy and program for the natural resources and agricultural potential of the country's liberated territories, FAO Representative in Azerbaijan Nasar Hayat told Trend.

In an interview with Trend on the sidelines of the World Food Day 2026 event, jointly organized by ADA University, Azerbaijan's Ministry of Agriculture, and FAO on Friday, Hayat discussed cooperation between the organization and Azerbaijan.

He said FAO was cooperating with the Ministry of Agriculture on artificial intelligence solutions, technological innovations, and digital technologies for the agricultural sector. The organization is also working with the ministry to develop a strategy and program to make use of the natural resources and agricultural potential of the liberated territories.

Hayat said FAO was considering a number of projects for implementation in Azerbaijan. The organization's main priority is to support the Ministry of Agriculture in achieving the objectives set under the Agricultural Development Program.

"At the same time, the agricultural sector faces various challenges, including climate change, water scarcity, and soil health. These are just a few of the challenges. We intend to provide support across all these areas," he said.

According to Hayat, cooperation should help the ministry achieve the program's intended results while also addressing the needs of Azerbaijan's population and farmers.

He said artificial intelligence was becoming an increasingly useful tool in various sectors, including agriculture.

Hayat stressed that introducing innovations, using technology, and advancing digitalization were essential for the agricultural sector. These opportunities are not limited to the most advanced agricultural technologies but also cover various aspects of farmers' daily activities.

"We can also look at areas such as early warning, climate change, efficient water use, and market information. These are some of the areas where technology can provide real support to farmers in achieving better results and producing better crops with fewer resources," he said.

Hayat also noted that FAO had the capacity to support the development and application of artificial intelligence solutions for agriculture in Azerbaijan.

"We are working with the Ministry of Agriculture on artificial intelligence solutions, as well as other technological and digital innovations. We have extensive capabilities not only in our office in Azerbaijan but also in our subregional office in Ankara, our regional office in Budapest, and our headquarters in Rome," the FAO representative said.

He also addressed support for the development of sustainable agriculture in Azerbaijan's liberated territories, noting that FAO approaches the region from the perspective of agriculture and natural resource management.

"We are currently working with the Ministry of Agriculture to develop a strategy and program on how the natural resources and agricultural potential of that area can be developed," Hayat said.

Having visited Karabakh several times, Hayat described the region's agricultural production potential as substantial.

"I have been to the Karabakh region many times. The region has great potential. It is very rich in both natural and water resources and has considerable potential for agricultural production," he said.

Hayat emphasized the importance of attracting more young people to agriculture to help ensure food supplies for the population.

He said one of the main tasks was to explain to young people the connection between agriculture and technology.

"Most young people, especially those living in cities, think that agriculture is still the same activity their grandparents were engaged in. However, agriculture has undergone tremendous development over the past two generations," he said.

The FAO representative noted that modern agriculture had become a sector that uses drones, artificial intelligence, digital solutions, and satellite imagery.

"Today, this sector is connected with drones, artificial intelligence, digital solutions, and satellite imagery. In other words, agriculture is just as modern as any other sector," Hayat said.

Azerbaijan became a member of FAO on October 20, 1995.
