World.title: Uzbekistan proposes business forum with Slovakia to boost investment ties
World.content:
Photo: The Ministry of Agriculture of Uzbekistan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 16. Uzbekistan has proposed holding a bilateral business forum with Slovakia in 2027 to strengthen business ties, explore investment opportunities, and promote joint projects, at a meeting of the Intergovernmental Commission held on October 15 in Bratislava.

This was reflected in the statement by Uzbekistan's Ministry of Agriculture.

According to the Ministry, during the meeting, representatives of Uzbekistan and Slovakia’s Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development reviewed opportunities to broaden bilateral cooperation in the agricultural sector.

Particular attention was given to improving the professional skills of agricultural specialists, advancing scientific cooperation, sharing best practices, and strengthening collaboration in plant quarantine.

Moreover, the parties discussed prospects for increasing trade in agricultural products and expanding trade and economic ties between the two countries.

As part of efforts to strengthen business contacts, the Uzbek side proposed organizing an Uzbekistan-Slovakia business forum in 2027. The event is expected to bring together companies from both countries to explore investment opportunities, establish new partnerships, and develop mutually beneficial projects.

The discussions focused on translating bilateral agricultural cooperation into practical initiatives and expanding economic ties between Uzbekistan and Slovakia.

"Negotiations were aimed at developing trade and economic relations in the agrarian sector and expanding practical cooperation between Uzbekistan and Slovakia," the ministry said in the statement.

World.title: Innovations can boost Azerbaijani farmers' incomes – FAO
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 16. Innovative solutions can help farmers in Azerbaijan use water resources more efficiently, reduce crop losses, and increase their incomes, FAO Representative in Azerbaijan Nasar Hayat said at the World Food Day 2026 event on Friday, Trend's correspondent reports from the event.

The event was jointly organized by ADA University, Azerbaijan's Ministry of Agriculture, and the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO).

Hayat said that more efficient irrigation management, timely weather information, improved farming practices, and digital links with buyers offer important opportunities for agricultural development.

"Innovation does not always mean a complex or expensive solution. A simple solution that saves water, reduces losses, or helps farmers earn more is also an innovation. The key criterion is whether it works on the farm," Hayat emphasized.

Speaking about the role of young people in this process, the FAO representative cited KendMart, a digital platform developed by 14-year-old Azerbaijani student Leyla Heydarova. He said the platform was designed to connect local farmers directly with consumers and help small farms find customers.

Hayat also highlighted the role of universities, including ADA University, stressing the importance of linking education and scientific research to farmers' practical needs. He said combining modern scientific knowledge with the experience farmers have accumulated over generations helps preserve agrobiodiversity, improve production, and strengthen resilience.

The FAO representative also emphasized the importance of expanding access to finance, training, technology, and markets for rural women, small-scale farmers, and young people.

He noted that 645 million people worldwide faced hunger in 2025, while approximately one-third of the global population could not afford a healthy diet. In this context, ensuring that existing solutions are accessible and useful to those who need them remains a key challenge.

Hayat said FAO remained committed to working with the Azerbaijani government and its partners to translate the organization's priorities of better production, better nutrition, a better environment, and a better life into practical action.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s Central Bank discusses potential cooperation with BlackRock
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 16. The Central Bank of Azerbaijan (CBA) discussed the prospects for potential cooperation with BlackRock.

This was announced in a statement published by the CBA.

According to the statement, a delegation led by Central Bank Governor Taleh Kazimov met with BlackRock executives during a working visit to Bangkok.

During the meeting, the parties exchanged views on initiatives aimed at further strengthening the country’s investment climate and deepening the capital market, as well as on the priorities the Central Bank has identified regarding the diversification of funding sources.

The prospects for potential cooperation were also discussed at the meeting.

“BlackRock” is a U.S.-based investment management firm that operates internationally. The company provides institutional and private clients with asset management services, investment strategy development, and access to financial markets. Its clients include pension funds, insurance companies, financial institutions, and private investors.

The company offers a variety of investment products, including solutions for investing in stocks, bonds, and exchange-traded funds (ETFs). The ETFs offered by BlackRock under the “iShares” brand are widely used in international financial markets. These products are designed to simplify investors’ access to various asset classes and markets.

Asset management companies are involved in allocating funds among various investment instruments, managing investment portfolios, and helping institutional investors achieve their financial goals.

Given the Central Bank of Azerbaijan’s priorities regarding the deepening of the capital market and the diversification of funding sources, the meeting with BlackRock is of great importance for discussing international best practices in investment management.

World.title: Freshly unearthed abuse claim ahead of notorious paedophile's prison release
World.content:
A freshly unearthed allegation against one of WA's worst serial paedophiles who molested dozens of teenage boys is under scrutiny by authorities, just weeks out from a decision on his release from prison after 15 years.

Dennis McKenna abused students in the 1970s and '80s while he was the warden at St Andrew's Hostel, a boarding lodge in the town of Katanning, 290 kilometres south-east of Perth.

McKenna used a combination of favouritism, intimidation and threats to abuse teenage boys under a veil of secrecy at the hostel.

Justice Marcus Solomon is weighing up what life will look like for McKenna when his sentence of more than 15 years expires later this year.

But in an extraordinary development outside court on Friday, McKenna's victims claimed there may be at least one more abuse survivor who complained to police.

Tony Buti says High Risk Serious Offender applications are conducted independently by the State Solicitor's Office. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

Attorney-General Tony Buti has confirmed to the ABC that information about the complaint had been provided to the State Solicitor's Office.

"They are considering it," he said.

Prosecutors have sought to declare McKenna a high-risk serious offender, which could have him jailed indefinitely or see him face tough restrictions for the rest of his life upon release.

"Dennis McKenna's offending against children is abhorrent, and I condemn his behaviour in the strongest possible terms," Mr Buti.

"If anyone has allegations against Mr McKenna I would strongly encourage them to go to the police so the allegations can be properly investigated."

Freshly unearthed allegation

McKenna's brazen and repetitive offending of hostel students was revealed over the course of four separate court cases between 1991 and 2015.

Dennis McKenna has spent more than 15 years behind bars. (ABC News)

McKenna was jailed in 1991 but released after a year and 10 months on parole. Police laid further charges in the late 2000s and he was jailed in 2011 for a 15-and-a-half year term.

Expert evidence given to the court by a forensic psychologist and psychiatrist pointed to a lack of offending between 1993 and 2011 as a reason that McKenna would be a low risk of committing a serious offence in the future.

But Maggie Dawkins, a whistleblower who worked in Katanning during McKenna's period of offending, said today that she knew of a police report made in 2004 or 2005 by a man who claimed he was assaulted by the paedophile.

Maggie Dawkins (right) says another man claimed to have been assaulted by McKenna. (ABC News: Jake Sturmer)

McKenna was not charged in relation to that matter, meaning it was not disclosed or taken into account in the proceedings.

But Ms Dawkins questioned how a decision about McKenna's release could be made based on the belief he had not offended between 1993 and 2011, given the police report.

"We know that this man went to the police and made a police complaint. There is an incident number," she said.

"The expert witnesses haven't had a chance to even know that information."

Maggie Dawkins hugs a supporter outside court. (ABC News: Jake Sturmer)

That complaint is the one now under consideration by the State Solicitor's Office.

The deciding factor

Justice Solomon is deciding whether to declare McKenna a high-risk serious offender, which would see him face tough restrictions as to where he could go and who he could socialise with.

He could impose a continuing detention order, meaning McKenna would be locked up for life, but state prosecutor Brett Tooker and McKenna’s lawyer Joel Grinceri said a restriction order would be more appropriate.

Joel Grinceri is representing McKenna in court. (ABC News: Jake Sturmer)

The court heard from various experts about McKenna's capacity to reoffend. Among them was forensic psychiatrist Peter Wynn Owen, who considered the risk low, primarily due to his advanced age and lack of offending between his 1991 and 2011 jail sentences.

Survivors watch as 'house of horrors' hostel demolished Demolition has begun at the site of one of state's worst cases of institutionalised child sexual abuse, where dozens of boys were harmed by paedophile Dennis John McKenna.

But Dr Wynn Owen said the serial paedophile continued to "categorically" deny any offending after 1981.

"[He] attributes blame to victims, suggests victims in fact instigated aspects of the offending," he told a hearing in July.

"If an individual is denying offending, it suggests they are not going to be able to engage with treatment."

Dr Wynn Owen said McKenna continued to hold distorted views that, in his mind, minimised or justified his offending.

"This distortion … enabled him to continue to offend over a long period of time," he said.

Justice Solomon's decision is due to be handed down in November, weeks before McKenna’s sentence is due to expire.

World.title: Lithium mine expansion could rival global leader
World.content:
A West Australian mining company will spend more than $1 billion on an expansion in the state's north-west despite falling prices for the commodity.

In a statement to the Australian Stock Exchange (ASX), PLS Group Limited announced it would push ahead with plans to increase spodumene concentrate production to about 2 million tonnes per annum at its Pilgangoora lithium mine, 140 kilometres south-east of Port Hedland.

The company is investing $1.9 billion in the project, which will include building a new processing facility named Jimmagunya by Nyamal elders, meaning spring country.

The PLS Pilgangoora site in WA will expand. (Supplied)

PLS managing director and CEO Dale Henderson said in the statement he was determined to ensure the company was competitive in the lithium market.

"Pilgangoora has grown significantly over the past decade and as we look ahead, we are continuing to invest in the infrastructure needed to support the long-term potential of this world-class asset," he said.

"These [changes] are expected to reduce operating costs, improve productivity, and strengthen the existing operation while also providing the infrastructure capacity required to support the increased scale of P2000."

The company has also announced a $600 million infrastructure investment over three years.

That includes upgrading access roads, co-funded by the state government, building a new 1,200-bed permanent workers' village and a mine services facility.

Funding for both will be underpinned by the company's existing cash balance and operation cashflows from existing production.

The statement said lithium had been a strong growth market over the past decade, with forecasts for it to grow by 8 per cent per annum until 2040.

Demand high, while price low

If the company's predictions are correct, the expansion would make the PLS mine rival Talison's Greenbushes mine in WA's South West as Australia's largest hard rock lithium mine.

Talison Lithium operates the Greenbushes mine in the state's South West. (ABC South West WA: Jon Daly)

PLS predicts Pilgangoora will produce 2 million tonnes per year of spodumene concentrate when it is fully operational in 2029.

Mining analyst Peter Strachan said demand for lithium had been steadily growing, but costs were falling.

"Despite the fact that the demand for lithium is strong because of the strong electric vehicle demand globally, the price of spodumene concentrate has fallen," he said.

"The market for lithium miners in Australia has been quite weak on the back of this falling commodity price."

Lithium prices have now almost halved from their May highs of $US3,000 per tonne to $US1,505 per tonne for spodumene and about $US15,500 per tonne for lithium carbonate.

Peter Strachan says demand for lithium is high due to EVs. (Supplied: Peter Strachan)

"Mines which were closed two or three years ago when the price really fell are now coming back online," Mr Strachan said.

"It's a supply issue that's been pushing down the price of lithium."

Mr Strachan said Talison Lithium, which owns the Greenbushes mine, would likely rein in operations to reduce its own costs off the back of the announcement.

"They will scale back, they'll choose to do the lowest cost operation," he said.

State government backs expansion

The WA government has welcomed the news, saying the expansion would create 1,000 jobs during construction and a further 500 ongoing operational roles.

"This is exactly the kind of investment that keeps Western Australians in work today and creates the jobs of tomorrow," Premier Roger Cook said.

Pilbara Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson said the move was a vote of confidence in the region.

Amber-Jade Sanderson says there will be more opportunities for Pilbara workers. (ABC News: Benjamin Gubana)

"The creation of about 1,500 jobs will deliver real opportunities for Pilbara workers, local businesses, and communities while strengthening the region's position as a global critical minerals powerhouse," she said.

WA's lithium industry sold almost 4 million tonnes of spodumene concentrate in 2025, the highest volume on record.

World.title: State authorities threaten legal action over council's homeless camp in park
World.content:
A Queensland government agency has threatened legal action against the City of Moreton Bay for "illegally" allowing homeless people to camp at a public park.

Economic Development Queensland (EDQ) issued the council a show cause notice, which gives the council an opportunity to explain why legal action should not be taken.

It comes after the City of Moreton Bay council turned Wyllie Park in Petrie into a free, designated campsite for homeless people in August.

An EDQ spokesperson said the site's lawfully approved purpose was as green space, and not as a homeless camp.

Wyllie Park was supposed to be a place where homeless people did not need to fear eviction. (Supplied: Beau Haywood)

"EDQ has responsibilities under the Act to regulate and ensure land is used lawfully within the Moreton Bay Central PDA," they said.

"The Queensland Government has available a range of support services for those experiencing homelessness with over $1 billion being invested in support services and crisis accommodation over the next four years."

Wyllie Park is in the Moreton Bay Central Priority Development Area, which means it falls within EDQ's remit.

Government not consulted

In August, Housing Minister Sam O'Connor criticised the City of Moreton Bay's decision to turn Wyllie Park into a designated homeless camp.

He told 612 ABC's Breakfast program clustering vulnerable campers in one area would cause safety risks and strain emergency services.

"We had no idea and we weren't consulted on it either. We found out through the council's press release," Mr O'Connor said.

"We weren't asked about it, and if we were asked about it we would have expressed some serious concerns about this model.

"We've had other councils look at this and we've expressed that concern to them, and they haven't gone forward."

Human rights violations

In March, the City of Moreton Bay was found guilty of violating the human rights of homeless campers by evicting them and destroying their belongings.

Wyllie Park falls within EDQ's jurisdiction as a priority development area. (Supplied: Beau Haywood)

The Supreme Court ruled that the council should not have evicted the campers when they did not have anywhere else to go.

None of the homeless campers involved in the court case had been offered social housing when they were threatened with fines and forced to move.

Peter Flannery says the camp was an alternative place to go. (612 ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

In August, Mayor Peter Flannery told 612 ABC's Drive program the camp would provide a place for homeless people to sleep without fear of eviction.

"We did learn from the court case that we shouldn't have been asking them to move when there wasn't somewhere else to go," Cr Flannery said.

"This is providing that somewhere else to go."

Evictions on the horizon

The Wyllie Park campsite was supposed to be a 12-month trial, offering 30 sites for up to 60 campers at a time.

The site would offer toilets, bins, lighting, CCTV, 24/7 security, and access to a range of government services and local charities.

Beau Haywood is worried about the future of Wyllie Park's campers. (612 ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

Beau Haywood runs the charity Nourish Street, which feeds homeless people in Wyllie Park and across Moreton Bay.

Mr Haywood said he feared this latest news could mean another wave of homeless evictions.

"I'm disappointed in the Queensland government," Mr Haywood said.

"Although the situation in Wyllie Park wasn't perfect, it was thinking outside the square.

"My concern now is for the residents of Wyllie Park, and I really hope the Queensland government is planning on providing these people with accommodation."

The ABC has contacted the City of Moreton Bay for comment.

World.title: Marilyn Wallman inquest suspended after emergence of new witness
World.content:
A coroner has suspended an inquest into the disappearance of missing Mackay schoolgirl Marilyn Wallman after the emergence of a new witness.

Coroner David O'Connell said he anticipated Marilyn's family would suggest two brothers, Noel and Tommy Morris, were involved in her disappearance.

Noel Morris, who was married to Marilyn's cousin, had previously been identified as a person of interest but Tommy Morris was not scheduled as a witness.

The 14-year-old girl was last seen on March 21, 1972, while she was riding her bike to school.

A piece of her skull was found in a cattle paddock two years later at McGregor Creek, 40 kilometres from Mackay.

Members of the Wallman family outside the Mackay Court House. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

The Wallman family is represented at the inquest by Marilyn's brother Rex, who can sit at the bar table and question witnesses.

Mr O'Connell said he expected suspicions about the two members of the Morris family would be raised in the court.

"I am anticipating, from the division within the wider Wallman-Morris family, that there may be a suggestion put to me at the end of the inquest," Mr O'Connell said.

"That perhaps Noel Morris and Tommy Morris had some involvement in Marilyn's disappearance."

Noel Morris and his solicitor Robert Beamish. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

The court heard Tommy Morris was believed to have left Mackay for South Australia in the months after Marilyn's disappearance.

Mr O'Connell said the two brothers were yet to appear and would need a chance to respond to any allegations.

"Accordingly, when we recommence, Mr Noel Morris and Mr Tommy Morris will have to be available to give evidence," he said.

The inquest will resume on December 8.

New public information

Mr O'Connell said new information from the public also had to be investigated before the inquest could continue.

He told Rex Wallman he realised the difficulty this may cause.

"But this is possibly our last opportunity to make progress for the matter," the coroner said.

Marilyn Wallman's siblings Rex, David and Lenore. (ABC Tropical North Danielle Jesser )

The court had heard progress in the inquest was slow because some witnesses and investigating officers were dead and others had cognitive decline.

Mr O'Connell said Michael Anthony Frances and Arthur Stanley Brown, whose involvement in Marilyn's disappearance was being considered, had also died.

He said those matters would "have to rely on investigation material".

Relatives search sugarcane farm

Witness Lyle Wright said he and his cousin Noel Morris were employed at the Goonyella coalmine, 145 kilometres west of Mackay, around the time Marilyn went missing.

Mr Wright told the court he decided to leave work early on the morning Marilyn disappeared and he drove to Mackay with her uncle, Tom Watson, to help search the Wallman farm.

Witness Lyle Wright leaving Mackay Court House. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

Solicitor Robert Beamish, representing Noel Morris, queried changes in Mr Wright's statements to police.

He said that, in 2015, Mr Wright told police he could not recall who travelled with him and that it "could have been 'Noelly' and Tom [Watson]".

In June this year, Mr Wright told police he recalled Noel Morris was in Mackay for the birth of his daughter on the day Marilyn disappeared.

Mr Beamish questioned the reliability of the recent statement, saying it was likely Mr Wright's evidence was more accurate in 2015.

" What we're getting at, is that his evidence becomes more certain over time as opposed to what ordinarily happens over the years. "

Car colour debated

The court heard Mr Wright told investigators in 2016 that Noel Morris drove the same type of Holden sedan police were looking for.

Mr Beamish said that, at the time, the witness described Mr Morris's car as a light-blue pastel colour Holden HD with a lighter coloured roof.

However, in a statement from 2015 shown to the court, Mr Wright described Noel Morris's car as a "bluey-greeny" 1965-model Holden.

Mr Wright told the court police had "sprung" the interviews on him, and that he had spent more time thinking about the events leading up to Marilyn's disappearance since then.

"I've probably contradicted myself over the years; I've been thinking about it."

World.title: Bush pub that inspired Slim Dusty's 'Humpty Doo Waltz' hits the market
World.content:
Once just a convenient place to pull in for a pint, the Humpty Doo Hotel has become a Northern Territory landmark.

For more than 50 years thirsty travellers have stopped at the pub, about 40 kilometres south-east of Darwin, on their way to Kakadu National Park.

Despite having what are claimed to be the largest buffalo horns in the Southern Hemisphere hanging behind the bar, it is not stereotypical Aussie pub charm that put the Humpty Doo Hotel on the map.

Rod Parry has been behind the bar at the Humpty Doo Hotel for almost 40 years. (ABC News: Courtney Barrett-Peters)

"It's the name," licensee Rod Parry says.

"Where do you find another Humpty Doo Hotel? You'll find a Railway, a Commercial, a Royal, but you'll never find [another] Humpty Doo Hotel."

Mr Parry has decided it's time to call last drinks and is putting the hotel up for sale after four decades of ownership.

"I think it's time I had a rest, let someone else take over the reins," he says.

"Thirty-nine years is half my lifetime."

Horses, crocs and a beer-sculling bull

Established in 1971, the pub survived Cyclone Tracy and is believed to be one of the Northern Territory's longest-licensed premises.

The pub has been a Territory landmark for many years. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Since Mr Parry purchased it in 1987 the venue has inspired bush ballads such as Slim Dusty's Humpty Doo Waltz and former NT administrator Ted Egan's The Man from Humpty Doo.

Mr Parry has seen plenty of patrons come through the doors in his time, including those with four legs.

"Horses stand at the bar with their riders, their riders have a couple of beers, and the horses stand there very quietly, maybe they watch the TV," he laughs.

"We've had a pig in here. The other day the girls called me and said, 'There's a wallaby in the men's toilet' — and the crocodile, last wet season, out the front of the bottle shop.

"It never stops."

Perhaps most notably, the hotel's Darwin Stubby drinking competition in 1988 was won by Norman the Brahman bull, who sculled a 2.25-litre stubby in 47 seconds, according to an ABC report.

Norman the imbibing Brahman at the 1988 Humpty Doo Hotel Darwin Stubby drinking contest. (ABC News)

Norman reportedly proceeded to wash that down with "half a dozen tinnies and a meat pie".

In 2016, a tiny donkey, a pony and a cow walked into the premises and police had to ask them to leave.

But Mr Parry says the customers he will miss the most are those with two legs — the generations of Top End locals who have grown up in the venue.

"A lot of those guys have passed away, but their children still drink here and their children's children come in," he says.

"I will miss the locals and I'll miss my staff, because some of them have been here for so many years."

Rod Parry says his staff have come to be like family. (ABC News: Courtney Barrett-Peters)

General manager Alex Taylor says the feeling is mutual.

"Working with him for 10 years, he has definitely become more of a family than anything else," she says.

"I don't really see Rod as my boss.

"He's helped me a lot through my career and my development and he's always been there just in general as well."

'World famous' pub

Although the business was "devastated" by the COVID-19 pandemic, in the past year the Humpty Doo Hotel has recorded more than 50,000 visitors.

It says staff turn around an average of 400 lunch meals every day during the dry season.

The bar area has remained untouched under Rod Parry's ownership. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

But the hotel's success can no longer just be purely attributed to its food and beverage sales, with its name recognisable worldwide.

"We send [shirts] to America, England, New Zealand, just in the mail. They buy them online," Mr Parry says.

"My daughter, years ago, was at Mount Everest Base Camp and she had a Humpty Doo Hotel shirt on there and she passed a guy on the track and he said, 'I've been there, that's great pub.'"

The apparel, emblazoned with buffalo horns, has also become a drawcard for Australian holiday-makers such as Perth road-tripper Mel Catchpole, who stopped in for a "nostalgic visit".

Mel Catchpole and her husband Nathan grabbed some merch during their visit. (ABC News: Courtney Barrett-Peters)

"As a child, my uncle lived in Humpty Doo and I was fortunate to travel up when I was very young — 11 — and then again at 18 years of age," she says.

Her husband, Nathan Catchpole, is visiting for the first time and says it's "a bit sad" to hear the hotel is up for sale.

"It's an iconic pub and [it's] sad to see it go to new owners," he says.

"It's an outback pub and we want to keep it that way."

Rowdy reckons the new owners shouldn't change a thing. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

The news has also saddened Humpty Doo local Rowdy, who has been a regular patron for more than 45 years.

"It's handy and a good place to come to," he says.

"You can't change it much. Just keep it going how it is."

Looking for the right fit

Since purchasing the hotel all those years ago, Mr Parry has added a bottle shop, RV park, gaming machines and a bistro.

One thing he hasn't touched is the bar, which he hopes the new owners will also respect.

"It's an iconic pub. You can't change it," Mr Parry says.

"What are you going to do? Put carpet in here? It's not going to be the same.

"It'd just be like every other hotel in town if it's, like, air-conditioned, carpet, tiles — just doesn't work for Humpty Doo.

"We just walk in here with a firehose, hose it out in the morning, squeegee it, turn the fans off to dry the concrete — simple."

Brisbane-based hotel broker JLL put the 2.3-hectare property up for sale on Wednesday.

So far Mr Parry has been fielding interest from people all over Australia, but says he isn't willing to let it go to the wrong person.

The cast and crew from Top End Bub filmed part of the show at the Humpty Doo Hotel. (Supplied: Screen Territory)

"I had a call from a guy who owns a car yard. Mate, I don't think it's your bag to run a hotel," he says.

"You need to have some hospitality experience, because these days you need to have so many licences."

Expressions of interest for the new licensee will be open for a month.

World.title: Teen reported for assault after Glenelg beach fight, police say
World.content:
Police say they have reported a 14-year-old boy after an investigation into an alleged assault at Glenelg Beach.

Officers were called to the beach on September 29 to reports of "several hundred youths surrounding a fight on the beach".

SA Police said a woman had attempted to intervene during the disturbance when she was hit by a bottle.

Police will allege the bottle was thrown at the woman, causing a minor cut to her hand.

Police said in a statement the woman was identified and reported the incident to police.

"On Thursday 8 October, police attended Glenelg Beach regarding an unrelated matter, where they identified the suspect allegedly involved in the assault," police said.

Police said a 14-year-old Valley View boy was reported for aggravated assault today.

He is expected to appear in the Adelaide Youth Court at a later date.

World.title: Carnival Cruises axes half of Australian fleet
World.content:
Carnival Cruises has announced it will remove two of its four Australian cruise ships from March 2028, despite more than 1.4 million Australians going on a cruise last year.

Carnival, which is the only major cruise company operating full-time in Australia, announced it was pulling the Carnival Adventure and the Carnival Luminosa.

The Carnival Encounter (pictured) and Carnival Splendor will remain in the Australian fleet. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Other major cruise operators such as Disney and Royal Caribbean no longer operate full-time in Australia.

Carnival said ship schedules were considered years in advance and it was considering "long-term certainty and globally competitive operating conditions to support itinerary planning and investment".

The decision was an economic one, according to Chris Frame, a maritime historian.

" Australia is an end-of-the-line destination, and it's a huge investment. "

Mr Frame said higher levels of regulation, such as tough biosecurity rules, and little cruise infrastructure made it hard for cruises to stay profitable in Australia.

All other major cruise lines, including Disney, Norwegian Cruise Line and Royal Caribbean have pulled their full-time ships from Australia. (Facebook: Pieter Klaas de Boer)

"Berthing fees are higher than other markets, refuelling is higher and provisioning the ship with food is higher, as you just don't have the economies of scale."

He said that for the company, the ships were assets and "they can always be redeployed somewhere else more profitable".

New changes to cruise laws

The moves comes after a decades-old temporary exemption, allowing cruise ships to circumvent Australian labour laws, was extended earlier this month, but with new protections added for workers for the first time.

Earlier this year, an ABC News investigation revealed that workers had accused the company of 12-hour work days for seven days a week, medical neglect, not providing safe drinking water and wages less than $3 an hour. Carnival denied the allegations.

Punishing conditions face Carnival crew Passengers boarding a Carnival cruise ship are promised a world of endless food, relaxation and oceanic luxury. But for the crew, life is vastly different.

Carnival's country manager Peter Little said in a statement the company had "greater exposure to changes in local market and operating conditions" than other cruise lines. Carnival did not respond to requests for comment.

However, Jake Field of the Maritime Union of Australia claimed this was the third time Carnival had threatened to withdraw from Australia, and that it was a negotiating tactic.

"There are 80 cruise vessels that are scheduled to come to Australia, only four of them don't have collective agreements with their crews, and those are the four Carnival ships," he said.

World.title: Live: Jillaroos on track for big win in World Cup opener
World.content:
— reporting by AAP

Samoa have opened their World Cup campaign by crushing France in a 78-4 win that gives an early boost to the Pacific nation's hopes of reaching the knockout stages.

In a 14-try-to-one victory in which centre Stephen Crichton kicked 11 goals and Melbourne flyer Sua Fa'alogo crossed four times, the Samoans barely worked up a sweat at Western Sydney Stadium in Sydney on Friday.

Taking on a French side mostly made up of Super League players, the star-studded Samoan team raced out to a 28-0 lead inside 20 minutes.

The only blemish for coach Ben Gardiner was the sight of Brisbane winger Deine Mariner going off in the first half with a suspected injury.

And while they had lapses of discipline and concentration with the result sewn up — France scored their sole try through winger Guillermo Aispuro-Bichet — the heavy win will increase Samoa's points differential and their hopes of making it to the semi-finals.

One of Samoa, England or Tonga will miss the knockout stages as a result of the new tournament format, in which the top two teams from across group B and group C make it to the last four.

Samoa face Papua New Guinea in Port Moresby next week before concluding their pool games in an all-Pacific match-up for the ages against the Tongans.

The Kumuls on home soil and Tonga in Sydney will provide a much sterner test than the French, who were left for dead in a blistering opening quarter.

Mariner scored the opening try for the Toa in the third minute soon after his father Lapi had sung the country's national anthem that brought stars including Jarome Luai and Spencer Leniu to tears.

Benaiah Ioelu, Jermaine McEwen, Fa'alogo, and Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow all crossed in the next 15 minutes as the French defence was cut to shreds.

Aispuro-Bichet briefly stemmed the bleeding before Fa'alogo went in again just before halftime to make it 34-4 at the break.

The French had little resistance in the second period, with Fa'alogo adding two more while Crichton, Chanel Harris-Tavita, Shawn Blore, Izack Tago, Francis Molo and Ioelu all went over.

World.title: Cities impacted by longer, more severe bushfires: study
World.content:
NationalQueenslandBushfires Cities impacted by longer, more severe bushfires: study Courtney Kruk October 16, 2026 — 9:23pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Bushfires are impacting Queensland’s urban air quality more frequently and more severely than previously understood, new research has found, with pollution travelling further across the state, and for longer, increasing public health risks. The study led by researchers from the Queensland University of Technology analysed air quality data from 22 urban monitoring sites across Queensland between 2008 and 2023. It found bushfire smoke can increase fine particle pollution (PM2.5) by up to 160.5 per cent during a fire event, and ozone levels by up to 33.2 per cent during fire-active seasons (July to December). A QUT-led study found bushfire smoke is affecting Queensland urban air quality more often and more severely than previously understood. Nick Moir Between 2018 and 2023, bushfire-impacted hours during the fire-active season were approximately three times more frequent, compared with 2008–2017.



Lead researcher Dr Zijun Li said climate change has increased the frequency and ferocity of bushfires, with longer burn times increasing pollution levels. Related Article Exclusive

Pollution Air pollution kills 1 million a year – hundreds of whom are Australians “Climate change and heatwave conditions are favouring the conditions of the bushfires,” Li said. “Bushfire smoke is not only a problem for communities located near fires. “Our research shows emissions can travel hundreds or even thousands of kilometres and significantly affect air quality in urban areas far from the source.



“As climate change increases the frequency and intensity of bushfires in many regions, understanding how smoke affects urban air quality is becoming increasingly important.” PM2.5 – the fine particle matter emitted during wildfires – is small enough to penetrate deep into the lungs and bloodstream, and is linked to respiratory and cardiovascular health impacts. Gold Coast University Hospital doctor Yian Zhao moved from China to Australia as a child because of his asthma. Gold Coast University Hospital Gold Coast University Hospital doctor Yian Zhao has suffered asthma since early childhood, and moved from China to Australia when he was 11 because of the difference in air quality. “Industrial smoke and allergies are the main [asthma] triggers for me,” Zhao, who grew up in Adelaide, said.



“[In China] we lived in a heavily industrialised area as well. The dust, smoke, air quality … some days you could barely see five metres in front of you because of how bad it was. “So my parents made the decision to move over to Australia.” Since moving from South Australia to Queensland, Zhao said his exposure to bushfire events has been minimal. But he can feel changes to air quality, and worries about the impact of longer and more severe bushfire seasons. “I look at it from both sides, as a doctor and a patient myself,” he said. “For me, it gets a little bit harder to breathe whenever there’s smoke in the air, to the point where I’ll probably preemptively take some more of my puffers.



(Left to right) Huon Morton, Dr Zijun Li, Adjunct Professor Zoran Ristovski and Mr Hongzhi Zhang worked on the study analysing air quality data from 22 urban monitoring sites in Queensland. Queensland University of Technology “[In the public health system] the number of resources that we do have is finite … so an increase in bushfires would definitely put a stress on both things.” Li said the research also revealed insights into how bushfire smoke behaves and affects communities, with stronger fires affecting urban pollutants. “Ozone formation is complex. We found bushfire emissions can interact with local urban emissions, particularly nitrogen oxides from vehicles and industry, to increase ozone concentrations,” Li said. “This means bushfire smoke can worsen air quality even when the fires are a long way from the city.”

A planned 51-storey hotel tower above Brisbane’s landmark Victory Hotel CBD pub has received council approval, paving the way for a major accommodation development ahead of the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games. Brisbane City Council approved Precision Group’s proposed Victory Tower, a 206.6-metre development behind and above the heritage-listed hotel, on Monday. As part of the approval, Precision Group would be required to pay almost $2 million in infrastructure charges to the council. Precision Group is planning a new tower behind the Victory Hotel in Brisbane Bureau Proberts The new tower would be built on the site of the pub’s popular beer garden.



The approval marks a significant milestone for the project, which would transform the site into a 284-room hotel with restaurants, function spaces, wellness facilities, a rooftop bar and a swimming pool on the 40th floor. The 16,000-square-metre tower will be built on a 924-square-metre site and occupies the area currently used as the Victory’s Charlotte Street-facing beer garden. Precision Group founder and chief executive Shaun Bonett said the development would help address Brisbane’s hotel room shortage as the city prepares for the 2032 Games. “The critical shortfall of hotel rooms in Brisbane is well documented and the demand for accommodation is accelerating,” he said. “The Victory Hotel is one of Brisbane’s most recognised hospitality landmarks.



“Our vision is to honour that history while giving the site a new future, bringing together heritage, hotel accommodation, hospitality, wellness and rooftop experiences in a way that contributes to the city well beyond 2032.” A year ago, Brisbane 2032 president Andrew Liveris said a lack of sufficient accommodation was something that kept him up at night and, just last month, industry leaders discussed innovative ways, such as cruise ships and camping, to address the expected shortfall. The new Victory Tower would include a rooptop bar. Bureau Proberts Designed by Bureau Proberts, the slender tower has been positioned in the north-eastern corner of the site at the corner of Edward and Charlotte streets. Planning documents argued the design’s narrow footprint and setbacks would preserve views of the historic pub, which has operated on the site since 1855 and was recognised by the council as the oldest remaining pub in Brisbane’s CBD.



The project was supported by heritage architect Ruth Woods, who previously advised that the development would not compromise the prominence of the Victory Hotel or neighbouring heritage-listed buildings, including the former Metro Arts building. Related Article Pubs ‘Remarkable hotel’: Plans for a rooftop bar, balcony at the Victory If built, the tower would include a publicly accessible rooftop bar with panoramic city and river views, along with hospitality spaces intended to connect with the refurbished hotel below. Precision said restoration work at the Victory Hotel was already under way. The heritage pub was being reconfigured into four venues – a sports bar and beer garden, a rooftop garden bar, a steakhouse restaurant and a basement speakeasy with a gaming room.



The company took direct control of the hotel’s operations earlier this year and said discussions were continuing with prospective hotel operators. “We are already seeing strong interest from respected hotel operators who recognise the strength of the location, the heritage of the Victory Hotel and the opportunity to help shape a new hospitality destination for Brisbane,” Bonett said. “Getting that partnership right matters. It will help ensure Victory Tower is not only successful as a hotel but also contributes meaningfully to the wider CBD precinct.” The construction timetable would not be confirmed until an agreement was reached, but Precision expected the tower to be completed before 2032. World.title: ‘Just business’: Brethren leaders admit meeting far-right – and Trump
World.content:
NationalInvestigations ‘Just business’: Brethren leaders admit meeting far-right – and Trump Sherryn Groch and Michael Bachelard Updated October 16, 2026 — 8:22pm ,first published 6:24pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The son of the Exclusive Brethren’s world leader has admitted meeting with far-right agitators and belonging to secret chats where neo-Nazi associates and Brethren elders plotted an “election influence” campaign of stunts targeting left-leaning MPs at the last election. But, in a fiery three-hour hearing before a parliamentary inquiry on Friday, Gareth Hales claimed the meetings were “just business”, and not about campaigning. Hales appearing via video link at the inquiry. Alex Ellinghausen In his own testimony before the joint standing committee examining the 2025 election, Exclusive Brethren leader Bruce Hales revealed that members of the secretive sect have met with US President Donald Trump in New York. Senators questioning the Hales were frequently interrupted by Coalition MPs who slammed the inquiry as a “witch hunt” and religious discrimination – a line that is also being pushed by far-right lobby group Turning Point in America.



Gareth Hales confirmed that he had met then opposition leader Peter Dutton and his staffers in 2025, though he called the encounter “brief”. Both Gareth and Bruce Hales insisted their church, which is now known as the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church, did not directly order members to turn out in their thousands around the country and covertly campaign for the Coalition, as revealed by this masthead. Committee chair, Labor’s Jerome Laxale, and independent Monique Ryan were among MPs who said they were not persuaded by the Haleses’ evidence. “It had all the credibility of a Melbourne weather forecast,” said Ryan, after the hearing. “I’m not buying what you’re selling,” independent and former Nationals MP Andrew Gee told Gareth Hales flatly before proceedings wrapped. The father and son of the normally secretive church were called to give evidence, under threat of subpoena, by the parliamentary committee after leaked messages published by this masthead revealed that Gareth was among the church elders party to a secret stunt campaign where far-right agitators were paid to ambush MPs at campaign events and hotels.



The investigation found Brethren elders followed the prime minister’s car and plane and fed “private intel” on his location to neo-Nazi associates. Gareth Hales’ company Sante Global was also implicated in the stunt operation. A meeting of Brethren elders and far-right figures at a Sydney golf club was booked in the company’s name in April last year. Bruce Hales (top row, centre) appears via video link during the inquiry on Friday. Alex Ellinghausen Hales claimed that the meeting was about business, not the election. But he also confirmed that he had met with key far-right figures involved in the Brethren stunt operation, Chris De Bruyne and Morgan C Jonas, including at his Sante offices. De Bruyne and Jonas endorsed Brethren posters and ads that appeared during the election, including the mysterious “Make Australia smile again” signs which reflected a phrase used by Bruce Hales.



Asked about the phrase, Bruce Hales told the committee that “there was a certain amount of discontent, as I viewed it, with the present government” in 2025 ahead of the election, but he denied his catchcry of “Make Australia smile again” was a direction to his sons to campaign rather a general comment about the government. Loading Both Bruce Hales and his son failed to answer repeated questions about whether they would investigate or take any action about revelations of Brethren involvement in the election, including the influence operation with neo-Nazi associates. Bruce Hales said he had not read the articles about the stunt campaign, but at times launched blistering attacks on one of this masthead’s reporters, Michael Bachelard. Loading



Gareth Hales, meanwhile, stressed he was giving testimony to the committee as a “private citizen” and claimed to have no formal role in the church, although he said he was its most senior figure. Related Article Exclusive

Investigations ‘Tail, film, heckle’: Inside the Brethren’s secret election influence plot with the far-right He said he was “not active” in group chats with the far-right and other Brethren elders co-ordinating the stunts, and that he campaigned “alongside many others” in 2025. Simply “campaigning alongside someone else does not mean adopting every opinion they have ever expressed”, he said. Gareth also claimed that he never asked Brethren members to campaign, prompting interjections from chair Laxale when Gareth Hales later conceded that he had encouraged them. Leaked videos of Gareth and his brothers urging Brethren to “man polling booths” and “dominate the play” on the campaign trail were just meant to “encourage people to get out in their democratic right,” Gareth said.



“I might have offered a little bit of encouragement [to the Brethren campaigning] but in no way did I direct them all.” Loading He also claimed he would have called out poor behaviour such as intimidating MPs, and repeated the Brethren line used throughout the election that members campaigning, including himself, were simply “businessmen ... concerned about the direction the country was heading”. Gareth Hales was himself photographed among the Brethren who donned blue Liberal Party T-shirts to campaign on the ground for a Coalition victory. Bruce Hales told the committee that he first realised Gareth’s involvement in the campaign when he saw that photo published by this masthead, and had no idea about the stunt operation with the far-right.



“I can understand how you might find it hard to believe,” he told MPs. But “I had no knowledge of those events before. I had no part in planning them, I think if they’d asked me about them, and asked permission, I would have denied it.” Gareth Hales (centre) campaigning for the Liberals at the last federal election. “So do you think that your sons deliberately didn’t ask you about it?” Labor senator Corinne Mulholland pressed. “Quite likely,” Hales replied. He conceded his sermons were rarely misinterpreted by his flock – when quizzed about his recent preaching to Brethren members of the need to keep “our secrets” from “men in the world”.



Gareth Hales denied there was any link with his father’s Scripture and the subsequent election campaign. Bruce Hales was also questioned about his history of statements defined by some Jewish groups as antisemitism, including calling Jews “wicked … infidel”. He said the church had been praying for Israel since the outbreak of war in the Middle East and that he himself had Jewish heritage in his family. But he added “there’s quite a bit of history ... to the Jewish matter or the Jewish question”, saying that “the Jews aren’t exactly referred to favourably because they were the ones that finally clamoured publicly for Christ to be crucified”. Lester Sharples, a Brethren elder who confirmed his involvement in the far-right stunts to this masthead, was also called to give evidence but declined to attend, as did two other senior Brethren figures called. Both Gareth and Bruce claimed not to have spoken to Sharples recently.



Gee accused Liberal MP Ben Small of “running a protection racket” for the Brethren as Small and Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie led Coalition interruptions supporting the church leaders throughout the hearing, but he later withdrew the remark. “This is beginning to look like religious discrimination,” McKenzie shouted at one point. “This isn’t the Spanish Inquisition!” Tensions flared again when Gee asked Bruce Hales whether his testimony was truthful. “Who’s asking that?” Bruce Hales immediately demanded to know, and later told the committee he felt he was being “targeted”.



Gee also expressed doubt about Gareth Hales’ testimony. “Given that the evidence before this committee is that thousands of members of your church actively participated in a co-ordinated way in the 2025 federal election campaign, can you understand how people might find the church’s denial that it had any role … very difficult to believe? It defies belief,” he said. Hales said he understood that “it’s difficult to believe”. “But they weren’t members of the church. They were members of concerned business groups and … private citizens. They weren’t there on behalf of the church,” he said. Gee’s attempts to ask Gareth Hales about whether the Brethren were given access, or tried to get access, to an Australian Electoral Commission database was met with repeated interjections from Small.



“If members of your church are being given access to the Australian Electoral Commission database, I think that is an issue of national concern,” Gee said. Gareth Hales said: “Well, now that you’ve said concerned five times, yes I’m very concerned.” Former and current members of the Brethren, many of them watching the hearings online, have spoken out in horror since the relevations of the far-right plot by church elders emerged. Some say the Brethren is a controlling sect, not a religion. Former prime minister Kevin Rudd and the current PM, Anthony Albanese, both described the Exclusive Brethren as a cult, as have many former members. “I thought it was a bit rough,” Gareth Hales told the committee. “Mr Rudd, Mr Albanese branded [the Brethren] as a cult … they haven’t ever sat down with us and chatted to us or talked to us.”



Labor has slammed the “intimidation” campaign against Labor and other Coalition opponents as an attack on democracy, while extremism experts have called for an investigation and teal donor Climate 200 has referred the church to the charity regulator for investigation. Committee members expressed scepticism about an apparently coincidental meeting Gareth Hales had with then-opposition leader Peter Dutton. Labor MP Shayne Neumann asked how Hales happened to be at a petrol station in Carlingford for Dutton’s fuel announcement. “I had no telephone conversations with those people,” Hales answered. “So magically and mysteriously, you just happened to have turned up to a petrol station where the leader of the opposition and his staff were?” Neumann said.



“It wasn’t magic or mysterious. It was just known that he was going to turn up there,” Hales said. Neumann said election campaigns did not work that way, with even the press gallery only told about leader events at short notice. “Have you heard, Mr Neumann, of word of mouth?” replied Gareth. Bruce Hales also confirmed during the hearing that Brethren members have met with US President Donald Trump. “I understand there have been some members in the New York area who have met Mr Trump briefly. I have never met him, nor have I ever directed anybody to,” he said.



Related Article Investigations Brethren a controlling sect, not a religion, former and current members say Hales said he was not sure if senior Brethren had also trained in election campaigning with Trump’s MAGA movement in the US, as reported by this masthead, and was asked to take the question on notice. Independent MP Monique Ryan asked Bruce Hales whether church members believed that he was “a direct messenger from God?”. “Well, I would think that they would say that what I get, I get from the Lord,” he replied. Ryan also asked about how he became the leader of the church – which Hales said arose “spontaneously” from his flock globally.

Located opposite the heritage-listed Hunter Baillie Memorial Church, Hunter House features symmetrical curves, pointed roof forms, glazing and six-metre ceilings. The materials are also striking. Built from double brick, concrete and steel, the interiors feature walnut joinery, marble, terrazzo and Venetian plaster. Other features include four bedrooms, a wellness room or a gym and a four-car garage. 74 Davidson Avenue, Concord NSW



This brand-new double-brick Concord home features a stylish, statement facade with curved lines and arched windows. Like something from an architectural magazine, the resort-style exterior features a sunken lounge overlooking a circular swimming pool, a spa and established greenery. Inside, high ceilings, glazing, floor-to-ceiling windows and a marble staircase stand out, along with premium finishes such as a marble kitchen and a wine cellar. The property backs onto Central Park and is close to Majors Bay Road Village and public transport. 1/15 Woodlands Avenue, Breakfast Point NSW



Originally built c. 1915 for the AGL gasworks and now heritage-listed, The Plumber Workshop was converted in 2021 into 14 residences, with number one currently for sale. The residence wraps around the building’s corner over two levels. The original brick exterior is a show-stopping feature in its own right, as are the arched, steel-framed windows and the living and dining room, which rises two storeys. The master bedroom suite occupies the entire upper floor and includes a bedroom with a round-arched window overlooking the void, a media room lined with library joinery, a fitted walk-in robe and an en suite.



Membership of the Breakfast Point Country Club is included with the apartment and provides access to the pools, gym, tennis and sauna. 15a Milner Crescent, Wollstonecraft NSW This contemporary terrace offers family luxury with five bedrooms, including a master with a large en suite and a balcony. Set across two levels, the home uses curves and mixes materials in its facade and interior.



There is an expansive living, dining and kitchen area, with the latter equipped with quality cabinetry, Calacatta Amore marble benchtops, premium appliances and a butler’s pantry. Other highlights include double-glazed windows, oak timber floors, 100 per cent wool carpets, and a private, landscaped rear garden with a natural-stone-paved entertaining area. 31 Vale Street, Gordon NSW With approximately 1650 square metres of private grounds, a full-size tennis court, a swimming pool with a waterfall and a concealed wellness room, this property makes you feel as if you are living in your own resort.



The interiors are largely the same, with a sunlit music room, a sauna and a formal lounge featuring an open fireplace, a ceiling-mounted projector and a motorised screen. World.title: ‘It means everything’: How Melbourne scientists are fighting to save Poppy’s sight
World.content:
NationalVictoriaMelbourne Assembly ‘It means everything’: How Melbourne scientists are fighting to save Poppy’s sight Henrietta Cook October 16, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Melbourne Assembly brings together the people, ideas and conversations shaping the future of our city. See all stories .

When Poppy Stevens was just a few months old, she received a devastating diagnosis. After failing her newborn hearing test, genetic testing confirmed the little girl had Usher syndrome, which meant she might also lose her vision. Poppy Stevens and her mother Ali. Poppy, 5, has a faulty gene too big for gene therapy. Ben Jones “It was a second wave of devastation,” reflects her mother Ali Stevens, who lives in Melbourne’s south-east.



“Suddenly I’m thinking, ‘is my child going to be blind?’ We were going through the worst-case scenarios ... Is she going to work? Is she going to drive? Will this make it harder for her to have a family? Is she going to live with us for the rest of her life?” A team of Melbourne researchers is determined to alleviate these anxieties and provide a cure for the vision loss faced by children like Poppy, who is now five and uses a hearing aid. Usher syndrome is the primary cause of deafblindness in Australia and impacts about one in 6000 children. Children are typically born with hearing loss, and then progressively lose their vision during their adolescence and early adulthood. At the Centre for Eye Research Australia, managing director Professor Keith Martin and Professor Guei-Sheung (Rick) Liu are creating a treatment called EDITRA that aims to correct the tiny spelling mistake in a person’s genetic code that causes Poppy’s variant of Usher syndrome, type 2A. The project, developed by the centre’s new spin-out company Adara Bio, overcomes a major barrier to treatment for patients with Usher syndrome, whose mutated genes are too large to fit into current gene therapies.



By fixing the cell’s genetic instructions (known as its RNA) instead of replacing the large gene that causes the syndrome, the treatment fits inside a single modified virus that is injected into the eye. As part of the next week’s Melbourne Assembly civic forum, The Age has been exploring big ideas for the future of the city, including how to maintain and enhance Melbourne’s status as a global leader in medical research and innovation. Loading Martin, who is also chair of the Association of Australian Medical Research Institutes Victoria, left his job at the University of Cambridge and moved to Melbourne seven years ago because he was attracted to the city’s “biotech ecosystem”. “Melbourne’s cluster of medical research institutes, universities, industry and the start-up ecosystem is really attractive,” he said.



Related Series

City life Melbourne Assembly He says the city rivals Boston and London as one of the world’s top research destinations, with its medical research institutes employing more than 7500 people and delivering more than $600 million to the state’s economy every year. This eclipses the annual economic benefit of the Australian Open ($566 million) and the Grand Prix ($350 million). But the sector is not without its problems. Martin warns that Victoria risks losing its edge as a global biotech hub without stronger state and federal investment and more local manufacturing facilities.



“There’s sometimes a complacency from the Victorian government that we’re world leading and will remain world leading,” he says. “Unless we support this with more funding, we’re going to lose our preeminence within Australia and globally. It’s not easily recoverable.” Modelling commissioned by the peak body indicates that without a significant funding increase, 10 of the state’s 14 independent medical research institutes will be at risk of closure by 2030. They receive their funding from federal government grants, philanthropy, commercial activities and the state government. The Hudson Institute of Medical Research in Clayton. Luis Enrique Ascui Last month, The Age revealed the 66-year-old Hudson Institute of Medical Research would stop operating independently and cut at least 75 jobs. Victorian Minister for Medical Research Anthony Carbines said at the time that the government had increased funding for the state’s research institutes by $24.6 million over two years, with more than $47.7 million flowing to the sector last financial year. This, he says, is the largest amount of funding for indirect research costs provided by any Australian state or territory.



Despite these funding concerns, ground-breaking research continues. Martin and his team are testing their treatment for Usher syndrome on miniature eye models they have grown in a lab. They hope to start clinical trials within three years. The technology has the potential to fix other inherited retinal diseases, including genetic forms of macular degeneration. Poppy Stevens, 5, (front, centre) and her mum Ali, sister Evie, 7, and dad Ben. Poppy has a genetic condition called Usher syndrome which leads to hearing and vision loss. Ben Jones “It’s beautifully controllable, it’s like molecular surgery,” Martin explains. “We can very precisely change the gene to correct those errors.”



The research has provided hope to the Stevens family. “It could completely change Poppy’s future,” Ali says. “Instead of planning for her going blind, our plans can be about where we are going to travel and what we are going to do together. It means everything.” Just a few blocks away from the lab where scientists are working on a treatment for Usher syndrome, a young man with electrodes strapped to his shaved head recites a series of nonsense sentences in a Faraday room, which blocks electromagnetic fields. Scientist Dean Freestone is developing a brain-computer interface that translates intended speech from neural signals into communication. Luis Enrique Ascui “These days chicken leg is a rare dish,” Jay Marinis says from the carpeted room in the Aikenhead Centre for Medical Discovery, which is co-located at St Vincent’s Hospital Melbourne and accelerates the commercialisation of medical and health research.



“A zestful food is a hot cross bun.” Related Article Melbourne Assembly How innovation hubs at Parkville and Clayton can put Melbourne on top of the world Marinis is being paid $40 an hour to read these sentences aloud, then mouth them and then think them. It’s all in the name of research – he’s helping a team of Melbourne scientists and entrepreneurs create a device called Fluent that translates what a person intends to say from brain signals into communication. If the innovation kicks off, it would transform the lives of 100 million people around the world who have lost the ability to speak or have a profound speech deficit. This includes people with throat and mouth cancer, cerebral palsy, Motor Neuron Disease, Parkinson’s, non-verbal autism and those who have suffered a stroke. While the device might seem like the stuff of science fiction, Dean Freestone, the co-founder and chief technology officer of Fluent, aims to launch it in 2030.



“The device goes under the skin and is completely invisible – similar to a cochlear implant,” he says, referring to bionic ear which was developed at the University of Melbourne in 1978. “It’s inserted through a small incision, unfurls under the scalp, and can be done in an outpatient clinic in 20 minutes.” While the project has an ambitious timeline, many years of research underpins it. Fluent co-founders Dean Freestone and Tim Mahoney with Lachlan Hill, who is wearing their tech. Jason South Freestone previously helped create a device that is implanted beneath the scalp’s surface which predicts seizures among patient with epilepsy. Within the space of eight years, the Epiminder device went from basic research through to regulatory approvals and is now available in the US.



With the assistance of artificial intelligence, researchers discovered that the brain measurements detected by this technology could also be used to decode intended speech. “It’s not reading your background inner monologue,” Freestone says. “It’s the signals that go from our brain to our speech muscles.” While Freestone views Melbourne as a world-class clinical research hub, he says it’s constrained by a small local market and a lower appetite for risk among investors. “It’s just chalk and cheese compared to Silicon Valley,” Freestone says. “Australians want to invest in things that are going to have an expected return within a few years, whereas a medical device will take longer.” Melbourne Assembly will be held from October 19 to October 21. More information is available on the Melbourne Assembly website.

World.title: Why this seven-year-old, $34 shot might just be poised to spring an almighty Everest upset
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Why this seven-year-old, $34 shot might just be poised to spring an almighty Everest upset Craig Kerry October 16, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Clayton Douglas didn’t expect to have 2022 Everest winner Giga Kick back for another assault two years later, when it was runner-up – let alone for a third attempt on Saturday at seven years old. And he is not expecting the winner of $15.5 million to upset “generational” talent Ka Ying Rising or brilliant mare Tempted in the $20 million Everest (1200m) at Randwick. Clayton Douglas with Giga Kick in 2023, when he was the defending Everest champion. Louise Kennerley But on a potential heavy surface, the Victorian trainer is daring to dream that his wet-track marvel can add another successful chapter to his Everest story. “He’s actually got the best record out of this field in this race ... so far,” Douglas said, with the prospect of Ka Ying Rising likely winning back-to-back titles on Saturday to join Redzel as the only two-time champions.



“Third would be a great result, but you know how Sydney works. If they get a downpour raceday, it’s a wet track and Ka Ying doesn’t handle it, something happens with Tempted, you just don’t know. It’s still a horse race. “You saw Sheza Alibi get beat the other day, and no one thought she would get beat by Land Legend [in the Might And Power]. They are animals, and they can have an off day – although he’s going to have to have a very off day to get beat. Giga Kick winning the 2022 Everest. Getty Images “I’m under no illusions. He’s a seven-year-old and this Ka Ying Rising is a generational horse, and there’s nothing to suggest he might even be better on soft ground. And what price would Tempted be if he wasn’t there? The way she won the Premiere, she’d be odds-on. “The times he’s been running are freakish. But I can’t fault Giga Kick, he’s going great. He’s the same weight as when he ran second to Bella Nipotina [in 2024]. He’s trialled good. I think the blinkers might give him an edge, a point of difference in the twilight of his career. He’s finally got a gear change.



“He’ll run really well and hopefully there is a bit more rain to come.” Randwick was a soft 7 on Friday afternoon after almost 100mm of rain in the past week. Predicted scattered showers could keep it in that range. The likelihood of a rain-affected track has given Ka Ying Rising’s rivals, Douglas included, a glimmer of hope, given 20 of his 22 wins have come on good Sha Tin surfaces. Giga Kick’s trainer Clayton Douglas and jockey Craig Williams with The Everest trophy in 2022. Getty Giga Kick is one of just two three-year-olds to win the Everest, a victory he achieved on a soft 6 track. A muscle tear ruled then him out for 12 months, before he returned for second place on a soft 5 in the 2024 Everest. He was also second in the TJ Smith Stakes over the Randwick 1200m on a heavy 9 and soft 7. His most recent win, in the Champions Sprint (1200m) at Flemington last November, was on a “real bog track”. That came after a poor winter campaign and delayed return, which cost him an Everest call-up last year.



“I’ve got him back on the right leg this time around, and it’s good to see him there. To get to three Everests, not many have done that,” he said. “I didn’t think he’d back as a five-year-old running in it, after he hurt himself. Then to get beat a short margin in 2024, it just goes to show he’s an amazing horse, a champion.” Giga Kick wins the Champions Sprint at Flemington last November. Getty Images Douglas admitted it was a surprise to see Giga Kick picked up late to replace the injured Guest House in Coolmore’s slot, following a four-lengths eighth in the Manikato Stakes (1200m). He was 10th first-up in the Moir (1000m). Douglas was confident, though, the veteran was going better than his recent form reads. “He ran the fourth fastest last 600m in the Moir,” he said.



Related Article Opinion

The Everest The Rising part II: We know how this movie should end, but wet track could deliver Everest boilover Ally Mosley Expert analyst for Sky Racing and presenter for the Nine Network “The thing outside him annoyed him, and he likes a bit of room. And he needed the run. He was really big in condition, and he’s not a 1000m horse. “Then in the Manikato we drew low with the rail out 13 metres, which wasn’t a great set up for us. Then the expected rain didn’t come. He didn’t run bad.” As for the extreme outside draw, he said: “I don’t think barrier 12 is too much of a problem. There looks to be a lot of speed, so he should be able to get an OK run off the back of them.” Giga Kick, with Sydney jockey Dylan Gibbons aboard, was $34 with TAB.



‘No Pride Of Jenni’: Likely leader to go his own pace in King Charles Victorian trainer Gavin Bedggood says Just Folk won’t be doing a Pride Of Jenni in the $5 million King Charles III Stakes (1609m) as the veteran mudlark searches for a hefty cheque. Much to the dismay of racing fans, front-running hero Pride Of Jenni was scratched from the race late on Thursday because of a leg infection. Just Folk, left, winning the 2024 Hawkesbury Cup. Getty Images The prospect of the nine-year-old setting a cracking tempo for superstar Autumn Glow and two-time King Charles champion Ceolwulf to chase was set to make the six-horse race a highlight of the Everest program. With her out, Chris Waller-trained Autumn Glow, Australia’s champion of last season, firmed into $1.28 and Ceolwulf drifted to $3.70.



Trainer Joe Pride was confident Ceolwulf, which has surged to victory from back in the field the past two years, would get his chance to challenge Autumn Glow in a truly run race on wet ground. While the soft track remains, Ceolwulf’s chances of a solid tempo up front now look to sit with 10-year-old Just Folk ($26) – a go-forward horse and the only other challenger not from Waller’s stable. Just Folk has three wins and four placings from 10 heavy track runs, and finished top three 16 times in 23 attempts on soft. Those wins include the Doncaster Prelude and Ajax Stakes in Sydney and he has placed in his past five runs. Bedggood said the wet track at Randwick and prizemoney on offer prompted the trip north, but he was not planning a Pride Of Jenni-style breakaway out front. The King Charles offers $125,000 for fifth, while third takes home $425,000. “I’m a realist and I wouldn’t think that we could run in the top two, but third or fourth is a definite possibility,” Bedggood said.



“He loves wet ground and any rain over the next 24 hours is only going to help his cause. “His racing pattern is obviously laid bare. He goes forward and he looks the leader in that race, and what will be, will be. “He’s definitely not a Pride Of Jenni. We will just be riding him where he’s comfortable. “Jamie Mott knows my horse and I don’t have to tell him too much. He knows how he needs to be ridden and we won’t be doing anything out of the normal. “He just needs to go a good, even gallop. Not go too slow, or too quick.



Related Article The Everest The WhatsApp message, the deal, the pressure and perks: The tell all on Ka Ying Rising “He’s been a great money spinner for his connections and he will run well again.” Mott and Bedggood also combine at Randwick with Tempesti ($21) in the St Leger Stakes (2600m). A recent addition to Bedggood’s Cranbourne stable from Matt Cumani, the eight-year-old has six wins and two thirds from nine heavy track starts. “It’s his first run for us and we haven’t had him long, but he’s pleased us,” Bedggood said. “He’s had a gap between runs and he’s got form on wet ground, so that’s why we are taking him up. There’s options in Victoria but our tracks are getting firm.”

World.content:
PropertyNewsVictoria residential property Five of the best Melbourne homes that stand out from the crowd Shona Hendley October 16, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 Gift this free article Share full article with anyone — no subscription needed to read it. Whether it’s a mixed-material facade, a statement entry, landscaped gardens, feature lighting, bold palettes, or distinct architectural focal points, homes that stand out from the crowd capture attention and offer a unique point of difference. Here are five of the best Melbourne homes that stand out from the crowd. 251-255 Moray Street, South Melbourne VIC This landmark South Melbourne warehouse definitely leaves an impression!



“Irish Linen House” ca. 1920 comprises three separate addresses across its two titles and two independent residences and offers both residential and commercial zoning. From its triple-frontage facade to its interiors, its warehouse origins run through both levels of 253-255. A renovation preserves these features, including high reclaimed-timber ceilings with Oregon beams, while transforming the building into a contemporary residence. Number 251 is an entirely independent two-bedroom residence with its own living and dining areas, kitchen and private courtyard. 18 Dominion Road, Mount Martha VIC



With attention to detail like no other, “Handmade House”, as it is called, was almost entirely hand-built by Ross Bakker of Bakka Constructions for his own family. Baker hand-laminated rare, furniture-grade West African Danta into the rafters and stair treads, while architect and furniture maker Adam Markowitz turned the rest into joinery, cladding and lighting, including a copper-sleeved stair rail. The house’s H-plan floorplan epitomises mid-century design, separating living from sleeping areas with two courtyards at the centre. The main living zone and main suite are upstairs to capture the northern light and offer views of Port Phillip Bay. 41 Elizabeth Street, Malvern VIC



Recently completed, this architect-designed Malvern residence features softly rendered Krause brickwork on the exterior facade. Natural limestone, limewash walls, a French oak staircase, and Patagonia natural stone are among the materials used throughout the home’s interiors. High ceilings and a double-height void flood the home with natural light. The kitchen stands out for its richly toned cabinetry, Miele appliances, a butler’s pantry, and window seating that offers views of the outdoors. The exterior is equally impressive, with landscaped pool and grounds by Kate Patterson. 28 Old Mornington Road, Mount Eliza



Set behind landscaped gardens, this single-level home features four-metre ceilings and clerestory windows, creating a naturally lit interior. The open-plan living, dining, and kitchen areas feature polished concrete floors and a stone-clad fireplace that opens to a covered, decked alfresco area overlooking an active-edge pool and spa. A second entertaining area, with a barbecue and outdoor kitchen, faces an outdoor lounge, and a showcase double garage alongside has glass doors that stack into the wall cavity. The property is located close to Mount Eliza Village and local schools.

26 Euston Street, Malvern VIC With a bold architectural facade, this Luciano Bologna-designed home features raw materials and a contemporary design.



Set over three levels, the basement level features a home office and a guest bathroom, while the ground floor is home to one bedroom and an open-plan living, dining and kitchen area, and the four remaining bedrooms, including the master, are located on the first floor. The home utilises timber flooring, high ceilings, light wells, raw materials and refined finishes. Outside, there is a north-facing alfresco and established gardens.
