World.title: Cities impacted by longer, more severe bushfires: study
World.content:
NationalQueenslandBushfires Cities impacted by longer, more severe bushfires: study Courtney Kruk October 16, 2026 — 9:23pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Bushfires are impacting Queensland’s urban air quality more frequently and more severely than previously understood, new research has found, with pollution travelling further across the state, and for longer, increasing public health risks. The study led by researchers from the Queensland University of Technology analysed air quality data from 22 urban monitoring sites across Queensland between 2008 and 2023. It found bushfire smoke can increase fine particle pollution (PM2.5) by up to 160.5 per cent during a fire event, and ozone levels by up to 33.2 per cent during fire-active seasons (July to December). A QUT-led study found bushfire smoke is affecting Queensland urban air quality more often and more severely than previously understood. Nick Moir Between 2018 and 2023, bushfire-impacted hours during the fire-active season were approximately three times more frequent, compared with 2008–2017.



Lead researcher Dr Zijun Li said climate change has increased the frequency and ferocity of bushfires, with longer burn times increasing pollution levels. Related Article Exclusive

Pollution Air pollution kills 1 million a year – hundreds of whom are Australians “Climate change and heatwave conditions are favouring the conditions of the bushfires,” Li said. “Bushfire smoke is not only a problem for communities located near fires. “Our research shows emissions can travel hundreds or even thousands of kilometres and significantly affect air quality in urban areas far from the source.



“As climate change increases the frequency and intensity of bushfires in many regions, understanding how smoke affects urban air quality is becoming increasingly important.” PM2.5 – the fine particle matter emitted during wildfires – is small enough to penetrate deep into the lungs and bloodstream, and is linked to respiratory and cardiovascular health impacts. Gold Coast University Hospital doctor Yian Zhao moved from China to Australia as a child because of his asthma. Gold Coast University Hospital Gold Coast University Hospital doctor Yian Zhao has suffered asthma since early childhood, and moved from China to Australia when he was 11 because of the difference in air quality. “Industrial smoke and allergies are the main [asthma] triggers for me,” Zhao, who grew up in Adelaide, said.



“[In China] we lived in a heavily industrialised area as well. The dust, smoke, air quality … some days you could barely see five metres in front of you because of how bad it was. “So my parents made the decision to move over to Australia.” Since moving from South Australia to Queensland, Zhao said his exposure to bushfire events has been minimal. But he can feel changes to air quality, and worries about the impact of longer and more severe bushfire seasons. “I look at it from both sides, as a doctor and a patient myself,” he said. “For me, it gets a little bit harder to breathe whenever there’s smoke in the air, to the point where I’ll probably preemptively take some more of my puffers.



(Left to right) Huon Morton, Dr Zijun Li, Adjunct Professor Zoran Ristovski and Mr Hongzhi Zhang worked on the study analysing air quality data from 22 urban monitoring sites in Queensland. Queensland University of Technology “[In the public health system] the number of resources that we do have is finite … so an increase in bushfires would definitely put a stress on both things.” Li said the research also revealed insights into how bushfire smoke behaves and affects communities, with stronger fires affecting urban pollutants. “Ozone formation is complex. We found bushfire emissions can interact with local urban emissions, particularly nitrogen oxides from vehicles and industry, to increase ozone concentrations,” Li said. “This means bushfire smoke can worsen air quality even when the fires are a long way from the city.”

World.content:
NationalQueenslandHotels Victory for developers planning new tower over popular CBD pub Cameron Atfield October 16, 2026 — 9:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. A planned 51-storey hotel tower above Brisbane’s landmark Victory Hotel CBD pub has received council approval, paving the way for a major accommodation development ahead of the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games. Brisbane City Council approved Precision Group’s proposed Victory Tower, a 206.6-metre development behind and above the heritage-listed hotel, on Monday. As part of the approval, Precision Group would be required to pay almost $2 million in infrastructure charges to the council. Precision Group is planning a new tower behind the Victory Hotel in Brisbane Bureau Proberts The new tower would be built on the site of the pub’s popular beer garden.



The approval marks a significant milestone for the project, which would transform the site into a 284-room hotel with restaurants, function spaces, wellness facilities, a rooftop bar and a swimming pool on the 40th floor. The 16,000-square-metre tower will be built on a 924-square-metre site and occupies the area currently used as the Victory’s Charlotte Street-facing beer garden. Precision Group founder and chief executive Shaun Bonett said the development would help address Brisbane’s hotel room shortage as the city prepares for the 2032 Games. “The critical shortfall of hotel rooms in Brisbane is well documented and the demand for accommodation is accelerating,” he said. “The Victory Hotel is one of Brisbane’s most recognised hospitality landmarks.



“Our vision is to honour that history while giving the site a new future, bringing together heritage, hotel accommodation, hospitality, wellness and rooftop experiences in a way that contributes to the city well beyond 2032.” A year ago, Brisbane 2032 president Andrew Liveris said a lack of sufficient accommodation was something that kept him up at night and, just last month, industry leaders discussed innovative ways, such as cruise ships and camping, to address the expected shortfall. The new Victory Tower would include a rooptop bar. Bureau Proberts Designed by Bureau Proberts, the slender tower has been positioned in the north-eastern corner of the site at the corner of Edward and Charlotte streets. Planning documents argued the design’s narrow footprint and setbacks would preserve views of the historic pub, which has operated on the site since 1855 and was recognised by the council as the oldest remaining pub in Brisbane’s CBD.



The project was supported by heritage architect Ruth Woods, who previously advised that the development would not compromise the prominence of the Victory Hotel or neighbouring heritage-listed buildings, including the former Metro Arts building. Related Article Pubs ‘Remarkable hotel’: Plans for a rooftop bar, balcony at the Victory If built, the tower would include a publicly accessible rooftop bar with panoramic city and river views, along with hospitality spaces intended to connect with the refurbished hotel below. Precision said restoration work at the Victory Hotel was already under way. The heritage pub was being reconfigured into four venues – a sports bar and beer garden, a rooftop garden bar, a steakhouse restaurant and a basement speakeasy with a gaming room.



The company took direct control of the hotel’s operations earlier this year and said discussions were continuing with prospective hotel operators. “We are already seeing strong interest from respected hotel operators who recognise the strength of the location, the heritage of the Victory Hotel and the opportunity to help shape a new hospitality destination for Brisbane,” Bonett said. “Getting that partnership right matters. It will help ensure Victory Tower is not only successful as a hotel but also contributes meaningfully to the wider CBD precinct.” The construction timetable would not be confirmed until an agreement was reached, but Precision expected the tower to be completed before 2032. World.title: ‘Just business’: Brethren leaders admit meeting far-right – and Trump
World.content:
NationalInvestigations ‘Just business’: Brethren leaders admit meeting far-right – and Trump Sherryn Groch and Michael Bachelard Updated October 16, 2026 — 8:22pm ,first published 6:24pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The son of the Exclusive Brethren’s world leader has admitted meeting with far-right agitators and belonging to secret chats where neo-Nazi associates and Brethren elders plotted an “election influence” campaign of stunts targeting left-leaning MPs at the last election. But, in a fiery three-hour hearing before a parliamentary inquiry on Friday, Gareth Hales claimed the meetings were “just business”, and not about campaigning. Hales appearing via video link at the inquiry. Alex Ellinghausen In his own testimony before the joint standing committee examining the 2025 election, Exclusive Brethren leader Bruce Hales revealed that members of the secretive sect have met with US President Donald Trump in New York. Senators questioning the Hales were frequently interrupted by Coalition MPs who slammed the inquiry as a “witch hunt” and religious discrimination – a line that is also being pushed by far-right lobby group Turning Point in America.



Gareth Hales confirmed that he had met then opposition leader Peter Dutton and his staffers in 2025, though he called the encounter “brief”. Both Gareth and Bruce Hales insisted their church, which is now known as the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church, did not directly order members to turn out in their thousands around the country and covertly campaign for the Coalition, as revealed by this masthead. Committee chair, Labor’s Jerome Laxale, and independent Monique Ryan were among MPs who said they were not persuaded by the Haleses’ evidence. “It had all the credibility of a Melbourne weather forecast,” said Ryan, after the hearing. “I’m not buying what you’re selling,” independent and former Nationals MP Andrew Gee told Gareth Hales flatly before proceedings wrapped. The father and son of the normally secretive church were called to give evidence, under threat of subpoena, by the parliamentary committee after leaked messages published by this masthead revealed that Gareth was among the church elders party to a secret stunt campaign where far-right agitators were paid to ambush MPs at campaign events and hotels.



The investigation found Brethren elders followed the prime minister’s car and plane and fed “private intel” on his location to neo-Nazi associates. Gareth Hales’ company Sante Global was also implicated in the stunt operation. A meeting of Brethren elders and far-right figures at a Sydney golf club was booked in the company’s name in April last year. Bruce Hales (top row, centre) appears via video link during the inquiry on Friday. Alex Ellinghausen Hales claimed that the meeting was about business, not the election. But he also confirmed that he had met with key far-right figures involved in the Brethren stunt operation, Chris De Bruyne and Morgan C Jonas, including at his Sante offices. De Bruyne and Jonas endorsed Brethren posters and ads that appeared during the election, including the mysterious “Make Australia smile again” signs which reflected a phrase used by Bruce Hales.



Asked about the phrase, Bruce Hales told the committee that “there was a certain amount of discontent, as I viewed it, with the present government” in 2025 ahead of the election, but he denied his catchcry of “Make Australia smile again” was a direction to his sons to campaign rather a general comment about the government. Loading Both Bruce Hales and his son failed to answer repeated questions about whether they would investigate or take any action about revelations of Brethren involvement in the election, including the influence operation with neo-Nazi associates. Bruce Hales said he had not read the articles about the stunt campaign, but at times launched blistering attacks on one of this masthead’s reporters, Michael Bachelard. Loading



Gareth Hales, meanwhile, stressed he was giving testimony to the committee as a “private citizen” and claimed to have no formal role in the church, although he said he was its most senior figure. Related Article Exclusive

Investigations ‘Tail, film, heckle’: Inside the Brethren’s secret election influence plot with the far-right He said he was “not active” in group chats with the far-right and other Brethren elders co-ordinating the stunts, and that he campaigned “alongside many others” in 2025. Simply “campaigning alongside someone else does not mean adopting every opinion they have ever expressed”, he said. Gareth also claimed that he never asked Brethren members to campaign, prompting interjections from chair Laxale when Gareth Hales later conceded that he had encouraged them. Leaked videos of Gareth and his brothers urging Brethren to “man polling booths” and “dominate the play” on the campaign trail were just meant to “encourage people to get out in their democratic right,” Gareth said.



“I might have offered a little bit of encouragement [to the Brethren campaigning] but in no way did I direct them all.” Loading He also claimed he would have called out poor behaviour such as intimidating MPs, and repeated the Brethren line used throughout the election that members campaigning, including himself, were simply “businessmen ... concerned about the direction the country was heading”. Gareth Hales was himself photographed among the Brethren who donned blue Liberal Party T-shirts to campaign on the ground for a Coalition victory. Bruce Hales told the committee that he first realised Gareth’s involvement in the campaign when he saw that photo published by this masthead, and had no idea about the stunt operation with the far-right.



“I can understand how you might find it hard to believe,” he told MPs. But “I had no knowledge of those events before. I had no part in planning them, I think if they’d asked me about them, and asked permission, I would have denied it.” Gareth Hales (centre) campaigning for the Liberals at the last federal election. “So do you think that your sons deliberately didn’t ask you about it?” Labor senator Corinne Mulholland pressed. “Quite likely,” Hales replied. He conceded his sermons were rarely misinterpreted by his flock – when quizzed about his recent preaching to Brethren members of the need to keep “our secrets” from “men in the world”.



Gareth Hales denied there was any link with his father’s Scripture and the subsequent election campaign. Bruce Hales was also questioned about his history of statements defined by some Jewish groups as antisemitism, including calling Jews “wicked … infidel”. He said the church had been praying for Israel since the outbreak of war in the Middle East and that he himself had Jewish heritage in his family. But he added “there’s quite a bit of history ... to the Jewish matter or the Jewish question”, saying that “the Jews aren’t exactly referred to favourably because they were the ones that finally clamoured publicly for Christ to be crucified”. Lester Sharples, a Brethren elder who confirmed his involvement in the far-right stunts to this masthead, was also called to give evidence but declined to attend, as did two other senior Brethren figures called. Both Gareth and Bruce claimed not to have spoken to Sharples recently.



Gee accused Liberal MP Ben Small of “running a protection racket” for the Brethren as Small and Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie led Coalition interruptions supporting the church leaders throughout the hearing, but he later withdrew the remark. “This is beginning to look like religious discrimination,” McKenzie shouted at one point. “This isn’t the Spanish Inquisition!” Tensions flared again when Gee asked Bruce Hales whether his testimony was truthful. “Who’s asking that?” Bruce Hales immediately demanded to know, and later told the committee he felt he was being “targeted”.



Gee also expressed doubt about Gareth Hales’ testimony. “Given that the evidence before this committee is that thousands of members of your church actively participated in a co-ordinated way in the 2025 federal election campaign, can you understand how people might find the church’s denial that it had any role … very difficult to believe? It defies belief,” he said. Hales said he understood that “it’s difficult to believe”. “But they weren’t members of the church. They were members of concerned business groups and … private citizens. They weren’t there on behalf of the church,” he said. Gee’s attempts to ask Gareth Hales about whether the Brethren were given access, or tried to get access, to an Australian Electoral Commission database was met with repeated interjections from Small.



“If members of your church are being given access to the Australian Electoral Commission database, I think that is an issue of national concern,” Gee said. Gareth Hales said: “Well, now that you’ve said concerned five times, yes I’m very concerned.” Former and current members of the Brethren, many of them watching the hearings online, have spoken out in horror since the relevations of the far-right plot by church elders emerged. Some say the Brethren is a controlling sect, not a religion. Former prime minister Kevin Rudd and the current PM, Anthony Albanese, both described the Exclusive Brethren as a cult, as have many former members. “I thought it was a bit rough,” Gareth Hales told the committee. “Mr Rudd, Mr Albanese branded [the Brethren] as a cult … they haven’t ever sat down with us and chatted to us or talked to us.”



Labor has slammed the “intimidation” campaign against Labor and other Coalition opponents as an attack on democracy, while extremism experts have called for an investigation and teal donor Climate 200 has referred the church to the charity regulator for investigation. Committee members expressed scepticism about an apparently coincidental meeting Gareth Hales had with then-opposition leader Peter Dutton. Labor MP Shayne Neumann asked how Hales happened to be at a petrol station in Carlingford for Dutton’s fuel announcement. “I had no telephone conversations with those people,” Hales answered. “So magically and mysteriously, you just happened to have turned up to a petrol station where the leader of the opposition and his staff were?” Neumann said.



“It wasn’t magic or mysterious. It was just known that he was going to turn up there,” Hales said. Neumann said election campaigns did not work that way, with even the press gallery only told about leader events at short notice. “Have you heard, Mr Neumann, of word of mouth?” replied Gareth. Bruce Hales also confirmed during the hearing that Brethren members have met with US President Donald Trump. “I understand there have been some members in the New York area who have met Mr Trump briefly. I have never met him, nor have I ever directed anybody to,” he said.



Related Article Investigations Brethren a controlling sect, not a religion, former and current members say Hales said he was not sure if senior Brethren had also trained in election campaigning with Trump’s MAGA movement in the US, as reported by this masthead, and was asked to take the question on notice. Independent MP Monique Ryan asked Bruce Hales whether church members believed that he was “a direct messenger from God?”. “Well, I would think that they would say that what I get, I get from the Lord,” he replied. Ryan also asked about how he became the leader of the church – which Hales said arose “spontaneously” from his flock globally.

World.title: This man is a political candidate. Seriously?
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters This man is a political candidate. Seriously? October 16, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Megan Herbert To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. ONE NATION I have always been proud to call myself Australian and to live in a country that prides itself on respecting societal values which include respect for individuals, equal opportunity, democracy and a fair go.

Now, I read about the One Nation candidate for Melbourne who has a history of promoting far-right rhetoric about waging religious wars against Muslims, uses misogynistic language and spreads COVID-19 conspiracy theories (“One Nation urged ‘decolonisation’ of Muslim countries” 16/10).

What is happening in our country when we allow such outrageous behaviour to be forefront as a possible parliamentary voice? Freedom of speech is also a core Australian value, but surely, freedom of speech should be one that builds, not destroys.

Julie Ottobre, Brunswick East Selection criteria bemusing

Re The Age report on the One Nation candidate for Melbourne, Matthew Collins. This is a man who carries a medieval shield and calls for a crusade between Christians and Muslims.

By the way, he also refers to women as ″⁣foids″⁣ (″⁣female humanoid organisms″⁣).

What criteria does One Nation use to choose candidates, one of whom holds views that would be anathema to most ordinary Australians?

Of course, everyone knows the views of Pauline Hanson. But it seems that One Nation selection committees are prepared to accept anyone, regardless of their beliefs.

In a democratic society, we can vote for anyone who runs for election, but why would you vote for such a disparate mob of obsessive extremists as One Nation?

Damien Ryan, Berwick



Crusaders need to brush up on history

Pauline Hanson and her bunch of merry Crusaders need to brush up on their history a bit. The Crusades were not a one-sided affair, and the Muslims acquitted themselves very well.

As the Americans, the world’s greatest superpower, has recently rediscovered, a smaller nation like Iran can still punch well above its weight, even bringing the mighty US military to heel.

My advice to the Crusaders: stay safely at home and keep your wild fantasies quietly to yourselves.

Mark Kennedy, Sebastopol Encourage kindness, never cruelty

Waleed Aly writes with poignant accuracy (“More Australians believe in political violence than go to church each week”, 16/10). Political violence is in a cultural context which should not keep normalising violence.

It’s a terrible choice to choose violence over peacemaking.

All we can do is encourage people to think, speak and act in ways that are kind, never cruel.

We have this freedom to make choices that only heal and never harm. As is conveyed in places of spiritual practice, do to others what we would have them do to us. Under no circumstances do anything else.

Bishop Philip Huggins, Point Lonsdale THE FORUM More hare, less snail

There seems to be a generally held view that Anthony Albanese and others in the government want Labor to be the “natural form″⁣ of government for Australia. This is unsurprising given the prime minister is a machine politician. Yet, such governments essentially move along doing nothing, wishing to offend nobody.

But given the changing world and the fundamental problems we face with climate change, the American alliance, housing, the budget and the overwhelming need for redistribution of income from the wealthy to the poor and middle classes, something more radical must be done.

The government cannot continue moving along at a snail’s pace. It must begin moving and fast even at the risk of wrecking it aspiration to be the natural form of government.

Greg Bailey, St Andrews Greens’ Ukraine sell-out

Oh, pardon me, David Shoebridge, I thought the Greens were a party of the environment which would fight for urgent climate change action, not a ″⁣party of peace″⁣.

Opposing Australia’s support for Ukraine is a disgraceful sell-out of the unbelievably brave Ukrainian people and their staunch leader who have endured four years of death, destruction and misery at the hands of a communist dictatorship which will not stop at overrunning Ukraine.

And the Ukrainian people keep fighting, despite Trump’s latest disgraceful attempts to sabotage their efforts by reducing access to essential data (″⁣Zelensky’s fury at Starlink slowdown″⁣ 16/10).

The Greens aim to replace the Labor Party? I don’t think so. A decent, honourable Australia relies on a party of the middle ground where most people still sit - a country that fought in World War II to defend democracy and its allies.

Let’s hope Sarah Hanson-Young, who is an environmentalist and supports Ukraine, quickly replaces you.

Lynne Holroyd, East Hawthorn



Greens’ catch 22

Thank you, Senator Hanson-Young, for seeing sense on the Green’s position on Ukraine (″⁣Greens split over Ukrainian military aid as Sarah Hanson-Young breaks ranks″⁣ 13/10).

While most of us might support peace and non-violence as a general principle, David Shoebridge’s conclusion that that extends to declining military aid to embattled Ukraine strikes as extraordinarily inflexible. The fact that the Greens would agree to such support if it were backed by a UN Security Council resolution (which Russia would immediately veto) is straight out of the pages of Joseph Heller’s 1961 classic Catch 22. If the Greens ever form government, perhaps Heller’s masterpiece should be mandatory reading.

Ian Coltman, Torquay Stand up for Ukraine

President Donald Trump is acting like a spiteful bully, especially towards Ukraine, by buying diesel from Russia, which only encourages Putin to continue attacking it, and then taking away Ukraine’s early warning capability by restricting Starlink, causing the death of more civilians.

The Australian government can’t just stand by without condemning the United States, as well as Russia. It is time to stand up for justice and humanity and stop hiding behind whatever strategic advantage the government may think is to be gained by remaining silent.

As our politicians like to say, it’s the right thing to do.

Denny Meadows, Hawthorn Small business reality

The (now delayed) decision to stop credit-card payments to the Australian Tax Office could only have been made by those well accustomed to regular, guaranteed salaries. The small-business reality is ″⁣lumpy cashflow″⁣, which means low or no salary or payments some months, higher payments in others.

In turn, it reveals how out of touch some of the salaried are with the realities of small business. Most small business owners would prefer not to pay by credit card if they had the luxury of regular salary and income flow. But they don’t, so credit cards are used as a bridge until the funds owed to them come in.

Emma Borghesi, Rye Tax big companies

Instead of sending small businesses to the wall, why doesn’t the Labor government tax the companies that pay no tax, or very little? If small business doesn’t survive and therefore doesn’t employ people, the government is going to have to pay these people unemployment benefits from a smaller tax take. Currently, there is little incentive to start a business and try to build it when you barely make a wage.

Rita Reid, Port Melbourne Space to play

Your article ″⁣Finding city’s sporty kids a place to play″⁣ (16/10) suggests public schools share facilities with community sports clubs out-of-hours.

The comment is too simplistic as the school cannot afford to fund cleaning and security and lighting costs. We all know state schools are underfunded now and cannot afford a further impost from supporting community groups, some of which do not pay their way, leaving facilities unlocked and rubbish left behind. Sadly, there are schools that have had to kick sporting groups out for not paying their way, and to get cleaners in before school resumes; all costs beyond their remit.

Keith Hawkins, Point Lonsdale



Grounds not grand prix

It’s time private schools should also open their facilities for sport. They have used our taxes to build some of their magic sports arenas. It’s time for more equality in sport. No child should be disadvantaged as sport is also a medium for good mental health. The $100 million in government money spent on the grand prix each year could be used to acquire land and build sports facilities for our kids.

Nola Cormick, Albert Park Trapped by religion

After reading the article concerning the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church (″⁣Brethren boss faces inquiry over members’ election secrets″⁣ 16/10), I was appalled and at the same time amazed at what makes this church attractive.

The five demands the members have to adhere to sound very much like a dictatorship. I thought Christianity was loving, sharing and caring. The Brethren’s form of Christianity sounds like a prison with invisible walls.

Greg Bardin, Altona North Car rego by weight

In addition to the correspondent’s observation (Letters, “Plenty of potholes” 16/10) regarding the very large vehicles used in house construction and the resulting potholes on small roads, an investigation needs to be done regarding all modern vehicles.

The vast majority of vehicles driven today are heavier than the traditional sedan – SUVs, EVs, those ugly truck-like utes – to say nothing of the huge trucks driven through suburban streets. Of course, the same damage is done to country roads. How many people who choose these vehicles over a traditional sedan appreciate their contribution to the impossible task of preventing potholes without enormous expenditure?

Perhaps registration fees need to be scaled according to vehicle weight.

Margery Renwick, Brighton City’s stark contrasts

Congratulations to chef Hugh Allen, his investors and staff on Yiaga’s recent successes.

Wandering through the gardens in which the restaurant is nestled, I noticed a man sleeping rough beneath one of the magnificent old trees, just metres from the restaurant.

The contrast made me reflect on what we value as a city. Is it the number of chef’s hats our restaurants earn, or how we care for the most vulnerable?

Homelessness is not a problem for Hugh Allen, or any individual business, to solve. But the gulf between those who take their seats at Yiaga and those who sleep on the ground outside has rarely seemed as stark as it does in Melbourne today.

Kate Coughlan, East Melbourne Do better by women

It is an exceedingly depressing time to be female. A US comedian refers to women as ″⁣whores″⁣ because they dress to exercise. Abortion is once again being debated, when it is clearly a health issue. Gender-based violence and femicide are reported endlessly on the news cycle. We can and must do better.

Rosslyn Jennings, North Melbourne



AND ANOTHER THING Matt Golding Trump

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky says he feels ″⁣betrayed″⁣ by Donald Trump. Join the club.

Terry Kelly, Coburg In gun-happy America, the livestreaming of an execution by firing squad is called off, and minutes later there is another school shooting tragedy.

If Trump were a great president, he would proclaim “enough is enough″⁣, and maybe a Nobel Peace Prize would be his.

Margaret Skeen, Ocean Grove Let’s put a mark on the wall – Trump finally got it right and banned the livestreaming of an execution. Now, can he start supporting Ukraine instead of Russia?

John Walsh, Watsonia



Re ″⁣The disappearing women of the Trump administration″⁣ (16/10). It couldn’t have happened to a more deserving group. I assume others will follow, although there don’t appear to be many more left.

Marie Nash, Balwyn Futhermore

Whatever can help relieve the problems with hospital care for the elderly seems essential. To take action that would cause more elderly to rely on public health facilities is unwise.

Doris LeRoy, Altona

Have the multimillionaires and billionaires pay their taxes and Labor will have their $1.6bn-plus for aged care.

Robert Martin, Winchelsea South Could Jess Wilson please explain how the lives of First Nations people in Victoria will be improved by repealing the Treaty?

Jen Hooper, Nunawading Abortion into the political debate; Ben Carroll just lost the election.

Michael Brinkman



Finally

The AFL has decided all players will be hair tested for illicit drugs twice yearly. I suggest in order to lead from the top, all senior AFL and club personnel should subject themselves to the same process.

John Rawson, Mernda The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Victoria’s shocking funding gap ahead of what could be a horror fire season
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaEditorial Editorial Victoria’s shocking funding gap ahead of what could be a horror fire season The Age's View Editorial October 16, 2026 — 7:45pm

October 16, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Imagine having the strength of character to charge towards raging infernos. That’s the job of around 35,000 firefighters – the vast majority of them volunteers – to protect lives, property and the environment from fire and other emergencies. Now imagine doing so while unsure your equipment is up to the task or that a broken-down piece of machinery could put you or your colleagues at even greater risk. Fifty-seven per cent of the CFA’s fire trucks are more than 15 years old. AP This week, Victoria’s auditor-general detailed widespread cracking, caused by dangerous overloading, had forced half of the environment department’s fleet of fire trucks to be removed from service during our last fire season. It was striking that the audit noted that of the department’s 600-odd trucks, the ones off the road due to cracking, were considerably younger – with only 6.7 per cent more than 15 years old – than those used by Fire Rescue Victoria (FRV) and Country Fire Authority (CFA).



The audit found 57 per cent of the 2400 trucks used by FRV and the CFA are 15 years or older, and more than one-third are over 20 years old. FRV policy gives fire trucks a useful lifespan of 15 years, beyond which the authority says they should be replaced. Related Video Video icon 1:09 Bushfire threatens Victorian town This is clearly not being met. The audit further found that maintenance on those ageing trucks was falling behind. Victoria’s three fire authorities use this equipment to respond to more than 100,000 fire emergencies and other incidents every year and with which they are eyeing predictions of a hot El Niño summer. All up, fire authorities need $1.5 billion between 2024-25 and 2033-34 to address critical fire truck replacement and upgrade needs. Yet the auditor-general concluded fire authorities only have about one-quarter of the funding they desperately need. It’s a staggering shortfall for such a critical part of the state’s emergency response apparatus.



In response, Premier Ben Carroll acknowledged the report “clearly shows we have more work to do” and pointed to Labor’s recent election promise to commit another $167 million towards 150 new trucks by 2030, including 50 for FRV and 100 for the CFA. That still leaves a gap, once other commitments are included, of close to $1 billion over 10 years. Related Article Victoria bushfires 30-year-old fleets and cracking trucks: Why Victoria’s fire services are chasing billions Disappointingly, the opposition is, after years of critical commentary, saying only that it will put in “more” funding than Labor and that its policy will be released before the election. It has already said it will not find the $1 billion called for in the audit. This is the sharp reality of the state’s finances. Given the choice, the government has opted for record debt to fund infrastructure and left essential services literally cracking apart. This year’s state budget showed a government under fiscal pressure on all fronts, with Victoria’s net debt set to rise to $175.6 billion in 2026-27 and grow to $199.3 billion over the forward estimates.



When the Andrews government was elected in 2014, it inherited net debt of $22 billion, or about 6 per cent of the state’s economy. That percentage rose steeply with COVID-19 spending – including a $285 million bungle and cover-up revealed this week. How dearly the state’s fire agencies would like that money back right now. Even though the pandemic emergency has subsided, the big spend has not as The Age has noted previously with some concern. Debt now sits at about 25 per cent of the state’s economy. Victoria’s volunteer firefighters, such as this Ararat crew from 2024, respond to thousands of emergencies every year in ageing trucks. Simon Schluter The upcoming fire season could see the very real consequences of that debt for emergency preparedness and the operational firefighters on the front lines. Forecasters are predicting increased bushfire risk – particularly in Victoria’s south-west, Central Highlands, far-east Gippsland and western plains – throughout spring and into summer.





This year, as every year, they should be updating their farm map, doing an inventory of their emergency kit, clearing vegetation and low branches and checking their gates. They will need to make sure their roadside property number is visible to help fire crews locate it or orient themselves in the worst-case firestorm scenarios. But that’s just the domestic perspective of fire season preparedness. “We only need one bad day to have a bad summer,” said Country Fire Authority chief officer Garry Cook at his first event in the job this week. Without safe and reliable equipment that is fit for purpose and well maintained, that day could have consequences lasting much longer. Nobody will be able to say they were not warned. Whether featuring a mixed-material facade, a statement entry, landscaped gardens, bold palettes or distinct architectural focal points, standout homes capture attention and offer a unique point of difference. Here are five of the best Sydney homes on the market that stand out from the crowd. 40 Collins Street, Annandale NSW From its bold facade to its interiors, “Hunter House” makes a statement in contemporary Gothic style.



Located opposite the heritage-listed Hunter Baillie Memorial Church, Hunter House features symmetrical curves, pointed roof forms, glazing and six-metre ceilings. The materials are also striking. Built from double brick, concrete and steel, the interiors feature walnut joinery, marble, terrazzo and Venetian plaster. Other features include four bedrooms, a wellness room or a gym and a four-car garage. 74 Davidson Avenue, Concord NSW



This brand-new double-brick Concord home features a stylish, statement facade with curved lines and arched windows. Like something from an architectural magazine, the resort-style exterior features a sunken lounge overlooking a circular swimming pool, a spa and established greenery. Inside, high ceilings, glazing, floor-to-ceiling windows and a marble staircase stand out, along with premium finishes such as a marble kitchen and a wine cellar. The property backs onto Central Park and is close to Majors Bay Road Village and public transport. 1/15 Woodlands Avenue, Breakfast Point NSW



Originally built c. 1915 for the AGL gasworks and now heritage-listed, The Plumber Workshop was converted in 2021 into 14 residences, with number one currently for sale. The residence wraps around the building’s corner over two levels. The original brick exterior is a show-stopping feature in its own right, as are the arched, steel-framed windows and the living and dining room, which rises two storeys. The master bedroom suite occupies the entire upper floor and includes a bedroom with a round-arched window overlooking the void, a media room lined with library joinery, a fitted walk-in robe and an en suite.



Membership of the Breakfast Point Country Club is included with the apartment and provides access to the pools, gym, tennis and sauna. 15a Milner Crescent, Wollstonecraft NSW This contemporary terrace offers family luxury with five bedrooms, including a master with a large en suite and a balcony. Set across two levels, the home uses curves and mixes materials in its facade and interior.



There is an expansive living, dining and kitchen area, with the latter equipped with quality cabinetry, Calacatta Amore marble benchtops, premium appliances and a butler’s pantry. Other highlights include double-glazed windows, oak timber floors, 100 per cent wool carpets, and a private, landscaped rear garden with a natural-stone-paved entertaining area. 31 Vale Street, Gordon NSW With approximately 1650 square metres of private grounds, a full-size tennis court, a swimming pool with a waterfall and a concealed wellness room, this property makes you feel as if you are living in your own resort.



The interiors are largely the same, with a sunlit music room, a sauna and a formal lounge featuring an open fireplace, a ceiling-mounted projector and a motorised screen. With six bedrooms and five bathrooms, the home offers space for a large or multigenerational family, or for hosting guests. Other highlights include ducted air-conditioning, extensive underfloor heating, ample storage, a three-car automatic garage and remote-controlled, gated entry.

World.title: ‘It means everything’: How Melbourne scientists are fighting to save Poppy’s sight
World.content:
NationalVictoriaMelbourne Assembly ‘It means everything’: How Melbourne scientists are fighting to save Poppy’s sight Henrietta Cook October 16, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Melbourne Assembly brings together the people, ideas and conversations shaping the future of our city. See all stories .

When Poppy Stevens was just a few months old, she received a devastating diagnosis. After failing her newborn hearing test, genetic testing confirmed the little girl had Usher syndrome, which meant she might also lose her vision. Poppy Stevens and her mother Ali. Poppy, 5, has a faulty gene too big for gene therapy. Ben Jones “It was a second wave of devastation,” reflects her mother Ali Stevens, who lives in Melbourne’s south-east.



“Suddenly I’m thinking, ‘is my child going to be blind?’ We were going through the worst-case scenarios ... Is she going to work? Is she going to drive? Will this make it harder for her to have a family? Is she going to live with us for the rest of her life?” A team of Melbourne researchers is determined to alleviate these anxieties and provide a cure for the vision loss faced by children like Poppy, who is now five and uses a hearing aid. Usher syndrome is the primary cause of deafblindness in Australia and impacts about one in 6000 children. Children are typically born with hearing loss, and then progressively lose their vision during their adolescence and early adulthood. At the Centre for Eye Research Australia, managing director Professor Keith Martin and Professor Guei-Sheung (Rick) Liu are creating a treatment called EDITRA that aims to correct the tiny spelling mistake in a person’s genetic code that causes Poppy’s variant of Usher syndrome, type 2A. The project, developed by the centre’s new spin-out company Adara Bio, overcomes a major barrier to treatment for patients with Usher syndrome, whose mutated genes are too large to fit into current gene therapies.



By fixing the cell’s genetic instructions (known as its RNA) instead of replacing the large gene that causes the syndrome, the treatment fits inside a single modified virus that is injected into the eye. As part of the next week’s Melbourne Assembly civic forum, The Age has been exploring big ideas for the future of the city, including how to maintain and enhance Melbourne’s status as a global leader in medical research and innovation. Loading Martin, who is also chair of the Association of Australian Medical Research Institutes Victoria, left his job at the University of Cambridge and moved to Melbourne seven years ago because he was attracted to the city’s “biotech ecosystem”. “Melbourne’s cluster of medical research institutes, universities, industry and the start-up ecosystem is really attractive,” he said.



Related Series

City life Melbourne Assembly He says the city rivals Boston and London as one of the world’s top research destinations, with its medical research institutes employing more than 7500 people and delivering more than $600 million to the state’s economy every year. This eclipses the annual economic benefit of the Australian Open ($566 million) and the Grand Prix ($350 million). But the sector is not without its problems. Martin warns that Victoria risks losing its edge as a global biotech hub without stronger state and federal investment and more local manufacturing facilities.



“There’s sometimes a complacency from the Victorian government that we’re world leading and will remain world leading,” he says. “Unless we support this with more funding, we’re going to lose our preeminence within Australia and globally. It’s not easily recoverable.” Modelling commissioned by the peak body indicates that without a significant funding increase, 10 of the state’s 14 independent medical research institutes will be at risk of closure by 2030. They receive their funding from federal government grants, philanthropy, commercial activities and the state government. The Hudson Institute of Medical Research in Clayton. Luis Enrique Ascui Last month, The Age revealed the 66-year-old Hudson Institute of Medical Research would stop operating independently and cut at least 75 jobs. Victorian Minister for Medical Research Anthony Carbines said at the time that the government had increased funding for the state’s research institutes by $24.6 million over two years, with more than $47.7 million flowing to the sector last financial year. This, he says, is the largest amount of funding for indirect research costs provided by any Australian state or territory.



Despite these funding concerns, ground-breaking research continues. Martin and his team are testing their treatment for Usher syndrome on miniature eye models they have grown in a lab. They hope to start clinical trials within three years. The technology has the potential to fix other inherited retinal diseases, including genetic forms of macular degeneration. Poppy Stevens, 5, (front, centre) and her mum Ali, sister Evie, 7, and dad Ben. Poppy has a genetic condition called Usher syndrome which leads to hearing and vision loss. Ben Jones “It’s beautifully controllable, it’s like molecular surgery,” Martin explains. “We can very precisely change the gene to correct those errors.”



The research has provided hope to the Stevens family. “It could completely change Poppy’s future,” Ali says. “Instead of planning for her going blind, our plans can be about where we are going to travel and what we are going to do together. It means everything.” Just a few blocks away from the lab where scientists are working on a treatment for Usher syndrome, a young man with electrodes strapped to his shaved head recites a series of nonsense sentences in a Faraday room, which blocks electromagnetic fields. Scientist Dean Freestone is developing a brain-computer interface that translates intended speech from neural signals into communication. Luis Enrique Ascui “These days chicken leg is a rare dish,” Jay Marinis says from the carpeted room in the Aikenhead Centre for Medical Discovery, which is co-located at St Vincent’s Hospital Melbourne and accelerates the commercialisation of medical and health research.



“A zestful food is a hot cross bun.” Related Article Melbourne Assembly How innovation hubs at Parkville and Clayton can put Melbourne on top of the world Marinis is being paid $40 an hour to read these sentences aloud, then mouth them and then think them. It’s all in the name of research – he’s helping a team of Melbourne scientists and entrepreneurs create a device called Fluent that translates what a person intends to say from brain signals into communication. If the innovation kicks off, it would transform the lives of 100 million people around the world who have lost the ability to speak or have a profound speech deficit. This includes people with throat and mouth cancer, cerebral palsy, Motor Neuron Disease, Parkinson’s, non-verbal autism and those who have suffered a stroke. While the device might seem like the stuff of science fiction, Dean Freestone, the co-founder and chief technology officer of Fluent, aims to launch it in 2030.



“The device goes under the skin and is completely invisible – similar to a cochlear implant,” he says, referring to bionic ear which was developed at the University of Melbourne in 1978. “It’s inserted through a small incision, unfurls under the scalp, and can be done in an outpatient clinic in 20 minutes.” While the project has an ambitious timeline, many years of research underpins it. Fluent co-founders Dean Freestone and Tim Mahoney with Lachlan Hill, who is wearing their tech. Jason South Freestone previously helped create a device that is implanted beneath the scalp’s surface which predicts seizures among patient with epilepsy. Within the space of eight years, the Epiminder device went from basic research through to regulatory approvals and is now available in the US.



With the assistance of artificial intelligence, researchers discovered that the brain measurements detected by this technology could also be used to decode intended speech. “It’s not reading your background inner monologue,” Freestone says. “It’s the signals that go from our brain to our speech muscles.” While Freestone views Melbourne as a world-class clinical research hub, he says it’s constrained by a small local market and a lower appetite for risk among investors. “It’s just chalk and cheese compared to Silicon Valley,” Freestone says. “Australians want to invest in things that are going to have an expected return within a few years, whereas a medical device will take longer.” Melbourne Assembly will be held from October 19 to October 21. More information is available on the Melbourne Assembly website.

World.title: Toa Samoa give France a thrashing in World Cup opener
World.content:
Samoa kicked off their 2026 Rugby League World Cup campaign with a strong 78-4 win over France at the CommBank Stadium in Sydney on Friday night.

Toa Samoa scored 14 tries in the process, four through replacement winger Sualauvi Fa'alogo, and 22 points through the boots of Stephen Crichton, who kicked 11 goals.

Toa Samoa players showed a lot of emotions as their national anthem was sung and the Siva Tau battle challenge was laid down before kick-off.

And it took them just three minutes to get on the board with Deine Mariner running untouched out wide as the French defensive pattern was left wanting.

In the end the Blues of Samoa showed their fans and the world they are serious contenders, even though France was not as strong as many would have hoped for.

Co-captain and hard running forward Junior Paulo thanked the fans after the game, adding they are the reason the players do what they do.

"It's awesome to see the way they turn up," Paulo told Seven post match.

"It means everything to us.

"This is the reason why we play for our nation. To turn up here and see the crowd it means the world to us.

"We gotta dig deep out there; they are the reason."

Head coach Ben Gardiner told the players at halftime they needed to hang on to the ball longer, after their play had dropped heading into the last 10 minutes of the first 40.

Toa Samoa led 18-0 by the 10th minute mark, with two more touchdowns through Benaiah Ioelu in the sixth minute and Jermaine McEwen, in the eighth, as the team dominated play early.

Crichton kicked all three conversions for the 18-0 lead.

In the end they ran up 13 tries, with replacement winger Sualauvi Fa'alogo claiming four on the night.

Fa'alogo replaced Mariner early in the first half after the first try-scorer of the night had to leave the field after he pulled his hamstring.

Luai, Chanel Harris-Tavita, Tabuai-Fidow, Brian To'o and Crichton combined to run hard against the French.

Up front, co-captain Paulo, Connelly Lemuelu, Jermaine McEwen and Francis Manuleleua were on fire, gaining valuable yards and territory every time they had the ball in hand.

Luai was the mastermind, with Harris-Tavita being the other option to command play.

Fa'alogo claimed his first try in Toa Samoa colours after the 10th minute before Tabuai-Fidow got his name on the score sheet.

France had their first visit into the Samoan territory in the 23rd minute but dummy-half Benjamin Garcia passed the ball forward 10 metres from the Samoan line and gave away the team's first real momentum.

But they got their first points on the board when Garcia sent the ball right close to the Samoan line, which saw Louis Grossemy finishing with a try in the corner in the 24th minute.

That was after a good defensive set inside their own 20-metre line won them a penalty and the ensuing sets saw them get a second penalty 10 metres out from the Samoan tryline.

The try seemed to have lifted the French, as they forced the Samoans into errors and put them under pressure a few times.

That also saw a drop in the Samoans' game as they dropped passes and knocked the ball on a few times.

Fa'alogo grabbed his second try in the 37th minute after some straight-up-the-middle runs by the forwards and Crichton slammed his conversion from out wide through the uprights, sending Samoa into a 34-4 lead at halftime.

The second 40

Gardiner's pep talk at halftime fired the Samoans back into action in the second spell.

He told Seven before resumption of play that the side needed to keep the ball and work on their game.

The team responded.

Crichton got Samoa's seventh try, two and half minutes after the restart, before Francis Manuleleua got his name on the board too.

Fa'alogo got Samoa's ninth try and his third for the night, running on to another Luai long pass, with 15 minutes to go, before adding his fourth some minutes later.

Warriors playmaker Tavita was on hand to touch down between the posts after another Luai show of his deft footwork, before centre Izack Tago managed to get a try to his name with eight minutes to go, with Crichton adding his ninth conversion, as Samoa went further up to 66-4.

Big forward Francis Molo, who previously played for the Cook Islands, powered his way over the French line for Samoa's 70th point in the game.

Crichton kicked his 10th conversion, and Samoa went up 72-4.

It was Ioelu who scored Samoa's 14th try in the dying seconds of the game after he jumped high to collect the ball that had bounced off the upright, from Crichton's attempted penalty kick.

World.title: Employment Court ruling over Calendar Girls sets 'important precedent' for country, dancers say
World.content:
An Employment Court decision regarding a Wellington strip club has set an important precedent for the entire country's adult entertainment industry, the dancers who pursued the case say.

This week, the Employment Court ruled that five dancers were employees of Calendar Girls when they worked at its Wellington club, not contractors.

The dancers took an employment case against the chain of adult venues after being effectively fired for challenging changes to their work conditions.

Cherida Fraser, from the Aotearoa Sex Workers Collective, told RNZ's Checkpoint the dancers had been handed a contract on a work night that reduced their proportion of fees, while also increasing the overall fees.

"They grouped together to address it and engage in good faith with the club and wrote their letter and tried to get a meeting with them," Fraser said.

"But this was denied and they were just terminated immediately, which was grossly unjust.

"They lost their livelihoods overnight when they were actually just trying to engage in good faith."

During a hearing earlier this year, the dancers argued they were effectively being treated as employees, not contractors.

In its ruling, the court highlighted the level of control Calendar Girls had over the dancers, with numerous restrictions in place.

"The way they performed and the services that were on offer, they weren't able to choose how much they charged for the services they offered on top of the baseline club fees," Fraser explained.

"Their attendance, their sick leave, they were expected to do regular shifts, they weren't able to take breaks when they wanted to."

Even the dancers' appearances were subject to scrutiny, Fraser said.

"Someone wanted to change their hair colour and that wasn't allowed.

"As well as that, they were restricted from working anywhere else. So there were significant trade restraints."

Audio player for " Power imbalance between Calendar Girls and dancers laid bare " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/business/1958957%2Femployment-court-ruling-over-calendar-girls-sets-important-precedent-for-country-dancers-say

Power imbalance between Calendar Girls and dancers laid bare Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

Financial penalties were in place for breaches of those restrictions. Dancers would be fined $200 if they stayed in changing rooms for too long, $100 for misuse of a cell phone, and $100 for wearing a g-string.

The "coercive threat of financial penalty" was outrageous, Fraser said.

She said the women felt energised by the Employment Court's ruling that they were employees, not contractors.

"And deservedly, this doesn't happen without personal cost to them," Fraser told RNZ's Checkpoint.

The women had shown "absolute fortitude" by putting their lives on hold to pursue the case, Fraser said.

She shared a statement from the dancers, where they said they were proud to have stuck it out and received some hard-earned closure.

"We're even more proud to have played a part in something much bigger than ourselves.

"We believe this judgment sets an important precedent for the adult entertainment industry on the whole."

Fraser said the ruling meant the dancers could now be compensated for unfair dismissal.

She said the decision would put other clubs on notice to treat their workers better.

"I think this is a very strong signal to the clubs to ensure that the contracts and the practices that go with those contracts are truly independent.

World.title: Worst staffing shortage Starship Hospital nurses have seen, as cancer treatments delayed
World.content:
Nurses at Auckland's Starship Children's Hospital say this is the worst nursing shortage they've seen, as cancer treatments are delayed.

On Thursday, Health Minister Simeon Brown confirmed some treatments were delayed up to seven days.

Do you know more? Get in touch at: iwitness@rnz.co.nz

Earlier on Thursday morning, Health New Zealand's Starship Hospital director Dr Greg Williams said the paediatric haematology/oncology service has had to reschedule some treatments due to a shortage of nurses.

"These decisions are not made lightly and are based on clinical need," he said, adding: "Starship is recruiting experienced and new graduate nurses as quickly as possible".

But two nurses who spoke to RNZ on the condition of anonymity, said staffing had been a critical issue for over a year.

They said there was a lack of experienced staff as nurses needed to complete a certain amount of qualifications, hours and training to be competent in chemotherapies, high-risk therapies and monitoring.

"We're getting a lot of new graduates - which is brilliant - but we need the staff to support them.

"We want to keep our new nurses not scare them away.

"It doesn't really help with our workload, at the moment they can't give chemotherapy or those high-risk therapies, so we still have to do them, as well as train the new nurses.

"It's not just the amount of nurses that we're employing, its the experience we need them to have..."

The nurses said new graduates only got two or three weeks working with another more experienced nurse and observing, before they were "on their own on the floor" in a children's oncology ward.

"It's intense, it's emotional and it's a really high-risk area. I just don't think two to three weeks is enough and we're not giving them enough support that they need to keep our staff and staff retention is really important for our kids."

A spokesperson for Brown earlier told RNZ vacancies at Health NZ were the result of natural attrition such as parental leave and retirement, but the nurses disagreed.

"That is absolutely not the case."

They said some nurses left because they felt unsupported.

One thing the nurses did want to make clear to parents and the general public was patients would still receive support and care they needed.

"We will do everything we can to make sure we get those children seen and safely cared for," they said.

"The tricky thing is we're doing that at the detriment of our nurses.

"We want to reassure parents out there that their children will get the care and the treatment they need, the children are safe."

Following media reports in recent days, the nurses said many parents on the ward were stressed, worrying their children wouldn't get the care they needed.

"We want to reassure them all - and that is what we've spent most of the day doing... their kids will get the treatment that they need."

They said they wanted to thank the parents for messages of support they had received.

The nurses said however, they weren't currently able to spend the time really getting to know families like they used to, or spend time with the children and play with them.

"We purely come in now to do the treatment... and just get through the shift safely."

The bottom line they said, was they needed more experienced nurses.

"This is not a cry for money, we are not asking for another pay rise, we're crying out for more staff - and more staff who can train up our new starters."

They encouraged Brown to come to the hospital and meet with staff, to see what it was like in person.

"We'd be interested to speak to him if he's keen to, come and have a meeting with us, we'd be happy to have conversation."

They said Brown had not been to visit them in person before.

Brown said he had compassion and respect for all families supporting children at Starship Hospital and he was grateful to the staff who went "above and beyond every day".

"I am advised that all vacancies in ward 27B have been recruited with nurses either having already started in these roles or about to start. I expect Health NZ to ensure vacancies are recruited to as quickly as possible when they arise."

A spokesperson for Brown said he'd been in touch with people who had been at Starship in recent days and would soon be meeting with some parents of children receiving care there.

They said he had spoken with Health NZ's chief executive to seek an opportunity to meet with frontline staff and hear first-hand about "their important work and the care they provide to children and their families."

Health NZ have been approached by RNZ for comment.

On Thursday, a spokesperson for the minister said all children at Starship Hospital were still being treated, though a handful of chemotherapy sessions have been delayed for a few days - but no more than seven.

Two bone marrow transplants were moved "slightly", but both were still going ahead.

Williams said the oncology departments are being supported by staff in other parts of Starship and Auckland City Hospital.
