World.title: Guam declares 'Condition of Readiness 3' as tropical depression approaches
World.content:
Guam has been placed in 'Condition of Readiness 3' as Tropical Storm Champi moves towards the Mariana Islands, with residents warned to prepare for potentially damaging winds, heavy rain and flooding.

A Condition of Readiness 3 means that destructive or damaging winds are possible or forecasted within 48 hours.

Governor Lou Leon Guerrero ordered the alert.

The National Weather Service in Guam said the system, previously designated Invest 96W, is continuing to organise and strengthen.

Forecasters say the storm's track and intensity remain uncertain, but Guam could experience strong winds, heavy rainfall, flooding and hazardous marine conditions in the coming days.

Governor Leon Guerrero said the early declaration gives families, businesses and government agencies time to prepare before conditions deteriorate.

She has urged residents to secure their homes and ensure their families have essential supplies.

Residents are being advised to stock enough food, drinking water, medication and other emergency supplies for at least seven to 10 days.

They should also secure loose outdoor items, charge mobile devices, prepare flashlights and emergency radios, and review family emergency plans.

The governor has also urged the public to stay out of the water during storm conditions, warning that people who enter hazardous waters put both themselves and emergency responders at risk.

The Leon Guerrero-Tenorio administration, together with Guam Homeland Security and the Office of Civil Defense, is coordinating preparedness efforts with government agencies and emergency response partners.

Residents are urged to follow official updates from Guam Homeland Security and the National Weather Service.

Further announcements are expected as the system develops.

World.title: Cook Islanders urged to be prepared for potential cyclone
World.content:
Cook Islanders are being urged to get ready as a tropical depression brews in the country's waters, according to the Cook Islands Meteorological Service.

A tropical cyclone alert is now in force for the Cook Islands as TD01F moves towards the Southern Cook Islands.

The system is expected to strengthen and may develop into a category 1 tropical cyclone within the next 12-18 hours.

The Service's Director Maara Vaiimene said people should check around their houses for any loose objects that could become a problem when the wind comes.

"Make sure your house roof is steady, check on nearby trees that won't become a problem during strong winds," he said.

"Look at your communications, in terms of radio or tv, in the event the power goes out. People should also make sure they can communicate with neighbours or family to ensure they are safe, and that you are safe."

Vaiimene said the Emergency Cook Islands team has a response guideline for what people need to do in the event that the tropical depression becomes a tropical cyclone.

The Meteorological Service, which is working closely with the Fiji Meteorological Service, said the wind conditions associated with the tropical depression were similar to a tropical cyclone status.

"In the latest bulletin, they have indicated that the chances of the tropical depression forming in a tropical cyclone in the next day or two is high," Vaiimene said.

The Cook Islands is currently in an el nino climate situation.

Vaiimene said the El Niño weather phase over the region is contributing to the unusually early development of a possible tropical cyclone.

The official tropical cyclone season starts on November 1.

World.title: Thousands of people fled Europe for NZ during WWII. Survivors and descendants are reuniting for the first time
World.content:
Audio player for " Displaced European survivors of WWII gather in Palmerston North " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/community/1958055%2Fthousands-of-people-fled-europe-for-nz-during-wwii-survivors-and-descendants-are-reuniting-for-the-first-time

Displaced European survivors of WWII gather in Palmerston North Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

While Europe was in turmoil, New Zealand was embarking on an unprecedented period of growth.

As the babies boomed, almost 5000 displaced people from states such as Lithuania, Hungary and Poland arrived on our shores from 1949-1952, ready to get to work and blend in.

This weekend some survivors, and their descendants, are gathering in Palmerston North to mark an often overlooked chapter in Aotearoa's history.

Escape from Lithuania

Captured in a jaunty National Film Unit Weekly Review newsreel, a ship load of war-displaced people arrive in Wellington Harbour in 1949, after a long journey that began in Italy.

Video player removed for printing https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W_lDL7FrCws)

The New Zealand government had agreed to welcome them on humanitarian grounds and because the country needed labour.

Among those who arrived in 1949 was Jurgis Cibulskis, sister Audrone, and parents Mecisolvas and Stefanija, from Lithuania.

Jurgis Cibulskis soon adopted the first name George as his family began a new life, speaking a different language in an unknown country on the other side of the world.

"We left Lithuania in 1944 as the Russians were advancing," Jurgis, now 86, told RNZ this week.

Lithuania had already endured a brutal Nazi invasion before the tide of war turned.

"My father at that stage decided he wasn't going to face Russian occupation once more and he decided to get out.

"The whole family, without ever returning to the apartment we were living in, because that was going the wrong way, were given a horse and cart by relations who we were holidaying with and away we went."

Jurgis Cibulskis, with the book about his life that was published last year. RNZ/JIMMY ELLINGHAM

Perhaps too young to appreciate what was happening, Jurgis remembers the novelty of the horse and cart as his family joined a convoy of people leaving. He also remembers his parents looking after their children well, probably going hungry so the younger ones could eat.

They went to Germany, where Jurgis lost all the fingers on his right hand in an accident. He also learnt to speak fluent German.

His accident led the family to New Zealand, because Canada wouldn't take a child who might not be able to work as a physical labourer.

On arrival they were sent to the lower North Island town of Pahīatua, where they spent a few weeks learning English and how to be good New Zealanders at a camp best known for taking in Polish refugee children during WWII.

"We got good treatment. We couldn't complain," Jurgis remembered.

"Our first dinner in New Zealand - you wouldn't believe it, you know what they gave us? Good old New Zealand curry.

"We'd never smelt the curry flavour. We'd seen meat swimming in a light gravy, with raisins. Meat and raisins didn't feature in our diet."

They were hungry, so gratefully accepted the fare.

Daily life at the Pahīatua camp, from where the displaced people were sent to all parts of New Zealand SUPPLIED/HOLLAND FAMILY COLLECTION

The Cibulskis family were then sent to Auckland, where they settled. Jurgis' father initially worked as a dairy farmer in Northcote, before moving to other jobs, including carpentry.

The family ended up buying a home in Remuera, a suburb Jurgis still lives in, his apartment overlooking St Michael's church, where he married his wife of 58 years, Beverly. She died in 2022.

The pair had three children and six grandchildren.

Jurgis had a successful career in industry, including many years at Fibremakers New Zealand, and played plenty of sport. He captained Auckland's third grade rep softballers.

"I assimilated in New Zealand very quicky. I picked up the language, no problems. I had no accent almost immediately.

"The vocabulary took a while to develop, but I was able to make my way quite readily."

He did notice some resentment about New Zealand importing workers a couple of decades after the tough Depression years, though.

Jurgis is one of four original displaced people at this weekend's gathering, which includes a trip back to Pahīatua - although the camp there is long gone.

He'll travel to Palmerston North by overnight bus from Auckland and was looking forward to catching up with people from the Pahīatua camp, or their families.

Most displaced people had only about six weeks to learn English in classrooms at the Pahīatua camp. SUPPLIED/HOLLAND FAMILY COLLECTION

Workers wanted as New Zealand grew

Organiser Tania Kopytko, whose father Michael was a displaced person from Belarus, said there needed to be more recognition of this part of New Zealand history.

"This is the same period as the £10 Poms came. New Zealand needed manpower and it wanted to develop economically, and these people were part of that process.

"We're talking about 4000 who went through the Pahīatua camp, and a rapid turnover in some instances."

Many New Zealanders were kind to the new arrivals and helped them settle - others were not.

"It's sad to say, but in some instances where these people might not have spoken English very well and spoken to somebody up town, like their daughter in their own language, people felt quite happy about marching up to them and saying: 'You speak English in our country.'

Tania Kopytko and her father Michael in 1993. SUPPLIED/TANIA KOPYTKO

"I actually witnessed that myself," said Tania, who is in her early 70s and lives in Palmerston North.

"On the other hand, there was also extremely kind New Zealanders. My Aunty Lucy spent six weeks in the [Pahīatua] camp and still couldn't speak English, and was sent to work in a factory in Palmerston North. It was her neighbour who taught her to speak English."

Tania's father didn't go through the Pahīatua camp, instead meeting her mother, Olive, in London and returning to New Zealand with her.

The Palmerston North gathering, the first of its kind, is called Celebrating Our Stories, and Tania said the organisers were keen to know what further work was needed to record people's memories from this period, part of the wider Untold Stories project.

World.title: RNZ funder kept in dark for six days over finance chief's sudden exit
World.content:
RNZ's major funder has requested "better communication" from the public broadcaster after being kept in the dark for nearly a week about its chief financial officer's resignation.

NZ On Air confirmed it was first notified of Hilary Parker's unexpected departure in an email from RNZ's communications director on Thursday 8 October, six days after she resigned and left the building.

"We asked for better communication in future," an NZ On Air spokesperson said.

The funding agency received a further update on Monday 12 October but said it had not sought any more information.

"RNZ's financial performance is monitored by Treasury."

In response, an RNZ spokesperson said the failure to notify NZ On Air earlier had been "an omission".

"This was rectified as soon as it was brought to our attention and we apologised.

"As a Crown Entity, RNZ remains committed to keeping key stakeholders informed as appropriate."

NZ On Air is RNZ's main funding channel, providing just over $62 million of taxpayers' money in the 2025/26 financial year.

Parker's resignation on Friday 2 October triggered an emergency board meeting and the appointment of RNZ director Richard Dellabarca as interim finance chief.

Two weeks on, the circumstances of her exit remain unexplained, despite repeated requests for answers from RNZ, government agencies and ministers.

Her departure came as the publicly funded broadcaster was preparing its annual accounts, which must be completed by the end of the month.

In a company-wide message last week, chief executive Paul Thompson acknowledged the "keen interest in what is happening" and promised staff more details "as soon as we are able".

Asked for an update this Thursday, an RNZ spokesperson said there was "nothing further to add".

"We continue to be working through the normal year-end process."

Board chair Brent Impey also declined a fresh interview request, saying there had been "no other developments" since his comments last week.

Treasury confirmed it had "engaged with RNZ" over the finalisation of its annual report following Parker's resignation.

"RNZ have advised the Treasury that the annual report will be finalised within appropriate timeframes," a spokesperson said.

The Audit Office said it too was continuing to work with RNZ on its 2025/26 audit, including "asking for any relevant information" needed to complete the job.

"We cannot give specific details about the audit," a spokesperson said. "RNZ is best placed to respond to questions about this matter."

The office said only 16 of the 80 Crown entities with a usual 31 October deadline had completed their audits so far.

It said it was not unusual for many audits to be signed off close to the deadline, which this year would be treated as Monday 2 November because 31 October fell in the weekend.

The Public Service Commission also directed questions back to RNZ's board.

Broadcasting Minister Paul Goldsmith, who was notified of Parker's resignation under the no-surprises convention at the time, had no comment "at this stage".

Associate Finance Minister David Seymour, who holds shareholding responsibility for RNZ, confirmed he too had received a written briefing but referred questions to Goldsmith.

Impey last week told RNZ's Checkpoint that Parker had resigned of her own accord to acting chief executive Mark Stevens on Friday 2 October, before leaving the premises.

Thompson, who had been overseas, was informed on Saturday.

An emergency board meeting followed on Sunday, with director Richard Dellabarca appointed interim CFO.

World.title: PNG Chiefs to go ahead with NRL logo launch after court decision
World.content:
New Zealand's High Court has knocked back an application for an interim injunction on the PNG Chiefs NRL franchise using its name in the country.

New Zealand Rugby (NZR) had rushed to court before the PNG team's logo and jersey reveal in Port Moresby next week.

The organisation claimed use of the Chiefs name, which is also the name of the long-standing Super Rugby Pacific outfit, would cause confusion and damage to the brand.

But a judge at today's two-hour Wellington hearing turned down the application after hearing an injunction could harm the NRL expansion outfit's efforts to attract players ahead of a 2028 debut.

"The PNG Chiefs welcome today's decision in the New Zealand High Court and look forward to the launch of our inaugural logo and supporter jersey in Port Moresby on Wednesday,," PNG Chiefs CEO Lorna McPherson said.

NZ Rugby to protect 'Chiefs' name New Zealand Rugby has sought interim and final injunctions before the NRL's Papua New Guinea team is officially launched later this month.

"As the matter remains before the court, no further comment on this matter will be provided at this time."

The dispute continues, with an application for a final injunction still before the court and legal action in Australia under consideration.

ARLC executive chairman Peter V'landys last week labelled NZR's action one of "mind-blowing hypocrisy", using the example of the Auckland Blues' arrival decades after NSW "had been the Blues".

"Today's decision is not a judgment on the strength of our case and the matter will still be heard in full," NZR boss Steve Lancaster said.

"As the trademark holder, our responsibility to protect the Chiefs brand hasn't changed. We remain open to working with the ARLC on a solution."

NZR's lawyer Earl Gray argued today that the PNG Chiefs' use of "PNG Chiefs" and "Chiefs" interchangeably created confusion for fans of both codes and that, with no clear distinction between the two, it would strip the rugby Chiefs of brand exclusivity.

He said NZR had trademark protections for the Chiefs in New Zealand that the NRL had not acknowledged.

ARLC lawyer Clive Elliot argued that the request for an urgent injunction, about a year after NZR became aware of the PNG Chiefs name, was not appropriate.

He said an injunction now would cloud the franchise's reputation ahead of a recruitment blitz once free agency opened next month.

World.title: Surgery giving Kiwis hope of Ponga playing again in World Cup
World.content:
Kalyn Ponga will undergo surgery on his broken arm but will remain in camp, with New Zealand not giving up on the superstar fullback playing again in the Rugby League World Cup.

Ponga failed to finish his long-awaited Test debut for the Kiwis, departing in the 70th minute of the 24-22 loss after suffering the injury earlier in the second half.

Receiving clearance earlier this year to switch his allegiance to New Zealand, Ponga delivered a stand-out performance at Western Sydney Stadium as his side fell to Australia in the Thursday night thriller.

The Newcastle skipper scored two tries while running 253 metres from 16 runs, making three line breaks and five tackle breaks.

He has been booked in for surgery after breaking the radius in his left arm but Kiwis team doctor Greg Macleod sounded hopeful about the prospect of Ponga playing again through the tournament.

Australia's dominance looms over World Cup Ahead of the women's Rugby League World Cup, the dominance of the Jillaroos looms like a spectre.

"We wish Kalyn all the best with his surgery today," Macleod said in a statement.

"We'll see how that goes but for now he will remain in camp."

The 28-year-old is viewed as critical to the New Zealand's hopes of claiming their first World Cup since 2008.

Coach Stacey Jones, whose side will face the Cook Islands in Christchurch next week before wrapping up their group stages matches against Fiji, said Ponga had played through pain.

"He couldn't catch a ball or anything like that. He was in a bit of discomfort," Jones said.

Ponga was replaced by Keano Kini as he trudged off late in the match and was seen on the sidelines with his arm in a sling.

"He's obviously disappointed, but there's a bit of upbeat about him too. He really wants to still be involved," Jones said.

If New Zealand decide Ponga's tournament is over, the Kiwis have the option to ask for clearance to add an additional player to their squad.

"He's a tough guy and obviously has a lot of pride in the black and white jersey, and he doesn't want to let his teammates down," Kiwis captain James Fisher-Harris said.

"I thought he did an outstanding job. He's a freakish player, but he's also one of those tough players. We're feeling for him right now, but fingers crossed it's not too bad."

Jones said Kini would likely replace Ponga in next week's pool match.

The Kiwis' narrow loss to Australia was one that will burn Jones for a while.

Two of the Kangaroos' five tries were the result of interceptions and another two were from kicks.

The Kiwis dominated territory but lacked the polish to make Australia pay for their mistakes.

"Unfortunately, we were on the losing side, but we will learn from it, and we will get better and we will make some adjustments," Jones said.

"You go in that changing room and everyone's down, they're hurting.

"But you just bounce back and you get back into it. We know these boys, they work hard, they're professional. We'll be OK"
