World.title: Carlton suspends defender over high-range drink-driving charge
World.content:
Carlton has suspended defender Wade Derksen for drink driving on an off-season trip, allegedly blowing more than three times the legal limit.

The Blues suspended Derksen for all preseason games and up to round three of the AFL season next year.

The 25-year-old was charged with high-range drink-driving in Jabiru in the Northern Territory.

Derksen failed a roadside breath test late last month, allegedly returning a reading of 0.174.

Police said his licence was suspended and his case will be heard in court in the Northern Territory next month.

Cowan suspended by AFL The AFL hands down its sanction to Lachie Cowan following an investigation into his use of an illicit substance last weekend.

"While we acknowledge the upcoming legal process will carry its own penalty, Wade's conduct falls well below the standards we expect," Carlton general manager of football Chris Davies said.

"Wade is fully aware how disappointed we are in what occurred. We will continue to support him throughout this period as he takes full responsibility for his actions."

Derksen joined Carlton at the start of the season after GWS de-listed him at the end of last year.

He played 15 games for the Blues this season.

The AFL announced earlier today that Carlton's Lachie Cowan had been suspended for two games after an investigation into his use of an illicit substance last weekend.

World.title: Tahiti police gather evidence after pro surfer suspended over alleged incident
World.content:
Police in French Polynesia are gathering evidence following an alleged incident in Tahiti that has led world surf bodies to suspend a professional surfer from competitions.

Both the International Surfing Association (ISA) and World Surf League (WSL) announced this week they had suspended a male competitor after learning of the "serious" allegations.

Neither organisation has identified the suspended surfer, and the ABC has not independently verified their identity.

The Outerknown Tahiti Pro attracts international professional surfers. (AFP: Jerome Brouillet)

The WSL said the alleged incident happened at a private gathering in Tahiti in August, which was not affiliated with the organisation.

Surfing World magazine, which reported the suspension this week, said it understood the alleged incident occurred at a party after the final day of the Outerknown Tahiti Pro surfing event.

The alleged incident involved a teenage Australian female surfer and at least three men, it reported.

"[Surfing World] understands that NSW police have been advised of the allegations and have been in contact with surfing authorities," it reported.

However, Australian and French Polynesian police appear at odds regarding who has jurisdiction over the matter.

The ABC understands law enforcement officials in Tahiti believe they do not have jurisdiction, because the alleged victim reported their complaint to police in Australia.

It is also understood that local police in French Polynesia are now gathering evidence relating to the alleged incident to have ready for Australian law enforcement, but are yet to receive a formal request for information.

The World Surf League said its discipline committee suspended the professional competitor. (AFP: Martin Bureau)

NSW Police has declined to comment on the matter, saying that French Polynesian police have jurisdiction and carriage of the investigation.

The Australian Federal Police also said enquiries should be directed to local authorities.

'Serious allegations of abuse'

The ISA on Thursday said it had decided to provisionally suspend the professional surfer from "ISA-sanctioned" events "pending further investigation and review".

"The International Surfing Association is deeply concerned by recent reports of serious allegations of abuse within the surfing community," it said in a written statement on Thursday.

"This precautionary decision has been taken in the interest of athlete safety and welfare, and does not constitute a determination of wrongdoing.

"The ISA remains committed to respecting due process, confidentiality, and the rights of all individuals concerned.

" The ISA firmly believes that all athletes have the right to participate in sport in a safe and respectful environment, free from harassment, violence and abuse of any kind. "

The WSL, which was first to suspend the surfer, on Sunday said it had suspended a surfer on the 2026 Men's Championship Tour after it was made aware of "allegations of a deeply serious nature involving the competitor".

It said it had offered to assist relevant authorities.

World.title: Teen killed in cricketing tragedy 'died by misadventure', coroner finds
World.content:
The grieving family of a 17-year-old boy who died in a cricketing tragedy say they are relieved a coroner will not recommend changes to the rules of the game their son loved.

Ben Austin was hit in the neck by a ball thrown with a side arm device while practising in the nets at Wally Tew Reserve in Ferntree Gully, in Melbourne's outer east, in October last year.

Cricket authorities confirmed at the time he was wearing a helmet but not a stem guard, which protects the neck.

Ben later died at the Monash Children's Hospital.

Coroner Simon McGregor on Friday confirmed the 17-year-old died as a result of misadventure by well-meaning young people using proper equipment at a "caring, well-run club".

Ben's parents Tracey and Jace wiped away tears as the facts were read at a directions hearing in the Coroners Court of Victoria, with legal teams for Cricket Australia and Cricket Victoria also present.

Jace and Tracey Austin speak to media outside the Coroners Court of Victoria. (ABC News)

The coroner confirmed no adverse comments would be made about anyone's behaviour and "no individuals or organisations contributed to the cause of Ben's death".

He added that no recommendations or comments about rule changes would be made, paving the way for the summer cricket season to continue "in the normal way".

The coroner proposed commending the fact that some clubs and leagues had made safety changes without waiting to be told, with one bringing in neck guards and another banning the use of side arms.

But he said there was still some misunderstanding about individual clubs' ability to make safety changes, with some under the mistaken impression authorities would tell them what to do in response to safety issues.

The coroner is considering making a comment about the governance structure and how safety and best practice messages are conveyed.

The teenager's death shocked Ferntree Gully and the wider Melbourne cricket community. (ABC News)

Speaking after the hearing, Jace Austin said the lack of adverse findings and rule changes were exactly what Ben would have wanted.

"There's no way we want to change this great game," he said.

"But on the other hand, we don't want another Benny or Phil [Hughes, who died in similar circumstances in 2014].

"From what we've heard, it's exactly what we wanted."

With the anniversary of Ben's death nearing, he said the family would be coming together to reflect.

"Every day's tough, but when this comes to an end, this will be Benny's full stop, so you sort of want it to drag out."

"Every day's brutal to be honest."

Tracey Austin wore a necklace bearing her son's name.

"I've got him close to my heart," she said.

Jace and Tracey Austin say their family will be coming together to reflect on Ben's death. (ABC News: Wayne Hammond)

Cricket Victoria's Nick Cummins said the organisation would work through the coroner's initial comments and later findings.

"What we didn't want to do is go out and start finding solutions before we understood the coroner's findings," he said.

"Cricket is a safe sport. It's always been a safe sport. We have measures in place to make sure that's the case.

"But it's always important to have an open inquiry around incidents like this."

Cricket Victoria chief executive Nick Cummins attended the hearing on Friday. (ABC News)

He said the cricketing community had come together after Ben's death, with the Austin family raising $180,000 at a fundraiser last week.

"It's been incredibly heartening to see how cricket brings people together," he said.

The coroner's formal findings will be handed down before Christmas.

World.title: Cowan handed AFL suspension following illicit substance investigation
World.content:
The AFL has suspended Carlton's Lachie Cowan for two matches following an investigation into his use of an illicit substance last weekend.

The league said "the circumstances in which the matter subsequently became public" were also the subject of the investigation.

Cowan was found guilty of conduct unbecoming.

He will be suspended for the first two home-and-away matches of the 2027 season and issued with a $5,000 fine.

Two Carlton AFL players hospitalised in Melbourne The club has confirmed Lachie Cowan and Will Hayward have been admitted to hospital under separate circumstances.

No action was taken against Cowan's Blues teammate Will Hayward, who was also admitted to hospital on Sunday due to a separate incident.

Cowan's sanction was handed down as the AFL confirmed its new illicit drugs policy would come into effect in January.

The league said all players would be hair tested upon their return to training in January, "with readings going as far back as three to six months prior".

Cown said he should not have put himself "in such a vulnerable situation".

"I want to apologise for the impact my actions have had on my family and the football club," Cowan said in a Carlton statement.

"I also want to thank the medical professionals who helped me on the night, the football club for their ongoing support and everyone who took the time to reach out and make sure I was okay.

"This is a wake-up call and I am just so grateful to now be in a position to learn from this."

The AFL Players' Association (AFLPA) released a statement in the wake of the AFL handing down its suspension.

"This has become a public matter because private information regarding players seeking medical treatment has been shared," AFLPA chief executive James Gallagher said in the statement.

"That is unacceptable."

Gallagher said Cowan's suspension could discourage players from seeking emergency medical assistance.

"We don't want players using illicit substances and that is why the [AFL's] illicit drugs policy is so important, with its overarching purpose to change behaviour and minimise harm," he said.

"However, it is contrary to this health and wellbeing model to sanction players after they have sought medical treatment, particularly in an emergency.

"As an industry, we need to encourage help-seeking behaviour, not penalise or disincentivise it."

The Blues said Cowan's wellbeing remained the club's priority.

"Most importantly we are thankful that Lachie is okay and received the medical attention he needed," Carlton general manager of football Chris Davies said.

"We have been in regular contact with Lachie this week and he has taken ownership of his mistake.

"Lachie understands that it is his responsibility to ensure he makes better decisions moving forward."

Lachie Cowan issued an apology via the Carlton Football Club. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Michael Willson)

Cowan will be required to undertake further education above the current mandated training on illicit substances and their effects.

The league said the matter would "constitute a notifiable adverse finding under the AFL's illicit drugs policy".

"AFL players have a responsibility to themselves and their professional careers to uphold community expectations," AFL chief operating officer Tom Harley said in a league statement.

"They are well-educated when it comes to the harms associated with the use of illicit substances.

"Lachlan admitted his mistake and understands he must be accountable for his actions."

World.title: Supercars to return to Phillip Island, plugging hole left by MotoGP exit
World.content:
Supercars will return to Phillip Island next year, helping plug an economic gap left by MotoGP's move to Adelaide.

Victorian Major Events Minister Anthony Carbines today announced a five-year deal to host a Supercars Championship final series round.

It will be the first time since 2019 that the island has hosted Supercars.

"We know Supercars fans are wrapped with this news. We know our drivers are wrapped because they love Phillip Island, they love the circuit and they can't wait," Mr Carbines said.

"It was critical that we got back out there and made sure we locked in something that was going to make a big difference to the community of Phillip Island and the vast coast, but also to bring Supercars back to the Island."

Phillip Island will host its final MotoGP from October 23 to 25.

The track has hosted the event since 1989, but lost it to South Australia after the Victorian government rejected a request to move it from Phillip Island to Melbourne's Albert Park.

It later lost the Australian round of the FIM Superbike World Championships, which will be held on Phillip Island for the last time in 2027.

The loss of the two events has created anxiety in the local business community, which relies heavily on event-driven tourism.

Local tourism body Destination Phillip Island says racing is worth $80 million to the local economy.

Phillip Island will host a Festival of Motoring in March next year, with Labor and the Coalition both promising to back the event.

Opposition major events spokesperson David Southwick today said the Coalition would provide $100,000 to fund the event if it wins November's state election.

Victorian opposition major events spokesperson David Southwick and Bass Liberal candidate Rochelle Halstead say the Coalition will back a motoring festival on Phillip Island. (ABC Gippsland: Madeleine Stuchbery)

"We know the government has announced supercars today from Federation Square," Mr Southwick said on Phillip Island.

"They don't care about Bass Coast, they don't care about the island.

"We're here today because we care and we know it all starts with homegrown events."

Motorsport central to Phillip Island

President of the Association of Motoring Clubs Keith Mortimer said motoring culture connected many people to Phillip Island.

He said the goal for the next 12 months was to ensure the first motoring festival's success and make sure the event "is here to stay".

He said motorsport, whether it's bikes, classic cars, or Supercars, connected many visitors to the island.

Keith Mortimer says motorsport connects many visitors to Phillip Island. (ABC Gippsland: Madeleine Stuchbery)

"There are some wonderful things to see here, around Churchill Island, around the chocolate factories, around the local produce," Mr Mortimer said.

"It really does have something for everyone."

Destination Phillip Island chief executive Kim Storey said one in four jobs on the island were connected to the visitor economy.

She said the five-year commitment will boost confidence in local accommodation, hospitality, retail and tourism.

"Supercars represents meaningful progress towards rebuilding major event visitation," she said.

"There is still important work ahead to replace lost demand across the year and support the broader economic transition facing Phillip Island and San Remo."

World.title: World Cup opener a reminder of Test rugby league's glory days
World.content:
The Sydney Football Stadium is as modern a football temple as you'll find, but Australia's opening match in the 2026 Rugby League World Cup was like a trip back in time.

The game against New Zealand was played in the shadow of the Sydney Cricket Ground, where the Kangaroos have played ever since rugby league arrived in Australia in 1908.

It remains the site of so many sepia-toned memories of furious, blood-and-thunder battles because Test matches were the biggest, best and most brutal spectacles the game had to offer.

They would give these matches names like the Rorke's Drift Test or the Swinton Massacre, making them sound like wars.

Aussies win, Ponga suffers suspected broken arm Australia has won an all-time Rugby League World Cup classic, with a hat-trick from debutant Jack Bostock earning a thrilling 24-22 win over New Zealand.

Those days are past, swallowed by the twin beasts of State of Origin and the ever-expanding club competition, but last night's 24-22 win for Australia is proof they can live again, even if only for a night.

The crowd of 41,225 was the biggest attendance for any Test match in Sydney since 1974, and this was a game that reminded everyone of how it used to be as the two teams put on an utter classic.

The journey to the green and gold's victory was studded with indelible moments like Casey McLean's acrobatic opening effort and the twin length-of-the-field intercept efforts from Jack Bostock and Tom Trbojevic.

Tom Trbojevic scored one of Australia's two length-of-the-field intercepts. (Getty Images: Matt King)

But none were better than Kalyn Ponga's three battles with Reece Walsh, which were the kind of one-on-one duels that exist in the brief moments when a team game becomes an individual sport.

If they were gunslingers, this would have been high noon.

Walsh won their first meeting, bundling Ponga over the sideline in a try-saving tackle after the Kiwi debutant made a break in the first half.

But Ponga's revenge was beautiful. In the second half, after slicing through again, he left Walsh chasing ghosts with a left-foot step they should write songs about en route to scoring his second try of the night.

It was a glorious moment, but few bathe in glory like Walsh.

His reply was a length-of-the-field effort in which he stepped Ponga and Jahrome Hughes so comprehensively they ran into each other.

It was a gut-busting effort from Walsh, literally. He went for the technicolour yawn afterwards, so much so that Latrell Mitchell had to take the sideline conversion.

In the end, it was Bostock's third try, the Dolphin flyer's debut for good measure, sealing the deal for Australia as the World Cup began with one of the best matches — NRL, Origin or otherwise — of recent times.

It was a spectacle a long time coming. This was the Kangaroos' first game at the new SFS, which has been open for four years.

It was their first game against New Zealand in Sydney since 2014, and they'd only played there twice in the past decade before last night.

That absence began as a symptom of the decline in fan interest in the national side — the punters just stopped showing up — until it became a cause.

Jack Bostock was magnificent in his Test debut. (Getty Images: Matt King )

Taking the show on the road is important, and in recent years Australia has played all across its own land and beyond. They are a team for the nation, not just for the cities with the big, fancy stadiums.

But to stay in people's hearts and minds, to feel large in the life of a sport, to remind them how big this can be and how important it's supposed to feel, sometimes you need to play the old songs, the ones everyone used to know, in the big house.

Australia has so many wins it's hard for them to stand out, but this one will. Apart from Bostock's two aerial efforts, every try they scored originated inside their own quarter as they ran to victory from the back of beyond.

New Zealand will be filthy with itself for losing a game where its vaunted forward pack did everything it was expected to do as it trampled all over Australia.

Australia and New Zealand are expected to meet again in the final. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

The Kiwis finished with five line breaks to one, and more than 300 extra run metres. They scored 22 points but left more on the board with some sub-par execution in the attacking 20.

A poor end to a set from Hughes, who had plenty of time on the last inside the red zone but came up with a kick that led to a seven-tackle set before Bostock's leap to heaven, will loom large in their minds.

Against Australia, even if they lose a key player like Mitchell Moses to injury, even if their forwards get bashed, and even if they're the better team for great swathes of the game, you cannot ever give them an inch.

They can and will get better. After talk about the Kiwis and the Pasifika nations dominated the lead-up, Australia reminded us all that it is still its tournament to lose.

Tom Bostock was man of the match in a famous Test debut. (Getty Images: Matt Kind )

A rematch between these two in the final seems likely, but it's a long road to get there. Ponga's late departure with a suspected broken arm might put paid to the Kiwis' chances of claiming a second World Cup.

But before we look to the future, let us sit in the present a little longer as we bask in this glorious reminder of the past.

This was the good stuff. This is what it's all about. This is how it used to be and perhaps can be again.

One great match does not make a World Cup, and the international game cannot be taken back to its most legendary nights in just 80 minutes, no matter how good they might be.

Rugby league needs more of this: the best teams in the world, filled with the best players dancing on the edge of the blade, in the biggest and best stadiums when the stakes are highest.

It's a simple recipe, but the appetite for it is mighty. The crowd alone is proof of that, and there should be more of it to come.

Samoa and Tonga are almost certain to provide it when they play the latest round of a rivalry older than time in their sold-out pool match in a fortnight.

Less can be more for Rugby League World Cup The Rugby League World Cup exists in a constant state of change but ahead of the tournament opener between Australia and New Zealand the much-maligned tournament can prove less can be more.

The semifinals, which will almost definitely pit Australia and New Zealand against one of the two island nations or England, have the potential to be like the tournament opener.

In rebuilding the prestige of international football — its oldest treasure — the sport can strike gold again.

Rugby league gave up that prize once when it took Test matches for granted for years.

What happened last night gives it an electrifying shot in the arm and a taste of what it gave up, a sin this epic Australian victory proves would be madness to repeat.

Tech.title: Time is a-changin’: say goodbye to the leap second
Tech.content:
An important change will soon be made to global timekeeping that aims to prevent potential infrastructure failures akin to the Y2K bug scare. On Thursday, the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM) voted to scrap the leap second, an ad hoc time adjustment that’s occasionally added so tracked time standards mirror the Earth’s real (and inconsistent) rotation.

BIPM members previously agreed in 2022 to cease using leap seconds on or before 2035, but this is now being expedited to take effect on May 20th next year, aligning with World Metrology Day. There’s an unprecedented reason for its retirement being brought forward: changes to the Earth’s rotation may soon require timekeepers to subtract time instead of adding it in order to keep astronomical time in line with atomic time. This has never been attempted before, and there are concerns that doing so could wreak havoc on critical infrastructure that relies on time synchronization.

Those fears aren’t unfounded given Foursquare, Reddit, LinkedIn, Yelp, and many other tech platforms have suffered outages in the past when leap seconds have been added. Companies including Meta, Google, Microsoft, and Amazon have all supported efforts to scrap the system. Following the BIPM vote, timekeepers will instead switch to using “leap hours,” allowing atomic and astronomical time to gradually drift apart until an entire hour needs to be added — which isn’t expected to happen for around 3,000 years.

Tech.title: The Tesla Roadster flew, drove upside down, and hit 60mph in under a second
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Elon Musk promised a flying car. And the Tesla Roadster did exactly that.

Tesla demonstrated its next-generation Roadster at an event in Waco, Texas, where the electric supercar drove upside down, briefly flew, and accelerated to 60mph in under a second. It was an impressive demonstration of a car that likely will come with some heavy caveats and restrictions if it ever goes into production.

The event was less than 30 minutes and felt more like a stunt show than a product reveal. Indeed, there was no mention of price, release date, or other such mundane details. Musk promised the hypercar would go into production in 2028, but after nearly nine years who’s counting. The people were here to see a car fly, and that’s what Tesla gave them.

Previous Next







1 / 5

First, the Roadster drove up a very tall, multi-story ramp, using its incredible downforce to cling to the vertical roadway. When it reached the top of the ramp, it flipped around using its cold-gas thrusters to bring it gently back down to earth. The car uses a fan-based suction system, supplied by SpaceX and mounted underneath the vehicle, which is capable of generating up to two Gs of suction force.

Next, the Roadster flew over the rest of Tesla’s lineup, including the Model 3, Model Y, Cybertruck, Semi, and Cybercab — doing what Tesla VP for Engineering Lars Moravy called “a kick flip” in the process. Musk explained that it features attitude-control thrusters as well as main thrusters at the rear, giving the Roadster rocket-like capabilities.

“So it can basically fly like a rocket,” Musk said. “And it could do rolls. It could do, like, crazy gymnastics. Whatever you want, really. Now, I should say that this is not necessarily a safety-optimized car. But it takes the fun meter to 11 out of 10.”

The Roadster two ultra-high pressure air tanks with a combined volume of 600 liters, containing approximately 250 kilograms of air, and uses 10 nozzles to execute its maneuvers. The Roadster can even recharge its own tank, without requiring a specialized chemical propellant. The stored compressed air supplies the thrust needed to lift the car and perform the demonstrated maneuvers.

Musk claimed “This will be an actual car that’s on the roads” — though later the company admitted it would not be road legal. This seems obvious, of course. Imagine having to satisfy strict regulatory requirements from the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. The Roadster could go into production in 2028, as Musk promised — or it could be another decade of missed deadlines and broken promises. Again, who cares? Car flew.

As for the Roadster itself, Musk called it “the last best driver’s car.” Moravy said that Tesla drew inspiration from aerospace designs such as the SR-71 reconnaissance aircraft. It’s a two-seater, with seats molded directly into the chassis. Its steering and driving controls use steer-by-wire technology, including a steer-by-wire yoke, brakes, and throttle. The rear of the car features the thrusters and fans housed around the diffuser area. And it has a retractable rear wing for added downforce.

Previous Next











1 / 7

Tesla has also said that the Roadster can accelerate from 0-60mph in less than a second. And during the event, the company claimed it did so in 0.81 seconds. Musk explained that increasing the applied force while reducing the vehicle’s mass help boost acceleration. In fact, Musk says the production Roadster should improve on the demonstrated result, although he acknowledged the extreme forces involved and the need to avoid subjecting occupants to extreme acceleration.

“You’ve got to crack halfway to the speed of sound, I think,” Musk teased. “Mach 0.5. Maybe a little higher.”

After the event, Tesla updated its website with details about the three distinct performance tiers for the next-generation Roadster, outlining how its controversial cold-gas thruster systems scale across the lineup:

Performance (Road Ready): The entry-level variant seats two passengers and relies on an active aerodynamics package paired with a multi-mode suction system to maximize downforce on and off the track. It claims a 0–60 mph time under 1.6 seconds and a target range exceeding 300 miles.

Thrust (Race Ready): Also a two-seater, this mid-tier version pairs the multi-mode suction system with rear-mounted cold-gas thrusters. The additional propulsion cuts the vehicle’s 0–60 mph acceleration to under 0.9 seconds. Tesla says this configuration will be in “limited release.”

Rocket (Air Ready): The single-seat flagship model expands the hardware to a full perimeter-mounted array of cold-gas thrusters. In addition to driving forward and upward acceleration, the thrusters enable lateral and rotational movement in midair — enabling the short, low-altitude stunts showcased at the event. This top-spec version reaches a top speed over 230 mph and pushes 0–60 mph acceleration to under 0.59 seconds. Tesla says this version will be “invite only,” but also “not approved for public road use.”

The next-gen Roadster certainly took the scenic route in getting here. A prototype version was announced as a “one more thing” style surprise during the 2017 Tesla Semi event. The specs sounded ludicrous even back then: 0-60 mph in 1.9 seconds, a top speed over 250 mph, a 200 kWh battery delivering up to 620 miles of range, and a $200,000 starting price tag. Musk said deliveries would start in 2020, which sounded perfectly doable at the time.

Early adopters quickly threw down $50,000 deposits (or $250,000 for the limited Founders Series), effectively interest-free loans to help fund Tesla’s scaling ambitions. But then Tesla seemed to forget about the Roadster, as cementing its status as the ultimate vaporware. Production deadlines slipped as Tesla prioritized mass-market vehicles like the Model Y, while also wrestling with the overly complicated Cybertruck. Occasionally, when Musk would remember that the Roadster existed, he would up the ante about its capabilities. This culminated in the “SpaceX package” that would equip the supercar with cold-gas thrusters, bestowing hover powers and a 0-60 time under one second.

Musk has also sought to downplay the Roadster’s significance, calling it a “small potato situation” that will not “move the needle in a major way financially.” He’s framed the supercar more as a joint engineering collaboration between Tesla and SpaceX, even questioning whether it’s “even a car anymore” given its experimental nature. Some analysts theorize that the decision to re-release the Roadster is an attempt to set the stage for a rumored Tesla-SpaceX merger.

Tesla’s failure to bring the Roadster to market allowed other automakers to slip past the company with their own hyper-powered EVs. Rimac has smashed performance records with the Nevera, Porsche has refined electric performance with the Taycan, and Chinese giants like BYD are producing track-ready supercars at a fraction of the cost. The Roadster is no longer shocking the world as an impossible prototype; it’s playing catch-up to an industry that spent nine years building what Tesla merely rendered.

But then again, none of those cars flew.

Tech.title: Steam can now show game achievements in separate ‘sets’
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Valve is introducing a major new feature for Steam achievements called “achievement sets” that lets developers list different groups of achievements for a base game and DLCs.

“In games that support sets, you still unlock achievements by playing the game as usual,” Valve says. “But when you browse what you have unlocked afterward, Steam will break the long list of game achievements into the developer-created sets, making it easier to see what you have completed and to find other related achievements you can unlock next.” Achievement sets have their own progress bars, and if you finish a set, you’ll get a “set complete” trophy that’s visible on your profile.

Steam will support seasonal achievement sets that developers can archive, too. “We think there are a lot of fun ways games can take advantage of the temporary nature this can add, such as adding achievements to season-based games or enabling time-limited holiday achievements,” Valve says.

Look below the progress bar — you can see the different sets there.

A handful of games already support achievement sets, per Valve:

Against the Storm Age of Wonders 4 American Truck Simulator Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Crusader Kings III DREDGE Euro Truck Simulator 2 Forza Horizon 5 Flock Around He is Coming LEGO Batman: Legacy of the Dark Knight Left 4 Dead 2 Portal 2 PowerWash Simulator PowerWash Simulator 2 Team Fortress 2 Victoria 3

The company is also refreshing the Steam Achievements page to show “a summary of your overall progress, progress in each achievement set, and details on individual achievements.”

The updated Steam achievements page. Image: Valve

The new achievements features are available in the latest Steam client beta, Valve says.

Tech.title: ChatGPT can peek at your Chrome tabs now
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

OpenAI’s ChatGPT Atlas browser is gone, but now ChatGPT’s Google Chrome extension is getting some upgrades that allow it to use the browser tabs you already have open. With the extension installed, OpenAI says ChatGPT can now view your browser tabs when you tag Chrome in ChatGPT’s web or desktop app, posting a demo video showing someone asking ChatGPT to compare the three tabs they have open with sofas they’re considering.

Here are some of the sample queries OpenAI listed for using the upgraded add-on:

Use the details in this event brief to fill out the registration form, and stop before submitting.

Put the vendors in these tabs into my comparison sheet, with pricing, key features, and source links.

Look at all the tabs I have open and compare the contractor services. Then draft an email to the one that fits my home renovation.

Fill out the form I have open in @chrome ahead of seeing my new dentist. Also, can you add the appointment to my work and personal calendar.

It’s also updated ChatGPT in the sidebar, with “the full power of ChatGPT” and your entire conversation history in Chat or Work to use without leaving the page you’re viewing. It also enables ChatGPT Work to “control” your Chrome tabs for tasks like “sending messages, filling out forms, or downloading files,” similar to Google’s Gemini-powered “auto browse” feature, as well as organize or group open tabs.

Tech.title: Sega pulls Total War: Shogun 2 remaster from sale following disastrous launch
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Sega is removing Total War: Shogun 2 — Complete Edition from storefronts following a disastrous launch where users complained about issues like bugs and upscaling that appears to have been done by AI.

Complete Edition, a remaster of the 2011 strategy game, launched on Tuesday, and it bundled the main game and all of its DLC with promised upgrades including “improved visuals,” “1440p and 4K UI scaling,” and modernized controls. It has an “Overwhelmingly Negative” rating on Steam, where it has already been pulled, and posts on Reddit showcase artwork that users believe AI messed up.

“We’re aware that Total War: Shogun 2 – Complete Edition has fallen short of both your expectations and our own standards,” Sega and developer Creative Assembly wrote in a post. “We’ve seen your feedback, comments, and reviews. We agree that the current experience is not where it needs to be.” The two companies say they will “reinstate the original game,” and existing owners will “still be able to access” Complete Edition.

Sega and Creative Assembly say that they are “working closely with our development partner to identify the causes of these problems, deliver improvements, and ensure Shogun 2 - Complete Edition meets the quality standards players expect from Total War.” A studio called Mataboo is also listed as a developer for the game on Steam, and Mataboo highlights its work on the game on its website.

Tech.title: The tech backlash is now in theaters
Tech.content:
is a reporter focusing on film, TV, and pop culture. Before The Verge, he wrote about comic books, labor, race, and more at io9 and Gizmodo for almost five years.

Even though some of these movies are fictionalized dramas, each of them draws from the wealth of critical reporting that has revealed their subjects to be less-than-savory characters. You get the sense that these filmmakers are trying to tell stories that are meant to resonate with audiences whose views of Big Tech have long since begun to dim. But it also feels like some of Hollywood’s biggest studios are finally embracing the idea that the tech backlash isn’t letting up anytime soon.

Especially when you compare them to classics like The Social Network, the latest wave of cinematic dramas based on Silicon Valley power struggles has been far less sympathetic to their central figures. David Fincher’s 2010 film starring Jesse Eisenberg presented Zuckerberg as a complicated and misunderstood savant, but The Social Reckoning builds its story around the idea that the Facebook / Meta head is a man whose obsession with growth poses an existential threat to democracy. By focusing on the allegations leveled by whistleblower Frances Haugen, the movie is able to highlight Zuckerberg’s public transformation into a powerful executive who wields autocratic control over a multibillion-dollar social media empire.

What The Social Reckoning lacks in timeliness (The Wall Street Journal began reporting Haugen’s warnings in 2021) and stylistic flair, it makes up for in the way it connects Facebook / Meta’s past internal decisions to events that are still playing out in real time. The movie’s scenes that dig into Instagram’s negative impacts on teens’ mental health and the relationship between Facebook’s algorithm and the spread of misinformation feel as if they’re speaking directly to present-day concerns about how much influence Meta has over people’s lives. Similarly, Gibney’s Musk documentary acts as both a chronicle of the xAI / SpaceX head’s past and an inquiry into why the public was ever willing to let Musk accrue so much power within governments across the world.

Musk’s response to Gibney’s film has been telling. X has blocked the feature from being advertised on the platform, and Musk — a self-proclaimed “free speech absolutist” — has threatened to take legal action against Gibney for producing a “hit piece.” It wasn’t entirely surprising to see Musk personally badmouthing a project that casts him in a negative light, but it was curious to see the Musk ads initially missing from other social media platforms, including YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok.

Though the Meta subsidiaries and YouTube ultimately reversed their decisions, TikTok has stuck to its guns — which feels notable given the company’s indirect connections to the Trump administration by way of Skydance Corporation CEO David Ellison. David’s father — Oracle cofounder Larry Ellison — is a longtime Donald Trump supporter and one of the American billionaires who led the consortium of investors that purchased TikTok’s US business late last year. Ellison has reportedly promised Gibney that Musk will air on HBO (now a part of Skydance) sometime next January. The film is currently screening in select theaters, but it is hard to argue that it hasn’t had to deal with an unusual amount of outside interference in the weeks leading up to its release.

What sets Fielder’s You Can See Everything apart from each of these other recent tech films is how direct a view it gives you into the actual life of its subject. The documentary’s production began well after Holmes had already been sentenced to more than 11 years in prison, and Fielder uses his access to grill her about why she doesn’t believe that she defrauded Theranos investors. Invited to live with Holmes and her partner William Evans in a rental home during the month before she was set to begin her sentence, Fielder allows himself to become a character who can’t entirely tell whether his hosts’ supposed wish for radical transparency is genuine.

That central tension turns You Can See Everything into a surprisingly fascinating watch that challenges you to consider who’s actually in control of the documentary. Throughout the movie, Fielder repeatedly wonders if Holmes is using him as part of her recent PR campaign, and he leaves the audience to draw their own conclusions.

It often feels like Fielder is asking viewers to really listen to how Holmes presents herself on camera and then reconcile that person with what you might have read about Holmes in the news or seen in Hulu’s The Dropout. Whether or not Holmes is really just a committed performer who’s trying to manipulate the public shapes every beat of the film, and it makes You Can See Everything feel like a truly in-depth and honest examination of one of Silicon Valley’s most infamous figures — one who’s already captured so much of the public’s attention.

Tech.title: Trump posts AI-edited photo to brag about White House restoration work
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

President Donald Trump posted a series of photos on Truth Social showing off renovations to the White House — but one of them appears to be modified with AI. The picture, which compares an old White House column to a “restored” one, has several discrepancies and was flagged by Google’s AI detector as “made or edited with OpenAI.”

As pointed out by users on Reddit, the picture of the “restored” column has an uneven number of steps on both sides of the structure. The number of steps also doesn’t match up with the ones in the “before” photo. Additionally, the before and after photos appear nearly identical in angle and detail; the reflection in the windows is nearly the same, and the protective cardboard at the bottom of the column seems to be in the same spot as well. Not to mention that the “newly-painted” one looks unnaturally smooth.

Google’s SynthID detector flagged it as made or edited with OpenAI’s tools. Screenshot: Emma Roth / The Verge

The Verge can confirm that the photo posted to Truth Social is flagged as AI-generated when uploaded to Google’s SynthID Detector, which scans images, videos, and audio for an invisible watermark that indicates it was “created or edited” with AI.

Real pictures show people painting the front of the White House in June, so it’s possible the column actually did get a fresh coat of paint — the White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. The SynthID watermark wasn’t detected on other pictures Trump posted, which show the White House facade and heliport. Trump is no stranger to AI tools, though, as he often posts AI-generated caricatures of himself, while the White House has been known to post racist AI memes and at least one photo deceptively edited to make a protester appear distraught.

Tech.title: Bluesky’s AI tool now lets you make games and apps to share on social
Tech.content: Bluesky’s Attie AI tool, which initially launched earlier this year as a way to use AI to build your own feeds, now lets you make “small” social apps like games, polls, and dashboards that you can then share with others as their own websites. In an interview at TechCrunch Disrupt, Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider said to think of Attie as “social vibe coding or vibe coding for your community.”

Tech.title: Even Benchmark thinks AI is eroding the venture pact against backing rivals
Tech.content:
For decades, the unwritten rule of venture capital was that a firm doesn’t back two companies that compete head-on. But speaking at TechCrunch Disrupt earlier this week, the partners of Benchmark readily acknowledged that the AI boom is straining that rule.

It’s been on the verge of snapping for some time. The towering AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic share dozens of the same investors at this point. Then, at the end of September, Factory, a startup that builds an AI agent to write software, said it was firing board observer and adviser Chris Degnan for “unethical conduct involving Cognition,” its direct rival and the maker of the Devin coding agent. Factory’s CEO alleged Degnan had discussed a job at Cognition while privy to Factory’s board-level discussions. Degnan said he had already resigned and denied sharing anything confidential. Soon after, he announced he was joining Cognition as chief revenue officer. Powerhouse investor Vinod Khosla sided with Degnan on X, blasting Factory’s CEO and calling the company “a struggling second tier competitor.” Khosla Ventures backs both companies.

Even Benchmark, a firm whose reputation rests on 10-to-15-year partnerships with founders at the earliest stage, said the old rule can no longer be counted on. Asked at Disrupt whether the pact against backing rivals still holds as portfolio companies expand into each other’s territory, its partners described the conflicts as a matter of necessity, not preference.

“The harsh reality of this world is every company is evolving very quickly,” said Eric Vishria. Companies pivot and change, he said, and “you are going to get conflicts, and that’s just the reality of the current dynamic.”

Vishria said Benchmark stays committed to each founder and keeps what it learns confidential, and he downplayed how much a VC could pass along anyway: “We are not product or technology experts.” Seemingly referring to the Factory-Cognition dispute, he said Benchmark has been fortunate not to land in “that type of insane direct conflict.” Exclusivity, he said, remains “really important” at the very early stage Benchmark favors. “But things are evolving. There’s no doubt about that.”

Chetan Puttagunta said AI is accelerating the problem. As the cost of building software “effectively goes to zero,” he said, founders are “incredibly ambitious.” Because they now see a “surface area” and want to claim all of it, he continued, “[i]t’s probably going to happen more, where you start to run into each other.”

He drew a line between a direct competitor at the outset, which he called “an easy answer,” and a portfolio company that expands into another’s turf over time. “That happens,” he said.

Peter Fenton called the issue “kryptonite” and the firm’s toughest problem. He described a spectrum of how investors relate to their companies. At one end is the co-founder, who would never work on a competing company. At the other is the public-market stock picker, who can own several rivals because he is merely allocating capital, not shaping any of them. Benchmark sits nearer the co-founder end, Fenton said, and treats transparency as a golden rule. “There shouldn’t be the surprise after the fact.” If a conflict does emerge, a founder should never feel shortchanged, he added.

Benchmark isn’t declaring the pact dead. At the same time, when a firm that built its name on loyalty says conflicts are coming, founders might rightly wonder who else will be this candid.

Tech.title: Tesla reveals SpaceX-powered Roadster that flies and falls with style
Tech.content:
Tesla just revealed its redesigned second-generation Roadster with SpaceX thrusters, a vehicle CEO Elon Musk has called “the best of the last of the human-driven cars.”

Musk showed off the car at an event outside Waco, Texas, with a demonstration that saw the car use a mixture of high-powered fans and thrusters to drive up an inverted ramp, spin around, and ease itself to a landing on the pavement below. The car also used the thrusters to lift itself over a Cybercab, Cybertruck, Tesla Semi, Model Y, and Model 3 while in motion.

“This will be the actual car that’s on the roads,” Musk said of the car, which Tesla showed accelerating 0 to 60 miles per hour in one second. “It literally is just going to puff itself up, and uh, and be able to do this, these maneuvers whenever you’d like.”

Musk said Tesla will finally build the long-delayed vehicle in 2028, but didn’t name a price. Tesla will offer it in three trims. The first is “Performance,” which Tesla describes as “road ready.” It seats two, has active aerodynamics, and features a “multi-mode suction system for next-level performance on and off the track.” The second trim is “Thrust,” which is “race ready” and seats two, and has rear-mounted cold-gas thrusters that enable sub-one-second 0-to-60 mph accleration. The third is “Rocket,” which is “air ready” and seats one, and has 10 cold-gas thrusters positioned around the car.

All three trims will have 300 miles of range and be capable of speeds exceeding 230 miles per hour.

Tesla’s website showed Thursday the company is taking reservations for the car, charging $50,000 just to reserve the Performance, and $250,000 for Thrust. The Rocket trim is billed as “invite only.”

Tesla Roadster-starman Image Credits:Tesla /

Engineering VP Lars Moravy said at the event that the Roadster uses 10 thrusters connected to 600 liters of compressed air to lift and spin the car in midair. The air tank can be recharged, he said. “Every usable void in the car is packed with Carbon Fiber Overwrapped Pressure Vessels (COPVs),” Tesla wrote in a post on X, referring to the type of pressure vessel that has been at the root of multiple SpaceX rocket explosions. The company said “every usable void” in the car is filled with these vessels.

Musk also said at the event that Tesla may try to jump the Snake River Canyon — the site of Evel Knievel’s famous attempt to cross the gorge in a steam-powered rocket.

Musk has positioned the Roadster as a true halo car for Tesla, saying at one point that he’s “not sure it moves the needle massively from a revenue standpoint.” But he has previously said that “safety is not the main goal” with the new Roadster.

“If you buy a Ferrari, safety is not the number one goal. I say, if safety is your number one goal, do not buy the Roadster,” he said on a podcast earlier this year. Tesla would “aspire not to kill anyone in this car,” he said.

“This is the culmination of incredible work by Tesla and SpaceX Engineers working closely together to make something you haven’t seen in any movie, better than any James Bond car,” Musk said at the event. “I’ve never seen anything like this. You know when I suggested this to the team, I thought, ‘Am I crazy?’”

Tesla-roadster-event Image Credits:Tesla /

Musk had previously claimed that the car “will be very different from what was shown previously” and promised the demo would be the “most exciting, whether it works or not, demo ever of any product.”

The design changes were notable. The car, shown in stark white, now has a more angular design reminiscent of a Lamborghini or the famous Lotus Esprit used by the James Bond character in The Spy Who Loved Me — a car Musk owns, which was on display at the event.

In another post, Tesla said the design was inspired by the SR-71 reconnaissance aircraft and the F-35 fighter jet.

“Our design language has evolved since the last reveal: from S3XY to Cybertruck, Cybercab & Optimus,” the company wrote.

Tesla held the event almost nine years to the day after the company first revealed the second-generation Roadster, a modernized take on its first-ever car. Unveiled as a surprise at the end of the Tesla Semi reveal in 2017, the revamped Roadster was supposed to be delivered in just a few years. Tesla allowed customers to place $50,000 deposits to reserve the car. Some even paid $250,000 to reserve one of 1,000 “Founders Series” versions.

Musk first talked about adding thrusters to the car in 2018. “SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car,” he wrote on Twitter that year. “These rocket engines dramatically improve acceleration, top speed, braking & cornering. Maybe they will even allow a Tesla to fly …”

But the Roadster project took a back seat. In 2018, Tesla suffered through what Musk eventually dubbed “production hell” with the Model 3 sedan. The company then moved onto other projects like the Model Y SUV, which became the best-selling vehicle in the world, and the Cybertruck, which was a commercial flop by Tesla’s own standards. Along the way, Musk delayed the new Roadster in 2020, 2021, 2023, and 2024.

As more time passed following the launch of those new vehicles, Musk started talking about the second-generation Roadster again. Late last year, he said on Joe Rogan’s podcast that he wanted to reveal it by the end of 2025. One week later, at the shareholder meeting where he was awarded a $1 trillion pay package, he delayed it to April 1, 2026. Musk said holding an April Fools’ Day event would give him “some deniability” if Tesla delayed the event again.

“Like, I could say I was just kidding,” he said at the time. Tesla wound up pushing back the reveal again. It attempted to hold the event on October 1, but severe weather forced yet another delay.

These repeated delays caused a number of high-profile customers to speak out over the years, including YouTuber Marques Brownlee and OpenAI head Sam Altman.

“They really just got on stage and said this newly designed 4000+ pound car can do flips and go half the speed of sound (380+mph) and will ship in 2028,” Brownlee posted Thursday. “This is a prank, right?”

Tech.title: When it came to Cal AI’s viral success, a small army of influencers paid off
Tech.content:
Zach Yadegari has enjoyed an immense amount of success for someone who only recently graduated from high school. Founder of the AI-fueled calorie tracking app Cal AI, Yadegari is only 19 but his company has rocketed to viral fame over the past two years. At TechCrunch Disrupt on Thursday, Yadegari shared details of that surprising rise to prominence.

Cal AI, which was founded in 2024, exploded onto the internet thanks largely to Yadegari’s strategy of deploying a small army of influencers to promote the brand. The company generated over $30 million in revenue in two years and was acquired by MyFitnessPal for an undisclosed amount of money in March.

Discussing his social strategy onstage, Yadegari noted that an early sign of success came when an influencer’s post about them led to approximately a thousand new users over the course of two days.

“From there, we figured out, okay, this can actually work for us, and so we started recruiting influencers as fast as we could — paying as many people as possible to start posting for us,” he said. “What we saw was that it was a clear formula. It was pretty linear, but it was extremely fast. I guess linear in the sense that every post they did would get a certain number of viewers that would convert.”

The Forbes 30 Under 30 alumnus told the audience that part of his company’s strategy was to negotiate rates with influencers, promising them certain payouts for a certain scale of reach. A lot of influencers are “broke college kids” who “just want cash,” Yadegari added. “You just ask them, okay, we’ll pay you this, but we need to get us at least this amount of use and keep posting until you get there.”

Another important component of success was finding the right influencers whose reach can be quantified. “The biggest thing for us was finding influencers that had very tight communities,” the founder said.

Yadegari, whose father was in the audience, also credited his family with giving him the freedom to go after his ambitions. Does he also credit higher education for his success? Not so much.

“I think the only real reason to go to college is if you want to have a fun social time as a kid and be with other people,” he said, to audience laughter.

Earlier this month, Yadegari also launched Persona, a new AI agent startup that has already raised $10 million.

Yadegari said the “overarching mission” with Persona is to “make computing seamless with human life.” The company’s personal AI assistant will “live anyplace with internet connection,” he said, including “iMessage, app, email, phone call.” He added that part of what distinguishes the company’s plans for this AI assistant is to build a “hardware ecosystem around” the app.

Tech.title: And the winner of Startup Battlefield at Disrupt 2026 is: Intero Biosystems
Tech.content:
For three days this week in San Francisco, 20 eager startups participated in the Startup Battlefield at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026. The top 20 were chosen to represent the best of the Startup Battlefield 200, and they competed for a chance to take home the Startup Battlefield Cup and $100,000. With that intense pitching now complete, we have a winner.

These startups were handpicked to compete in Startup Battlefield, and all of them presented a live demo in front of VCs and tech leaders who served as judges.

After hours of deliberation, TechCrunch editors pored over the judges’ notes and narrowed the list down to five finalists: Apate, Flox Intelligence, Intero Biosystems, Industrial Next, and Satlyt.

The final five made their way to the finale to demo in front of our final panel of judges: Alexa von Tobel of Inspired Capital, Chi-Hua Chien of Goodwater Capital, Dayna Grayson of Construct Capital, Karl Alomar of M13, and Stacy Brown-Philpot of Cherryrock Capital.

We’re now ready to announce that the winner of TechCrunch Startup Battlefield 2026 is:

Winner: Intero Biosystems

Intero Biosystems is a Denver-based startup founded by Charlie Childs and Madeline Eiken that spun out of the University of Michigan. It’s developing 1mm human intestinal “organoids,” lab-grown tissue that mimics the gut, offering another way to study how drugs and other compounds might affect the human body before they are tested in people. The startup sells its flagship product, GastroScreen, to pharmaceutical, biotech, food, and chemical companies for testing drugs and other compounds.

Read more about Intero Biosystems in our separate post here.

Runner-up: Apate

Apate is an Australian startup founded by Dali Kaafar, who came up with the idea while doing research at Macquarie University in Sydney, Australia. It deploys thousands of AI agents that masquerade as innocent victims, answering scam calls, responding to shady messages and emails, following phishing links, and joining social media groups to bait fraudsters. In addition to access to Apate’s fleet of agents, customers get an insights portal that offers intelligence and analytics on scams targeting their end users or employees, brands, products, and more.

Read more about Apate in our separate post here.

These two companies now join the ranks of Startup Battlefield winners and finalists like Trello, Discord, Cloudflare, and Mint on the Disrupt Stage. With more than 1,700 alumni having participated in the program, Startup Battlefield Alumni have collectively raised over $30 billion in funding with more than 200 successful exits.

Tech.title: Amazon devices chief Panos Panay on the importance of failure and bouncing back from it
Tech.content:
Amazon executive Panos Panay has a message for startup founders: Failure is an inevitable, required part of building a successful product.

Panay, Amazon SVP of Devices, Alexa, and Leo, shared that advice onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco, drawing on his own experience at Microsoft, where he spent more than 19 years and weathered one particularly expensive failure.

“You have to be willing to fail, and actually, not just willing, you actually have to go fail,” Panay said. “If you haven’t failed, you probably haven’t pushed the boundary. It’s literally about harvesting the lessons learned when you fail. You have to be willing to face it, and as you face it, learn from it.”

Panay said it’s possible to recover from all sorts of failures, even catastrophic ones, noting that he experienced one himself at Microsoft. He described the launch of the Surface RT, Microsoft’s first tablet computer, as a significant failure during his tenure at the company, one that ultimately led to a nearly $1 billion write-down.

“I remember being on the front cover of a newspaper, and it just said failure,” Panay said. “But, here’s the thing, it was easy to admit failure. The trick was, and always is, did you harvest the learnings and understand what happened? All right. What did you learn? Because the failure wasn’t that moment. It was decisions that led up to it two years before that, whether the software wasn’t complete or the inventory was wrong or how we balanced into retail. There were all these steps along the way.”

Image Credits:Kimberly White / Getty Images

He said founders need to be willing to understand what went wrong, and avoid making excuses, and ultimately accept the failure.

“Here’s the other side of it,” he said. “You want to succeed, yeah? You take that failure, but you don’t let go of your vision. That’s it. Surface has done pretty well. You don’t let go of your vision. You don’t break it.”

Panay emphasized the importance of staying committed to a vision, learning from experience, and moving quickly. He believes that by embracing failure and learning from setbacks, founders can adapt and make progress faster, even as they encounter new obstacles.

“It goes back to the same fundamental, like, have you learned?” he said. “Were you learning along the way? Because if you were learning, then you just change your vector. Usually, it’s not 180 degrees. Usually, it’s just 30 degrees. Take your lessons learned, change a little bit, adapt your vision where it needs to be, and then go. I believe there’s people that hang on too long, but it’s because they haven’t accepted the moment of failure at all.”

Tech.title: Meta launches an open-weight AI model that runs on Macs
Tech.content:
Meta has launched what it calls the “most capable” open-weight model in the United States. Dubbed Muse Spark Open, the model also has the distinction of having been designed to work with Macs.

The new model, which leverages 816 billion parameters and a 1 million token context window, claims to offer superior performance to other popular open-weight models, according to evaluation results released by Meta on Thursday.

Muse Spark Open is natively multimodal and built for complex coding tasks and agentic labor. It has also been designed to run locally on Apple’s computers. However, you will still need a lot of power to run the model locally, with a requirement of at least 1 terabyte of RAM, per Engadget. The model will run best via the Mac Studio that comes equipped with the M5 Ultra chip.

Still, if you can muster the memory, Muse Spark Open may prove a significant work horse for coding and other desktop tasks. Meta says that it paired the model with Muse Code, its AI coding terminal, and deployed it to various agentic workflows, including coding fixes for a Mastodon client that included “bug fixes, new features, [and] full build.”

The company says it also deployed it in the service of running DaVinci Resolve, the high-end video editing software, revealing that the model was capable of reviewing and cropping footage.

Open-weight models provide a number of distinct industry advantages that aren’t afforded by closed and proprietary models. Open-weight models can be significantly more cost-efficient and can also offer transparency and flexibility that closed source models don’t allow.

Meta is making the new model available now through a number of different API platforms.

Tech.title: Amazon devices chief Panos Panay sees a future where AI devices replace the need to use apps
Tech.content:
Amazon is placing its bets on ambient computing, not apps, as the future of personal AI.

Alongside the launch of the company’s new AI wearables from Bee, Panos Panay, who serves as Amazon’s SVP of Devices, Alexa & Leo, took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt on Thursday to talk more in depth about where he sees personal computing headed.

“A lot of times, what you’re doing right now — what we all do right now — is we have to remember what we’re asking our tool to do for us,” Panay began, explaining that this is how we engage with our modern smartphones. “It’s like point, shoot, return,” Panay continued. “I think where we’re headed is a world [that] starts with ambient devices.”

By “ambient devices,” he means those that work quietly in the background, using sensors and AI to help you figure out what needs to be done, instead of the other way around, where you’re telling the device what you need to do.

“As it works in the background, you’re able to stay more present. You’re able to get more done. You’re about to spend more time with people … you’re not afraid if you miss something. It’s incredibly powerful,” Panay said.

Amazon’s biggest entry into this space is the set of new Bee devices it introduced on Thursday, which include a band you can wear on your wrist or detach to wear as a pendant, as well as a new credit-card-sized device that attaches magnetically to the back of your smartphone.

These gadgets passively record audio and take notes about your day, finding the to-dos, reminders, and insights you may later need to refer back to. To balance the need to be useful with user privacy, Bee’s devices don’t actually store the raw audio from your conversations; they process the audio in real time and then delete it when done. Transcripts of conversations are encrypted using keys that your device creates and controls. That means no one else, including Amazon employees, can access those files unless you intentionally share them.

Panay said that privacy was a key consideration for how these new ambient devices should work.

“You have to give customers that control,” he said. “Every product is different, but for Bee specifically, as an example in the ambient space like that, you have to design with privacy in mind. And that’s what we do. That’s critical.”

The executive, who came to Amazon after 19 years at Microsoft where he oversaw the development of Surface devices, has spent a lot of his life thinking about how personal computing will evolve. With Bee — and ambient computing more generally — Panay also envisioned a future where the idea of interacting with apps becomes less important, as more tasks are handled via AI.

“Do I think we have a future where there’s a bit of a balance — a whole generation that doesn’t say ‘give me the app’ for that, but says it should just understand what I need? Yeah, I do. I think that transformation is coming. I think that is the next generation,” he said.

That doesn’t necessarily mean the smartphone itself won’t continue to be an important personal computing device (as much as Amazon would like it to be an Alexa tablet or Echo smart speaker), Panay pointed out. Rather, he believes a new crop of devices will emerge that use sensors to understand users better, and to bring intelligence to the world around you.

“I’m not a proponent that says one form factor is going to replace another. I don’t think that’s the case,” he clarified. “I think there’s an intelligence layer that connects it all … and it has to be useful.”

Tech.title: Bluesky wants to make it easier to buy, sell, and fundraise on the network
Tech.content:
Bluesky plans to introduce payments in the coming months, a first step in its strategy to make money without relying on advertising. CEO Toni Schneider and COO Rose Wang outlined the plans Thursday at TechCrunch Disrupt, explaining how the company hopes to build on the commerce and fundraising activity already happening on its decentralized social network.

“People are actually selling things, fundraising very successfully, supporting each other on the network,” Schneider said. “We want to make that easier, and the way we’re going to do this is if you see something on the network that you like and support, you can support that monetarily, and we want to do it in a way that works for Bluesky and for all the other apps out there as well, so that it works across the entire network.”

Schneider, the former CEO of Automattic, took the reins of the company in March after longtime CEO Jay Graber stepped down. He said, while onstage, that he was surprised by the reaction to his appointment, with some users joking that it marked the beginning of the end for the platform. Those comments reflected fears that a leadership change would bring unwanted changes to Bluesky.

Schneider said he understands that users can leave Bluesky for another platform if the company introduces features or changes they dislike, a reality that he said keeps the leadership team accountable as it prepares to introduce monetization in the coming months.

The executives argued that advertising isn’t the only viable business model for a social network.

Image Credits:Kimberly White/Getty Images for TechCrunch

“I think there’s a story around monetization that feels like advertising is the inevitable thing we have to do that will ruin the network,” Wang said. “What was really promising about having Toni join us is he built at WordPress Automatic a $10 billion business where a billion of it goes back to the parent company and the rest of it goes to the ecosystem.”

Wang also pointed to Bluesky’s status as a Public Benefit Corporation (PBC), which she said puts the company’s mission at the center of its business strategy.

“Yes, we need to make money, but because of our infrastructure, we cannot lock people in,” Wang said. “And so the thing that really matters for us is the people who are creating value on the networks these days are the ones who are getting the value that is coming in or the money that’s coming in. And I kind of think of it as like feudal society where we’re working for a few landlords and they dictate everything, and then we have to pay up our dues as tariffs.”

Bluesky aims to give users ownership of their digital identities and control over their networks while creating a more open internet where value and revenue can flow directly to the people who generate them.

“First, we’ll start with payments, but I think it’s about disrupting the actual infrastructure layer, which is what we’re doing, and not just building another app,” Wang said.

Tech.title: Jabra Enhance Select M3 Review (2026): A Big Price for Small Wins
Tech.content:
This fall, hearing-aid manufacturers have been busily rolling out new and improved devices en masse, including Jabra, a leading maker of direct-to-consumer, over-the-counter devices. The brand has replaced its entire product lineup with all-new gear, swiftly retiring the Jabra Enhance Select 700, 500, 300, and 50R, all of which were only a year or two old. Three new models replace them: Enhance Select M3, M2, and M1. Each of the M-series hearing aids looks and works about the same as the models from last year and the year before that. Most of the updates here happen under the hood—but even those changes are hardly extreme, as I learned with the M3 pair I tested.

Historically, a more expensive device has meant a slightly smaller chassis—not so with Jabra's new hearing aids. Each of the three new models weighs the same: 2.12 grams, give or take a few hundredths of a gram, depending on the ear tip you choose. While the M2 and M1 share an identical form factor, the M3 is a bit squatter in design, measuring a few millimeters shorter than its siblings. Even so, all three are virtually indistinguishable unless you look at the fine print. That is, unless you select the red model; it's an M3 giveaway, as the M1 and M2 aren't available in that color.

Tech.title: The New Fan’s Guide to the Unreal World of Nathan Fielder
Tech.content:
There has been no shortage of coverage on Elizabeth Holmes, the Silicon Valley fraudster whose biotech startup Theranos reached a peak valuation of $9 billion in 2014 before its supposedly groundbreaking blood test machine was revealed to be vaporware. Books, magazine articles, documentaries, TV dramatizations—the exposés have piled up high.

So, you might ask yourself, why the hype for the forthcoming You Can See Everything, yet another documentary about Holmes, and one that spans three hours?

The excitement is thanks to Nathan Fielder, one of the film’s directors. (Fielder codirected the documentary with Lance Oppenheim). Fielder is a cult-favorite television auteur whose devotees have awaited his showdown with Holmes ever since rumors about him visiting her in prison surfaced last year.

Now that Fielder appears poised to break the containment of an obsessed fan base and conquer the cineplex, it behooves you to get caught up. This will not be a typical documentary: Fielder has made a career of heightened unreality, sowing confusion wherever he goes. To give you some notion of what to expect from his analysis of Holmes, here’s a rundown of his unusual and captivating style.

Business Bona Fides

One reason Fielder makes sense as an interlocutor for big tech’s most notorious con woman is his own history of corporate chicanery. In his breakout TV series Nathan for You (2013–2017), he contrived and implemented bizarre publicity stunts for struggling small businesses. (While he jokes that he “graduated from one of Canada's top business schools with really good grades,” the fact remains he did graduate, unlike Holmes, a Stanford University dropout.)

Andrew Bricker, an associate professor of English at the University of Ghent and academic coordinator for the research project Democratic Literacy and Humour, writes in an email that it’s important to recognize that, throughout his career, Fielder has always played the same altered version of himself, leaving us unsure just who he really is.

Fielder “has made the borderlands of persona and person so ambiguous, so indeterminable, so indefinable, that none of us is entirely in on the joke,” Bricker says.

Tech.title: Egypt’s Climate-Resilient ‘Super Corals’ Are Starting to Feel the Heat
Tech.content:
As coral reefs have undergone massive bleaching events across the globe, the corals of Egypt’s Red Sea have offered some hope. They’ve been unusually resilient to rising water temperatures, and if the oceans continue getting hotter, some scientists even predict that Egypt’s northern reefs could become the world’s last-remaining corals.

That’s what Mahmoud Hanafy, a professor of marine biology at Suez Canal University and consultant for the Hurghada Environmental Protection and Conservation Association (HEPCA), has previously predicted. But in the summers of 2023 and 2024, heat waves strained Red Sea coral ecosystems. A HEPCA survey led by Hanafy found bleaching throughout the Red Sea corals in 2024. In the northern areas, less than a tenth of coral colonies surveyed were affected, but further south, bleaching took out half the corals.

Scientists are racing to piece together what these events mean for reefs long described as “super coral” for their unparalleled hardiness. But now the question is not just how much heat they can withstand, but what has protected them until recently—and whether that protection will hold.

In overly warm waters, the algae nestled amongst the corals’ polyps begin to produce toxic substances. As a defense mechanism, the corals eject the algae. This is what is referred to as coral bleaching, and because these microscopic organisms are corals’ primary food source, bleaching events leave corals to starve.

That’s among other negative impacts hot seas may be having on corals, which is an issue not just for the corals, but all the other life among the reefs. According to the United Nations Environment Program, reefs cover less than 1 percent of the seafloor yet support at least 25 percent of marine species—some that are only just now being discovered.

For many years, northern Red Sea reefs remained quite stable as temperatures rose, while other coral ecosystems suffered bleaching. Eslam Osman, a marine ecologist at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST), points to the Egyptian corals’ evolutionary history as a likely explanation for their heat tolerance.

Corals are believed to have spread into the Red Sea through the Bab al-Mandab Straight, which lies at the southern point of the sea between modern-day Djibouti and Yemen. Crossing through these especially warm waters acted as a natural filter, Osman posits. Heat-tolerant species and genotypes survived, and their offspring spread northwards into cooler waters.
